title: Three copies of the same HTTP code, and how one Go engine fixed it
description:
A free API client for REST, GraphQL, gRPC and WebSocket, and what building it taught me about SSRF, sandboxing other people's JavaScript, and keeping secrets away from AI agents.

It started with a login screen.

I wanted to send one request to my own API, running on localhost, on my own machine. The API client I'd used for years asked me to sign in first. Then it wanted to sync my workspace. Then a banner told me that running a collection against a CSV file was a paid feature.

I wasn't even angry, I was curious. How hard can an API client be?

That was April 2025. The answer turned out to be "a lot harder than it looks", and also way more fun than I expected. The weekend project became Gostman, a free and open source (MIT) API client for REST, GraphQL, gRPC and WebSocket. It runs as a desktop app, in the browser and as a CLI, and there's no account, no telemetry in the app and no paid tier.

This isn't a feature tour. It's the engineering story: one decision I got wrong, the rewrite that fixed it, and three problems that looked small and really weren't.

If you only read one paragraph, read this one. Every request, from every surface (desktop, browser, CI, an AI agent), goes through one Go function. A small Policy value carries what's different about each environment. The public web proxy checks the IP it actually connects to, which closes the DNS rebinding hole that URL checks leave open. Scripts from imported collections run in the CLI inside a pure-Go JavaScript engine with time and memory limits. And secrets get matched by their value, including their common encodings, and replaced before anything reaches an AI agent.

So yeah, why Go?

An API client is mostly networking. Timeouts, redirects, TLS, proxies, cookies, cancellation, streaming. Go's standard library already has all of it, net/http, crypto/tls, context, a cookie jar, and none of it is magic.

I also wanted gostman run to work in any CI pipeline without telling people to install Node.js first. Go gives you one static binary. Build it, copy it, done.

For the desktop app I picked Wails. The backend is Go, the UI is React, and you don't ship a whole Chromium like Electron does. What I didn't appreciate at the time is that this meant the same Go code could sit behind a native window and behind a serverless function. That ended up being the entire story.

THE ARCHITECTURE:

Four ways in, one way out. The desktop app, the browser, a CI job and a coding agent all end up in the same function. It definitely didn't start like this though.

Phase 1: A desktop app that sends requests

Version one was pretty much what you'd guess. A Wails app with React on top. The UI builds a request object and hands it to Go, Go makes the HTTP call and sends back status, headers, body and timing.

Everything was saved locally on your machine, no database and nothing in the cloud. (Much later, collections became plain YAML files in a folder, so you can commit them next to your code.)

It worked, it was fast, and I was happy with it. Then people started asking for a version they could try without installing anything.

Phase 2: The browser version, and my biggest mistake

Which is fair. I wouldn't install a random app from a stranger on Reddit either.

So I built a web version. A browser can't call any API you type in because of CORS, so requests from the web app go through a small Go proxy function on Vercel.

This is where I messed up. The web frontend got its own JavaScript copy of the request preparation: variable substitution, query params, GraphQL bodies, auth headers, curl parsing. And the Go code that actually sent the request now existed twice too, once in the desktop backend and once in the Vercel proxy. Three copies of "basically the same code".

It was not basically the same code.

Copies of the same logic don't stay the same for long. Mine drifted slowly and quietly, and then all at once.

Binary responses (images, PDFs, anything that isn't text) came back corrupted, because both Go copies did string(bodyBytes) on the response and handed the UI mangled text.

Big integers changed value on the way out. Variables and GraphQL variables were decoded into floats, JSON.parse on the JavaScript side and json.Unmarshal into map[string]any on the Go side, and a 64-bit float can't hold every integer above 2^53. So a database ID like 9007199254740993 got sent as 9007199254740992. A different ID, with no error anywhere. That one was really fun to track down.

And cookies set during a redirect just vanished. Neither copy had a cookie jar, so a Set-Cookie on the first hop was never sent to the second.

Every bug I fixed in one copy was still sitting in another one. I was maintaining three API clients and telling myself it was one.

Phase 3: One engine

The fix was boring on purpose. There is now exactly one piece of code that builds and sends a request, a Go package called engine/, and from the outside it's one function:

func Send(ctx context.Context, r Request, policy Policy) Response

The desktop app calls it through a Wails binding. The Vercel proxy now just calls it too, and the JavaScript copy is gone. When the CLI and the MCP server came along, they called it as well. Nothing else builds its own http.Request.

All the hard stuff lives behind that function: variable substitution, a dozen auth schemes (Basic, Bearer, OAuth 2 with PKCE, AWS SigV4, Digest, NTLM, Hawk and more), body encoding, redirects, the cookie jar, proxies and client certificates.

The Policy struct

The obvious question: if the desktop app and a public web proxy run the same code, how does the desktop app still reach localhost:3000 while the public proxy refuses to?

Everything that's different between environments goes into one value:

type Policy struct {
    BlockPrivate      bool
    MaxResponseBytes  int64
    MaxTimeout        time.Duration
    Permit            func(host string) bool
    RevealSecrets     bool
    MaxStreamDuration time.Duration
    RunCommands       bool
    RawSockets        bool
    ...
}

The desktop app passes a relaxed one. The hosted proxy passes this:

var Policy = engine.Policy{
    BlockPrivate:      true,
    RecordBody:        true,
    MaxResponseBytes:  3 << 20,
    MaxTimeout:        30 * time.Second,
    MaxStreamDuration: 60 * time.Second,
    MinStreamRetry:    time.Second,
}

The engine never asks "am I running on a server right now?". It asks the policy. Supporting a new place to run means writing a new Policy, not adding if isWeb checks all over a package of nearly 9,000 lines.

Why it works

The big one for me: if a request passes in the desktop app, gostman run in CI builds and sends it the same way. Only the limits differ, and those are explicit in the policy. "Works in the GUI, fails in the pipeline" just stopped happening. Bugs get fixed once too. The binary body bug became "keep bytes as bytes and base64 them for the UI". The big number bug became decoder.UseNumber(), which keeps the digits as text. And new front ends got cheap. The CLI and the MCP server were mostly wiring, because the hard part was already there.

Phase 4: Putting a proxy on the internet (the SSRF problem)

Here's the scary part. The web proxy fetches whatever URL a stranger sends it. Without care, anyone can ask my server to fetch http://169.254.169.254/ (the cloud metadata endpoint) or something on an internal network. That's SSRF, server-side request forgery.

The obvious fix is to parse the URL, resolve the hostname, check the IP is public, and then send the request. It looks right. It isn't.

DNS doesn't have to give you the same answer twice. A hostname can resolve to a perfectly normal public IP while you check it, and to 127.0.0.1 a few milliseconds later when the HTTP client actually connects. That's DNS rebinding, and the check-then-connect approach walks right into it.

So the check moved into the dialer. The IP you check is the IP you connect to, with no second lookup in between (slightly simplified):

func guardedDial(ctx context.Context, network, address, family string) (net.Conn, error) {
    host, port, err := net.SplitHostPort(address)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    addresses, err := net.DefaultResolver.LookupIPAddr(ctx, host)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    for _, candidate := range addresses {
        if isBlockedIP(candidate.IP) {
            return nil, errBlockedAddress
        }
    }
    for _, candidate := range addresses {
        conn, err := dialer.DialContext(ctx, network, net.JoinHostPort(candidate.IP.String(), port))
        if err == nil {
            return conn, nil
        }
    }
    ...
}

Two details turned out to matter a lot more than I expected.

First, refuse the host if any of its addresses is blocked, not just the first one. Otherwise a record with one public and one private address gets through the moment the client falls back to the second one.

Second, the standard library checks are a good start but not enough. An address is blocked if it's not IsGlobalUnicast() (that catches loopback and link-local, including the 169.254.169.254 metadata endpoint) or if it's IsPrivate(). That still misses carrier-grade NAT (100.64.0.0/10), the benchmarking range (198.18.0.0/15), NAT64 (64:ff9b::/96), 6to4 (2002::/16), IPv4-translated IPv6 (::ffff:0:0:0/96) and a handful of reserved ranges. Several of those are ways to reach an internal IPv4 address through something that doesn't look like one. So there are 22 extra ranges on top. (Plain IPv4-mapped addresses like ::ffff:127.0.0.1 are already handled, because Go normalises them to 4 bytes before those checks run.)

This guard is a policy switch, not a law of nature. It's on in the hosted proxy, and off by default on the desktop, where reaching localhost is the whole point. Because it lives in the engine's dialer, it covers every request the proxy makes: HTTP, GraphQL, SSE, gRPC, calls to MCP servers, and every redirect hop too. (WebSockets in the web app connect straight from your browser, so there's no server in the middle to protect.)

Phase 5: The CLI, and running a stranger's JavaScript

Once the engine existed, gostman run was the obvious next step. It runs a whole collection in CI, writes JUnit or HTML reports, and exits non-zero when a check fails.

People coming from Postman expect pre-request and post-response scripts with test() and expect(). In the apps, those run in a Web Worker. In the CLI I really didn't want "install Node.js" to be a setup step, so scripts run in goja, a JavaScript engine written in pure Go. The CLI embeds (//go:embed) a bundle built from the same JavaScript modules the apps run, so the test()/expect() helpers exist once. Same lesson as Phase 2: one copy, so nothing can drift.

The catch is that scripts come from imported collections, which means from strangers. And strangers write things like

while (true) {}

or my personal favourite

const a = []; for (;;) a.push(a)

Neither one is allowed to hang your CI job or eat your laptop's memory.

goja can stop a running script with vm.Interrupt(), so every script runs under a watchdog with two limits:

func watch(vm *goja.Runtime, limit time.Duration) *watchdog {
    guard := &watchdog{vm: vm, ticker: time.NewTicker(memoryInterval), done: make(chan struct{})}
    guard.timer = time.AfterFunc(limit, func() { guard.interrupt(errExpired) })
    ceiling := heapInUse() + memoryAllowance
    go guard.audit(ceiling)
    return guard
}

Time is the easy one, time.AfterFunc interrupts the VM when it runs out. Memory is a compromise. goja can't tell you how much one runtime has allocated, so a goroutine reads the process heap from runtime/metrics every 50 ms and interrupts the script if the heap is more than 512 MB above where it was when the script started.

To be honest about it: this is a tripwire, not an isolation boundary. It measures the whole process, so a parallel run's allocations count too, and one huge allocation can land between two samples. A subprocess with OS limits would be stricter, but it would break the single-binary story. For runaway loops like a.push(a) it does exactly what I need. It turns "the CI runner got OOM-killed and nobody knows why" into "script exceeded its memory allowance", and I'll take that trade.

Phase 6: Letting AI agents in without leaking your keys

This is the bit I'm most excited about.

gostman mcp serves a collection over the Model Context Protocol, so Claude Code, Codex or Cursor can call your saved requests. You can say "hit the staging login endpoint and check the response shape" and it just does it.

The problem is that responses, error messages and request timelines are full of secrets. Anything that reaches the agent can end up in a model's context, and I didn't want anyone having to explain why the AI saw their production API key.

My first attempt redacted by name: hide the Authorization header, hide fields called password. That broke constantly. Tokens show up in query strings, inside JSON bodies, in error messages that echo the URL back, and base64-encoded inside a Basic auth header.

So the matching works on values instead. Names still decide what gets learned, like environment variables, secret-manager references (Vault, AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, 1Password, Bitwarden, KeePassXC) and auth fields. But what gets matched in the output is the actual value, plus the common forms it takes once encoded:

func variants(value string, shortest int) []string {
    candidates := []string{value}
    candidates = append(candidates, percentEncoded(value)...)
    candidates = append(candidates, jsonEscaped(value)...)
    candidates = append(candidates, base64Encoded(value)...)
    ...
}

That's percent-encoding, a few JSON-escaped forms, and base64 at all three byte alignments, which is what catches a password buried inside a Basic auth header. Then any text on its way out, whether it's a response body, a header, a timeline entry or an error, has every known form swapped for a marker like {{apiKey}}. Overlapping matches get merged so a token sitting inside a longer token can't leave half of itself visible.

The agent sees that {{apiKey}} was used and that the request came back 200, and it never sees a value Gostman knows about. The limit is just as clear: it can't redact something it never learned, or a value that's been transformed into something else, like an HMAC signature.

The thing nobody warned me about: Go versions

The Wails v2 CLI can't load packages on Go 1.25 or newer. So the whole module is pinned to Go 1.24.5, and that one constraint spread. goja is pinned to the last commit that still builds on 1.24. The official MCP Go SDK needs 1.25, so the mcp/ package is a small MCP implementation I wrote myself.

Writing my own MCP server felt like a step backwards at first. But Gostman only needs a small part of the protocol (stdio by default, Streamable HTTP on loopback with a bearer token if you want it), and the small surface made it easy to keep every tool result and error flowing through one place in the tool layer, which is where the redactor sits.

What I'd tell myself in April 2025

Put the differences between environments in a value, not in if statements. The Policy struct is the only reason this didn't turn into four engines.

Check security at the point where the connection actually happens. Checking a URL and checking a socket are not the same thing.

Copies of the same logic will drift. Not "might". Will.

And figure out your toolchain constraints early. One GUI framework's Go version ended up shaping three other dependencies.

Try it

Gostman is free and open source, and a solid Postman alternative if you don't want an account. Data-driven runs, load testing, a mock server, a gRPC client with a GUI, secret managers and the MCP server are all in the free version.

Source code (MIT): github.com/kunalgoesbyken/gostman

Test an API online with no sign-up: gostman.com/web

If you've built something like this, especially an SSRF guard or a script sandbox, I'd love to hear how you approached it. And if you try Gostman and something's missing, open an issue, I read all of them.

title: Small SaaS Queue Delivery Explained: Node.js HTTPS Push or Polling Across 2 Regions
description:
Short answer: for a small SaaS sending shipment updates to subscribers, choose queue push when each worker already has a stable public HTTPS endpoint; choose polling when the worker is private, local, or easier to operate as a continuously running process. In both designs, commit the business result before acknowledging the message, and deduplicate by an application event ID because duplicate delivery can happen.

Delivery guarantees decide this choice. Push removes the consumer loop, but it moves the recovery boundary to public webhook ingress. Polling keeps ingress private and makes local inspection less awkward, at the cost of a worker that must stay alive. Europe and US deployment labels don't alter that mechanism; the actual endpoint and worker topology do.

For a bounded set of shipment subscribers with public endpoints, I would try Infrai at the queue boundary because one API key covers 295 routes across 20 modules and its contract can remain stable when the vendor behind that capability changes. That matters to a small team more than shaving a line from a worker. It provides one REST API for your entire backend: plain HTTP, no SDK to install, and the same interface from any language or runtime. One bill covers the queue and cron trigger in this recovery path, so they don't add separate billing accounts or SDK upkeep. The catch is important, though: there is no native topic that sends one event to many subscribers, so this design needs one queue per subscriber.

Can a small SaaS recover HTTPS queue push or a polling worker?

Start with one unglamorous question: can the receiving worker be reached over public HTTPS for its entire operating life? If yes, push subscription is usually the easiest setup because the application can receive delivery in the same server that already handles webhooks. If no, stop there. A polling consumer avoids inbound access and is the better fit for a private service, a laptop during development, or an internal staging worker.

Don't choose from an API-style preference. Draw the data flow: a shipment service publishes an update, each subscriber has an isolated queue, and either a public handler receives that subscriber's copy or its worker consumes it. The application records shipmentId:eventVersion:subscriberId before applying side effects. Now trace one awkward case all the way through. Shipment shp_1842 reaches subscriber warehouse_eu, the worker claims version 7, and the process loses its connection before delivery is acknowledged. The same payload may return. A durable claim lets the receiver identify the repeated event, skip the notification, and report success; a log line saying "already processed" does not. The operator can then compare the event key, stored completion state, and delivery attempt without guessing whether a second customer email escaped. With polling, the claim sits between consume and ack. With push, it sits inside the HTTPS request before the successful response. The transport changed, but the business invariant did not.

Duplicates are normal; duplicate shipment updates are not.

This is where the fan-out requirement changes the answer. The service has no topic primitive, so ten subscribers mean ten queues and ten publishes. That can be acceptable for a small, known subscriber set because isolation makes a slow recipient easier to contain. It is not suitable when subscriber count is large or dynamic; use a topic-oriented specialist such as Google Cloud Pub/Sub in that case. If the job needs a durable workflow graph, joins, or compensating steps, stick with Temporal or another workflow engine rather than stretching a queue into an orchestrator.

I'm not sure which delivery mode is simpler for a particular SaaS until its public ingress and worker deployment are mapped. A one-page inventory of endpoints, subscriber count, and ownership resolves that uncertainty quickly.

Build the publish and receive path

The smallest useful implementation is the receiver, not the subscription setup. The following Node.js handler uses an application-owned event schema and a filesystem marker created with exclusive-write semantics. It deliberately does not assume vendor-specific webhook headers. In production, put the same unique key in Postgres or another durable store shared by every instance; the local directory keeps this example runnable and makes the ordering visible.

import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { mkdir, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { join } from "node:path";

type ShipmentUpdate = {
  shipmentId: string;
  eventVersion: number;
  subscriberId: string;
  status: "packed" | "shipped" | "delivered";
};

const ledger = join(process.cwd(), ".shipment-deliveries");

function required(name: string): string {
  const value = process.env[name];
  if (!value) throw new Error(`${name} is required`);
  return value;
}

function retryDelay(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const retryAfter = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  if (retryAfter) {
    const seconds = Number(retryAfter);
    if (Number.isFinite(seconds)) return Math.max(0, seconds * 1_000);
    const dateDelay = Date.parse(retryAfter) - Date.now();
    if (Number.isFinite(dateDelay)) return Math.max(0, dateDelay);
  }
  return 250 * 2 ** attempt;
}

async function publishShipment(): Promise<void> {
  const body = required("INFRAI_QUEUE_REQUEST_JSON");
  JSON.parse(body);

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${required("INFRAI_API_KEY")}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": required("SHIPMENT_EVENT_ID"),
      },
      body,
    });

    if (response.ok) return;
    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
      await new Promise((resolve) =>
        setTimeout(resolve, retryDelay(response, attempt)),
      );
      continue;
    }

    throw new Error(
      `queue publish returned ${response.status}: ${await response.text()}`,
    );
  }
}

function isShipmentUpdate(value: unknown): value is ShipmentUpdate {
  if (typeof value !== "object" || value === null) return false;
  const event = value as Record<string, unknown>;
  return (
    typeof event.shipmentId === "string" &&
    Number.isInteger(event.eventVersion) &&
    typeof event.subscriberId === "string" &&
    ["packed", "shipped", "delivered"].includes(String(event.status))
  );
}

function safePart(value: string): string {
  return value.replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9_-]/g, "_");
}

async function claim(event: ShipmentUpdate): Promise<boolean> {
  await mkdir(ledger, { recursive: true });
  const key = [
    safePart(event.shipmentId),
    event.eventVersion,
    safePart(event.subscriberId),
  ].join("-");

  try {
    await writeFile(join(ledger, key), JSON.stringify(event), { flag: "wx" });
    return true;
  } catch (error) {
    if ((error as NodeJS.ErrnoException).code === "EEXIST") return false;
    throw error;
  }
}

async function notifySubscriber(event: ShipmentUpdate): Promise<void> {
  process.stdout.write(
    `notify ${event.subscriberId}: ${event.shipmentId} is ${event.status}\n`,
  );
}

const server = createServer(async (request, response) => {
  if (request.method !== "POST" || request.url !== "/shipment-update") {
    response.writeHead(404).end();
    return;
  }

  try {
    const chunks: Buffer[] = [];
    for await (const chunk of request) chunks.push(Buffer.from(chunk));
    const event: unknown = JSON.parse(Buffer.concat(chunks).toString("utf8"));

    if (!isShipmentUpdate(event)) {
      response.writeHead(400).end("invalid shipment update");
      return;
    }

    if (await claim(event)) await notifySubscriber(event);
    response.writeHead(204).end();
  } catch (error) {
    process.stderr.write(`${String(error)}\n`);
    response.writeHead(503).end("delivery not committed");
  }
});

server.listen(3000, "127.0.0.1", () => {
  process.stdout.write("shipment receiver listening on http://127.0.0.1:3000\n");
});

if (process.env.INFRAI_QUEUE_REQUEST_JSON) {
  await publishShipment();
}

Use the request JSON emitted by the public discovery example as INFRAI_QUEUE_REQUEST_JSON; keeping that payload outside this listing avoids freezing an undocumented field guess into application code. Run the receiver behind the app's existing HTTPS ingress, then configure push delivery from the discovered schema. The handler responds only after the deduplication claim and subscriber action complete. A duplicate gets the same successful response but no repeated action. Short path, clear boundary.

There is one nuance I wouldn't ship unchanged: the file claim precedes the example notification, so a real notification failure would require recovery state. In production, use a database transaction or an outbox with states such as claimed, completed, and retryable. That is an application design limitation in this minimal sample, not a transport failure.

Recovery ownership changes by product

The useful comparison is what an operator does after a duplicate, a stalled subscriber, or lost worker capacity. Product names matter less than those mechanics, but they still shape the amount of platform-specific code a tiny team owns.

Option Best fit here Delivery and recovery trade-off
REST queue push A bounded subscriber set with stable public HTTPS handlers Less consumer-loop code and a stable REST boundary; requires one queue per subscriber and idempotent receivers
REST polling consume Private or locally debugged workers No inbound public access; requires a continuously running worker and explicit consume/ack control
AWS SQS FIFO An AWS-centered system that specifically needs documented FIFO and deduplication semantics A specialist choice; validate its queue semantics and operating model against the shipment key
Google Cloud Pub/Sub A GCP-centered system or native topic fan-out Better aligned with many subscribers; it introduces a provider-specific integration boundary
BullMQ A Node.js team already operating Redis Keeps queue control in the application stack; the team owns that Redis and worker operation
Celery A Python worker fleet A natural language-stack candidate; it does not remove worker and broker operations
Inngest Event-driven application workflows Evaluate when step orchestration matters more than a plain subscriber queue
Temporal Multi-step shipment workflows with joins or compensation Use it for orchestration rather than treating queue delivery as a workflow engine

The standard queue is at-least-once, so consumer idempotency is mandatory. Its FIFO deduplication window is five minutes, which does not replace the durable application key: a delayed replay can arrive after that window. Messages are limited to 256KB, delay is capped at seven days, and retention is at most 30 days with deletion on acknowledgment. There is no Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups. Those boundaries are reasonable for compact shipment events, but poor for an audit stream that must be replayed months later.

Rate limits belong in the same recovery design. Any client making queue API calls should treat HTTP 429 as backpressure, honor Retry-After when present, and use exponential backoff. Writes should carry an idempotency key. The platform specifies Idempotency-Key with a 24-hour default deduplication window, but the shipment event key still belongs in the consumer because transport deduplication and business idempotency solve different problems.

Operate the failure ledger

First, verify that every push target is public HTTPS; private network endpoints cannot receive push delivery. Then replay the same application event ID and confirm that the observable business action occurs once. Stop and restart a polling worker to confirm it resumes cleanly. For API-side 429 responses, confirm the client waits instead of looping. Finally, inspect queue age and dead-letter work as part of the normal on-call path, not as an emergency improvisation.

Keep the regional check concrete. Infrai's API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required; its response exposes capability regions and vendor readiness. Validate the current scheduling entry for the Europe and US locations you actually deploy rather than inferring coverage from a marketing label. Each documented capability includes its request schema and runnable TypeScript example. This also makes the vendor-swapping claim testable: your application keeps one contract while readiness behind that capability remains visible.

For scheduled shipment sweeps, remember the separate limits: a cron execution is capped at 900 seconds, accepts only a public HTTP target, and does not replay triggers missed while paused. Longer work should use cron only to enqueue compact jobs, then let push handlers or polling workers process them. There is no native debounce or throttle, and no fan-out/join primitive hiding behind the scheduler.

The decision rule stays blunt. Use push for a small fixed set of public receivers. Use polling for private workers and local control. Pick Pub/Sub when topic fan-out dominates, SQS FIFO when its AWS-native FIFO model is the requirement, and Temporal when the shipment process has become a workflow. Don't let a convenient endpoint erase the recovery model.

If this boundary fits the deployment, start with the Infrai push-versus-polling guide and verify the live schema before wiring production traffic.

References

  • AWS SQS FIFO queues
  • Google Cloud Pub/Sub overview
  • BullMQ documentation
  • Celery documentation
  • Inngest documentation
  • Temporal documentation

title: Your product depends on one AI provider: when it cuts you off, what does your code do?
description:
On October 28, an internal tool I wrote for my own prospecting stopped drafting. The provider was not down. My claude.ai login had expired. Every call failed with "401 OAuth access token has expired". An API key was configured right next to it. My code never tried it.

TL;DR: an AI provider goes down, changes its quotas or refuses your login. Your product must not go down with it. Send every AI call through one router. Give it several backends in a stable order. When a backend refuses the login, bench it for ten minutes. The next one takes over, and nobody has to redeploy.

Incidents and versions: snapshot as of November 3, 2026.

This article is for developers and product teams whose code calls a language model.

The provider lets you down more often than you think

Look at the history on status.claude.com. On October 24 and 25, it lists five "Elevated errors" incidents on several models. Each one lasted between ten and thirty-five minutes. Thirty minutes is short for a provider. For your user, it is a button that stops answering.

On October 1, the incident was of another kind. Credit purchases were slow to show up in account balances. Requests failed for "insufficient credit balance". The incident stayed open from 16:20 to 22:36 UTC. Your code had no bug. It got errors anyway.

The Claude API documentation lists the cases. A 401 means your key is malformed, revoked or expired. A 429 means you hit a rate limit or a spend cap. A 529 means the API is overloaded. Three different causes, one result: your feature returns nothing.

A serious product needs a degraded mode. That is a state where your product delivers a reduced service instead of an error. For an AI feature, the simplest degraded mode is another provider.

On October 28, my router picked the backend that no longer worked

My tool runs on a Rust backend. It calls a model to classify messages, qualify emails, draft replies and summarize threads. An AI backend here is one model provider my code knows how to call. The tool knows four: the Claude Code CLI, the Anthropic API, the OpenAI API and a local Ollama.

The Claude Code CLI is the default backend. It bills my subscription, not each request. It is the cheapest provider for a tool only I use.

That morning, my claude.ai login had expired. An OAuth login is a time-limited authorization. When it expires, a human has to sign in again. The CLI wrote the error inside its JSON stream on standard output. Then it exited with code 1 and an empty standard error.

My router did not look at that result. It saw the CLI installed, so available. It picked it on every call. Drafts, rewrites and CV and dossier generation all broke. An Anthropic API key was configured in the settings. It was never used.

The fix comes down to two ideas. A refused login benches the CLI for ten minutes. And the router moves on to the next backend while the bench lasts.

The backend that refuses the login is benched, the next one takes over. Every feature goes through the router. A timeout or a rate limit benches nothing.

One entry point for every AI call

Every AI feature in the tool goes through one method: Clients::ai(settings). It returns the backend to use for this call. Nothing calls a provider directly. That is what makes the fix possible: a rule written once protects every feature.

The ai_provider setting picks the primary provider. The others follow in a stable order:

let order: [&str; 4] = match settings.ai_provider.as_str() {
    "anthropic_api" => ["anthropic_api", "claude_code", "openai", "ollama"],
    "openai" => ["openai", "claude_code", "anthropic_api", "ollama"],
    "ollama" => ["ollama", "claude_code", "anthropic_api", "openai"],
    // Default: the Claude Code CLI (subscription billing).
    _ => ["claude_code", "anthropic_api", "openai", "ollama"],
};

Every client is optional. Without its environment variable, the client does not exist and the feature is off. Boot logs it once, then stays quiet. Ollama only joins the rotation if a five-second ping succeeded at boot.

A sibling method, ai_availability(), tells the settings screen which backends are usable right now. The user sees what the router sees. A provider that is down is not a surprise at click time.

This router is part of the harness, the code around the model. I covered it in the article on the harness: the harness decides what the model sees. Here, it also decides which model answers.

Only a refused login benches a backend

The CLI client keeps one date: the last time its login was refused. Two constants and one function are enough:

/// Hard cap on a CLI invocation.
const EXEC_TIMEOUT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(600);

/// How long the router leaves the CLI out after its login was refused.
const AUTH_BENCH: Duration = Duration::from_secs(600);

/// True when the CLI failed because its claude.ai login is missing or expired.
fn is_auth_failure(error: &str) -> bool {
    error.contains("Failed to authenticate")
}

signed_in() returns false for AUTH_BENCH after a refusal. The router skips the CLI while it is false. The next backend, usually the API key, takes over. A successful call clears the date. The CLI is back in the rotation without a restart.

Only one kind of error triggers the bench. A timeout or a rate limit does not. The reason is simple. A timeout may pass on the next call. A rate limit lifts on its own. A refused login does not: it will refuse every call until a human signs in again.

That is why the bench lasts ten minutes. Long enough to cover the calls coming in. Short enough to retry without anyone stepping in. It is a circuit breaker cut down to one case. I did not count errors or compute a rate. A date and a comparison are enough.

The test replays the real outage

The unit test replaces the CLI with a shell script. The script mimics what the real CLI returned on October 28. A JSON result with the error message, then exit code 1.

#!/bin/sh
if [ -f ok ]; then printf '%s\n' '{"result":"fine"}'; exit 0; fi
printf '%s\n' '{"type":"result","result":"Failed to authenticate. API Error: 401 OAuth access token has expired. Re-authenticate to continue."}'
exit 1

The test an_expired_login_benches_the_cli_until_a_run_succeeds does three things. It checks that the client believes it is signed in at first. It runs the script, sees the error and checks that signed_in() turned false. Then it creates the ok file, runs the script again and checks that signed_in() is true again.

A second test, other_cli_failures_keep_the_cli_in_the_rotation, protects the other half of the rule. It feeds three messages to is_auth_failure. The message "Failed to authenticate. API Error: 401 OAuth access token has expired." returns true. "claude timed out after 600 s" returns false. "rate limit reached" returns false too.

Here is the useful part. The test holds the real output of the real incident. If the CLI ever changes its message, the test breaks before my product does.

The same rule in Go

This blog is mostly about Go, so here is the same pattern in Go. An interface for the backends, a slice in a stable order, one bench date per backend.

// Backend is one AI provider the product knows how to call.
type Backend interface {
    Name() string
    Generate(ctx context.Context, system, user string) (string, error)
}

// ErrAuth marks a refused login. Only this error benches a backend.
var ErrAuth = errors.New("login refused")

type Router struct {
    backends []Backend // stable order, primary first
    bench    time.Duration
    mu       sync.Mutex
    until    map[string]time.Time // backend name -> benched until
}

func NewRouter(bench time.Duration, backends ...Backend) *Router {
    return &Router{backends: backends, bench: bench, until: map[string]time.Time{}}
}

func (r *Router) Generate(ctx context.Context, system, user string) (string, error) {
    err := errors.New("no AI backend available")
    for _, b := range r.backends {
        if r.benched(b.Name()) {
            continue
        }
        var out string
        out, err = b.Generate(ctx, system, user)
        if err == nil {
            r.set(b.Name(), time.Time{}) // a success clears the bench
            return out, nil
        }
        if errors.Is(err, ErrAuth) {
            r.set(b.Name(), time.Now().Add(r.bench))
        }
    }
    return "", err
}

func (r *Router) benched(name string) bool {
    r.mu.Lock()
    defer r.mu.Unlock()
    return time.Now().Before(r.until[name])
}

func (r *Router) set(name string, until time.Time) {
    r.mu.Lock()
    defer r.mu.Unlock()
    r.until[name] = until
}

Each adapter translates its own refusal into ErrAuth. For the CLI, that is the "Failed to authenticate" message. For the API, that is a 401 authentication_error. The adapter returns fmt.Errorf("%w: %v", ErrAuth, err). The router never needs to know the providers.

This version goes one step further than my Rust. When a backend fails, it tries the next one in the same call. My tool returns the error of the first refused call. Only the following calls go to the API key. Both work. The Go version avoids one visible error.

A gateway is one more dependency

You can also buy this router. An LLM gateway talks to dozens of providers, measures costs and fails over on its own. That is useful when you have many providers and many teams.

But a gateway sees every one of your keys go by. On October 21, 2026, version 1.107.0 of LiteLLM, one of those gateways, was published on PyPI with a credential stealer. It collected system, browser, cloud and AI tool secrets, then sent them to an external domain. The version was pulled in under three hours. Anyone who installed it in that window has to rotate every key.

The suspected cause deserves a pause. According to LiteLLM, a coding agent could write the user's GitHub token into a response body. And the gateway logged those response bodies. The token ended up in the logs. The component that centralizes your AI calls also centralizes what leaks.

This is not a verdict against gateways. It is a reminder: every component between your code and the provider is a dependency that holds your secrets. My tool has four clients and a router of about sixty lines. For a product with two or three backends, that is often enough.

And the less you call the model, the less you depend on the provider. I wrote about why you should put the LLM last in the pipeline. A router protects the calls that remain.

The checklist

An AI provider is a dependency that fails. Code as if that were true.

  • [ ] Send every AI call through one function
  • [ ] Declare the backends in a list, in a stable order
  • [ ] Make every backend optional: no key, no client, one log line at boot
  • [ ] Detect the refused login: 401, "Failed to authenticate", expired key
  • [ ] Bench that backend for a fixed time, and skip it in the router
  • [ ] Never bench on a timeout or a rate limit: retry
  • [ ] Put the backend back in play as soon as one call succeeds
  • [ ] Show the user which backends are available right now
  • [ ] Replay the real output of the real outage in a test

The takeaway

An AI provider goes down, changes its quotas or refuses your login. The question is not if, but when. On that day, your code has two options: return an error, or move to the next backend. The second one costs a router, a list and a date.

Open your code and look for the places that call a provider directly. Each one is a feature that will go down with it.

Want an outside look at the reliability of your AI features? See my services, or let's talk.

Sources: Incident history, status.claude.com · Incident "Delayed credits on the Claude Platform", October 1, 2026 · Incident "Elevated errors for Claude Sonnet 5.5 and other models", October 25, 2026 · Claude API documentation, error codes · The Hacker News, LiteLLM 1.107.0 compromise (October 22, 2026)

title: How to merge Shift_JIS, UTF-8 BOM, and Windows-1252 CSVs without guessing the encoding
description:
How to merge Shift_JIS, UTF-8 BOM, and Windows-1252 CSVs without guessing the encoding

A shop export from Japan, another from the UK, a third from a US system, and a Chinese marketplace file. You want one table. pandas.read_csv() with the default UTF-8 encoding fails on three of the four files. Dates arrive as 2026/3/2, 20260310, 2026年3月14日, and 3/15/2026. Two rows are exact duplicates, one row is empty, and one amount is written in full-width digits (２４９).

This article walks through that exact problem using sheetstack-lite, a small MIT-licensed Python tool. Every command below was run against the repository's fictional sample files. The output is copied from those runs, not reconstructed from memory.

sheetstack-lite is a free, in-memory merge-and-clean utility. It is not a tax tool, and this article does not claim compatibility with Google Sheets or WPS.

What the sample files actually contain

Clone the repo and install the two dependencies (pandas and openpyxl). Python 3.10 or later is required.

git clone https://github.com/ebhow9986-ctrl/sheetstack-lite.git
cd sheetstack-lite
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate   # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

The samples/ folder ships with five fictional CSVs (none of the rows are real customer records):

File What the tool reported What is messy about it
store_us.csv utf-8-sig (UTF-8 with a BOM) Mixed date formats, a blank row, a duplicate US-1002
store_uk.csv cp1252 The word “Café” is a single 0xE9 byte; one date is 3/6/2026; UK-2003 is duplicated
store_jp.csv shift_jis Japanese headers (伝票番号, 日付, 商品名…); dates such as 2026年3月14日 and 20260310; JP-3005 is duplicated
store_cn.csv gb18030 Chinese headers; a full-width amount ２４９; a date written as 2026年3月13日
customers_messy.csv utf-8-sig Duplicate ids, an empty row, mixed dates, a full-width ０８ in the points column

The README describes the four store files as “GBK” for the Chinese export. When the CLI sniffed the same file, it printed gb18030 (a superset of GBK). The rest of this article uses the string the tool actually printed.

Why a default pandas read fails

On the same machine, pd.read_csv(path) with no encoding= argument succeeded only for the UTF-8 BOM file. The other three store exports raised UnicodeDecodeError:

store_cn.csv: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xb6 in position 0: invalid start byte
store_jp.csv: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x93 in position 0: invalid start byte
store_uk.csv: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xe9 in position 67: invalid continuation byte

That last one is the é in “Café”. If you force latin-1 or cp1252 onto the Japanese file, the read may “succeed” and give you mojibake instead of an error. Encoding has to be chosen per file, then the headers have to be lined up, then the dates and duplicates have to be cleaned. Doing that by hand for every export is the tedious part.

This is a well-worn problem — the Stack Overflow thread “UnicodeDecodeError when reading CSV file in Pandas” has been viewed more than a million times. The usual advice is “pass encoding=...”. That works when you already know the encoding and you only have one file. It does not merge four different code pages, or rename 伝票番号 and Order ID into the same column.

Merge the four store exports

The tool is invoked as python3 sheetstack_lite.py. Two subcommands exist: merge and clean.

Point merge at the four store files, ask it to normalize header aliases, and write a single CSV:

python3 sheetstack_lite.py merge \
  samples/store_us.csv \
  samples/store_uk.csv \
  samples/store_jp.csv \
  samples/store_cn.csv \
  -o stores.csv \
  --normalize-headers

Exact output from the run:

Merged 4 file(s), 21 rows, 7 columns
  - store_us.csv: 7 rows / encoding utf-8-sig
  - store_uk.csv: 5 rows / encoding cp1252
  - store_jp.csv: 6 rows / encoding shift_jis
  - store_cn.csv: 3 rows / encoding gb18030
Wrote stores.csv

--normalize-headers maps common aliases onto one English name. In these samples that means, among others:

  • Order ID / 伝票番号 / 订单编号 → order_id
  • Date / 日付 / 成交时间 → order_date
  • Item / 商品名 / 商品名称 → product
  • Quantity / 数量 / 件数 → qty
  • Sales / 売上 / 销售额 → amount
  • Remaining / 在庫 / 库存数 → stock

A source_file column is added unless you pass --no-source. The merged file still has 21 rows, including the blank US row and the three duplicate orders. Dates are not rewritten during merge. “Café mug”, スマホスタンド, and 键盘 all sit in the same product column, and the file is written as UTF-8 with a BOM (utf-8-sig) so Excel on Windows will not treat the CJK text as mojibake.

If you follow the README literally and run python3 sheetstack_lite.py merge samples -o merged.csv --normalize-headers, the tool walks the whole folder. That includes customers_messy.csv, which has a different schema. In that run the CLI reported Merged 5 file(s), 29 rows, 12 columns. For a store-export merge, name the four files (or keep customers in a separate folder).

Clean dates, drop the empty row, remove duplicates 

python3 sheetstack_lite.py clean stores.csv \
  -o stores_clean.csv \
  --date-cols order_date \
  --dedupe-cols order_id

Exact output:

Cleaned 21 rows → 17 rows (empty 1, duplicates 3)
Detected encoding: utf-8-sig
Wrote stores_clean.csv

The 17 remaining order_id values are unique: US-1001 through US-1005, UK-2001 through UK-2004, JP-3001 through JP-3005, and CN-4001 through CN-4003. Every order_date is YYYY-MM-DD. A few examples of what changed:

Input (order_date) Output
2026/3/2 2026-03-02
20260305 / 20260310 / 20260318 2026-03-05 / 2026-03-10 / 2026-03-18
2026.3.9 2026-03-09
3/15/2026 2026-03-15
2026年3月14日 / 2026年3月13日 2026-03-14 / 2026-03-13

Cells are trimmed, and full-width digits are folded to ASCII, so the Chinese amount ２４９ becomes 249. Duplicate keys keep the first row (US-1002, UK-2003, JP-3005).

Ambiguous dates: 3/6/2026 is not obvious

UK-2002 is dated 3/6/2026. Without --dayfirst, the cleaner treated that as 6 March (2026-03-06). With --dayfirst, the same value became 3 June (2026-06-03):

python3 sheetstack_lite.py clean stores.csv \
  -o stores_clean_dayfirst.csv \
  --date-cols order_date \
  --dedupe-cols order_id \
  --dayfirst

Unambiguous values did not flip: 2026.3.9 stayed 2026-03-09, and 3/15/2026 stayed 2026-03-15 (there is no 15th month). If a file is known to be day-first, pass the flag. If a folder mixes US and UK exports, inspect the ambiguous rows before you trust a single convention. sheetstack-lite does not invent a locale per source file during clean; it applies one rule to the column you name.

A second, smaller clean: messy customer dates and duplicates

The customer list is a better illustration of empty rows and full-width numbers mixed with several date styles:

python3 sheetstack_lite.py clean samples/customers_messy.csv \
  -o customers.csv \
  --dedupe-cols customer_id \
  --date-cols signup_date

Exact output:

Cleaned 8 rows → 5 rows (empty 1, duplicates 2)
Detected encoding: utf-8-sig
Wrote customers.csv

The cleaned table is:

customer_id  signup_date  city      notes            points
U001         2026-02-01   Tokyo     paid             120
U002         2026-02-03   Osaka     pending          08
U003         2026-02-08   Nagoya    follow-up        56
U004         2026-02-11   Fukuoka   shipped          230
U005         2026-02-15   Sapporo   address needed   15

2026/2/1, 20260203, 2026年2月8日, 2026-02-11, and 2/15/2026 all became YYYY-MM-DD. The full-width points value ０８ became 08. Leading and trailing spaces (including a full-width space after Nagoya) were stripped. The second U001 and the second U003 were dropped; the blank row was dropped.

One thing not to do: after merging unrelated schemas, do not dedupe on a column that is empty for some of the rows. In a trial clean of the five-file merge, --dedupe-cols order_id treated every customer row (blank order_id) as a duplicate of the first blank key and deleted most of the customer data. Dedupe on a key that actually identifies the row, or clean each kind of file on its own.

What the free tool does not do

sheetstack-lite version 1.0.0-lite loads each file into memory. It will not help if Excel already refuses to open the file, and it has no chunked reads, no split-into-pieces command, and no Excel summary workbook. The tests in the repo (python3 tests/test_lite.py) cover the README examples; they passed on the same machine used for this article.

If you only need to repair a file's encoding and would rather not use the command line, there is a free CSV encoding fixer that runs entirely in the browser. The file never leaves your computer.

If you later need chunked reads for large CSVs, a split into Excel-friendly pieces, an Excel summary with conditional formatting, or a one-step run pipeline, those are in the paid toolkit (Sheetstack on Gumroad). The free repository does not include that source, and the two editions have different licenses.

For the everyday case — a handful of exports, mixed encodings, messy dates, a few duplicates — the commands above are enough, and they stay on your machine.

title: Introducing the MongoDB Vercel AI SDK Integration: Persistent Memory for AI Applications
description:
We are excited to announce the release of the MongoDB Vercel AI SDK integration, which provides AI applications and agents built with Vercel’s SDK with a persistent memory store in MongoDB Atlas. It's now open source and generally available on npm.

This integration adds MongoDB Atlas as the memory store in the existing Vercel AI SDK code. Once installed, the package connects Vercel AI SDK applications to MongoDB Atlas and automatically stores the application's memories in documents. This allows the application to retain memories about conversations, user facts, and past events that persist across sessions, users, and restarts.

What is the Vercel AI SDK?

The Vercel AI SDK is a TypeScript toolkit for building AI applications. It handles calling models, streaming responses, using tools, and running agents that work through multi-step tasks. The SDK doesn't include a database to persist memories between runs. Without memory, an AI application starts every conversation with no knowledge of the last one. It doesn't know who the user is, what they asked yesterday, or what it learned along the way. It doesn’t have any context.

Today, developers have to build their own tooling to store memories in a layer. That usually means designing a database schema, writing jobs to clear out old data, and setting up vector search so the application can find relevant past information by semantic meaning instead of just keywords. It's a lot of work to build an AI application that can remember context.

What types of memory does an AI application need?

An AI application needs five kinds of memory, each kept for a different length of time and retrieved differently. This integration automatically categorizes each type of memory and stores it in MongoDB Atlas; here are short definitions of the five memory types:

  • Session: The conversation an application or agent has in each session. This helps the application follow what the user just said.

  • Semantic: Facts about people, entities, and preferences, so users don't have to repeat themselves.

  • Procedural: Workflows and instructions, so the application carries out tasks the way you've defined them.

  • Episodic: Key events and outcomes, so the application can recall what happened before. Kept for one year of inactivity by default.

  • Scratchpad: Temporary notes for work in progress. They expire after an hour and can be promoted to episodic memory if they turn out to matter.

Semantic and procedural memories are versioned, so history is preserved when a fact changes. The semantic, procedural, and episodic tiers use MongoDB Vector Search, which finds stored memories by semantic meaning rather than by exact keywords.

This integration automatically creates the vector indexes and detects embedding dimensions at startup. Developers can use any AI SDK embedding model to create vector indexes, including Voyage AI, OpenAI, Cohere, or Google.

Figure 1. How the integration works with MongoDB Atlas and the Vercel SDK interface.

How should memory age?

Each category of memory has its own retention policy, so short-lived notes expire quickly, and long-term facts are stored for longer. The MongoDB Vercel AI SDK integration ships with defaults for every category, which developers can customize if they desire.

Effective memory retention requires a balance. Keeping memories indefinitely can decrease retrieval performance and increase costs, while deleting them too early can cause applications to forget important context. This integration includes features to help developers easily set the right balance:

  • Retention modes: Choose none (never expire), ttl (expire after a set time), ttl+importance (expire after a set time unless the memory is marked important), or dynamic, where you define your own forgetting time period.
  • Model-driven forgetting: With memory_forget, the model can delete a specific memory when a user says "forget that." Removal usually happens within about 60 seconds.

Because the memory is stored in MongoDB Atlas, application operational data, its memory, and the vector search that retrieves it run on one platform. Developers can secure, monitor, and scale a single database without bolting on a separate vector store or memory service alongside it.

What changes when you run the MongoDB Vercel AI SDK Integration in production?

This production release gives developers greater controls over their data and flexibility in how they use the integration:

  • Reliable session history: By default, the model decides when to save and read conversation turns, so it can occasionally skip one. For production, you can use the AI SDK hooks so that the application’s own code loads and saves the transcript at every turn. Every user, assistant, and tool message is saved exactly once.

  • Separate data per customer: Developers can add a filter field, such as tenant_id, to the application’s vector indexes to limit each search to a single customer's memories.

  • Application names and layout: Developers can rename collections and indexes to match the existing application schema or turn off indexing for unused categories. 

  • Open source: The package is licensed under Apache 2.0 and works with any AI SDK model.

Get started today

Developers can add memory to an existing Vercel AI SDK project in three steps. This integration works with AI SDK v6 and v7 and requires a MongoDB Atlas cluster.

  1. Install the package and its peer dependencies: npm install @mongodb-developer/vercel-ai-memory ai mongodb

  2. Create a memory instance with an Atlas connection string and an embedding model.

  3. Pass the memory tools to the application, scoped to a user and session.

From there, the model decides when to save and when to search for memories.

title: Draining Rate-Limited Job Pools — FIFO Deduplication and Idempotency in 5 Minutes
description:
Short answer: use FIFO deduplication for a five-minute duplicate window, then enforce an application idempotency key in your database or cache; exactly-once delivery is not a safe assumption. For many media workloads, a standard at-least-once queue with an idempotent worker is the simpler rate-limited jobs design.

The page usually arrives late. A worker pool is draining slowly, the provider starts returning 429, and the queue depth alert fires after the deadline has already slipped. Then a retry lands beside its original message. The on-call sees two thumbnails being rendered for one upload and has to decide which side effect to keep.

I start from that alert because it exposes the real contract: a queue controls delivery, while the consumer owns correctness. FIFO can suppress a duplicate message for five minutes. It cannot protect a replay after that window, and an acknowledged message is deleted.

Infrai fits this handoff when a media team wants queue calls over one plain REST API and one credential alongside its other backend services. That can remove SDK setup and key rotation work, but it doesn't change the at-least-once contract or the need for an idempotent consumer.

What should a rate-limited queue do when FIFO deduplication expires?

Treat the FIFO window as an optimization, not a ledger. Put a key tied to the external request or business object in durable storage before the side effect completes. A unique constraint such as media:resize:{asset_id}:{version} lets a second delivery become a no-op even when it arrives hours later. Set the key to processing, commit the result, then mark it done; a lease or timeout is needed so a crashed worker can be retried.

The five-minute detail matters operationally. A producer retry inside that interval may disappear at the FIFO layer, while a delayed provider callback or a manual redrive can arrive on day two. Retention is capped at 30 days, and delay is capped at seven days, so neither feature substitutes for your own record.

Do not build a replay-stream architecture for this workflow. Multiple consumer groups are outside the contract here.

The smallest worker loop that keeps retries boring

The API surface is deliberately small. This Go sketch creates a queue, publishes a message with an application key, consumes it, and acknowledges only after the idempotent write and side effect succeed. It uses the verified queue paths.

package main

import (
  "bytes"
  "encoding/json"
  "fmt"
  "io"
  "net/http"
  "os"
  "time"
)

var client = &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}

func call(method, path string, body any, idem string) ([]byte, int, error) {
  raw, err := json.Marshal(body); if err != nil { return nil, 0, err }
  for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
    req, err := http.NewRequest(method, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"+path, bytes.NewReader(raw)); if err != nil { return nil, 0, err }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json"); req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idem)
    resp, err := client.Do(req); if err != nil { return nil, 0, err }; data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body); resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests { time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second); continue }
    if readErr != nil { return nil, resp.StatusCode, readErr }; if resp.StatusCode >= 300 { return data, resp.StatusCode, fmt.Errorf("queue request failed: %s", resp.Status) }; return data, resp.StatusCode, nil
  }
  return nil, http.StatusTooManyRequests, fmt.Errorf("rate limit persisted after retries")
}

func main() {
  queue := "media-rate-limited"
  _, _, _ = call("POST", "/queue/create", map[string]any{"queue": queue}, "create-"+queue)
  key := "resize:asset-1842:v3"
  _, _, _ = call("POST", "/queue/publish", map[string]any{"queue": queue, "body": map[string]any{"asset_id": "asset-1842", "version": 3}, "deduplication_id": key}, key)
  msg, _, err := call("POST", "/queue/consume", map[string]any{"queue": queue, "max_messages": 1}, "consume-"+queue)
  if err != nil { panic(err) }; fmt.Println(string(msg))
  // Check the durable idempotency record before rendering, then ack after success.
  _, _, _ = call("POST", "/queue/ack", map[string]any{"queue": queue, "receipt": "receipt-from-consume"}, "ack-"+key)
}

The receipt is a value returned by the consume response; production code must parse it and pass the actual receipt. Your database transaction, not the queue acknowledgment, is the boundary that prevents duplicate rendering.

Choosing a queue without pretending delivery is exactly once

RabbitMQ gives mature routing and dead-letter exchanges, but you operate the broker and its topology. Amazon SQS offers managed standard and FIFO queues, with FIFO deduplication semantics that still require consumer safeguards. Google Cloud Tasks is a strong fit when each task targets an HTTP handler and per-queue rate limits are the main control. Infrai is worth trying when integration friction is the bottleneck: one REST API and one credential keep queue calls consistent with other backend capabilities, and its public discovery surface exposes schemas and runnable examples without an SDK install. Swapping the backend behind this contract does not force a rewrite of the worker.

Option Setup and credential surface Duplicate/retry posture Best fit
RabbitMQ Self-managed broker and topology At-least-once; DLX is explicit Teams needing routing control
Amazon SQS Managed AWS IAM and queue resources Standard at-least-once; FIFO has a five-minute dedupe window AWS-native workloads
Google Cloud Tasks Managed HTTP task targets Retry policy and dispatch throttling Per-handler rate limiting
Infrai queue API Plain HTTPS with one key; discovery supplies schemas FIFO window is limited; application idempotency remains required Teams reducing SDK and credential sprawl

The catch is scope. Infrai is not suitable when you need Kafka-style replay, multiple consumer groups, DAG orchestration, fan-out joins, or a private HTTP target; choose a specialist such as RabbitMQ, SQS, Cloud Tasks, Airflow, or Temporal. Standard queues with idempotent consumers are often enough for a media worker pool.

Instrument the signal and set the boundary before the next page

Track queue age, receive count, 429 rate, and the count of idempotency keys in processing longer than the worker lease. Alert on age plus sustained 429s, not on a single transient response. A low threshold creates noise; a high threshold hides deadline misses. I am not sure which threshold fits your provider without its rate-limit headers and job SLA, so start from the maximum tolerable delay and tune from observed traffic.

For longer work, use a cron trigger to enqueue jobs and let workers consume them; cron execution is limited to 900 seconds. Keep payloads under 256KB, delay under seven days, and remember that acknowledged messages are removed. Those constraints make the durable idempotency record part of the design.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the queue capability guide and verify the discovered schema before wiring a worker.

References

  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/dlx
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/FIFO-queues.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/tasks/docs/creating-appengine-tasks
  • https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html
  • https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt

title: Data freshness is a schema property: freezing the market price before kickoff
description:
Every prediction is a claim about a world state that does not exist yet, which makes its input side auditable in a way most ML pipelines never face: the feature vector must be reconstructable as of a timestamp strictly earlier than the event.

We run a football analytics platform with 209 models and 46,233 settled predictions. Hunting for time leakage, I found it in three places, none a model bug — all three schema problems: tables physically able to store a value that could not have existed at decision time. The audit came down to one question per input table: what stops a row from being written after the event it describes? Mostly, nothing.

Lead time is the cheapest detector

The gap between row creation and the event timestamp is the first thing to plot. Join to fixtures, bucket the delta.

WITH lead AS (
  SELECT p.id, p.hit,
         EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (n.match_time - p.created_at)) / 60.0 AS lead_min
  FROM ai_predictions p
  JOIN nami_matches n ON n.id = p.match_id
  WHERE p.settled
)
SELECT CASE WHEN lead_min < 0    THEN 'after kickoff'
            WHEN lead_min < 10   THEN '0-10 min'
            WHEN lead_min < 60   THEN '10-60 min'
            WHEN lead_min < 360  THEN '1-6 h'
            WHEN lead_min < 1440 THEN '6-24 h'
            ELSE 'over 24 h' END AS bucket,
       COUNT(*) AS n,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN hit THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 100, 2) AS hit_pct
FROM lead GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;
bucket rows share settled-hit %
over 24 h 14,908 32.25% 56.45
6-24 h 20,292 43.89% 57.28
1-6 h 9,491 20.53% 56.34
10-60 min 1,171 2.53% 58.84
0-10 min 290 0.63% 55.52
after kickoff 81 0.18% 69.14

Eighty-one rows were written after the fixture had started, settling at 69.14% against 56.9% for the rest. At n=81 that is a symptom, not a result: those rows come from a different code path, one close enough to the outcome to matter. The reading is not "late rows are better" but "we cannot tell what they saw, and should not have been able to write them".

Percentiles: p5 100.4 | p25 413.1 | p50 1,074.1 | p75 1,840.5 | p95 4,183 minutes. A 17.9-hour median is healthy; a p5 of 100 puts one row in twenty inside the window where the market is most informative — and most likely quoted from the wrong tick.

A change log with no as-of boundary is a time machine

The price store is a change log: 15,378,162 rows over 44,933 fixtures, 22.1 sources per fixture (median 19, max 87), median 140 ticks per fixture (p90 983). No is_prematch flag, no write guard — so the worker keeps appending after kickoff:

SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE e.changed_at > n.match_time) AS post_kickoff_ticks,
       COUNT(*)                                            AS total_ticks,
       COUNT(DISTINCT e.match_id)
         FILTER (WHERE e.changed_at > n.match_time)        AS affected_fixtures
FROM nami_europe_odds e JOIN nami_matches n ON n.id = e.match_id;

post_kickoff_ticks | total_ticks | affected_fixtures
             62,922 |  15,378,162 |            15,259

0.41% of rows across 15,259 fixtures — a third of the store, small per fixture (mean 4.1 ticks, max 443) and short (median worst-case lag 2.4 minutes, max 1,439.6). The issue is that ORDER BY changed_at DESC LIMIT 1 — the pattern in every dashboard, prompt and backfill — silently returns an in-play value and cannot know it.

The consequence: of 44,625 fixtures with a pre-kickoff tick, the last lands a median 3.0 minutes before kickoff but the mean is 444.9; 13,540 (30.3%) have nothing newer than six hours, 2,201 (4.9%) nothing newer than 24. Bimodal — the feed either tracks to the whistle or stopped last evening, and no column records which.

The stored price is not the decision-time price

ai_predictions carries opening_eu_home/draw/away; the name promises the fixture's first quote. Two reference sets, tolerance 0.005, same 45,819 settled rows carrying a stored price:

reference rows matching share
declared opening, any source 13,706 29.9%
pre-kickoff price within 2 h, any source 20,365 44.5%

A column called opening reconciles with a pre-kickoff price more often than with the opening. Backwards. So I restricted to the 15,487 rows whose fixture has a declared opening, giving both tests one denominator:

WITH declared AS (
  SELECT match_id, MAX(initial_eu_home) AS ini
  FROM nami_europe_odds WHERE initial_eu_home IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1
), prekick AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT e.match_id, e.eu_home
  FROM nami_europe_odds e JOIN nami_matches n ON n.id = e.match_id
  WHERE e.changed_at <= n.match_time
    AND e.changed_at >  n.match_time - INTERVAL '3 hours'
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS n,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM declared d
           WHERE d.match_id = p.match_id
             AND abs(d.ini - p.opening_eu_home) < 0.005)) AS hit_opening,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM prekick k
           WHERE k.match_id = p.match_id
             AND abs(k.eu_home - p.opening_eu_home) < 0.005)) AS hit_prekick
FROM ai_predictions p
WHERE p.settled AND p.opening_eu_home IS NOT NULL
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM declared d WHERE d.match_id = p.match_id);

n = 15,487 | hit_opening 849 (5.5%) | hit_prekick 7,942 (51.3%)

The innocent explanation is that prices rarely move. Control: of the 13,882 fixtures holding both a declared opening and a pre-kickoff price, only 1,273 (9.2%) are unchanged. With 90.8% moving, 51.3% against the pre-kickoff price and 5.5% against the opening cannot both come from stability.

A placebo run on the 3,000 most recent rows — matching each stored price against the next fixture's pre-kickoff quote — returns 8.5%, the base rate of a 19-source grid; the same-fixture rate is 49.7%.

So opening_eu_home is filled at write time from whatever the feed currently says — usually the freshest quote. A timestamp-of-write price wearing a timestamp-of-event name:

Across 13,876 measured fixtures, the drift between those two ticks is a median 3.08 pp of implied probability, p90 10.93 pp, with 4,649 fixtures (33.5%) moving more than five points.

The reference column itself decays

Worse than a wrong name is a disappearing reference. Coverage of initial_eu_home by month:

month fixtures in store with declared opening coverage
2026-06 1,007 0 0.0%
2026-07 3,018 0 0.0%
2026-08 9,320 0 0.0%
2026-09 7,443 5,108 68.6%
2026-10 17,392 8,848 50.9%
2026-11 6,689 41 0.6%

Backfilled for two months, then abandoned — no migration, no alert. The store's semantics moved under its consumers: the most expensive kind of data debt, invisible to NOT NULL, and it turns every historical comparison into a comparison of different things.

Fixtures move too

match_time_audit exists because kickoff times are not stable: 42,378 fixtures, 141,111 changes, 13,500 of them carrying settled predictions. 2,056 predictions were created inside the window between the old and new kickoff — already running by the original schedule, not yet started by the revised one. Each has an unanswerable "was this pre-kickoff?" until the row records which copy of the schedule it used.

The fix: watermark, freeze, hash

1. A watermark, not a clock. Every price row carries the event time it describes (as_of) plus its fixture. Queries use as_of <= :decision_time, never changed_at. "Latest price" becomes "latest price as of a timestamp someone chose deliberately".

2. Freeze once, at kickoff, with a hash. One row per fixture, rejected at or after kickoff by the writer and by a constraint:

import hashlib, json
from datetime import datetime, timezone

def freeze(cur, match_id: int, as_of: datetime, prices: dict, source: str) -> str:
    """Insert the one and only frozen price for a fixture. Returns the hash."""
    cur.execute("SELECT match_time FROM nami_matches WHERE id = %s", (match_id,))
    kickoff = cur.fetchone()[0]
    if as_of >= kickoff:
        raise ValueError(f"{match_id}: as_of {as_of} is not before kickoff {kickoff}")

    body = {"match_id": match_id,
            "as_of": as_of.astimezone(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
            "source": source, "prices": prices}
    digest = hashlib.sha256(
        json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")).encode()).hexdigest()

    # the first freeze wins, forever
    cur.execute("""INSERT INTO frozen_prices (match_id, as_of, source, payload, sha256)
                   VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s, %s)
                   ON CONFLICT (match_id) DO NOTHING""",
                (match_id, as_of, source, json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True), digest))

    cur.execute("SELECT sha256 FROM frozen_prices WHERE match_id = %s", (match_id,))
    if cur.fetchone()[0] != digest:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{match_id}: frozen row exists with a different payload")
    return digest

3. Reference the freeze from the prediction. Store frozen_price_id and kickoff_at instead of three copied numbers; "which price did the model see" becomes a foreign key that survives every backfill.

One table already gets this right: odds_snapshot_ledger, 15.4M rows over 20,065 fixtures, write lag median 6 s and p95 34 s against the bucket it records, and zero rows in the last seven days whose live-tick timestamp postdates kickoff (2,083,478 checked). Same vendor, same worker — the difference is the schema, not the ingest code.

Invariants worth testing in CI

  1. Predictions with created_at >= kickoff_at = 0, and frozen prices with as_of >= kickoff_at = 0. Alert, not warn.
  2. Every settled prediction resolves through frozen_price_id to exactly one row, and the hash verifies.
  3. Stored price reconciles with at least one source quote at as_of — 100%, not 30%.
  4. Reference-column coverage measured monthly, alerted on any drop over 10 pp. A column that silently stops being populated is worse than one never added.
  5. Kickoff changes recorded before the window they invalidate; predictions carry the kickoff used.

None of these are modelling decisions. They are the arithmetic that makes a backtest mean anything — and all of them were failing on a system that produced 46,233 settled predictions without an alarm. Our 56.9% settled rate was computed against a price column that, in half the rows, holds a later price than the model saw. The model was not cheating; the schema left the door open and nobody checked who walked through it.

If you take one thing from this: data freshness is not a cron schedule, it is a column. A pipeline that refreshes every 60 seconds is still a time machine if the destination is not recorded on the row.

Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+
