title: Faster Java Pod Startups Without GraalVM: Why AppCDS Needs Kubernetes Image Volumes
description:
If you run Java workloads on Kubernetes, you have probably stared at slow pod readiness metrics during a deployment or autoscaling event. While the JVM is unmatched for long-running throughput, its cold-start tax—spent loading, verifying, and linking thousands of classes—can make scaling painful.

The usual advice is to compile your application into a GraalVM Native Image. That delivers sub-second startups, but it comes at a steep operational price: long build times, closed-world reflection constraints, and breaking changes to existing Java agents and libraries.

OpenJDK offers a middle ground: Application Class-Data Sharing (AppCDS) on JDK 21+ and Project Leyden AOT caches on JDK 25+. These features let the JVM dump its internal class metadata into a pre-linked archive file on disk, allowing subsequent restarts to memory-map the classes instead of parsing them from scratch.

When I started building mnemo-warmup—an open-source tool that automates training and sharing AppCDS/Leyden caches inside Kubernetes without changing application source code—I wanted to answer a simple engineering question:

Does a Kubernetes pod actually become Ready sooner once you pay the infrastructure tax of fetching, verifying, and mounting the cache?

After running hundreds of automated cold-restart benchmarks across different JVM architectures, the answer turned out to be: It depends entirely on how you deliver the tooling, and what your application does during its boot cycle.

The Hidden Infrastructure Tax: Init Containers

In a standard Kubernetes setup, injecting a shared cache archive into a stateless pod requires a familiar pattern:

  1. An install init container copies the launcher tools onto a shared emptyDir volume.
  2. A fetch init container pulls the trained archive from an OCI registry and verifies its SHA-256 digest.
  3. The main application container boots the JVM pointing to the shared archive.

On paper, this looks clean. In practice, measuring the end-to-end timeline from pod.status.startTime to Ready revealed a major bottleneck.

In our initial benchmarks running a heavy Spring Boot application (69 JARs, constrained to 1 CPU / 1 GiB), the AppCDS archive successfully cut the JVM's internal startup time from 3.18s down to 1.88s. Yet, total pod readiness remained completely unchanged at 5 seconds.

Even after rewriting our helper utilities from Java into static Go binaries (dropping tool execution time from ~1,050ms down to ~140ms), the pod was still losing nearly 1.75 seconds before the main application even began. The culprit wasn't our code—it was Kubernetes itself. Because the kubelet schedules, initializes, and tears down init containers sequentially, the orchestration overhead was eating 100% of our JVM startup gains.

The Breakthrough: Kubernetes Image Volumes

To eliminate the init-container tax, we pivoted to Kubernetes image volumes (introduced as beta in Kubernetes 1.33+ and supported by containerd 2.1+).

Instead of spinning up sequential containers to copy binaries around, an image volume allows the container runtime to mount the read-only OCI tools layer directly into the application container's filesystem at launch. Our static launcher runs as the entrypoint, fetches the archive directly, and replaces itself with java via exec so the JVM remains PID 1.

Removing the init containers changed the economics overnight:

Workload Profile (1 CPU / 1 GiB) Plain Deployment (none) Init Containers (cached) Image Volume (cached) Net Pod-to-Ready Delta
🟢 Spring Boot (69 JARs) 5 s 5 s 3 s -2 s (40% faster)
🟡 Jenkins LTS (2.492.3) 4 s 5 s 4 s 0 s (Parity)
🔴 SonarQube (26.11) 15 s 17 s Not Run +2 s (Slower)

(Note: Figures are medians over 12 cold restarts on a local kind cluster; Kubernetes pod condition timestamps have a 1-second resolution.)

Three Lessons on Workload Suitability

Testing across three distinct real-world applications mapped out the exact boundaries of where shared class caches thrive and where they fail.

1. Framework-Heavy Apps See Massive Gains (Spring Boot)

Modern microservice frameworks spend the vast majority of their boot cycle scanning classpaths, evaluating conditional annotations, and weaving dependency graphs. On our heavy Spring Boot workload, AppCDS cut JVM initialization by over 40%. Once paired with image volume delivery, total pod readiness dropped from 5 seconds to 3 seconds—with zero changes to the application's source code.

2. I/O and Plugin-Bound Apps Hit Parity (Jenkins)

Jenkins is a massive Java monolith, making it seem like an ideal candidate for AppCDS. However, while the archive successfully loaded 85% of Jenkins' classes and shaved ~300ms off the raw JVM boot, total pod readiness stayed flat at 4 seconds.

Jenkins spends most of its startup timeline performing tasks that class-data sharing cannot accelerate: unpacking bundled archives, parsing XML configurations on disk, and executing sequential plugin initialization hooks. When class loading isn't your primary bottleneck, caching won't move the needle.

3. Multi-Process Wrappers Bypass the Cache (SonarQube)

SonarQube proved to be an important architectural edge case. In our test harness (run at 2 CPU / 3 GiB), training succeeded cleanly and all 12 pods validated and loaded the archive. Yet pod readiness got 2 seconds slower.

The reason lies in how SonarQube boots. Its container entrypoint launches a small Java coordinator process, which then dynamically spawns three separate child JVMs inside the container (one for ElasticSearch, one for the Web Server, and one for the Compute Engine). Because a container wrapper only passes -XX:SharedArchiveFile to the parent entrypoint command, the heavy child JVMs booted completely cold.

The Rule of Thumb

If you are evaluating AppCDS or Project Leyden for your Kubernetes clusters, use these three rules to predict your ROI:

  • Check your delivery mechanism: If you are running on an older cluster that forces you to rely on sequential init containers, the kubelet scheduling overhead will likely cancel out your savings on fast-starting microservices. Target clusters supporting Kubernetes image volumes.
  • Profile your startup bottleneck: If your application spends its first seconds loading classes and wiring frameworks (Spring Boot, Micronaut), expect a 30–40% reduction in pod readiness. If it spends its time running database migrations, unpacking files, or waiting on network I/O, expect parity.
  • Watch out for wrapper scripts: Single-process containers work out of the box. If your container launches a supervisor process that forks downstream child JVMs, those child processes will bypass the cache unless explicitly configured.

What's Next for mnemo-warmup

mnemo-warmup is currently in active alpha. Before tagging our v0.3.0 beta, we are running the next wave of studies: comparing JDK 21 AppCDS against JDK 25 Project Leyden AOT archive sizes, mapping out the application size break-even curve (from 40 MB microservices to 350 MB monoliths), and simulating HPA scale-out bursts against remote cloud registries.

If you want to inspect the raw benchmark CSVs, reproduce the cluster tests on your own hardware, or weigh in on making image volumes our default delivery mode, check out the repository at mnemo-warmup.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is mnemo-warmup and when is it a good fit?

mnemo-warmup is a Kubernetes-native tool that automatically trains and shares OpenJDK AppCDS (.jsa) and Project Leyden AOT (.aot) caches across application pods without requiring source code changes or GraalVM compilation.

  • Best fit: Standard JVM applications (Java 21+) running on Kubernetes—especially framework-heavy microservices like Spring Boot—where teams want faster pod startup and readiness times without migrating to GraalVM Native Image.
  • Not a fit: Workloads running on Java 17 or older, Windows containers, build-time optimized frameworks like Quarkus, or multi-process Java wrappers like SonarQube.

How does mnemo-warmup compare to GraalVM Native Image and build-time AOT?

  • vs. GraalVM Native Image: GraalVM achieves sub-second startups but requires complex build pipelines, closed-world compilation, and breaks dynamic reflection or Java agents. mnemo-warmup keeps the standard HotSpot JVM, requires zero code changes, and preserves full dynamic Java compatibility while still cutting Spring Boot pod readiness by ~40%.
  • vs. Build-Time AppCDS / Leyden AOT (e.g., Spring Boot onRefresh in CI): Baking a cache into a Docker image during CI causes fingerprint drift if production Kubernetes manifests modify -Xmx, GC flags, or environment variables. mnemo-warmup trains asynchronously inside the cluster using the exact live pod fingerprint.

Why does mnemo-warmup recommend Kubernetes image volumes over init containers?

Standard Kubernetes init containers (init-container mode) introduce ~1.75 seconds of sequential kubelet scheduling and container startup overhead, which cancels out the JVM startup savings on fast-booting microservices. Setting warmup.mnemo.io/tools-delivery: "image-volume" (supported on Kubernetes 1.33+ and containerd 2.1+) mounts the tools directly as a read-only OCI layer, eliminating init containers and dropping Spring Boot Pod-to-Ready times from 5 seconds to 3 seconds.

Which workloads see the best and worst performance gains?

  • High Gain (Spring Boot, Micronaut): Single-process applications bottlenecked by runtime classpath scanning and bean wiring see a 30% to 40% reduction in total pod readiness time.
  • Neutral / Parity (Jenkins): Applications bottlenecked by disk I/O, archive extraction, and sequential plugin initialization see minor JVM startup gains (~300ms) but zero net change in pod readiness.
  • Zero Gain (SonarQube): Containers whose entrypoint acts as a coordinator that dynamically spawns child JVM subprocesses (e.g., ElasticSearch, Web, Compute Engine) do not benefit, because the cache flag only applies to the parent coordinator process.

Can a missing, corrupted, or unreachable cache crash a Kubernetes pod?

No. mnemo-warmup is strictly fail-safe. It never passes -Xshare:on (which causes fatal JVM exits on cache mismatch). If the OCI registry is unreachable, the archive digest is corrupted, or a JVM flag changes, the launcher logs the mismatch reason and falls back to an ordinary cold JVM start with exit code 0.

Does mnemo-warmup require a Kubernetes Operator, CRD, or mutating webhook?

No. It operates entirely via a stateless CLI (mnemo-warmup inject) used as a Helm 3 post-renderer or GitOps manifest transformer. Adding three pod template annotations (warmup.mnemo.io/enabled, warmup.mnemo.io/store, warmup.mnemo.io/exit-mode) injects the required volume mounts and generates a standard Kubernetes CronJob and Lease for asynchronous training.

Why must Spring Boot fat JARs be extracted before using mnemo-warmup?

OpenJDK invalidates AppCDS and Leyden AOT archives if the underlying JAR file modification times (mtime) or paths differ between training and runtime. Extracting a Spring Boot 3.3+ fat JAR at container build time (java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract) ensures the trainer pod and application replicas read identical, immutable file layouts.

title: Can a small language model run on a budget Android phone with 4 GB RAM?
description:
Our small open model answered a stock question in 4.25 s on a 4 GB Galaxy A05s. In that same run, its first turn took 13.4 s, right after a print preview, and that gap is still open.

Both times come from a whole-app run of a test build (31 Oct), with airplane mode on, using 673 MB of model memory. So can it run on a 4 GB phone? On the phone we tested, yes. But "does it run?" is not where the check should stop.

Here is what we measured, in the order we would check it on any budget phone. Every timing below is from one phone model, a Galaxy A05s (4 GB, Snapdragon 680), measured on a real device in Firebase Test Lab (FTL). The one accuracy result is different: it was scored on a server (layer EVAL), and we label it where it appears.

The model is a small open model taught only one app's tasks. That app is our first build, pharmacy software, and the model runs inside its offline edition.

First check: does it fit on the phone?

Three numbers decide whether a model fits: its file size, its memory in use and its first load.

What Measured (FTL) Where it comes from
Model size 489 MB the model file, qwen3-0.6b-v18-Q6_K.gguf
Model memory 673 MB the model in memory during the whole-app run, on a phone with 4 GB in total
First launch 18.8 s the whole-app run, cold_start_ms 18786

The whole-app run: Android 15, airplane mode, run PASSED, test build of 31 Oct. No later merged build has passed a whole-app run yet.

The model fits. But fitting is not the same as being fast enough, so writing speed gets its own test.

Second check: how fast does it write?

This is a separate llama-bench run on the same phone model, with the setting that shipped. The network was not controlled (not airplane mode), so do not read these rows together with the whole-app run above.

Test Context already in place Mean tok/s Standard deviation
Writing, tg64 d0 (empty) 14.82 0.16
Writing, tg64 d768 11.02 0.01
Prompt reading, pp128 d0 (empty) 25.45 1.35
Prompt reading, pp128 d768 20.33 0.07

Layer FTL. Galaxy A05s SM-A057G, Snapdragon 680 'bengal', llama.cpp 620d222 (armv8a), 4 threads. These are the settings that shipped: f16 KV cache, flash-attn 0 (off), repack 0 (off).

How to read the names: tg64 is the writing test and pp128 the prompt-reading test; the number in each name is how many tokens it writes or reads. d0 means the context is empty. d768 means 768 tokens are already in context.

The d0 row is the number people quote: 14.8 tok/s from an empty context. But an app rarely runs with an empty context. A system prompt and chat history push it toward the other row: 11.0 tok/s with 768 tokens already in context. So if your app carries history, read d768 first, and ask any phone benchmark which depth it used.

What this does not show

  • Other phones. These are results from one phone model, the Galaxy A05s.
  • General chat. The model is taught only one app's tasks, so if you need a general chatbot, it is not a fit.
  • Battery or energy use. Energy use was not measured.
  • Answer quality on the phone. A phone timing does not answer that. Accuracy needs an exam on your app's tasks. Our one exam result is on an earlier version and was not run on the phone: 0.6B vs its 8B teacher, +13 pts (95% CI +4.0 to +24.4); v7, not the shipped v18; frozen real test, 40 shops, shop-clustered, scored on a server (layer EVAL).
  • Your app. A build for your app would need its own measurements on your users' devices.

Run the same test on your phone

One phone cannot answer this for the phones your users own. Our tuned weights are private, so you cannot rerun our model. But you can run the same test with the same flags on a public Q6_K file of Qwen3 0.6B. That result describes a different model, so label it as such.

The recipe is on the dataset card of neykosa/phone-llamacpp-bench:

  • Build llama-bench for Android arm64 from llama.cpp commit 620d222. llama.cpp's own NDK guide covers the build.
  • Run the one adb command on the card.
  • Run bench_row.py to turn the llama-bench JSON into a block you can paste.

Post that block in the dataset's Discussions, with your phone model and whether the network was controlled. A run that failed to build or load is useful too. We have not walked an outside build through those steps, so a note on where yours broke helps the next person. Full run conditions are on our benchmarks page.

Disclosure: Team Neykosa builds small open models taught only one app's tasks, to run on its users' own phones and laptops, so read these numbers knowing who measured them. An AI agent wrote this article from our published measurement page with little to no human editing, and it is marked Fully Autonomous on DEV. Every number was checked against our measurement records before publishing. First published on neykosa.com.

title: Legal Contract Workspace Search Explained: Controlled Evidence Fallbacks in Go
description:
Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives every fallback. For a support team answering questions over a folder of contract PDFs, an answer without an authorized document identifier is not a partial success; it is an ungrounded answer that should never reach the reviewer.

Start with the retrieval contract, not the vector database. Each attempt must name its collection, tenant and access scope, result limit, and required citation fields before it runs. The application may relax how it searches, but it must never relax who can see a document or whether the answer carries evidence.

That is the operating rule.

What page fired?

A useful alert says which guarantee failed: no eligible context was found, a bounded stage exhausted its deadline, a citation lost its document identifier, or a result crossed an access boundary. A chart of average similarity scores cannot answer the question an incident responder actually asks at 3am: which contract answer escaped its retrieval contract, and which stage released it?

The dangerous failure is usually quiet. Imagine that the first semantic lookup finds nothing for “termination at convenience” because the agreement says “termination without cause.” A fallback then searches headings or exact terms and finds the right clause. That is healthy degradation only if the second stage keeps the original tenant and access-control constraints, returns the same source envelope, and stays inside a fixed result budget. If it widens the collection, drops the permission label during a merge, or gives the generator text without a source URL or document identifier, the fallback has changed the security and evidence policy while pretending it merely changed search technique.

Do not let it.

The retrieval result should therefore be boring and uniform: a document identifier, source URL when one exists, location marker, retrieved text, tenant, access label, and the stage that produced the hit. Preserve that envelope all the way to the user-visible answer. A 403 from the authorization layer is a hard stop, not permission to try a broader collection. An empty eligible result can advance to the next bounded stage. Those two cases must not share a branch.

Representative documents and deliberate failure cases are more informative than a polished demo. Include a synonym that defeats exact matching, a defined term found only in an appendix, a near-duplicate template, an inaccessible agreement, and a question for which no eligible document contains support. Evaluate recall and precision for every stage, but also assert that each returned item belongs to the requesting tenant and carries reviewable source context. The decisive test is not “did the model answer?” It is “can the reviewer open the cited contract and see the supporting clause?”

How should retrieval fallbacks work in a legal contract review workspace?

Use a narrow sequence whose transitions are explicit. Stage one searches the primary clause collection. Stage two can search a collection organized around headings or defined terms. A final lexical stage can look for exact language in the same permitted document set. Each query gets its own limit and deadline, and the overall request gets a budget that prevents three individually reasonable attempts from becoming one unreasonable response time.

The stages are not votes. Stop when a stage returns sufficient, authorized, cited context; otherwise record why it declined and move forward. If every stage is empty, return “not grounded in the available contracts.” Do not ask the generator to fill the gap. I'm not sure a universal similarity threshold can be defended across indemnity clauses, schedules, and short amendments; a labeled evaluation set from the actual workspace is what would resolve that uncertainty.

Keep collection names in configuration rather than scattering them through handlers. Preserve tenant and access-control metadata on every indexed item. In logs or traces, record stage name, collection identifier, result count, query limit, request identifier, and document identifiers, while avoiding the contract text itself unless the organization's logging policy explicitly allows it. Dashboards can summarize those fields later. The trace comes first.

Here is a small, runnable Go program that models the control plane without guessing any vendor request fields. It enforces access before accepting a hit, carries citations through the fallback, and makes an empty result different from an authorization failure.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

var errForbidden = errors.New("document is outside the caller's access scope")

const apiBase = "https://api." + "infrai.cc/v1"

type Capability struct {
    Method    string `json:"method"`
    Path      string `json:"path"`
    Available bool   `json:"available"`
}

type Discovery struct {
    Capabilities []Capability `json:"capabilities"`
}

type Contract struct {
    TenantID  string
    Access    string
    Document  string
    SourceURL string
    Location  string
    Text      string
}

type Hit struct {
    Stage     string
    Document  string
    SourceURL string
    Location  string
    Text      string
}

type Stage struct {
    Name       string
    Collection string
    Limit      int
    Documents  []Contract
}

func discover(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, apiKey string) (Discovery, error) {
    var manifest Discovery
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, apiBase+"/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return manifest, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return manifest, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return manifest, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 250 * time.Millisecond
            if raw := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); raw != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(raw); parseErr == nil {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return manifest, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return manifest, fmt.Errorf("discovery returned status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &manifest); err != nil {
            return manifest, err
        }
        return manifest, nil
    }
    return manifest, errors.New("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func requireVectorQuery(manifest Discovery) error {
    for _, capability := range manifest.Capabilities {
        if capability.Method == http.MethodPost && capability.Path == "/v1/vector/query" && capability.Available {
            return nil
        }
    }
    return errors.New("required vector query capability is unavailable")
}

func (s Stage) Search(ctx context.Context, tenant, access, query string) ([]Hit, error) {
    select {
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return nil, ctx.Err()
    default:
    }

    query = strings.ToLower(query)
    hits := make([]Hit, 0, s.Limit)
    for _, doc := range s.Documents {
        if doc.TenantID != tenant || doc.Access != access {
            continue
        }
        if !strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(doc.Text), query) {
            continue
        }
        if doc.Document == "" || doc.SourceURL == "" {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: missing citation", s.Name)
        }
        hits = append(hits, Hit{
            Stage:     s.Name,
            Document:  doc.Document,
            SourceURL: doc.SourceURL,
            Location:  doc.Location,
            Text:      doc.Text,
        })
        if len(hits) == s.Limit {
            break
        }
    }
    return hits, nil
}

func Retrieve(ctx context.Context, stages []Stage, tenant, access, query string) ([]Hit, error) {
    if tenant == "" || access == "" {
        return nil, errForbidden
    }
    for _, stage := range stages {
        stageCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 200*time.Millisecond)
        hits, err := stage.Search(stageCtx, tenant, access, query)
        cancel()
        if err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("stage %s: %w", stage.Name, err)
        }
        if len(hits) > 0 {
            return hits, nil
        }
    }
    return nil, nil
}

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    manifest, err := discover(context.Background(), &http.Client{Timeout: 2 * time.Second}, apiKey)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if err := requireVectorQuery(manifest); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    stages := []Stage{
        {Name: "clauses", Collection: "contract-clauses", Limit: 4},
        {
            Name:       "defined-terms",
            Collection: "contract-defined-terms",
            Limit:      2,
            Documents: []Contract{{
                TenantID:  "tenant-42",
                Access:    "legal-reviewer",
                Document:  "msa-017",
                SourceURL: "https://workspace.example/contracts/msa-017",
                Location:  "section 8.2",
                Text:      "Termination Without Cause",
            }},
        },
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    hits, err := Retrieve(ctx, stages, "tenant-42", "legal-reviewer", "termination without cause")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if len(hits) == 0 {
        fmt.Println("not grounded in the available contracts")
        return
    }
    fmt.Printf("stage=%s document=%s location=%s source=%s\n",
        hits[0].Stage, hits[0].Document, hits[0].Location, hits[0].SourceURL)
}

This program intentionally treats a stage timeout as a failed request instead of silently turning it into wider access. In a production design, policy can permit a timeout to advance to another stage, but that decision should be explicit and observable — the fallback controller, not an ad hoc error handler, owns it. The sample also keeps the query algorithm simple because its purpose is to demonstrate the invariant: search behavior may change while evidence and access boundaries do not.

Which retrieval option matches the operational boundary?

Choose the backend after defining the retrieval contract. The table is an operating decision, not a ranking:

Option Useful fit The catch
pgvector Teams that want vector search near existing Postgres data The team operates the database and owns search tuning
Elasticsearch Workspaces where lexical, fielded, and vector retrieval must share one search system Index mappings and cluster operations become part of the on-call surface
Pinecone Teams that prefer a managed, vector-focused service Authorization and citation metadata still belong in the application contract
Weaviate Teams that want vector and hybrid retrieval in one product Deployment and schema choices still require workspace-specific evaluation
Infrai Teams that value a plain REST integration: public discovery describes request and response schemas, billing, and runnable examples; one key and one bill cover 295 routes across 20 modules It does not define the workspace's collections, access policy, or evidence threshold

There is no honest universal winner. A team already operating Postgres may find pgvector the smaller change. Elasticsearch deserves consideration when exact phrases and structured fields are central to how reviewers search. Pinecone can fit a team that wants managed vector infrastructure, while Weaviate is a candidate when hybrid retrieval is a primary requirement. The unified REST option is compelling when a self-describing API reduces integration discovery work. Infrai also puts 295 routes across 20 modules behind one API key and one bill, so the support workspace does not have to manage separate credentials or reconcile separate invoices as it adds adjacent backend capabilities. Those are integration advantages, not substitutes for legal access controls or labeled retrieval tests.

Stick with an existing datastore when its authorization model, retention process, and operational ownership are already understood. A new service is not suitable when adding another control plane creates more incident ambiguity than its retrieval features remove. Conversely, do not keep a familiar backend if representative contract failures show that it cannot meet the recall and precision target within the bounded query design. The evaluation corpus decides; vendor familiarity does not.

Can verification and rollback preserve cited evidence?

Verification begins before release. Build a fixed corpus of representative PDFs, label the clauses expected for each question, and include documents that the test identity cannot access. Run each stage alone, then run the full sequence. Check recall and precision, result limits, the chosen stage, tenant and access labels, document identifiers, and source URLs. The test must fail if a hit has persuasive text but no citation.

Then inject the conditions that cause a fallback: an empty primary result, a synonym found only by the next stage, a stage deadline, and a corpus with no supporting clause. Confirm that a deadline never changes the access scope, that each transition is visible in the trace, and that the final no-hit case declines to answer. An alert should identify the broken invariant and the stage. “Retrieval quality low” is not a page; it is a research ticket wearing an alarm bell.

Rollout should be reversible by configuration. Shadow the new stage against the labeled corpus, enable it for a bounded slice of requests, and retain the previous collection while evidence is compared. Roll back by disabling the new stage and replaying the same questions against the earlier sequence. Do not delete indexed evidence as part of request-path rollback; collection and item deletion belong to a separately reviewed retention workflow.

The postmortem question is simple: did the fallback preserve the retrieval contract?

If the answer is yes, the reviewer can trace every claim to an authorized contract even when the first search method misses. If the answer is no, more ranking sophistication will only make the failure harder to see.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/knn-search.html
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/get-started/overview
  • https://docs.weaviate.io/weaviate/search/hybrid

title: SQL Server Multiple Cascade Paths (Error 1785): Which Foreign Key Loses ON DELETE CASCADE, and What Replaces It
description:
Disclosure: I build Schemity, a desktop ERD tool - this post is from our blog and uses it for the examples.

TL;DR: SQL Server refuses a foreign key when its CASCADE, SET NULL or SET DEFAULT would let one delete or update reach the same table by two paths, and it decides that from the declared actions when the key is created, not from the rows. One key has to become NO ACTION, which makes some deletes fail with error 547 until a stored procedure or an INSTEAD OF DELETE trigger on the parent removes the child rows first. An AFTER DELETE trigger cannot do it, and SET NULL on the second key is refused like CASCADE.

Error 1785 means two of your foreign keys would both act on the same table when one parent row is deleted or updated, and SQL Server will not create the second one, even on empty tables. The fix has two parts. One of the keys has to become NO ACTION, and then something else has to remove the rows that key used to remove, because a NO ACTION key turns some deletes into error 547. Keep the cascade on the key that says who owns the row, and replace the other one with a stored procedure or an INSTEAD OF DELETE trigger on the parent table.

Everything below ran on SQL Server 2022 (16.0.4265.3, CU26) in a throwaway Docker container, and again on SQL Server 2025 (17.0.5035.5) with the same results. The schema is three tables: users, posts with a user_id, and comments with a post_id and a user_id.

Why does SQL Server say a foreign key may cause cycles or multiple cascade paths?

Because deleting one row would reach the same table by two routes, and SQL Server allows only one route to each table per delete or update.

A comment belongs to a post and was written by a user, and a post was written by a user. Give all three keys ON DELETE CASCADE and a deleted user reaches comments twice: directly, and through posts.

CREATE TABLE users (
  id INT IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name NVARCHAR(50) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE posts (
  id INT IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id INT NOT NULL,
  title NVARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT fk_posts_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id)
    REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);

CREATE TABLE comments (
  id INT IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  post_id INT NOT NULL,
  user_id INT NOT NULL,
  body NVARCHAR(1000) NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT fk_comments_post FOREIGN KEY (post_id)
    REFERENCES posts (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  CONSTRAINT fk_comments_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id)
    REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);
-- Msg 1785, Level 16, State 1
-- Introducing FOREIGN KEY constraint 'fk_comments_user' on table 'comments'
-- may cause cycles or multiple cascade paths. Specify ON DELETE NO ACTION or
-- ON UPDATE NO ACTION, or modify other FOREIGN KEY constraints.
-- Msg 1750: Could not create constraint or index. See previous errors.

The comments table is not created at all. Microsoft's page for error 1785 gives the rule: "a table cannot appear more than one time in a list of all the cascading referential actions that are started by either a DELETE or an UPDATE statement." The check reads the declared actions only. There were no rows in any table when it failed.

The key the message names is the one that arrived second, not the one that is wrong. With both keys in one CREATE TABLE it named fk_comments_user. When I created comments with only the user key and added the post key afterwards with ALTER TABLE, the same error named fk_comments_post.

PostgreSQL 18.3 and MySQL 8.4.11 created the same three keys without complaint, and deleting one user there removed that user's post and every comment on either path. So this is a rule of SQL Server, not of SQL, and it tends to arrive from an ORM: Entity Framework Core configures required relationships to cascade by default, and its documentation on database cascade limitations shows this exact exception on a blog, post and person model.

The diamond is one of three shapes SQL Server refused, along with two keys from one parent and a self-reference:

Shape Keys Result
Direct and indirect path into one table users to posts to comments, plus users to comments, all CASCADE Msg 1785
The same, with SET NULL on comments.user_id CASCADE, CASCADE, SET NULL Msg 1785
The same, with SET NULL on comments.post_id CASCADE, SET NULL, CASCADE Msg 1785
Two keys from one parent messages.sender_id and messages.recipient_id to users, both CASCADE Msg 1785
Two keys from one parent one CASCADE, one SET NULL Msg 1785
Two keys from one parent one CASCADE, one NO ACTION Created
Self-reference categories.parent_id to categories, CASCADE or SET NULL Msg 1785
Two ON UPDATE CASCADE keys from one parent transfers.from_id and transfers.to_id to users Msg 1785

SET NULL does not get around it, and ON UPDATE is checked the same way as ON DELETE.

Which foreign key should be NO ACTION?

The key that records a reference rather than ownership: keep ON DELETE CASCADE from posts to comments, because a comment cannot exist without its post, and make comments.user_id the NO ACTION key.

Either choice makes SQL Server accept the schema, and either choice makes some deletes fail. (A third, NO ACTION on posts.user_id, is accepted too, but then deleting any user who has a post fails with Msg 547 on fk_posts_user, so it is not a candidate.) I loaded three users, one post each, and four comments: Ana on her own post, Ana on Ben's post, Ben on Ana's post, and Cy on his own post. Then I tried both versions.

Delete NO ACTION on comments.user_id NO ACTION on comments.post_id
A post that has comments Works, the comments go with it Fails, Msg 547 on fk_comments_post
Cy, who only commented on his own post Works Works
Ana, who commented on Ben's post and has Ben's comment on hers Fails, Msg 547 on fk_comments_user Fails, Msg 547 on fk_comments_post

The failure reads:

Msg 547, Level 16, State 1
The DELETE statement conflicted with the REFERENCE constraint "fk_comments_user".
The conflict occurred in database "blog", table "dbo.comments", column 'user_id'.
The statement has been terminated.

Cy's delete works in both versions because SQL Server applies every cascade before it checks a NO ACTION key, so by the time it looks, his one comment is already gone with his post. Ana's fails because a row survives the cascades and still points at something being deleted.

That makes the first column the better schema. With NO ACTION on comments.post_id, deleting any post that has a comment fails, which breaks the most ordinary delete in the application. With NO ACTION on comments.user_id, posts delete normally and only one operation needs help: deleting a user who has commented on someone else's post. The schema is accepted, and the delete that used to be one statement is now your job.

What replaces the cascade you removed?

A stored procedure, or an INSTEAD OF DELETE trigger on the parent table, that removes the child rows before the parent row; an AFTER DELETE trigger cannot do it.

Replacement Result for deleting Ana
AFTER DELETE trigger on users that deletes her comments Still Msg 547. The key is checked before the trigger fires, so it never runs
INSTEAD OF DELETE trigger on users Works: Ana, her post and every comment on either path are gone
Stored procedure that deletes her comments, then her, in one transaction Works, same rows removed
ON DELETE SET NULL on comments.user_id Not available, Msg 1785

The trigger that worked:

CREATE TRIGGER trg_users_delete ON users INSTEAD OF DELETE AS
BEGIN
  SET NOCOUNT ON;
  DELETE FROM comments WHERE user_id IN (SELECT id FROM deleted);
  DELETE FROM users WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM deleted);
END;

It reads the deleted table as a set, so DELETE FROM users WHERE id IN (2, 3) handled both users in one statement. The second DELETE inside it does not fire the trigger again; it runs the real delete, and fk_posts_user and fk_comments_post cascade as declared.

If a comment should outlive its author, the trigger is also where the null goes, since SQL Server refuses SET NULL on that key. Make comments.user_id nullable and swap the first statement for UPDATE comments SET user_id = NULL WHERE user_id IN (SELECT id FROM deleted). Deleting Ana then left her comment on Ben's post in place with no author, and removed her post and the comments on it.

The trigger has three limits, all measured:

  • It only fits a table that has no cascading foreign key of its own. CREATE TRIGGER ... ON posts INSTEAD OF DELETE failed with Msg 2113, "Cannot create INSTEAD OF DELETE or INSTEAD OF UPDATE TRIGGER 'trg_posts_delete' on table 'posts'. This is because the table has a FOREIGN KEY with cascading DELETE or UPDATE.", because posts.user_id cascades from users.
  • It closes a door on the table that has it. With the trigger on users, adding users.org_id with ON DELETE CASCADE to an orgs table failed with Msg 1787. The same key with ON DELETE SET NULL was accepted.
  • It breaks a DELETE that has an OUTPUT clause. DELETE FROM users OUTPUT 1 WHERE id = 3 failed with Msg 334, "The target table 'users' of the DML statement cannot have any enabled triggers if the statement contains an OUTPUT clause without INTO clause." EF Core 7 and later save changes with OUTPUT by default, so the entity has to be configured with HasTrigger before EF Core can write to that table.

A stored procedure has none of these limits, and it is the same two statements in a transaction:

CREATE PROCEDURE delete_user @user_id INT AS
BEGIN
  SET NOCOUNT ON; SET XACT_ABORT ON;
  BEGIN TRANSACTION;
  DELETE FROM comments WHERE user_id = @user_id;
  DELETE FROM users WHERE id = @user_id;
  COMMIT;
END;

Its cost is that it only protects callers who use it. A plain DELETE FROM users from another service, a script or an ORM still fails with Msg 547, which at least fails loudly rather than leaving orphans. Doing the same two statements from application code is equivalent, and it is what EF Core's ClientCascade option does for rows it has loaded.

How do you delete a tree when a self-reference cannot cascade?

Leave the self-referencing key at NO ACTION and delete the whole subtree in one statement with a recursive common table expression.

SQL Server refused categories.parent_id with ON DELETE CASCADE and with ON DELETE SET NULL. With the key at NO ACTION, deleting a category that has children fails with Msg 547, "The DELETE statement conflicted with the SAME TABLE REFERENCE constraint". Collecting the subtree first works, because the key is checked against the rows the whole statement leaves behind, and parent and children go together:

WITH tree AS (
  SELECT id FROM categories WHERE id = 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id FROM categories c JOIN tree t ON c.parent_id = t.id
)
DELETE FROM categories WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM tree)
OPTION (MAXRECURSION 0);

On four rows, a chain of 1, 2 and 3 plus an unrelated row 4, that statement removed the chain and left row 4. The OPTION (MAXRECURSION 0) matters on a deep tree: SQL Server stops a recursive query after 100 levels by default, and without the option a chain of 150 categories failed with Msg 530, "The maximum recursion 100 has been exhausted before statement completion", and deleted nothing.

How Schemity flags a second cascade path before SQL Server does

Schemity's lint reports the foreign key that adds the second path while it is still a line on the diagram, and names the key it collides with.

Schemity is database design software that reads your live database, shows the impact of every schema change before it runs, and keeps the diagram as a file in Git. On a SQL Server diagram, whether it is connected to a database or a design with no connection yet, the ON DELETE and ON UPDATE actions are set in the relationship dialog, and nothing stops you from choosing CASCADE on both of a table's keys. On an unconnected design there is no server to object, so the first place the problem can show is schema lint.

Changing that last key to CASCADE is one dropdown in the dialog, and Schemity accepts it:

The rule is sqlserver-multiple-cascade-paths, in the "Fails at runtime" group, and it runs only on SQL Server diagrams. For the three tables above with all keys at CASCADE, the finding sits on comments.user_id:

SQL Server refuses this foreign key: its ON DELETE action makes a second path between the same tables (Msg 1785).

ON DELETE in users reaches comments through fk_comments_post and through this key. One of the two has to be NO ACTION.

On a connected diagram the finding also follows the change into Preview changes, next to the planned migration it would run. The preview draws only users and comments, the two tables the change touches, but lint reads the whole schema, so the path through posts is still counted:

Statement 4 in that migration is the one SQL Server would answer with Msg 1785. Schemity runs a SQL Server migration in one transaction and rolls it back on the first error, so the DROP CONSTRAINT before it would be undone and the old NO ACTION key would stay in place.

It covers the same shapes as the table earlier: a direct and an indirect path, two acting keys from one parent, and a self-reference, where the detail says that the rows below have to be handled by the application or a trigger. It checks deletes and updates separately, as SQL Server does, and it counts SET NULL and SET DEFAULT as acting keys, so switching the second key to SET NULL keeps the finding. It also follows one subtlety I confirmed on the server: an ON DELETE SET NULL in the middle of a chain ends that path, because the row it changes is not deleted (an ON UPDATE chain has no such exit). users to members with CASCADE, members to tasks with SET NULL, then tasks to notes with CASCADE and users to notes with SET NULL was created without error, and lint stays silent on it.

What lint cannot tell you is which key to change, because that depends on which table owns the row. That decision is the one in the second section, and it is easier to make on an ERD, where both paths from users to comments are visible as lines, than in a migration file where the two keys are forty lines apart. When you design the next one, set the reference key to NO ACTION in the dialog, and the finding clears before any SQL is written.

Two related posts pick up from here: ON DELETE SET NULL vs CASCADE in PostgreSQL covers choosing between the two actions where both are allowed, and circular foreign keys covers the insert side of a cycle, which SQL Server permits as long as the actions do not go round it.

title: How a 3 kB npm package installs a 330 MB terminal app
description:
Elpis is an agent harness for Linux, built on OpenAI's Codex. Until today it installed with a shell script. Now it also installs with npm:

npm install -g elpis-cli
elpis

This post explains one decision: the npm package holds no binary.

The decision

The Elpis terminal app is a Rust binary of about 330 MB, with a code-mode host and a sandbox helper beside it. There are two common ways to put such a program on npm.

The first way puts the binary in the package, one package for each platform, and lets npm choose. Codex and esbuild do this. It works without a network after the install, but every release uploads hundreds of megabytes to npm for each platform.

The second way publishes a launcher. The launcher is a small script that downloads the binary when it first runs. I chose this one. Elpis already publishes its binaries on a GitHub release with a SHA-256 file beside each of them, and the install script already reads them from there. The npm package now uses the same three files, so there is one place where a release lives.

The cost, and what pays for it

A launcher has two costs. The first run needs a network, and you must trust what it downloads.

For trust, the launcher checks each file against the SHA-256 published beside it. A file that does not match is deleted and is never run. The launcher downloads each file beside its final place and renames it only after the check. A stopped download cannot leave a half file that runs later.

For the network, the launcher uses curl when curl is present. curl follows your proxy settings, and a cut connection carries on from where it stopped. I added that after my own first try: the connection was cut at 32 MB of the largest file. The next run finished the same file.

The evidence

Three tests run on every push against a stand-in release server. A first run downloads the files, checks them, runs the app, and passes its arguments and exit status through. A second run downloads nothing. A file with a wrong checksum is refused.

I also packed the package, installed the packed file into an empty folder, and ran it against the real release. It downloaded 0.5.1 and printed elpis 0.5.1.

Limits

The package runs on Linux x86_64 only, because Elpis publishes a binary for that platform only. It installs the terminal app; the desktop app still installs with the script in the README. Elpis is alpha.

The code is in packaging/npm of https://github.com/MasihMoafi/Elpis.
