title: "By Friday" Is Not a Timestamp: Resolving Dates in Chat-Created Tasks
description:
Somebody sends this message to a team chat:

Can you send the client report by Friday?

A human reads it and knows what to do. Software has to decide a lot of things at once. Which Friday? Friday in whose time zone? Friday at what time? And what if the message was sent on a Friday?

If your product creates tasks from chat messages, you are answering those questions whether you meant to or not. Usually the answer is "whatever the model guessed", and that is how you end up with deadlines that are off by a day and a very confused customer.

This post is about taking that decision away from the guesswork and putting it somewhere you can test. The examples are TypeScript with Luxon, but the ideas don't depend on either.

Four kinds of date phrases

"Parse the date" sounds like one problem. In practice, chat messages contain at least four different kinds, and they need different handling.

Kind Examples Difficulty
Absolute "Nov 20", "20/11" Locale and format ambiguity (03/04?)
Weekday "Friday", "this Friday", "next Friday" Needs a clear policy
Relative "tomorrow", "in 3 days", "end of week" Needs a reliable anchor
Fuzzy "EOD", "ASAP", "after the launch" Often shouldn't be resolved at all

Most bugs come from treating all four the same way.

Don't let the model do the date math

Language models are good at spotting that a message contains a deadline. They are a poor place to do calendar arithmetic. A model may not know today's date unless you tell it. It may do the arithmetic slightly differently on Tuesday than on Monday. And you can't write a reliable unit test against "usually right".

A cleaner split looks like this:

  1. The model extracts what the person said, as structured data.
  2. Plain code resolves that into a real date, against an anchor you control.

The extraction output is small and boring:

{ "kind": "weekday", "weekday": 5, "modifier": "none", "raw": "by Friday" }

Everything after that is deterministic. That means it's testable, and when it's wrong you can find out why.

The anchor is more than "now"

Relative phrases only mean something relative to a moment and a place. Your anchor needs three things.

1. The time the message was sent, not the time you processed it. If a message arrives at 11:58 PM and a queue delay means you handle it at 12:02 AM, "tomorrow" has shifted by a whole day. Always anchor on the message's own timestamp.

2. A time zone you actually know. Take it from the user's profile, not from guesswork in the message. Store an IANA name like Asia/Kolkata, not an offset like +05:30. Offsets don't know about daylight saving.

3. Workday conventions. When does the week start? What does "EOD" mean here, 5 PM or 6 PM? Make these settings, with sensible defaults, rather than constants buried in a function.

import { DateTime } from "luxon";

export function makeAnchor(sentAtUtc: string, userZone: string): DateTime {
  return DateTime.fromISO(sentAtUtc, { zone: "utc" }).setZone(userZone);
}

A resolver that is allowed to say "I'm not sure"

The most important design choice is the return type. A resolver that always returns a date will eventually return the wrong one with total confidence. Let it return three outcomes instead:

export type Precision = "date" | "datetime";
export type Candidate = { at: DateTime; precision: Precision };

export type Resolution =
  | { status: "resolved"; value: Candidate }
  | { status: "ambiguous"; reason: string; options: Candidate[] }
  | { status: "unresolved"; reason: string };

export type Modifier = "none" | "this" | "next";

const day = (at: DateTime): Candidate => ({
  at: at.startOf("day"),
  precision: "date",
});

Now the weekday rules. These are policies, so write them down rather than leaving them implicit:

  • Plain "Friday" means the nearest upcoming Friday.
  • If today is Friday, plain "Friday" is ambiguous. Don't guess.
  • "This Friday" means the Friday of the current week. If it has passed, say so.
  • "Next Friday" means the Friday of the following calendar week. 
// weekday uses Luxon numbering: Monday = 1 ... Sunday = 7
export function resolveWeekday(
  anchor: DateTime,
  weekday: number,
  modifier: Modifier
): Resolution {
  const today = anchor.startOf("day");

  if (modifier === "this" || modifier === "next") {
    const target = anchor
      .startOf("week")
      .plus({ weeks: modifier === "next" ? 1 : 0, days: weekday - 1 });

    if (target < today) {
      return { status: "unresolved", reason: "That day has already passed this week" };
    }
    return { status: "resolved", value: day(target) };
  }

  const daysAhead = (weekday - today.weekday + 7) % 7;

  if (daysAhead === 0) {
    return {
      status: "ambiguous",
      reason: "The weekday named is today",
      options: [day(today), day(today.plus({ weeks: 1 }))],
    };
  }

  return { status: "resolved", value: day(today.plus({ days: daysAhead })) };
}

"EOD" gets the same treatment. If it's already past your configured end of day, don't quietly push it to tomorrow.

export function resolveEod(anchor: DateTime, endHour = 18): Resolution {
  const eod = anchor.startOf("day").set({ hour: endHour });

  if (anchor >= eod) {
    return {
      status: "ambiguous",
      reason: "End of day has already passed",
      options: [{ at: eod.plus({ days: 1 }), precision: "datetime" }],
    };
  }
  return { status: "resolved", value: { at: eod, precision: "datetime" } };
}

A date-only deadline is not an instant

This is the bug I would check for first in any task system.

"By Friday" is a date. It isn't "Friday at 00:00 UTC". If you store it as a UTC timestamp, a user west of UTC can see the deadline show up as Thursday. People often get a date shifted by exactly one day and spend an hour blaming the front end.

Store date-only deadlines as dates, alongside the zone that gave them meaning:

{ "dueDate": "2026-11-13", "dueTime": null, "timeZone": "Asia/Kolkata" }

That's why Candidate carries a precision flag. A weekday gives you date. "EOD" gives you datetime. Your storage and your display should treat them differently.

Days and hours are not the same unit

A small Luxon detail worth knowing, because it's easy to get wrong in any library: adding "a day" and adding "24 hours" are different operations when daylight saving ends.

const ny = DateTime.fromISO("2026-10-31T21:00", { zone: "America/New_York" });

ny.plus({ days: 1 });   // 2026-11-01T21:00 (same wall-clock time)
ny.plus({ hours: 24 }); // 2026-11-01T20:00 (an hour earlier on the clock)

For "tomorrow", you want calendar days. For "in 24 hours", you want elapsed time. Your resolver should know which one the person meant.

Whose Friday is it?

When one person assigns a task to someone in another time zone, "by Friday" has two reasonable readings. One is the assigner's Friday, where the sentence was written. The other is the assignee's Friday, where the work happens.

I'd default to the assigner's zone, because the phrase was theirs, but the more important rule is to never leave it implicit. Show both zones when they differ. A task that says "Friday 5:00 PM IST (Friday 11:30 AM in London)" prevents a conversation that would otherwise happen on Thursday night.

Echo the result back

The cheapest safeguard is also the best one. After you resolve a date, tell the person what you understood, in a format that's hard to misread:

export function echo(c: Candidate): string {
  const fmt = c.precision === "date" ? "cccc d LLL" : "cccc d LLL, h:mm a";
  return `${c.at.toFormat(fmt)} (${c.at.zoneName})`;
}

// echo(resolved) -> "Friday 13 Nov (Asia/Kolkata)"

Two details matter here. First, build the text from the resolved value, not from the model's wording. Second, include the weekday and the date. "Friday 13 Nov" lets a human catch a mismatch in half a second. "13 Nov" alone doesn't.

When not to resolve

Some phrases should stay unresolved: "ASAP", "soon", "after the launch", "when you get a chance". They aren't dates, and inventing one creates a deadline nobody agreed to.

Better options are to leave the task undated, or to ask one short question: "Do you want to set a date for this?" An honest "no date yet" is more useful than a confident wrong one.

Test it with a fixed clock

None of this is worth much without tests, and the nice thing about a deterministic resolver is that tests are easy. Fix the anchor, and never depend on the real current time.

import { DateTime } from "luxon";
import { expect, test } from "vitest";

const at = (iso: string, zone: string) => DateTime.fromISO(iso, { zone });

test("plain weekday resolves to the upcoming one", () => {
  const r = resolveWeekday(at("2026-11-12T10:00", "Asia/Kolkata"), 5, "none");
  expect(r.status).toBe("resolved");
  if (r.status === "resolved") expect(r.value.at.toISODate()).toBe("2026-11-13");
});

test("weekday named on that weekday is ambiguous", () => {
  const r = resolveWeekday(at("2026-11-13T10:00", "Asia/Kolkata"), 5, "none");
  expect(r.status).toBe("ambiguous");
});

test("'next Friday' means the following calendar week", () => {
  const r = resolveWeekday(at("2026-11-09T09:00", "Asia/Kolkata"), 5, "next");
  if (r.status === "resolved") expect(r.value.at.toISODate()).toBe("2026-11-20");
});

test("anchor on sent time, not processing time", () => {
  const sent = makeAnchor("2026-11-12T18:28:00Z", "Asia/Kolkata"); // 23:58 IST
  const late = makeAnchor("2026-11-12T18:32:00Z", "Asia/Kolkata"); // 00:02 IST next day
  expect(resolveTomorrow(sent)).toMatchObject({ value: { at: expect.anything() } });
  // 'tomorrow' differs by a day depending on which timestamp you trust
});

test("days vs hours across a DST change", () => {
  const ny = at("2026-10-31T21:00", "America/New_York");
  expect(ny.plus({ days: 1 }).hour).toBe(21);
  expect(ny.plus({ hours: 24 }).hour).toBe(20);
});

A useful habit is to add one test for every date bug that reaches a user. Over time, that list becomes the most valuable documentation in the module.

Where this shows up

Any assistant that lets people create tasks from a conversation has to settle these questions somewhere, whether the front end is a chat window, an email thread or WhatsApp. That includes assistants like Atlas in ProjTL, where users can add tasks and assign them to teammates through WhatsApp. The questions are the same regardless of product: what is the anchor, which policy applies, and what happens when the answer is unclear.

The short version

  • Let the model extract the date phrase. Let plain code resolve it.
  • Anchor on the message's sent time, a known IANA zone, and explicit workday settings.
  • Return resolved, ambiguous or unresolved, not always a date.
  • Store date-only deadlines as dates, not UTC instants.
  • Use calendar days for "tomorrow" and elapsed time for "in 24 hours".
  • Echo the result back with weekday, date and zone.
  • Don't invent dates for "ASAP" and friends.
  • Test with a fixed clock.

What's the strangest date phrase your users have typed that your parser had to deal with? I'd like to hear it in the comments.

title: Ping64|What My Parents Actually Did With the Shared Streaming Account This Year
description:
During the holidays I did something I had been quietly putting off for a while. I opened the settings of our family streaming account and actually looked at the device list. Not because anything seemed wrong. Pure professional curiosity, the kind that makes an IT person glance at the guest Wi-Fi list at a party. What I found was a small anthropology project, and honestly, a fairly gentle audit report on how my parents use technology day to day.

The account started years ago as a simple favor: one subscription, two profiles, my parents get their movies, everybody happy. What it became over time is something nobody designed and nobody manages. It just grew, the way shared things in families and in companies tend to grow when the original owner stops looking.

What the device list actually showed

Eleven devices, for a household of two. Two of them were TVs that had been replaced years ago and never signed out. One was a tablet my mother insists she has never owned, in a tone that closed the discussion. There were sessions from two different countries, both eventually explainable and both worth a conversation over dinner. The password, it turned out, was the same one they use for their email, which is the finding that made me put my coffee down very carefully.

The profiles were their own chapter. Instead of the clean two we had planned, there were five, with names like Mom 2 and Guest and one labeled Test that neither of them could explain. Subtitles had been switched to a language nobody in the family speaks. Autoplay had been set to maximum enthusiasm by someone, presumably during a long winter. None of this was malicious, or even careless in any meaningful sense. It was just what happens when a thing is shared and nobody owns it.

Why shared things drift like this

Nobody in my family ever sat down and decided to make the account messy. Each change made sense in the moment. A new TV needed signing in, and the old one was not worth the effort of signing out. A cousin visited, got a quick profile, and left behind a small legend. The password was reused from email because remembering two passwords felt like a tax with no visible benefit. These are the same small, locally reasonable decisions that turn a tidy tool stack into a sprawl at work, one exception at a time.

There is no family IT department, of course. Ownership defaults to whoever set the thing up originally, which is me, which means the drift stays invisible until I look. The same pattern shows up in every team I have worked with: shared resources do not decay because people are careless. They decay because maintenance belongs to no one and costs something small every single time it is postponed.

The work parallel I could not shake

Reading that device list, I kept thinking about how the same pattern plays out in professional settings. Accounts accumulate. Credentials get reused for reasons that felt sensible locally. The inventory exists, but nobody opens it without a prompt or an audit. Some teams try consolidated platforms like Ping64 to reduce the daily busywork of multi-tool security stacks. While a streaming account is a much smaller beast, the underlying instinct is the same one: fewer scattered places, fewer stale sessions, fewer passwords quietly standing in front of something that matters. Even at the scale of two retirees and a smart TV, consolidation beats collection.

A few fixes that survived contact with reality

I installed a password manager for my parents and had them practice the master password twice. One password to remember instead of eleven, and the reuse problem mostly evaporated on the spot.

We signed out the ghost devices together, which took ten minutes, produced one moment of genuine mystery, and one good laugh about the tablet from the country that shall remain unnamed.

Each person got one profile with a PIN. My mother has already appointed herself the administrator of ratings, which was not the plan but seems stable, so I am leaving it alone.

The streaming password is now unique and stored, not memorized. If it ever leaks, it leaks one thing instead of everything, which is the entire point and the easiest sell of the whole visit.

A tidier account, and a nicer visit

The account is tidier now, and more to the point, my parents understand it better, which was the actual goal all along. They did not need a lecture about credential hygiene. They needed someone to sit with them for an afternoon and treat their digital household with the same patience I would give a client’s environment. That is a lesson worth carrying back to work too: most sprawl is not a failure of intelligence or care. It is simply what happens in the absence of someone who occasionally looks, tidies up, and brings the snacks.

References

  • https://www.cisa.gov/secure-our-world
  • https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0006/
  • https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/61/r2/final

title: How OpenEvidence scales medical search for 650K doctors
description:
OpenEvidence on Vercel

  • Serves 650,000 doctors with medical search

  • Completes production deployments in about five minutes

  • Absorbs traffic spikes without additional capacity provisioning

  • Reduced serverless spend by 90% with Fluid compute

  • Updates doctor- and patient-facing applications independently

OpenEvidence helps physicians find medical evidence during care, whether they’re checking a dosage on intensive care rounds or handling a case outside their specialty without a specialist nearby. Answers draw on peer-reviewed literature and include citations, so doctors can examine the sources behind them.

OpenEvidence’s small team began using Vercel to get early experiments online and kept that workflow as the product grew, relying on the platform to handle web deployments and capacity.

Building software physicians depend on

The stakes are different when software helps inform medical decisions. An incorrect answer can affect how a doctor treats a patient, while an unavailable application can cut off access to evidence when it is needed.

OpenEvidence supported more than 20 million clinical consultations in January 2026. The company also reported that more than 100 million Americans were treated by doctors using OpenEvidence in 2025.

"Honestly, life or death is not inaccurate," says Kush Khosla, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. "We operate in situations where it's an ER and they really need to know what's going on. Uptime is very, very important to us."

"A lot of doctors and medical professionals are used to really outdated software," says Andy Yoon, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. A more modern experience still needs to meet physicians' expectations of speed, stability, clarity, and information they can trust. The small team needs a way to test updates to the web application before putting them into production and to roll back if something goes wrong.

Keeping releases simple as the audience grows

Andy recalls why Vercel suited the team he joined at OpenEvidence. "I was pretty much the only engineer on our team coming from an actual frontend background," he says. "Most of our team works in Python and machine learning." He adds, "Given the makeup of our engineering team, Vercel really scaled with our needs so well."

The team builds its physician-facing web application with the Next.js framework. When engineers push changes to a development branch, Vercel builds and deploys a preview, giving them a link they can use for live demos and share with colleagues to try new features. Pushing or merging into the production branch then triggers the production build and deployment. If a release needs reverting, the team can roll back to a previous deployment.

That workflow lets the team release multiple times a day, with each change becoming available to a physician audience that Kush thinks about whenever he ships something:

More doctors without more provisioning

Keeping that application available means handling demand the team can’t always anticipate. Andy was scrolling through Slack when he saw the message that OpenEvidence had gone viral on TikTok, reaching around two million views in under a week. He watched traffic climb and checked the logs. Response times stayed fast and error rates remained near zero, and with no additional capacity to provision, he went back to his work.

Beyond sudden spikes, the team has accommodated sustained growth without rebuilding the web application.

"Not once have I had to think, now that we have five times as many doctors, what's happening to page loads or time to first paint," Kush says. "The scaling has happened so naturally that we end up focusing on other things."

A 90% drop in serverless spend

As usage grew, VP of Engineering Micah Smith was watching compute costs. The team enabled Fluid compute for its functions on Vercel, and Micah described the result alongside the wider infrastructure budget:

"We reduced our serverless spend by 90% while maintaining the same performance, and even as we've scaled up to 1000x growth, Vercel is less than 5% of our overall infra spend."

Fluid compute lets multiple requests share a running function instance, so it can handle other work while a request waits for another service, such as a database or an AI backend, to respond. With Active CPU pricing, that waiting time doesn’t incur CPU charges, though memory remains billed while requests are in progress.

A familiar workflow for a new audience

Take Home, OpenEvidence’s first patient-facing application, lets a doctor translate a clinical answer into plain language and share it with a patient, who logs in to review and save the evidence. Clinical-trial matching is also part of the application’s planned direction.

To support this expansion, the team uses a pattern established through dozens of early proofs of concept, each deployed as its own Vercel project with a custom domain. Stakeholders could open those applications and test the workflows for themselves. Getting new projects online in minutes helped the team find product-market fit and made it easier to win early enterprise partnerships.

Take Home has its own project and domain too, so engineers can update the patient experience without deploying the other applications.

With Take Home, evidence that helps a doctor during a consultation can become something a patient returns to afterward.

About OpenEvidence: OpenEvidence helps healthcare professionals find medical evidence at the point of care, with answers sourced, cited, and grounded in peer-reviewed literature. Physicians use it daily across more than 10,000 hospitals and medical centers in the United States. Its mission is to help doctors save lives and improve patient care. Learn more at openevidence.com.

Announcement

On October 22, 2026, we released an updated version of Apigee (1-18-0-apigee-7).

Note: Rollouts of this release began today and can take four or more business days to complete across all Google Cloud zones. Your instances might not have the features and fixes available until the rollout is complete.

Security

Bug ID Description
573663408 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the ingress gateway to patch security vulnerabilities.
N/A Security fix for Apigee infrastructure.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
568535165 Skip main_task_wait_time and nio_task_wait_time metrics for the first 12 Prometheus scrapes during Message Processor startup warmup.
573602919 Fix generated OpenAPI specs' servers[] to carry the Apigee envgroup hostname instead of the backend target host.
562964081 The sgpUserIntentMatchingMode verdict-log field is now always present, including on dry-run policy records, and shows the mode used for the evaluation, including when sgpUserIntentMatching isn't set (CONSTRAINTS_AND_INTENT, or INTENT_ONLY when no policies match the tool call).
524115876 Fix an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests.
572025634 Responses with a compressed text/event-stream body to a proxy with an EventFlow now skip EventFlow processing and pass through intact instead of returning a corrupted body.
549078690 If no SGP policy is attributed for a denial, a customer sees the generic fallback message. This fix short-circuits to show the rationale instead when no matched policy has a configured denial message.
492041991 VerifyAPIKey and VerifyAccessToken now set the apiproduct.operation.llmTokenQuota.* flow variables only from the LLM operation(s) that matched the request; they are no longer set from unmatched LLM operations or for requests that match no LLM operation.
567244615 Semantic Governance now evaluates LLM requests it previously skipped, such as OpenAI requests whose message content is an array of parts, which can produce new denials and judge-model usage. It considers every system message rather than only the last, and a non-streaming OpenAI or an Ollama tool call whose arguments are not valid JSON is now an evaluation error.
567244615 Semantic Governance no longer evaluates a request or response with a field it cannot read when a tool call is involved. It records verdict ERROR naming the field, with status MODEL_ERROR. The inline SemanticGovernance policy instead raises GovernedLLMResponseParseError or GovernedLLMProviderDetectionFailed (HTTP 500), in DRY_RUN too unless continueOnError is true. It also reads every text part of a Gemini system instruction and Gemini tool parameters given as parametersJsonSchema, and no longer loses the rest of a Claude or Gemini request when one field has an unexpected shape.
560272924 Added continuous-scan bidirectional gRPC streaming support for the SanitizeModelResponse policy over Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams, preserving native LLM provider SSE JSON envelopes and event framing.
555332621 Model Armor policies now honor HTTPClient.managementplane.skip.proxy: with it set, Model Armor callouts bypass the forward proxy like other googleapis traffic. Streaming (ContinuousScan) Model Armor traffic uses the forward proxy.
158204922 VerifyJWT now rejects a JWT whose header contains "b64":false, with fault steps.jwt.InvalidToken, as RFC 7797 section 7 requires. Previously, such a token could be accepted if KnownHeaders listed b64, IgnoreCriticalHeaders was true, or the header had no crit.
158204922 GenerateJWS supports RFC 7797 unencoded payloads. GenerateJWS now raises MissingPayload, InvalidPayload or FailedToResolveVariable for payload errors, where it previously raised GenerationFailed. KnownHeaders and CriticalHeaders in the JWS and JWT policies accept names separated by whitespace, such as one per line. A b64 header supplied through AdditionalHeaders is now rejected, with steps.jws.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWS and steps.jwt.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWT. A proxy that set b64 through an AdditionalHeaders variable produced an RFC 7797 JWS before this change, and must move to UnencodedPayload, with DetachContent for the detached form.
158204922 VerifyJWS verifies RFC 7797 unencoded-payload JWS (b64:false), attached or detached. b64 in crit no longer needs a KnownHeaders entry. VerifyJWS rejects b64:false unless crit lists b64, with the new fault steps.jws.UnencodedPayloadNotCritical; IgnoreCriticalHeaders does not change that. DecodeJWS reports the raw payload of such a JWS.
559228730 ext_proc: ImmediateResponse now carries any Content-Type (raw body bytes + preserved Content-Type); replies too large to buffer use StreamedImmediateResponse.
544751120 Semantic Governance Policies marked as dry run are now evaluated and logged without blocking the request. Each dry-run policy adds a second judge evaluation per tool-calling response, whose tokens are billed. Dry-run verdicts are written to the semantic-governance-policy log as separate records flagged sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation=true; queries that count verdicts should add sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation != true to exclude them.
554114419 Fixed: an AssignMessage/HTTPModifier/RaiseFault policy that creates a new request (createNew="true") in an HTTP/2 flow can now set the :path and :authority pseudo-headers instead of failing with an invalid-header error.
567812025 FILESYSTEM persistence mode makes the synchronizer skip Cassandra entirely (no connections, reads, writes, or datastore health probes).
559009293 Fixed elevated OAuth latency and Cassandra read load for AppGroup apps, including access token verification and token and authorization-code generation, by caching AppGroup lookups in the message processor runtime, matching Developer behavior.
568860869 Fixed RegularExpressionProtection patterns of the form "...." whose middle section contains regular expression syntax (for example, ".?Exception in thread." or "(?i).<script.>.*") being matched as literal text instead of as regular expressions. Such patterns now raise steps.regexprotection.ThreatDetected for all matching input.
564945600 Enhance VerifyAPIKey policy to better handle leading spaces.
502231886 Fixed the default source templates for SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse so a policy that omits the source element extracts content correctly when IgnoreUnresolvedVariables is false.
562964081 Semantic Governance now honors the sgpUserIntentMatching AuthzExtension metadata key (ENABLED or DISABLED) to toggle user-intent matching in policy evaluation; DISABLED evaluates against constraints only.
565004219 Fixed Semantic Governance Policy skipping evaluation for Anthropic requests that send system as a content-block array (the form ADK and LiteLlm emit). Affected agents are now evaluated, which may produce new denials and new judge-model usage on the consumer project.
527517087 SGP policy logs written to your project now identify their originating region. resource.type changes from "global" to "generic_node" and the region appears in resource.labels.location. Anything selecting these entries by resource.type="global" must be updated -- including log-based metrics, sinks, exclusion filters and alerts, which stop matching silently rather than erroring.
575439485 JavaCallout policies that run remotely (per-contract offload) can now pass every value type allowed by the GCP-2025-023 setVariable restriction between policies (collections, maps, arrays, primitive wrappers including Character, Date, BigDecimal, UUID, java.time, atomics, JDK enums, Optional), with their types preserved, instead of failing with steps.remotepolicy.NonSerializableVariable.
575439485 Remotely executed (per-contract offload) JavaCallout policies with continueOnError="true" now continue the flow when the callout faults, instead of returning HTTP 500.
567244901 In enforce mode, Semantic Governance now blocks a tool call when the governance check cannot be completed, instead of letting it through.
573622417 Fixed an issue where istio-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
571679067 removes old version of ApigeeTelemetry CRD.
571378258 The Apigee Redis container is now built from the Valkey engine (BSD-3-Clause, Linux Foundation) at version 8.1.10. Wire protocol is unchanged (RESP2) and the redis-server/redis-cli binary names are preserved.

Announcement

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Argon becomes the default model for AlphaEvolve on October 26, 2026

On October 26, 2026, Gemini 4 Argon will replace Gemini 3.8 Flash as the default model for new AlphaEvolve experiments. AlphaEvolve uses the default model when you don't specify a model in the models field of generationSettings.

From that date, new experiments that use the default model are billed at Gemini 4 Argon token prices instead of Gemini 3.8 Flash token prices. To keep using Gemini 3.8 Flash, specify gemini-3.8-flash in the models field.

Announcement

Advanced reporting dashboards prerelease notes 6.24

Here are the pre-release notes for updates to the advanced reporting dashboards and other reporting in CCAI Platform. When we release these updates, we expect the new capabilities to be as shown here.

Important: The next version of the advanced reporting dashboards could be greater than 6.24.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where call and chat type names were cut off in the Dashboard Reports selector on wide-screen displays.

  • Fixed an issue where the Individual Call History and Individual Chat History reports, run for all agents, left out calls and chats that were never assigned to an agent (for example, abandoned, deflected, or expired calls) when only one agent or no agents had activity in the selected period. The All Call History and All Chat History files are now always included.

  • Fixed an issue where the Interactions Detail by Agent report omitted outbound calls placed without a queue when generated for all agents.

  • Fixed an issue where the Real-time Queue Monitoring and Campaign dashboards incorrectly displayed English queue names for French and Spanish interactions.

  • Fixed an issue where "wrap-up" and "hold" metrics in advanced reporting were displayed with inconsistent and inaccurate French Canadian (fr_CA) translations.

  • Fixed an issue where Spanish chat queues incorrectly displayed English names in Real-time Queue Monitoring and advanced reporting dashboards.

  • Fixed an issue where call disposition fields appeared blank on dashboards when viewing date ranges between 46 and 365 days.

title: Accept crypto payments in Node.js
description:
A step-by-step Moonvex integration in plain Node.js with the official @moonvex/node SDK: your server creates an invoice, the customer pays on a hosted page, and an HMAC-signed webhook marks the order paid. No framework, just node:http and PostgreSQL.

Step by step

1. Get an API key and a webhook secret

In the Moonvex dashboard go to “Integration” → “Create key” → type “Secret” (sk_live_…). The key is shown only once: store it on your server as MOONVEX_SECRET_KEY. On the same page add a webhook pointing to an https URL on your server and store its signing secret as MOONVEX_WEBHOOK_SECRET. The @moonvex/node SDK has no dependencies and needs Node.js 18+.

npm install @moonvex/node pg

# .env — server only, never commit it
MOONVEX_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_...
MOONVEX_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_...
DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/shop

2. Create a payment with the SDK

payments.create takes orderId, the amount as a string, currency and network. The second argument is idempotencyKey: a retry after a timeout returns the same payment instead of creating another one. The SDK itself retries network errors, 429 and 5xx with the same key. Errors are thrown as MoonvexError with status, code and detailsCode, for example DUPLICATE_ORDER when the order already has an active payment.

// moonvex.js
import { Moonvex, MoonvexError } from '@moonvex/node';

export const moonvex = new Moonvex({ apiKey: process.env.MOONVEX_SECRET_KEY });

/** Creates an invoice for the order; a retry with the same key returns the same payment */
export async function createPaymentForOrder(order, attempt = 1) {
  try {
    return await moonvex.payments.create(
      {
        orderId: String(order.id),
        amount: order.total, // a string such as "25.00", not a number
        currency: 'USDT',
        network: 'TRON',
        customerId: String(order.userId),
        expiresInMinutes: 30,
      },
      { idempotencyKey: 'order-' + order.id + '-' + attempt },
    );
  } catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof MoonvexError && err.detailsCode === 'DUPLICATE_ORDER') {
      // the order already has an active payment, return it
      const page = await moonvex.payments.list({ orderId: String(order.id), limit: 1 });
      if (page.data[0]) return page.data[0];
    }
    throw err;
  }
}

3. Send the customer to paymentUrl

paymentUrl is a hosted payment page: the exact amount including the fee, the address, a QR code, the official token contract and a timer, with a status that updates by itself. Open it with a redirect or in a new tab; it cannot be embedded in an iframe. A customer returning to your site is not proof of payment: mark the order paid only from a webhook or the status from GET /v1/payments/:id. Answering a POST form with 303 makes the browser open the payment page with a plain GET.

// server.js
import http from 'node:http';
import { db } from './db.js';
import { createPaymentForOrder } from './moonvex.js';

const server = http.createServer(async (req, res) => {
  const url = new URL(req.url, 'http://localhost');
  const pay = url.pathname.match(/^\/orders\/(\d+)\/pay$/);

  if (req.method === 'POST' && pay) {
    const { rows } = await db.query(
      'SELECT id, user_id AS "userId", total::text AS total FROM orders WHERE id = $1',
      [pay[1]],
    );
    if (!rows[0]) return res.writeHead(404).end();
    const payment = await createPaymentForOrder(rows[0]);
    // 303 makes the browser open the payment page with a GET
    return res.writeHead(303, { Location: payment.paymentUrl }).end();
  }

  if (req.method === 'POST' && url.pathname === '/moonvex/webhook') {
    return handleWebhook(req, res); // step 4
  }

  res.writeHead(404).end();
});

server.listen(3000);

4. Receive the webhook and verify the signature

Moonvex sends a POST with a Moonvex-Signature header: t=,v1=. The signature is a hex HMAC-SHA256 of the string “t.raw_body” keyed with the webhook secret. Compute it over the body bytes before parsing JSON, compare in constant time and reject events older than 5 minutes. For 24 hours after a secret rotation the header carries two v1 values; either one is valid. verifyWebhook from the SDK does all of this and throws WebhookVerificationError when something is off. It needs the raw body as a Buffer, not an object.

// server.js (continued)
import { verifyWebhook, WebhookVerificationError } from '@moonvex/node';
import { markOrderPaidOnce } from './db.js';

/** Raw request body: the signature covers the bytes, not parsed JSON */
async function readRawBody(req) {
  const chunks = [];
  for await (const chunk of req) chunks.push(chunk);
  return Buffer.concat(chunks);
}

async function handleWebhook(req, res) {
  const raw = await readRawBody(req);
  let event;
  try {
    // checks HMAC-SHA256, both v1 values during a secret rotation and the event age (5 minutes)
    event = verifyWebhook(raw, req.headers['moonvex-signature'], process.env.MOONVEX_WEBHOOK_SECRET);
  } catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof WebhookVerificationError) return res.writeHead(400).end('bad signature');
    throw err;
  }

  if (event.type === 'payment.confirmed' || event.type === 'payment.overpaid') {
    await markOrderPaidOnce(event.id, event.data.orderId);
  }
  // any 2xx within 10 seconds, otherwise Moonvex retries the delivery
  res.writeHead(200).end('ok');
}

5. Mark the order paid exactly once

A redelivered event keeps the same id, so store it in a table with a unique key in the same transaction as the order update: a duplicate then changes nothing. Fulfil on payment.confirmed and payment.overpaid, never on payment.detected. Respond with a 2xx within 10 seconds; on failure (5xx, timeout) Moonvex retries the delivery for about three days.

// db.js
import pg from 'pg';

export const db = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

// CREATE TABLE processed_events (
//   event_id   text PRIMARY KEY,
//   created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
// );

/** Marks the order as paid exactly once, even if the event is delivered again */
export async function markOrderPaidOnce(eventId, orderId) {
  const client = await db.connect();
  try {
    await client.query('BEGIN');
    const fresh = await client.query(
      'INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id) VALUES ($1) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING',
      [eventId],
    );
    if (fresh.rowCount === 1) {
      // first delivery of this event
      await client.query(
        "UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid', paid_at = now() WHERE id = $1 AND status <> 'paid'",
        [orderId],
      );
    }
    await client.query('COMMIT');
  } catch (err) {
    await client.query('ROLLBACK');
    throw err;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
}

6. Test the integration

Moonvex has no test network: everything runs on mainnets. The “Send test” button under “Integration” sends a webhook.test event, which is how you check the signature. Then pay a small invoice, for example 1 USDT on TRON: it is a regular payment and the money lands on your balance. The delivery log with response codes and a “Retry” button is on the same page.

Pitfalls

  • Pass the original Buffer to verifyWebhook. JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(body)) produces different bytes and the signature will not match.
  • Build idempotencyKey from the order number and attempt (order-1001-1) rather than a random UUID, so a retry after a process restart is safe too.
  • Amounts are strings. Read total from PostgreSQL as numeric::text instead of Number(): floats lose cents.
  • Do slow work (emails, granting access) after responding 200, in a queue. A response slower than 10 seconds counts as a failed delivery.

FAQ

Do I need the SDK, or is fetch enough?

You can skip the SDK: the API is plain HTTPS with JSON and an Authorization: Bearer header. The SDK adds TypeScript types, retries with the same Idempotency-Key and a ready-made verifyWebhook. See the Express guide for a version without the SDK.

Is there a test mode or a sandbox?

No, there is no test network: Moonvex runs on mainnets only. Check the signature with the “Send test” button (a webhook.test event) and the whole payment flow with a real payment of a small amount, for example 1 USDT on TRON.

What if the customer does not pay in time?

The payment moves to EXPIRED and you receive payment.expired. You can create a new payment for the same orderId with a new Idempotency-Key (for example, bump the attempt number at the end of the key). The payment window is set with expiresInMinutes: 5 to 1440 minutes, 30 by default.

Originally published at: moonvex.org/en/guides/nodejs

title: User Reminders Queue Duplicate Processing: At-Least-Once Retry and Message Idempotency
description:
Short answer: if the same user reminder is sent twice, assume the queue is delivering at least once, derive one stable send key from user_id + reminder_id + scheduled_at, persist that key before calling the email or SMS sender, and acknowledge the queue message only after the send is recorded safely.

Do not start by tuning visibility timeouts or blaming two workers. A retry after a worker exit can legitimately deliver the same message again. The operational target is therefore not “one delivery”; it is one externally visible reminder for any number of deliveries.

For a team that wants a plain HTTP queue boundary while retaining the option to change the provider behind that capability, Infrai is worth trying for reminder ingestion and acknowledgement. Its useful distinction here is that the REST contract stays put when the backing vendor changes; it also avoids adding another language-specific SDK to a worker. One API key and one bill cover its 295 routes across 20 modules, so a reminder service that later adds another backend capability does not create another credential-rotation runbook or invoice owner. The outbound email or SMS processor remains a separate trust boundary, and the consumer still owns idempotency.

The API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required; it returns the request schema, response schema, billing metadata, and runnable examples for a capability. Every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. That matters during an incident review because the transport contract can be checked without guessing at fields. Infrai provides one key for all backend capabilities and one bill. Its breadth is 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, a separate operational advantage that reduces credential rotation and billing reconciliation when this worker uses more than the queue capability.

What makes a user reminders queue retry the same message twice?

Start with a delivery state machine, not a boolean processed flag. The identity of the operation must describe the business effect. A queue message ID describes a delivery artifact and may change when work is republished; user_id + reminder_id + scheduled_at describes the reminder the user would recognize. Normalize the timestamp before composing the key so equivalent times don't acquire different textual forms.

Duplicates are normal.

The safe order is claim, send, record, ack. “Claim” means inserting the stable key in a durable store before contacting the sender. If the insert reports that the key already exists with a terminal sent state, skip the side effect and acknowledge the redelivery. If another worker owns an active claim, do not send concurrently. Once the sender accepts the reminder, persist the provider's receipt and terminal state, then ack.

There is still an ambiguity window between a remote sender accepting a request and the worker recording that acceptance. The strongest practical defense is to pass the same stable key to a sender that supports idempotent requests. Without that downstream contract, a process exit in that window cannot be distinguished from a request that never arrived. Don't disguise this as exactly-once delivery; it is an end-to-end property, not a queue setting.

FIFO deduplication narrows one part of the problem but does not close it. Its five-minute window cannot protect a retry outside that interval, and worker failures still require consumer idempotency. Standard queue delivery is at-least-once by design, so a duplicate should take the quiet, tested path rather than the incident path.

With Infrai, consume work, execute the state transition below, and acknowledge only a safely recorded send or a confirmed duplicate. Return retryable work to the queue. A transport response such as HTTP 429 is retryable; I wouldn't acknowledge it because doing so converts temporary backpressure into a missed reminder.

Consider one exact failure timeline. A worker claims user-42:renewal-7:2026-08-14T09:00:00Z, the email processor accepts the request, and the worker exits before writing receipt-001. The queue delivers the message again. A new worker can see the unfinished claim, but the ledger alone cannot prove whether the email crossed the processor boundary. If the processor recognizes the same idempotency key, the second request resolves to the original effect and the worker can safely record its receipt. If the processor has no such contract, neither an aggressive retry nor an ack is safe: the former may send twice, while the latter may lose the reminder. This is the case the runbook must reconcile, because a uniqueness constraint by itself only prevents two workers from starting together; it cannot make a remote side effect transactional with a local row.

Stop there.

Decide where reminder data may persist

Delivery guarantees are only half the review. Region, retention, deletion, and processor boundaries determine where customer contact data travels and how long copies survive. Keep full message bodies out of the queue when identifiers will do. Record which system holds the user address, which system renders the content, which processor sends it, and which deletion workflow removes each durable copy. An ack deleting a queue message does not delete the delivery ledger or a specialist sender's records.

Infrai exposes region and provider readiness through its public discovery surface, so inspect the selected capability rather than assuming a region from the platform name. Its queue can own transport and redelivery while the specialist email or SMS provider owns final delivery. Contractual residency, retention, and deletion commitments for that processor must be verified with the processor; an API routing layer cannot supply guarantees that are absent from the underlying agreement. I'm not sure a generic architecture diagram can answer that question. The current DPA, selected region, and deletion evidence can.

The limitation is concrete: stick with Kafka when replay or several independent consumer groups define the system. Choose Temporal when the reminder belongs to a durable multi-step workflow, or Airflow when DAG scheduling is the actual job. Infrai has no DAG orchestration or fan-out/join primitive, no native topic fan-out, and no Kafka-style replay. It is suitable when the boundary is queue transport plus an idempotent worker, not when those specialist semantics are the requirement.

Put the idempotent boundary in the worker

The following Go program first checks the configured Infrai queue through the verified queue-get route, with explicit authentication, status handling, and bounded 429 backoff. It then runs the part that has to remain stable regardless of queue vendor. The in-memory implementations keep the example runnable and focused; in production, Ledger.Claim and Ledger.MarkSent must use a durable database with a unique constraint on the key, while Sender.Send should forward that key through the sender's idempotency mechanism.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

var ErrAlreadySent = errors.New("reminder already sent")

type Reminder struct {
    UserID     string
    ReminderID string
    Scheduled  time.Time
    Channel    string
    Body       string
}

func (r Reminder) SendKey() string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("%s:%s:%s", r.UserID, r.ReminderID, r.Scheduled.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339Nano))
}

type Ledger interface {
    Claim(context.Context, string) error
    MarkSent(context.Context, string, string) error
}

type Sender interface {
    Send(context.Context, Reminder, string) (string, error)
}

func getQueue(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, apiKey string) ([]byte, error) {
    endpoint := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/get/user-reminders"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("get queue: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, errors.New("get queue: rate limit retry budget exhausted")
}

func Process(ctx context.Context, ledger Ledger, sender Sender, reminder Reminder) error {
    key := reminder.SendKey()
    if err := ledger.Claim(ctx, key); err != nil {
        if errors.Is(err, ErrAlreadySent) {
            return nil
        }
        return fmt.Errorf("claim %q: %w", key, err)
    }

    receipt, err := sender.Send(ctx, reminder, key)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("send %q: %w", key, err)
    }
    if err := ledger.MarkSent(ctx, key, receipt); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("record receipt for %q: %w", key, err)
    }
    return nil
}

type memoryLedger struct {
    mu    sync.Mutex
    state map[string]string
}

func (l *memoryLedger) Claim(_ context.Context, key string) error {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()
    if l.state[key] == "sent" {
        return ErrAlreadySent
    }
    if l.state[key] == "claimed" {
        return errors.New("send already in progress")
    }
    l.state[key] = "claimed"
    return nil
}

func (l *memoryLedger) MarkSent(_ context.Context, key, receipt string) error {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()
    l.state[key] = "sent:" + receipt
    return nil
}

type memorySender struct{}

func (memorySender) Send(_ context.Context, r Reminder, key string) (string, error) {
    fmt.Printf("send channel=%s key=%s body=%q\n", r.Channel, key, r.Body)
    return "receipt-001", nil
}

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        panic("set INFRAI_API_KEY")
    }
    metadata, err := getQueue(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}, apiKey)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("queue metadata: %s\n", metadata)

    ledger := &memoryLedger{state: make(map[string]string)}
    sender := memorySender{}
    reminder := Reminder{
        UserID:     "user-42",
        ReminderID: "renewal-7",
        Scheduled:  time.Date(2026, time.August, 14, 9, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC),
        Channel:    "email",
        Body:       "Your support plan renews tomorrow.",
    }

    if err := Process(ctx, ledger, sender, reminder); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if err := Process(ctx, ledger, sender, reminder); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

Run it with INFRAI_API_KEY set after creating the user-reminders queue. The program retrieves that queue, then receives the logical reminder twice but prints one send. The production schema should retain the key, state, claim time, attempt count, and sender receipt long enough to cover the full queue retry horizon. A stuck claimed record needs an explicit reconciliation policy: query the sender by idempotency key or receipt before deciding to retry. Blindly clearing claims makes duplicate sends possible.

Keep the queue payload small and boring: identifiers, the normalized schedule, the channel, and a version. Infrai queue messages are limited to 256KB and can be retained for at most 30 days; ack deletes the message. Seven days is the maximum delivery delay. These limits fit ordinary reminders, but they are poor storage semantics for a permanent audit record. Put the durable reminder and delivery ledger in your database, and treat the queue as transport.

Option Prefer it when The catch
Infrai queue A stable plain-HTTP queue contract and the ability to change the backing provider without worker code changes matter No Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups; retention is at most 30 days, and consumer idempotency remains mandatory
Google Cloud Pub/Sub Direct alignment with an existing Google Cloud trust boundary is more important than a provider-neutral contract Treat standard delivery as at-least-once and verify region, retention, and deletion settings against your requirements
Amazon SQS FIFO A five-minute FIFO deduplication window usefully filters rapid producer retries The window does not replace consumer idempotency or cover later retries
Temporal Reminder sending is part of a durable, multi-step workflow with orchestration requirements It is a larger workflow decision, not merely a queue swap
BullMQ The worker already runs on Node.js and Redis is an accepted operational dependency Its runtime and Redis boundary are a deliberate commitment rather than a provider-neutral HTTP contract
Sidekiq Ruby and Redis already define the job-processing stack It is the natural direct choice for that stack, not for a Go worker seeking plain HTTP
Celery Python task processing and its broker ecosystem match the existing service Broker and result-backend choices add trust boundaries that need their own retention review

Prove the retry path before enabling sends

Before enabling sends, publish the same logical reminder twice and confirm one sender call, one terminal ledger row, and two safely resolved deliveries. Then terminate a worker after claim, after the sender call, and after MarkSent; each injection should have a documented next state. Run the same checks with an HTTP 429 from the sender. The expected outcome is retry without an early ack, followed by one externally visible reminder once the sender accepts the stable key.

Watch three signals separately: queue delivery attempts, unique send keys, and sender receipts. If delivery attempts rise while unique keys and receipts remain flat, idempotency is absorbing retries. If receipts exceed terminal keys, stop consumption because the ambiguity window or sender contract is unsafe. If terminal keys exceed receipts, stop acking and reconcile potential missed sends. These are operational assertions, not vanity throughput charts.

Rollback is simple only if it is planned. Pause the consumers, leave unacknowledged work available for retry, and preserve the ledger. Do not purge the queue or delete claims during diagnosis. Revert the worker while keeping the send-key format stable; changing key composition during rollback turns old reminders into apparently new work. Resume at low concurrency, compare receipts to terminal rows, and increase concurrency only after the counts reconcile.

Also test the calendar edges: two schedules for the same reminder, equivalent timestamps with different offsets, and a retry beyond five minutes. Your mileage may vary on how long sender receipts remain queryable, which is why that retention promise belongs in the trust-boundary review and the runbook.

One retry is enough to expose a bad ordering.

The decision rule is short: use Infrai when a stable REST queue contract, provider substitution behind that contract, and no SDK dependency are valuable, and when 30-day maximum retention plus at-least-once delivery fit the reminder design. Use a specialist when replay, workflow joins, private-only push targets, or stronger provider-specific controls dominate. If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live capability schema before implementing the transport adapter.

References

  • RFC 2104: HMAC keyed-hashing for message authentication
  • Google Cloud Pub/Sub overview
  • Amazon SQS FIFO queue deduplication
  • Temporal documentation
  • BullMQ documentation
  • Sidekiq documentation
