title: Preparing iOS Apps for iOS 27.2 and iOS 27.3: Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode & Compatibility Testing
description:
Discussion topic for Swift and iOS developer communities | November 2026

Introduction

iOS 27.2 is now out, and the first developer beta of iOS 27.3 landed on November 3. On the surface, 27.2 is a user-facing release: it adds or refines features in six of Apple's own apps. The 27.3 beta is where things get more interesting for anyone who ships web content or hybrid apps, because Safari is gaining two features that change how pages are framed and rendered: Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode.

Point releases rarely come with big API announcements, but they regularly shift the environment our apps run in. This post walks through what changed, where I think the real risks are, and a testing checklist I am using. I would love to hear what others are seeing on the betas.

A note on scope: the 9to5Mac article this discussion is based on covers the iOS 27.2 app updates. Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode are Safari features in the iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3 and macOS 27.3 betas, reported separately by 9to5Mac on November 3. Release of 27.3 is expected around December.

1. What shipped in iOS 27.2

Here is a summary of the six app changes, with my take on where each one may touch third-party apps. Most are low-impact, but a couple deserve a quick regression pass.

App What changed Why developers might care
Messages Suggested Actions appear under messages and can propose calendar events, reminders, notes and more based on context. Users can tune which suggestion types appear. If your app shares text, invites or confirmations into Messages, check how that content reads when the system offers actions alongside it. Clear dates and times help.
Apple TV Profiles come to the TV app on iPhone and iPad, with a profile picker at launch (can be disabled). Mostly user-facing. Worth noting if your app hands off to the TV app or relies on its watch history.
FaceTime Dual Capture (front and rear cameras at once) now works in Group FaceTime on iPhone 17 and newer. Camera apps should re-test interruption handling when another app holds both cameras.
Home New 'Lock After Closing' automation and 'Door Left Open' alerts for compatible locks. HomeKit apps may see lock state change from automations users set in Apple's Home app. Make sure your UI reflects state changes it did not initiate.
Podcasts Up Next is split into New Episodes and Continue Playing. Low impact unless you document deep links or user flows that point at Up Next.
Games Home tab shows downloaded but unplayed games; achievements and leaderboards are easier to track. Game Center achievements and leaderboards get more visibility, so it is a good moment to audit their configuration and artwork.

A practical example from the FaceTime change: if your app uses the camera, a Group FaceTime call with Dual Capture can take camera access away from you. That path has always existed, but it is now more likely to occur in real usage.

Handling camera interruptions caused by another app (AVFoundation)

import AVFoundation

final class CameraController {
    let session = AVCaptureSession()
    private var observers: [NSObjectProtocol] = []

    func observeInterruptions() {
        let center = NotificationCenter.default

        observers.append(center.addObserver(
            forName: AVCaptureSession.wasInterruptedNotification,
            object: session, queue: .main) { note in
                let key = AVCaptureSessionInterruptionReasonKey
                guard let raw = note.userInfo?[key] as? Int,
                      let reason = AVCaptureSession.InterruptionReason(rawValue: raw)
                else { return }

                switch reason {
                case .videoDeviceInUseByAnotherClient:
                    // e.g. a FaceTime call is using the cameras
                    self.showCameraUnavailableBanner()
                case .videoDeviceNotAvailableWithMultipleForegroundApps:
                    self.showMultitaskingMessage()
                default:
                    break
                }
        })

        observers.append(center.addObserver(
            forName: AVCaptureSession.interruptionEndedNotification,
            object: session, queue: .main) { _ in
                self.hideCameraUnavailableBanner()
        })
    }

    private func showCameraUnavailableBanner() { /* ... */ }
    private func showMultitaskingMessage() { /* ... */ }
    private func hideCameraUnavailableBanner() { /* ... */ }
}

2. iOS 27.3 beta: Safari Vertical Tabs

What we know so far from the beta 1 coverage:

  • Tabs can be arranged along the left side of the window instead of across the top.
  • By default they show as icons to save space; the tab bar can be resized to show page titles.
  • Vertical Tabs work with Tab Groups and with Topics (the Apple Intelligence tab sorting introduced in iOS 27).
  • It is available on iPad and Mac, and on iPhone Duo in both portrait and landscape.
  • On iPhone it is enabled in Settings > Apps > Safari; on iPad and Mac also via Safari's View menu.

How this can affect web-based experiences

  • Narrower content area. A sidebar on the left reduces the width available to your page, especially when users expand it to show titles. A layout that sat comfortably at a desktop breakpoint on iPad may now fall into a tablet or mobile breakpoint. Fixed-width layouts and off-canvas menus are the usual suspects.
  • Favicons matter more. In icon-only mode, your site's icon is the main way a user finds your tab. Missing or low-resolution icons make your page harder to identify among many tabs.
  • Page titles matter more. In the expanded sidebar, titles are what users scan. Single-page apps that never update document.title on navigation will look identical across tabs.
  • Resize events. Toggling or resizing the sidebar changes the viewport width while the page is live. Any logic that measures layout only once on load can break.

Web side: icons, titles and width-change resilience

<!-- Give Safari a clear icon and title for icon-only vertical tabs -->
<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png">
<title>Order #4821 - Acme Store</title>

<style>
  /* Prefer container queries for components that live in variable-width areas */
  .product-grid { container-type: inline-size; }
  @container (max-width: 700px) {
    .product-grid .card { grid-column: span 12; }
  }
</style>

<script>
  // React to width changes when the tab sidebar is toggled or resized,
  // instead of measuring once on load.
  const ro = new ResizeObserver(entries => relayout(entries[0].contentRect.width));
  ro.observe(document.documentElement);
</script>

How this can affect app integrations

Native apps are not directly affected by Safari's tab layout, but a few integration points are worth checking:

  • Universal Links and Smart App Banners. Users who open your site in Safari and then jump into your app go through a slightly different chrome. Verify banners and "Open in app" flows still render correctly in the narrower viewport.
  • SFSafariViewController and ASWebAuthenticationSession. These present their own browser UI. Based on the coverage I have read, Vertical Tabs are a Safari app setting, so I would not expect them to appear here, but confirm on the beta rather than assume, especially for OAuth sign-in flows.
  • Your own WKWebView screens. If you host web content that is also used in Safari, test it at the narrower widths Safari may now give it, since the same CSS will be exercised in both places.

A quick SwiftUI harness for checking web layouts at several widths

import SwiftUI
import WebKit

/// Debug-only harness: render the same page at several widths to catch
/// breakpoint regressions that a narrower Safari viewport can expose.
struct WidthMatrixView: View {
    let url: URL
    let widths: [CGFloat] = [1024, 834, 700, 600]

    var body: some View {
        ScrollView(.horizontal) {
            HStack(alignment: .top, spacing: 16) {
                ForEach(widths, id: \.self) { width in
                    VStack {
                        Text("\(Int(width)) pt").font(.caption.monospacedDigit())
                        WebView(url: url).frame(width: width, height: 900)
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

struct WebView: UIViewRepresentable {
    let url: URL
    func makeUIView(context: Context) -> WKWebView {
        let view = WKWebView()
        view.load(URLRequest(url: url))
        return view
    }
    func updateUIView(_ uiView: WKWebView, context: Context) {}
}

3. iOS 27.3 beta: Adaptive Dark Mode

Adaptive Dark Mode lets Safari generate a dark version of websites that do not support Dark Mode on their own. When the device is in Dark Mode and you visit such a site, Safari shows a "Try" button; users can apply it per site or let it kick in automatically.

It is important to be precise about what this is: it is a Safari feature for web content. It does not recolor native SwiftUI or UIKit interfaces. So why should native developers care?

  • Your web surfaces may be recolored without your input. Marketing pages, help centers, account portals and web checkouts that only have a light theme are candidates for automatic darkening. Brand colors, logos on transparent backgrounds, charts and screenshots are where automatic transforms most often go wrong.
  • Users will notice inconsistency. If Safari renders your website dark, and the user then taps a Universal Link into an app that has weak Dark Mode support, the gap becomes very obvious.
  • Hybrid apps are an open question. The coverage describes the feature in Safari. Whether anything similar applies to WKWebView content is not documented as far as I can tell, so the safest plan is to make your web content support Dark Mode properly rather than rely on any automatic transform.

Apple has not, to my knowledge, documented exactly how Safari decides a site "doesn't support" Dark Mode. Declaring your support explicitly is the most reasonable thing to do, and it is good practice anyway:

Web side: explicit Dark Mode support

<!-- Tell the browser which color schemes your page supports -->
<meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">

<style>
  :root {
    color-scheme: light dark;
    --bg: #ffffff; --text: #1b1f24; --brand: #0a66c2;
  }
  @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
    :root { --bg: #111418; --text: #e6e9ee; --brand: #4c9cff; }
  }
  body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--text); }
</style>

<!-- Provide a dark variant for logos and illustrations -->
<picture>
  <source srcset="/logo-dark.svg" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)">
  <img src="/logo-light.svg" alt="Acme">
</picture>

Impact on SwiftUI interfaces

SwiftUI handles appearance changes well when you stay with semantic styles. Problems usually come from hard-coded colors or from assets without dark variants. This is a good moment to audit both:

SwiftUI: semantic styles, asset colors and dual previews

import SwiftUI

struct OrderSummaryCard: View {
    @Environment(\.colorScheme) private var colorScheme

    var body: some View {
        VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 8) {
            Text("Order #4821").font(.headline)
            Text("Arriving Friday").foregroundStyle(.secondary)
        }
        .padding()
        // Semantic background adapts automatically; avoid Color.white / Color.black
        .background(.background.secondary, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 12))
        // "BrandAccent" lives in the asset catalog with Any/Dark appearances
        .overlay(RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12).stroke(Color("BrandAccent")))
        // Use colorScheme only for things styles can't express, e.g. shadow strength
        .shadow(radius: colorScheme == .dark ? 0 : 4)
    }
}

#Preview("Light") { OrderSummaryCard().padding() }
#Preview("Dark") { OrderSummaryCard().padding().preferredColorScheme(.dark) }

Impact on UIKit interfaces

UIKit's classic Dark Mode bug is Core Animation properties. CGColor values are resolved once, so borders and shadows set on a layer stay in the old appearance when the user switches modes. Since iOS 17, registerForTraitChanges is the recommended way to respond, replacing the deprecated traitCollectionDidChange(_:).

UIKit: keeping layer colors in sync with appearance

import UIKit

final class CardView: UIView {
    override init(frame: CGRect) {
        super.init(frame: frame)
        backgroundColor = .secondarySystemBackground   // dynamic, auto-updates
        layer.cornerRadius = 12
        layer.borderWidth = 1
        applyLayerColors()

        // CGColor does not update on its own; re-resolve when appearance changes.
        let traits: [UITrait] = [UITraitUserInterfaceStyle.self,
                                 UITraitAccessibilityContrast.self]
        registerForTraitChanges(traits) { (self: Self, _) in
            self.applyLayerColors()
        }
    }

    required init?(coder: NSCoder) { fatalError("init(coder:) not implemented") }

    private func applyLayerColors() {
        let traits = traitCollection
        layer.borderColor = UIColor.separator.resolvedColor(with: traits).cgColor
        layer.shadowColor = UIColor.label.resolvedColor(with: traits).cgColor
    }
}

// A dynamic color defined in code, when an asset catalog entry isn't practical
extension UIColor {
    static let brandAccent = UIColor { traits in
        traits.userInterfaceStyle == .dark
            ? UIColor(red: 0.30, green: 0.61, blue: 1.00, alpha: 1)
            : UIColor(red: 0.04, green: 0.40, blue: 0.76, alpha: 1)
    }
}

If you host web content, a related annoyance is the white flash before a dark page paints. Two small settings take care of most of it:

WKWebView: avoiding the white flash in Dark Mode

let webView = WKWebView(frame: .zero, configuration: WKWebViewConfiguration())
webView.isOpaque = false                       // avoid a white frame before first paint
webView.backgroundColor = .systemBackground
webView.underPageBackgroundColor = .systemBackground // iOS 15+: overscroll area
// WKWebView passes the view's appearance to prefers-color-scheme,
// so web content that supports Dark Mode follows the app automatically.

4. Compatibility and regression testing

Here is the matrix I am working from. It is deliberately small; the goal is to catch the regressions point releases tend to cause, not to retest everything.

Dimension What to cover Notes
OS versions Your minimum deployment target, the latest 27.1.x, 27.2 (shipping), 27.3 beta Install your current App Store / TestFlight build on the beta, not just a fresh debug build.
Devices A small iPhone, a large iPhone, iPhone Duo if you support it, one iPad Vertical Tabs matter most on iPad, Mac and iPhone Duo, where the Safari sidebar takes width.
Appearance Light, Dark, Increase Contrast, appearance switch while the app is running Live switching is where CGColor and cached-image bugs appear.
Text size Default, the largest standard size, one accessibility size Combine with Dark Mode; truncation bugs and contrast bugs often show up together.
Web content Safari with Vertical Tabs collapsed and expanded, Adaptive Dark Mode on and off Include login, checkout and help pages, not only the homepage.
System interactions FaceTime call during camera use, Home automations changing lock state Covers the iOS 27.2 changes most likely to reach third-party apps.

Automating appearance checks

Rendering the same screen under both appearances in a unit test is cheap and catches most color regressions. You can pair this with whichever snapshot library you already use:

XCTest: verifying trait-dependent colors

import XCTest
@testable import MyApp

final class AppearanceTests: XCTestCase {

    func testCardRendersInBothAppearances() {
        for style in [UIUserInterfaceStyle.light, .dark] {
            let traits = UITraitCollection(userInterfaceStyle: style)
            let card = CardView(frame: CGRect(x: 0, y: 0, width: 320, height: 120))
            card.overrideUserInterfaceStyle = style

            traits.performAsCurrent {
                card.layoutIfNeeded()
                let expected = UIColor.separator.resolvedColor(with: traits).cgColor
                let name = style == .dark ? "dark" : "light"
                XCTAssertEqual(card.layer.borderColor, expected,
                               "Border color not resolved for \(name)")
            }
        }
    }
}

For UI tests, a launch argument that forces the appearance keeps the setup simple and works on any OS version:

UI tests: forcing an appearance via launch environment

// In the app (e.g. SceneDelegate or App init), debug builds only:
#if DEBUG
if let mode = ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment["UI_TEST_APPEARANCE"] {
    window?.overrideUserInterfaceStyle = (mode == "dark") ? .dark : .light
}
#endif

// In the UI test:
let app = XCUIApplication()
app.launchEnvironment["UI_TEST_APPEARANCE"] = "dark"
app.launch()

5. UI issues, API changes, performance and backward compatibility

Potential UI issues

  • Hard-coded .white / .black colors and images without dark variants.
  • Layer-based borders and shadows that do not update when appearance changes at runtime.
  • Web pages that assume a minimum width on iPad or Mac and break when the Safari sidebar is expanded.
  • Logos and screenshots on websites that look wrong after Adaptive Dark Mode recolors the page around them.

API changes

The coverage of iOS 27.3 beta 1 focuses on user-facing Safari changes and does not describe new developer APIs for Vertical Tabs or Adaptive Dark Mode. That does not mean there are none: check the Xcode and Safari release notes for the 27.3 SDK, and file Feedback early if you see behavior changes in WebKit. If you do adopt something new, guard it with availability checks so your minimum deployment target keeps working:

Availability checks and OS-version logging

if #available(iOS 27.3, *) {
    // Adopt new behavior or API introduced in the 27.3 SDK (per release notes)
} else {
    // Existing code path for earlier versions
}

// Logging the exact OS version helps when triaging beta-only reports
let v = ProcessInfo.processInfo.operatingSystemVersion
logger.info("OS \(v.majorVersion).\(v.minorVersion).\(v.patchVersion)")

Performance

  • Watch for extra layout passes in web content when the Safari sidebar is resized; ResizeObserver callbacks that do heavy work can cause jank.
  • Measure hangs and launch time on the beta with Instruments, and compare with MetricKit data from the shipping release once 27.3 rolls out.
  • Retest memory in WKWebView-heavy screens; WebKit changes in a point release can shift memory behavior.

Backward compatibility

  • None of these changes require raising your deployment target. Keep shipping builds made with the release SDK, and use the beta for testing your existing binaries.
  • Avoid user-agent sniffing to detect the new Safari features; feature-detect and use responsive CSS instead.
  • Treat Dark Mode support on the web and in the app as one design system, so behavior stays consistent across OS versions that do and do not have Adaptive Dark Mode.

Discussion questions

  • Vertical Tabs: Have you tested your web content or Universal Link flows in Safari with Vertical Tabs expanded on iPad, Mac or iPhone Duo? Did any breakpoints or fixed layouts break?
  • Adaptive Dark Mode: Has Safari offered to darken any of your sites, and how did the result look? Has anyone found a reliable way to signal that a site already supports Dark Mode, beyond the color-scheme declaration?
  • Hybrid apps: For apps built on WKWebView, have you seen any change in how web content renders in Dark Mode on the 27.3 beta, or does everything behave as it did on 27.2?
  • Testing workflow: How do you organize regression testing for point releases? Do you automate appearance and Dynamic Type checks, or rely on manual passes on beta devices?

Swift #SwiftUI #UIKit #iOSDev #iOS27 #iOS27_2 #iOS27_3 #Safari #WebKit #DarkMode #VerticalTabs #RegressionTesting #XCTest #Accessibility #AppleDeveloper

Sources

  • 9to5Mac, "iOS 27.2 adds new features in six iPhone apps, details here" (Nov 10, 2026)
  • 9to5Mac, "iOS 27.3 and macOS 27.3 add Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and more to Safari" (Nov 3, 2026)
  • Additional beta coverage: MacRumors via Daring Fireball, TechRadar, Macworld (Nov 3, 2026). Features in beta may change before release.

title: PostgreSQL 14 Reaches End of Support on November 12. What Should You Check First?
description:
The PostgreSQL Global Development Group lists November 12, 2026, as the final release date for PostgreSQL 14. After the final release, the upstream project will stop shipping security patches and bug fixes for the 14.x series. PostgreSQL versioning policy

If you run a managed database, check your provider’s timeline too. Maintenance schedules, supported upgrade paths, and extended support terms vary by service. Confirm when your provider’s coverage ends and whether that date affects your patching or compliance requirements.

If PostgreSQL 14 is still in your stack, start with an inventory. Find out where it runs, which applications depend on it, and how much time you’ll need to rehearse the upgrade and recover if something breaks.

1. Find every PostgreSQL 14 server and assign an owner

Start with your cloud database inventory, deployment manifests, and self-managed hosts. Check production, staging, QA, and disaster recovery environments. A standby replica that only gets attention during a failover is easy to miss.

From an application connection or SQL client, run this command to check the version of the server you’re connected to:

SHOW server_version;

For every PostgreSQL 14 instance, record:

  • The environment
  • The owning team and primary engineering contact
  • Connected applications, including scheduled jobs and BI or reporting tools that query the database outside normal traffic hours
  • Available maintenance windows

If an instance has no clear owner, assign someone to map its dependencies before scheduling changes.

2. Choose a target version your stack can support

Check which PostgreSQL major versions your hosting platform supports and how long each will receive upstream fixes. Then verify compatibility with the extensions, database drivers, and backup tools you rely on. If an application uses PostGIS, for example, confirm that the required extension version is available on your target platform before booking a maintenance window.

For self-managed deployments, pg_upgrade and dump-and-restore are two major upgrade paths. If you plan to use pg_upgrade, run pg_upgrade --check during rehearsal to identify issues the tool can detect before the upgrade. On a managed service, follow your provider’s documented upgrade path and confirm whether you can move directly from PostgreSQL 14 to your target version. PostgreSQL versioning policy

3. Rehearse the upgrade and define your rollback trigger

Rehearse with a representative copy of production data. Time the upgrade, test the application’s critical read and write paths, and run background jobs that execute less frequently. A successful login confirms basic connectivity. Run the nightly reporting job separately to check that it still has the permissions and extensions it needs.

Restore a backup in a test environment, record how long recovery takes, and compare the measured time with your recovery time objective (RTO). Before cutover, agree on two things:

  • When to roll back. Define a measurable trigger, such as an application error rate above an agreed threshold or an upgrade that exceeds the maintenance window.
  • How to handle post-cutover writes. If you redirect traffic to the old PostgreSQL 14 instance after the upgraded database has accepted writes, those transactions will be missing from the old instance unless you have a way to reconcile them.

Your action plan for this week

By the end of the week, aim to give every remaining PostgreSQL 14 instance an owner, a target version to validate, and a scheduled rehearsal date. If you only have time for one step today, verify the server version behind your primary production connection and confirm who owns the upgrade.

If your team has already moved off PostgreSQL 14, what took longer than you expected during the rehearsal?

Author’s note: I work in marketing at Advange and cover enterprise IT news for infrastructure and operations teams. I used AI assistance to draft and edit this post.

title: UI20 Inspection Photos: Build an Idempotent Review Ledger in Python
description:
An inspection team exports a folder twice because the first upload appeared to stall. Both transfers finish. The reviewer now sees twice as many rows, although the team visited the same assets. A second folder arrives with an unchanged filename but different bytes. One importer silently replaces the earlier file, including the image that somebody already accepted. The photo viewer works. The handoff record has lost the ability to say what was reviewed.

This tutorial builds a small SQLite ledger for an inspection team evaluating a UI20 aircraft configuration. The ledger runs after files have been delivered to the team. The UI20 aircraft listing identifies the product to discuss with a supplier. The manifest and all payload bytes below are synthetic, and the code assumes the team supplies its own capture identifiers. The example requires Python's standard library and no access to the aircraft.

Decide what must survive a second import

Start by asking what should happen when the same export is delivered under a different folder name. A successful second import should leave the same captures and reviews in the ledger. A file path is useful for finding a file in one transfer, but the receiver cannot assume that path survives archiving, renaming or copying through a different operating system. A filename can also be recycled by a camera or a person's export script.

Define the unit of work with a key such as job ID, required view ID and capture ID. The job separates deliveries for different work orders. The view identifies the evidence requested for a particular asset or inspection question. The capture identifies one attempt to supply that view. The team assigns those identifiers and records them in a manifest before sending files. A path in that manifest points to the bytes in the current delivery. It can change on another delivery without changing the key. If two assets each need a label photo, their view IDs should be distinct in the job requirements.

Give the bytes a separate identity

Hash the original byte stream with SHA-256. The digest lets the receiver detect byte-for-byte equality. Include the byte count for storage and inspection, and retain the original bytes somewhere the ledger can reference. A digest of a preview or an image decoded and saved again describes a different artifact. For example, a program that strips metadata from a photo creates a new byte sequence even when a person cannot see a difference in the displayed image. Store derived artifacts with their own digest and a reference to the source.

Two capture keys can point to the same digest. The ledger retains both keys and only needs one blob record for those bytes. That situation can occur when a sender attaches the same file to multiple manifest rows. It warrants a review of the assignment. The digest alone cannot tell whether the image is suitable evidence for either required view. Keeping the two identities separate allows the receiver to find repeated bytes without silently dropping work or counting duplicates as additional completed views.

Define the three import outcomes

An unseen capture key is a new capture. A known key with the same digest is a replay. A known key with a different digest is a conflict. Those outcomes can be checked without timestamps or filenames. In particular, a file marked newer by a transfer service could still be a renamed copy of an older image. The team's manifest contract should say who can issue a new capture ID and what the receiver should do with a conflict.

This example rejects the conflicting batch and leaves earlier committed imports and reviews available. In production, a receiver can place the batch and its manifest in quarantine and give a human the job, view and capture key together with both digests. The sender can explain which item the delivery intended to replace. A corrected capture gets its own ID or follows a documented amendment process. A policy that overwrites old rows during ingestion makes the correction look like the original bytes were never there.

Build the ledger in SQLite

The example stores a blob digest and size, a capture-to-blob association, and one decision for each reviewed capture. The fixture uses small byte strings as stand-ins for image files. It stores no original bytes in SQLite. For a real handoff, save them in durable storage, verify the hash computed from what was written, and keep the locator alongside the digest. Build that storage and reconciliation layer before depending on the database as an operational record.

The import does the inserts and the comparison inside one transaction. The capture insert can skip a key that already exists. The following query checks the digest stored under that key. If the bytes conflict, an exception rolls back the import, including any new blob rows from that batch. The review uses a conditional insert so that a request referring to a stale or missing digest cannot attach a decision to a different capture. Identical decisions can be replayed. Changing an accepted decision requires a separate revision process with its own record.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from hashlib import sha256
import sqlite3


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Capture:
    job_id: str
    view_id: str
    capture_id: str
    payload: bytes

    @property
    def key(self):
        return self.job_id, self.view_id, self.capture_id


def open_ledger():
    db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    db.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")
    db.executescript("""
        CREATE TABLE blob (
            digest TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL,
            byte_count INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (byte_count >= 0)
        );
        CREATE TABLE capture (
            job_id TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (length(job_id) > 0),
            view_id TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (length(view_id) > 0),
            capture_id TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (length(capture_id) > 0),
            digest TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES blob(digest),
            PRIMARY KEY (job_id, view_id, capture_id)
        );
        CREATE TABLE review (
            job_id TEXT NOT NULL,
            view_id TEXT NOT NULL,
            capture_id TEXT NOT NULL,
            digest TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES blob(digest),
            decision TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (decision IN ('accepted', 'rejected')),
            PRIMARY KEY (job_id, view_id, capture_id),
            FOREIGN KEY (job_id, view_id, capture_id)
                REFERENCES capture(job_id, view_id, capture_id)
        );
    """)
    return db


def import_export(db, rows):
    with db:
        for row in rows:
            digest = sha256(row.payload).hexdigest()
            db.execute("""
                INSERT INTO blob VALUES (?, ?)
                ON CONFLICT(digest) DO NOTHING
            """, (digest, len(row.payload)))
            db.execute("""
                INSERT INTO capture VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)
                ON CONFLICT(job_id, view_id, capture_id) DO NOTHING
            """, (*row.key, digest))
            stored = db.execute("""
                SELECT digest FROM capture
                WHERE job_id = ? AND view_id = ? AND capture_id = ?
            """, row.key).fetchone()
            if stored != (digest,):
                raise ValueError(f"Conflicting bytes for capture {row.key}")


def record_review(db, key, expected_digest, decision):
    if decision not in {"accepted", "rejected"}:
        raise ValueError("Unsupported review decision")
    with db:
        db.execute("""
            INSERT INTO review
            SELECT job_id, view_id, capture_id, digest, ? FROM capture
            WHERE job_id = ? AND view_id = ? AND capture_id = ? AND digest = ?
            ON CONFLICT(job_id, view_id, capture_id) DO NOTHING
        """, (decision, *key, expected_digest))
        stored = db.execute("""
            SELECT digest, decision FROM review
            WHERE job_id = ? AND view_id = ? AND capture_id = ?
        """, key).fetchone()
        if stored != (expected_digest, decision):
            raise ValueError(f"Review target or decision conflicts for {key}")


def missing_views(db, job_id, required):
    accepted = db.execute("""
        SELECT DISTINCT view_id FROM review
        WHERE job_id = ? AND decision = 'accepted'
    """, (job_id,))
    return sorted(set(required) - {view_id for (view_id,) in accepted})


if __name__ == "__main__":
    ledger = open_ledger()
    front = Capture("JOB-17", "cabinet-front", "C-1", b"synthetic front bytes")
    label = Capture("JOB-17", "asset-label", "C-2", b"synthetic label bytes")
    requirements = {"cabinet-front", "asset-label"}
    import_export(ledger, [front, label])
    import_export(ledger, [label, front])
    record_review(ledger, front.key, sha256(front.payload).hexdigest(), "accepted")
    print(missing_views(ledger, "JOB-17", requirements))
    record_review(ledger, label.key, sha256(label.payload).hexdigest(), "accepted")
    print(missing_views(ledger, "JOB-17", requirements))

Read the result as an evidence check

The first import records two views. The second import presents the same records in the opposite order and leaves the ledger unchanged. Accepting the cabinet front leaves ['asset-label'] in the missing-view report. Accepting the label then produces []. A populated capture table would have been a premature reason to call the job complete. The example checks required views against accepted reviews, so a file can be present while evidence is still due.

Decide what the report means before integrating it with a dashboard. An empty list says that the required view IDs passed this workflow's review rule for that job. That rule should be owned by a named person or role. A reviewer might need to verify that a label is legible, that the asset matches the work order, or that a close view includes the feature the request describes. A script can detect the missing decision. The decision itself depends on the acceptance criteria and the material presented.

Test retries and ambiguous inputs

Use at least one export fixture that includes a capture with a stable key and resend it in a different order. Compare the number of blob, capture and review rows before and after. Then create a batch with a new capture followed by a conflict for an existing key. Check that the new capture and its blob were rolled back, and that the accepted decision for the old capture still refers to the previous digest. This test catches a deceptively common bug where the importer commits each item and then reports that the overall batch failed.

Exercise a stale review request by changing its expected digest. The call should fail without creating a decision, even if another capture in the job has those bytes. Check that a rejected capture still leaves its view due. Check a second capture ID with the same bytes to confirm that capture identity and storage deduplication are independent. Finally, query the same required view in another job. Accepted views for the original work order should have no effect on a different work order.

Verify file integrity without overinterpreting a hash

A content hash can tell you that bytes changed between two measured points. It cannot tell you who assigned the capture ID or which asset appears in the photo. An operator could accidentally attach a valid file to the wrong manifest row. If the sender and receiver must agree on origin and authority, define a trusted manifest exchange with the parties responsible for its production and review. Store the received manifest and its revision alongside the receipt. Compare the hash of the stored original with the one used at review time.

If the manifest already includes a digest, compute the receiver's digest independently before accepting the claimed value. A failed match is useful evidence of a transfer or packaging problem. A passing match still leaves the human or a validated domain-specific check responsible for content acceptance. Keep timestamps for troubleshooting and audit, but state whether a timestamp describes image capture, export assembly, receipt or review. These times can differ without any defect in the delivered image.

Keep storage and review recoverable

A directory and a database cannot normally share one transaction. If a worker uploads a blob and then crashes before committing the capture association, the blob may be unreferenced. If it commits first and crashes before the upload, the ledger may point at an unavailable object. A practical sequence is to write and verify the blob first, commit its association second, and periodically reconcile unreferenced objects with a retention window. This example focuses on the database transaction and leaves storage operations outside the fixture.

Define the point where the system acknowledges a batch to the sender. If the importer acknowledges after commit but the reply is lost, the sender can present the same manifest again. If a conflict is found, a receipt can identify the exact row that stopped the import so the sender does not resend a corrected subset without understanding what was committed. Record whether the transaction policy is per batch or per item. Teams that mix those two policies have a harder time explaining counts after a restart.

Manage revisions with explicit review rules

An inspection request can change after some images were accepted. A maintenance engineer may ask for a closer view or specify that the asset tag must be visible together with a particular surrounding feature. Record the revised requirement under a version that the reviewer can see. Decide whether an earlier capture is still eligible under that version. A new revision of the request may change the missing-view report even when there is no new file. The important record is which requirement and which exact artifact justified the result.

The sample stores a single decision per capture and checks it against the expected digest. A team that allows two independent reviewers or wants to record a superseding decision can add append-only review events. Bind each event to the capture key, the source digest, the requirement revision and an event ID for retries. Define the projection that the dashboard uses to decide the current state. Otherwise, ordering by the latest row created can accidentally put a retried earlier decision ahead of a genuine correction.

Make the handoff fit the actual export

Ask for representative original files from the specific configuration under consideration. Have the person who builds the export show how stable identifiers are assigned and what happens when the same job is exported twice. When the aircraft, payload or downstream software does not produce a usable key, agree on where the team's manifest is assembled and who is authorized to correct it. Include at least one required view where an otherwise valid file is easy to mistake for a different asset. That makes the review criterion observable rather than a promise about the system.

Try the exercise with two deliveries and a deliberately conflicting row. Require the operator to identify the original decision and confirm that the database still points to the reviewed bytes. Ask the reviewer to demonstrate which view remains due after a rejected file. Finally, have another person repeat the procedure using only the work-order instructions and the retained export. If the second person cannot recreate the same result, write down which identifier or acceptance rule was implicit and make it part of the next handoff.

Record the limits before adding automation

This example uses a single local SQLite connection and an in-memory database. A production worker needs persistent storage, a clear writer policy, backup and restoration tests, and a rule for who can see the delivered material. Reuse the same logical keys even if files arrive by a different transport. Use file sizes and bounded reads to control how much work an unexpected export can demand. Keep personal, site-specific or sensitive image content out of application logs, and record only the fields needed for operational investigation.

If the team later automates parts of the review, introduce a distinct state for machine observations and specify when human approval is required. A failed image decoder, an uncertain asset match and an incomplete manifest have different meanings to the person doing the work. Report them independently. The ledger is most useful when someone can trace a readiness decision back to the work order, the exact original bytes, and the review criteria they agreed to use. That trace is what lets a second delivery become a safe replay rather than a new interpretation of the job.

title: A Claude Client in One Rust File, and the First Dependency
description:
The first three clients in this series had HTTP and TLS handed to them by their standard libraries. Rust does not. The spec says a language without them gets one named library for the transport and it counts towards size, so this post is the first time the leaderboard has to price a dependency. The transport is ureq with rustls, the parsing is serde_json, and together they bring in thirty-six crates. The result is still the smallest thing on the board so far.

The code is at github.com/AndyCross/claude-hot-path, and the spec every client passes is at /claude-hot-path/.

Choosing the transport

The usual answer for HTTP in Rust is reqwest, which is async and brings tokio and hyper with it. For a client that makes two sequential requests and streams the reply to stdout, async buys nothing and costs a runtime. ureq is the blocking alternative, it defaults to rustls so there is no OpenSSL to link, and version 3 exposes the response body as a Read, which is all the SSE loop needs.

One configuration line matters. By default ureq turns a 4xx or 5xx response into an Err, which would throw away the body that holds the API's error message. The spec wants that message on stderr, so the agent is built with status errors off and the client reads the status itself:

let agent: ureq::Agent = ureq::Agent::config_builder()
    .http_status_as_error(false)
    .build()
    .into();

The loop

The body reader goes into a BufReader and lines() does the rest. The let else on the prefix strip is doing the same job as the continue in Go, skipping event: lines, pings and blank separators:

let reader = BufReader::new(resp.body_mut().as_reader());
for line in reader.lines() {
    let line = line.unwrap_or_default();
    let Some(data) = line.strip_prefix("data: ") else { continue };
    let ev: Value = serde_json::from_str(data).unwrap_or_else(|e| {
        eprintln!("error: bad event: {e}");
        exit(1)
    });
    let index = ev["index"].as_u64().unwrap_or(0) as usize;
    match ev["type"].as_str() {
        Some("content_block_start") => {
            content.push(ev["content_block"].clone());
            partial.push(String::new());
        }
        Some("content_block_delta") => match ev["delta"]["type"].as_str() {
            Some("text_delta") => {
                let text = ev["delta"]["text"].as_str().unwrap_or("");
                out.write_all(text.as_bytes()).unwrap();
                out.flush().unwrap();
                let existing = content[index]["text"].as_str().unwrap_or("").to_string();
                content[index]["text"] = Value::String(existing + text);
            }
            Some("input_json_delta") => partial[index].push_str(ev["delta"]["partial_json"].as_str().unwrap_or("")),
            _ => {}
        },
        Some("content_block_stop") => {
            if content[index]["type"] == "tool_use" && !partial[index].is_empty() {
                content[index]["input"] = serde_json::from_str(&partial[index]).unwrap_or(json!({}));
            }
        }
        Some("message_delta") => stop = ev["delta"]["stop_reason"].as_str().map(str::to_string),
        _ => {}
    }
}

serde_json::Value with index syntax is the Rust equivalent of C#'s JsonNode, and I used it for the same reason: the shapes are dynamic and a typed struct per event would be longer than the client. Indexing a Value that lacks the key returns Null rather than panicking, so the as_str().unwrap_or chains read a missing field as empty and move on.

The out is a locked stdout, flushed after every delta. Rust's Stdout is line-buffered, and a text delta rarely ends in a newline, so without the flush the words would sit in the buffer until the stream ended. The harness catches that: the runner records when the first visible byte reached stdout and the mock records when it wrote each chunk, and a client whose first text lands after the stream finished fails conformance. I tried it with the flush removed, and it failed by a millisecond. With the flush it has eleven in hand.

The one thing the library does not have

Timezones again. Rust's standard library has no zoneinfo reader and chrono-tz or jiff would be a third dependency carrying a copy of the database. The platform has one at /usr/share/zoneinfo, in the TZif format from RFC 8536, and reading it is sixty lines: skip the version 1 block, take the 64-bit transition times from the version 2 block, find the last transition before now, and apply its offset. The civil date comes out of Howard Hinnant's days-to-date algorithm, which is nine lines of integer arithmetic. It is more code than any other part of the client, it is inside the rules, and it is the reason the turnaround column reads the way it does.

What it measures as

Rust C# Native AOT Go bash and curl
Artefact 1.4 MB 5.4 MB 5.8 MB 3.7 KB
Runtime 2.0 MB 2.4 MB 0 23.7 MB
Ship 3.3 MB 7.8 MB 5.8 MB 23.7 MB
Cold start, median of 100 1.1 ms 3.0 ms 1.7 ms 7.0 ms
Turnaround, median of 100 0.7 ms 1.4 ms 1.2 ms 19.1 ms
Client total, median of 100 3.2 ms 7.1 ms 4.8 ms 35.3 ms
Peak RSS 3 MB 7 MB 6 MB 11 MB
Lines of code 184 102 156 75
Third-party crates or packages 36 0 0 0

rustc 1.99.1, linux/arm64, Apple M4 Max under Docker. Release profile with opt-level = "z", fat LTO, one codegen unit, panic = "abort" and symbols stripped.

One point four megabytes for the binary, and that is with a complete TLS stack inside it. rustls and its crypto provider are most of it. The 2.0 MB runtime is glibc, libgcc_s and the loader, the same bill .NET paid, and a musl build would fold most of that into the binary and probably come out smaller overall. I have left it dynamic because the Debian image is what someone would actually deploy, and because the leaderboard already has one static entry to compare against.

Three megabytes of peak memory is half of Go's, the cold start is the fastest so far, and the turnaround is the fastest on the board by a clear margin. It did not start that way. The first version shelled out to date for the timezone and measured three milliseconds between turns, and when I replaced the process with the TZif reader above it only came down to about two. The rest was ureq: it resolves the hostname on every request, before it checks the connection pool, so each turn paid a DNS round trip to Docker's resolver for a socket it then reused. Pointing the client at the mock's IP instead of its name was how I found that, and the fix is the caching resolver, plugged in through Agent::with_parts. Thirty-six crates is the cost, and it is the first non-zero number in that column. Go and .NET got their HTTP stacks from a standard library maintained by one organisation. Rust got its from a dozen maintainers who have never met, and the series rules are not going to pretend that is the same thing. Both are real engineering positions. The column exists so you can weigh them yourself.

How to run it 

git clone https://github.com/AndyCross/claude-hot-path
cd claude-hot-path
./bench/bench.sh rust

Docker and Python 3, no key. The release build takes about fifteen seconds in the container. Next is Zig, which has HTTP and TLS in its standard library and a reputation for binaries measured in kilobytes, so the top of the board may not stay where it is.

title: Multi-tenant from day one: keeping one customer's chatbot data out of another's
description:
The first version of almost every B2B tool is single-tenant by accident. You build it for one customer, it works, a second customer arrives, and you add a customer_id column.

That column is now the only thing standing between your two customers' data. One forgotten WHERE clause and customer A's chatbot answers a question using customer B's internal pricing document. You will not get a second chance to explain that.

This is what I would set up on day one of a multi-tenant product, in the order the risk actually appears. It is written around a chatbot — vector search makes one of these problems unusually sharp — but most of it is the same for any SaaS.

1. Never pass the tenant id as an argument

The single highest-value change, and it is architectural rather than clever.

If getDocuments(tenantId, query) takes the tenant as a parameter, then every call site is a chance to pass the wrong one, or to forget it in a new function written at 1am. Humans do not reliably remember a rule 400 times.

Instead, resolve the tenant once, at the edge, from the authenticated session — never from a request body, a query string, or a header the client controls — and carry it in a context the data layer reads for itself:

// One place turns a session into a tenant. Nothing downstream takes it as an argument.
app.use(async (req, res, next) => {
  const session = await getSession(req);
  if (!session) return res.sendStatus(401);
  // The tenant comes from the session, never from req.body.tenantId.
  tenantContext.run({ tenantId: session.tenantId }, () => next());
});

// The data layer reads the context itself. There is no overload without a tenant.
function documents() {
  const { tenantId } = tenantContext.getStore() ?? {};
  if (!tenantId) throw new Error('No tenant in context — refusing to query');
  return db('documents').where({ tenant_id: tenantId });
}

That throw matters more than it looks. The failure mode you want for a missing tenant is a loud crash, not a query that quietly returns everything.

In Node this is AsyncLocalStorage. Most ecosystems have an equivalent. The point is not the mechanism — it is that the safe path is the only path, so a new developer cannot write the unsafe one without noticing.

2. Put the same rule in the database

Application-level filtering is one bug away from failing. A second, independent layer means a bug needs two mistakes to become a breach.

In Postgres that is row-level security:

ALTER TABLE documents ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE documents FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;   -- applies to the table owner too

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON documents
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid);

with the setting applied per transaction from the same context as above. FORCE is the line people miss: without it, the owner role bypasses the policy, and your application often connects as the owner.

This is defence in depth, not belt-and-braces theatre. The two layers fail for different reasons — one to a forgotten clause in code, the other to a misconfigured role — and it is unlikely you make both mistakes in the same hour.

3. Vector search is where isolation quietly breaks

Here is the chatbot-specific trap, and it is the one I would check first in anyone else's system.

A vector index does not have a WHERE clause in the way a SQL table does. Approximate nearest-neighbour search walks a graph and returns the k closest vectors it finds. If you then filter those results by tenant, two bad things happen:

  • Correctness: you asked for 20 and got 20 from across all tenants; after filtering, you might have 3 for this tenant, or none. The bot answers badly for no visible reason.
  • Safety: every piece of filtering logic between the index and the answer is a place to get it wrong.

Post-filtering is the wrong shape. The two shapes that work:

An index per tenant. Simplest to reason about, and the cross-tenant bug becomes structurally impossible — a query against tenant A's index cannot return tenant B's rows, whatever the code does. The cost is many small indexes, which is fine for hundreds of tenants and painful for a hundred thousand.

Pre-filtered search, where the tenant is a condition the index applies during the search, not after. pgvector does this naturally, because it is a Postgres query and row-level security already applies:

SELECT id, content, 1 - (embedding <=> $1) AS score
FROM   documents                      -- RLS already scopes this to the tenant
ORDER  BY embedding <=> $1
LIMIT  20;

Managed vector databases support metadata pre-filtering too — but read their documentation carefully and test it, because "filter" in some engines means post-filter, and the difference is exactly the one that matters here.

Write a test for this and never delete it. Two tenants, two documents, one query that would match the other tenant's document far better than its own:

test('a tenant never retrieves another tenant\'s content', async () => {
  await seed(tenantA, 'Our refund window is 30 days.');
  await seed(tenantB, 'Our refund window is 90 days.');

  const hits = await asTenant(tenantA, () => retrieve('how long is the refund window'));

  expect(hits).not.toHaveLength(0);                     // it still works
  expect(hits.every(h => h.tenantId === tenantA)).toBe(true);
  expect(hits.map(h => h.content).join(' ')).not.toMatch(/90 days/);
});

That last assertion is the one that catches a post-filter regression where the leak reaches the prompt but not the response object.

4. Secrets belong to one tenant each

Customers will give you API keys — their own model provider key, a WhatsApp token, an SMTP password. These need handling that plain columns do not give you:

  • Encrypted at rest with authenticated encryption, AES-256-GCM or equivalent, so a database dump is not a credential dump.
  • Decrypted only at the moment of use, never loaded into a general-purpose settings object that gets logged or serialised into an API response.
  • Masked everywhere they are displayed. Show the last four characters. There is no screen that needs to show the whole key, including the owner's own settings page — they have it already.
  • Scrubbed from errors. A provider's error object will happily include the request headers you sent.

5. Make the tenant visible in everything you operate

Isolation that you cannot observe is isolation you are only assuming.

  • Logs carry the tenant id on every line. Debugging a cross-tenant issue without it is guesswork.
  • Metrics and rate limits are per tenant. One customer's traffic spike should not degrade everyone, and a per-tenant limit is also your defence against a runaway loop in someone's integration costing you a fortune.
  • Background jobs carry the tenant explicitly, because they run outside the request that had the context. This is the most common place the whole scheme leaks: a cron job with no session, written months later.
  • Caches are keyed by tenant. A cache key of answer:${hash(question)} will serve tenant A's answer to tenant B, and it will do it intermittently, which makes it nearly impossible to reproduce.

That cache bug deserves emphasis. It is the one that gets shipped by careful teams, because the cache is added later as an optimisation, by someone who is thinking about latency rather than tenancy.

What it costs to do this on day one

Perhaps two days of work: the context plumbing, the RLS policies, the per-tenant index decision, the isolation test, the encrypted-secrets helper.

Retrofitting it onto a live product with real customers is weeks, because every query, job and cache written in the meantime has to be found and re-checked, and you cannot be sure you found them all. The second system is also the one where you are reading your own code wondering whether an untested path ever leaked.

The work is not hard. It is just much cheaper before the second customer than after the twentieth.

I build ChatNory, a multi-tenant AI chatbot that answers from each business's own content. The isolation test in section 3 exists because the post-filtering version looked completely fine until it did not. If you run vector search across tenants, go and check whether your engine pre-filters or post-filters — it is a five-minute check and it is worth doing today.

title: Build a polite mini SEO site auditor in Python with robots.txt and a tiny crawl
description:
Commercial SEO crawlers are excellent. You do not need one of them to learn the pattern: read robots.txt, fetch a few pages politely, measure a handful of on-page signals, and write the findings somewhere a human can act on.

In this tutorial we build a small, polite Python script that:

  1. reads robots.txt and stops if User-agent: * (and our bot) may not fetch the start URL,
  2. crawls a tiny site breadth-first with hard caps (pages, depth, timeout, body size),
  3. per page records title / meta description length, H1 count, canonical, meta robots / X-Robots-Tag, basic Open Graph presence, images missing alt, internal vs external link counts, HTTP status and redirect hops,
  4. checks a few broken internal links only (HEAD, with GET fallback),
  5. reads whether robots.txt names common AI crawlers (GPTBot, Claude-Web, Google-Extended, …) — read rules only, never impersonate those bots,
  6. optionally probes for llms.txt and sitemap.xml,
  7. writes CSV and JSON, and attaches a simple 0–100 score with plain-English fix hints.

Dependencies: Python 3.9+ (tested on 3.13) and requests. HTML and robots parsing use the standard library. The full script is at the end. Every figure below comes from live runs on 6 November 2026.

The checks are a small educational subset. They are incomplete on purpose. Treat them as teaching examples, not as a product rule catalogue.

Why pure Python (and only requests)

There is nothing wrong with Playwright, Scrapy or a hosted auditor. For a tutorial, a single file you can read top to bottom beats a framework:

  • urllib.robotparser and html.parser are in the standard library.
  • requests handles TLS, redirects and a session cookie jar without ceremony.
  • Hard caps (pages, depth, bytes, link-check budget) keep the script safe to point at a stranger's documentation site once.
  • You can paste the script into a throwaway venv and delete it when you are done.

If you later move the same ideas into an async service, keep the politeness contract: robots first, clear User-Agent, rate limit, capped bodies, no personal data.

What we will not do

  • Crawl a whole production site. Default caps are 10 pages and depth 2.
  • Log in, solve captchas, rotate proxies or ignore Disallow.
  • Harvest mailto: / tel: links, form contents or anything that looks like a person.
  • Send User-Agent: GPTBot (or any other third-party bot name) to see what happens. We only read those rules from robots.txt.
  • Pitch a hosted product. This is a standalone script you can read and run.

One site, several layers of signal

Take crawlee.dev from the live run on 6 November 2026. After robots.txt allowed our bot and *, an eight-page crawl (depth ≤ 2) returned:

Layer What showed up
Homepage HTTP 200, title 40 chars, meta description 146 chars, one H1, self-canonical, Open Graph present, score 100
Site extras sitemap.xml declared in robots and present; llms.txt HTTP 200
Deeper pages Blog title 107 chars (soft-max notice); a couple of JS/Python pages with images missing alt
Roll-up Average score 97.8 across 8 pages; no broken internal links in the sample

That mix is the point of the exercise. A homepage that scores 100 can still sit next to a blog index with a long title and no H1. A useful mini auditor shows both — still with a tiny crawl budget.

Step 1: be a polite bot

Identify yourself. The educational User-Agent in this tutorial is:

LindenwerkDataEducationalBot/0.1 (+https://dev.to/lindenwerkdata; educational tiny SEO site-audit tutorial; honours robots.txt)

Then honour RFC 9309-style robots rules with urllib.robotparser. The script fetches /robots.txt first (capped body size). Practical rules we use:

  • HTTP 404 / other 4xx on robots.txt → treat as no rules, allow the fetch (common convention; example.com returned 404 in our run and we continued).
  • HTTP 5xx on robots.txt → treat as disallow (conservative).
  • Otherwise parse the file and require both our bot name and User-agent: * to be allowed for the URL we are about to request.
  • Every later page and internal link check goes through the same parser.

On 6 November 2026, crawlee.dev and docs.python.org served normal robots files that allow / for * and our bot. A unit check of RobotFileParser with Disallow: / correctly returns False for /.

from urllib.parse import urlsplit, urlunsplit
from urllib.robotparser import RobotFileParser

def robots_allows(session, page_url):
    parts = urlsplit(page_url)
    robots_url = urlunsplit((parts.scheme, parts.netloc, "/robots.txt", "", ""))
    r = session.get(robots_url, timeout=15, stream=True)
    # ... read a capped body ...
    if 400 <= r.status_code < 500:
        return True, f"robots.txt {r.status_code} (no rules → allow)"
    if r.status_code >= 500:
        return False, f"robots.txt {r.status_code} (treat as disallow)"
    rp = RobotFileParser()
    rp.parse(body.decode("utf-8", "replace").splitlines())
    target = urlunsplit((parts.scheme, parts.netloc, parts.path or "/", parts.query, ""))
    allowed = rp.can_fetch("LindenwerkDataEducationalBot", target) and rp.can_fetch("*", target)
    return allowed, "robots.txt OK"

If robots say no, the site row is stored as robots_disallowed and no HTML crawl is started.

Step 2: a tiny breadth-first crawl 

from collections import deque

queue = deque([(start_url, 0)])
seen = set()
while queue and len(pages) < max_pages:
    url, depth = queue.popleft()
    if url in seen:
        continue
    seen.add(url)
    if not robots_allows_url(robots, url):
        continue
    # GET with timeout + 1 MB body cap, then parse …
    if depth < max_depth:
        for href in internal_hrefs:
            queue.append((href, depth + 1))

Defaults in the script: 10 pages, depth 2, 0.75 s pause between requests, 15 s timeout, 1 MB HTML cap. Query strings are stripped when discovering new URLs (keeps the frontier small). Static asset extensions (.png, .css, .js, …) are skipped. mailto: and tel: are never followed.

Live on 6 November 2026 with --max-pages 8 --max-depth 2:

  • example.com → 1 page (no further internal links)
  • crawlee.dev → 8 pages
  • docs.python.org → 8 pages
  • httpbin.org → 2 pages

Step 3: per-page on-page checks

An HTMLParser subclass collects <title>, meta tags, H1 count, rel=canonical, Open Graph keys, image alt presence and anchor hrefs — without walking mailto: / tel:.

For each page the script records:

Signal How we treat it (educational soft targets)
HTTP status / redirects 4xx/5xx = error; ≥2 redirect hops = warning
Title length missing = error; < 30 = warning; > 60 = notice
Meta description missing = warning; outside ~70–160 = notice
H1 0 = warning; > 1 = notice
Canonical missing = notice; cross-domain = warning; self vs other labelled
Indexability noindex in meta robots or X-Robots-Tag = warning
Open Graph no og:title / og:description / og:image / og:url = notice
Images count of <img> with missing/empty alt

example.com on 6 November 2026 is a useful teaching case. The live HTML is a short documentation stub: title "Example Domain" (14 characters), no H1, no meta description, no canonical, no Open Graph. Score 86. (Older textbook copies of that page had an H1 — the public page changed; the script reports what the network returns today.)

crawlee.dev/ scored 100 on the same day: title 40 chars, description 146, one H1, self-canonical, Open Graph keys present, 14 images all with alt text.

Step 4: a few broken internal links only

Full-site link checking is expensive and easy to abuse. The educational script keeps a small pool of internal URLs discovered during the crawl that were not already fetched as pages, then:

  1. skips any URL robots disallow,
  2. sends HEAD (falls back to a tiny GET if the host rejects HEAD),
  3. stops after --max-link-checks (default 15).

Broken samples land on the site row as broken_internal_links and contribute a site-level broken_internal_link issue. On our 6 November 2026 runs across example.com, crawlee.dev, docs.python.org, httpbin.org and cloudflare.com, the sampled internal links all responded OK — which is a fine outcome; the plumbing is what you are learning.

Step 5: read AI-bot rules (do not wear their badges)

Many sites now name AI crawlers explicitly in robots.txt. The script looks for a short list (GPTBot, ChatGPT-User, OAI-SearchBot, ClaudeBot, Anthropic-AI, Claude-Web, Google-Extended, PerplexityBot, CCBot, …) and, for each:

  • whether the name appears in the file,
  • whether RobotFileParser.can_fetch(bot_name, homepage) is true,
  • a one-line policy hint.

Important: page fetches and link checks always use our educational User-Agent. We never send User-Agent: GPTBot to "see what the CDN does". Impersonating another bot is rude, often against terms, and unnecessary for reading a public rules file.

On 6 November 2026, cloudflare.com/robots.txt explicitly named GPTBot, ChatGPT-User, Google-Extended, Anthropic-AI, Claude-Web, CCBot, PerplexityBot (and Cohere-ai) with Allow: / for each. The script reported named_in_robots: true and homepage_allowed: true for those entries. crawlee.dev and docs.python.org named none of the AI bots in our teaching list — they fall under User-agent: *.

Step 6: optional llms.txt and sitemap presence

Two cheap HEAD/GET probes (still rate-limited):

  • /llms.txt — present or not (reported as information; search engines may ignore it).
  • Sitemap — first Sitemap: URL from robots.txt, else /sitemap.xml.

Step 7: score, fix hints, CSV and JSON

Each page starts at 100. Unique issue ids subtract 10 (error), 4 (warning) or 1 (notice). Every issue carries a short fix string a non-engineer can read:

{
  "id": "title_short",
  "severity": "warning",
  "message": "Title only 14 chars (soft min ~30)",
  "fix": "Expand the title toward ~30–60 characters without stuffing."
}

Outputs:

  • JSON — site row (rowType: "site") plus one page row per URL (rowType: "page"), including the AI-bot matrix and broken-link samples.
  • CSV — flat spreadsheet of page metrics plus a [site] summary row with average score and top issue ids.

Soft length targets are teaching defaults, not Google policy quotes. Adjust them for your own style guide.

Limitations you should expect

  1. Client-rendered apps may ship an almost empty HTML shell. A single GET will under-count H1s and text. Headless browsers are out of scope here on purpose.
  2. Soft title/description ranges are conventions, not guarantees of ranking.
  3. Broken-link sample ≠ full link audit. Raising --max-link-checks still only samples the frontier; it is not a substitute for a dedicated checker.
  4. AI-bot matrix is a reading aid. Bot names change; keep the list short and honest.
  5. The rule list is tiny. Real auditors have dozens of rule types (hreflang, JSON-LD, thin content, mixed content, …). Growing yours is fine — keep evidence, keep caps, keep robots.

Scheduling a weekly re-audit

Companion file crontab.txt:

CRON_TZ=Europe/Berlin
30 7 * * 1 cd /path/to/code && ./venv/bin/python seo_audit.py -f domains.txt --max-pages 10 --max-depth 2 --out-dir out >> out/cron.log 2>&1

Keep max-pages low. A free shared runner is not a reason to hammer strangers. Diff this week's JSON against last week's if you want a change watch — the educational script itself does not ship a state file (unlike a one-page tech detector); a jq diff is enough to start.
