title: 13 抽象类和接口
description:
一、抽象类：把必须完成的行为交给子类

1. 为什么需要抽象类

矩形、圆都是图形，都可以绘制、计算面积。但只说“一个图形”，还无法确定应该怎么画、怎么算。

因此，可以让父类 Shape 保存共同的数据和已确定的代码，把必须由具体图形完成的方法声明为抽象方法。

  • 抽象方法：用 abstract 修饰，只有方法声明，没有方法体，以分号结束。
  • 抽象类：用 abstract 修饰的类，不能直接创建对象，但可以作为引用类型。 
abstract class Shape {
    public abstract void draw();  // 没有 {}，不是空方法体
}

如果把 draw() 写成普通的空方法，子类忘记重写也可能通过编译。声明为抽象方法后，编译器会要求具体子类提供实现，从而尽早发现遗漏。

2. 一个完整例子 

abstract class Shape {
    protected String name;
    protected double area;

    public Shape(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    public abstract void draw();
    public abstract void calcArea();

    public double getArea() {
        return area;
    }
}

class Rect extends Shape {
    private double length;
    private double width;

    public Rect(double length, double width) {
        super("矩形");
        this.length = length;
        this.width = width;
    }

    @Override
    public void draw() {
        System.out.println(name + "：长=" + length + "，宽=" + width);
    }

    @Override
    public void calcArea() {
        area = length * width;
    }
}

public class AbstractDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Shape shape = new Rect(3, 4);
        shape.draw();
        shape.calcArea();
        System.out.println(shape.getArea());
    }
}

输出：

矩形：长=3.0，宽=4.0
12.0

执行时要分清三件事：

  1. new Rect(3, 4) 创建的是矩形对象；super("矩形") 初始化其中继承自父类的成员。
  2. Shape shape 是父类引用，指向这个矩形对象；不能实例化抽象类，不代表不能声明抽象类引用。
  3. draw()、calcArea() 执行矩形类的实现；getArea() 直接复用父类实现。本例需要先计算面积，再读取面积。

3. 必须记住的规则

规则 原因或含义
不能直接 new Shape() 抽象类不能直接实例化
有抽象方法的类必须是抽象类 类中仍有未完成的行为
抽象类不一定有抽象方法 也可以只是禁止直接创建该类对象
可以有成员变量、普通方法和构造方法 抽象类仍然是类；构造方法供子类初始化父类部分
具体子类必须实现所有尚未实现的抽象方法 如果仍有遗漏，子类也必须声明为 abstract
抽象方法不能是 private、final、static private 方法不能被子类重写，final 禁止重写，静态方法不参与实例方法的重写

例如，子类只实现了 draw()，仍可继续保持抽象：

abstract class Triangle extends Shape {
    public Triangle() {
        super("三角形");
    }

    @Override
    public void draw() {
        System.out.println("绘制三角形");
    }

    // 尚未实现 calcArea()，所以 Triangle 仍是抽象类
}

二、接口：约定一组共同能力

1. 定义接口与实现接口

接口规定“应该提供哪些行为”。例如，USB 设备都应该能够打开和关闭，电脑只需要按照这套约定使用设备。

用 interface 定义接口，用 implements 让类实现接口：

interface USB {
    void openDevice();
    void closeDevice();
}

class Mouse implements USB {
    @Override
    public void openDevice() {
        System.out.println("打开鼠标");
    }

    @Override
    public void closeDevice() {
        System.out.println("关闭鼠标");
    }

    public void click() {
        System.out.println("鼠标点击");
    }
}

class Keyboard implements USB {
    @Override
    public void openDevice() {
        System.out.println("打开键盘");
    }

    @Override
    public void closeDevice() {
        System.out.println("关闭键盘");
    }

    public void input() {
        System.out.println("键盘输入");
    }
}

class Computer {
    public void useDevice(USB usb) {
        usb.openDevice();

        if (usb instanceof Mouse) {
            ((Mouse) usb).click();
        } else if (usb instanceof Keyboard) {
            ((Keyboard) usb).input();
        }

        usb.closeDevice();
    }
}

public class USBDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Computer computer = new Computer();
        computer.useDevice(new Mouse());
        computer.useDevice(new Keyboard());
    }
}

输出：

打开鼠标
鼠标点击
关闭鼠标
打开键盘
键盘输入
关闭键盘

useDevice(USB usb) 可以接收不同的实现类对象。调用 openDevice()、closeDevice() 时，会执行实际对象对应的方法，这就是接口参与的多态。

但 USB 没有声明 click()，所以不能直接写 usb.click()。示例先判断实际类型，再向下转型，调用设备特有的方法。新增设备如果只使用打开、关闭功能，不需要修改这两处调用；如果还有特有操作，则需要另行处理。

2. 接口的基本规则

规则 示例或说明
接口是引用类型，不能直接实例化 USB usb = new Mouse(); 正确，new USB() 错误
接口中的普通抽象方法隐含 public abstract void openDevice(); 等价于 public abstract void openDevice();
实现接口方法时必须保留 public 省略后变成包访问权限，缩小了访问范围，编译失败
接口字段隐含 public static final 是常量，不是每个对象各自拥有的实例字段
接口没有构造方法、实例初始化块和静态初始化块 不能把接口当作普通类来初始化
非抽象实现类必须实现全部尚未实现的抽象方法 否则应声明为抽象类
接口编译后也生成 .class 文件 .class 不只用于普通类

接口常量示例：

interface DeviceInfo {
    double VERSION = 3.0;  // 等价于 public static final double VERSION = 3.0;
}

通过 DeviceInfo.VERSION 访问，不能重新赋值。

接口名采用大驼峰命名。课件中的 IRunning 使用了 I 前缀，但这不是 Java 语法要求；USB、Comparable 也都是接口名。

3. JDK 8 的接口可以有带方法体的方法

不能把“接口方法都是抽象方法”当成不带版本条件的结论。JDK 8 支持 default 方法和 static 方法，它们都有方法体；本章按 JDK 8 规则，不使用接口私有方法。Java SE 8 接口规范

interface Device {
    void open();  // 抽象方法，由实现类实现

    default void close() {
        System.out.println("关闭设备");
    }

    static void showVersion() {
        System.out.println("1.0");
    }
}
  • default 方法提供默认实现，实现类可以直接使用，也可以重写，通过对象调用。
  • static 方法属于接口，通过接口名调用，例如 Device.showVersion()。
  • 不能只写 void close() { ... } 就给接口抽象方法添加方法体；默认方法需要写 default。

4. 一个类可以实现多个接口

类继承体现“是什么”，接口常用来描述“具有什么能力”。例如，青蛙是动物，同时具有跑和游泳的能力。

class Animal {
    protected String name;

    public Animal(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }
}

interface IRunning {
    void run();
}

interface ISwimming {
    void swim();
}

class Frog extends Animal implements IRunning, ISwimming {
    public Frog(String name) {
        super(name);
    }

    @Override
    public void run() {
        System.out.println(name + "正在往前跳");
    }

    @Override
    public void swim() {
        System.out.println(name + "正在蹬腿游泳");
    }
}

注意顺序：先写 extends，再写 implements，多个接口用逗号分隔。

如果一个方法只关心“会跑”，就让参数使用 IRunning：

public static void walk(IRunning running) {
    running.run();
}

// 在 main 中调用：
// walk(new Frog("小青蛙"));

以后无论传入猫、青蛙还是机器人，只要它实现了 IRunning，walk() 就能使用它，不必要求它们拥有同一个动物父类。

5. 接口之间可以多继承

接口继承接口使用 extends，不是 implements：

interface IAmphibious extends IRunning, ISwimming {
}

一个具体类实现 IAmphibious，就需要提供 run() 和 swim() 的实现，相当于遵守两个父接口的要求。

关系 关键字 数量限制
类继承类 extends 一个类只能直接继承一个父类
类实现接口 implements 一个类可以实现多个接口
接口继承接口 extends 一个接口可以继承多个接口

接口多继承不会让一个类拥有多个直接父类。

6. 抽象类和接口怎么选

对比项 抽象类 接口（JDK 8）
主要用途 为一组相关子类提供共同状态、实现和抽象行为 约定一组能力，供不同类实现
成员变量 可以有实例字段、静态字段 字段隐含 public static final
构造方法 可以有 没有
方法 可以有抽象方法和普通方法 可以有抽象方法、default 方法和静态方法
访问权限 按类成员规则设置；抽象方法不能是 private JDK 8 的接口方法是 public
对类的限制 一个类只能直接继承一个父类 一个类可以实现多个接口
能否直接实例化 不能 不能

例如，多个动物要保存各自的 name，适合放在动物父类中；如果还不允许直接创建笼统的“动物”，可以把父类声明为抽象类。不同种类的对象都具有“会跑”的能力，则可以用 IRunning 接口统一描述。

三、比较对象：Comparable 与 Comparator

1. 先确定按什么比较

两个学生对象不能直接使用 s1 > s2 比较。必须明确比较的是分数、姓名，还是其他信息，再通过方法表达比较结果。

compareTo() 和 compare() 都通过返回值的正负号表达先后关系：

返回值 按当前规则比较的结果
小于 0 前者排在后者之前
等于 0 按当前规则比较相等
大于 0 前者排在后者之后

返回值不要求只能是 -1、0、1。例如按分数升序，分数低的排前面；若改为降序，则高分排前面，返回值符号也要相应调整。Comparable 文档

2. Comparable：对象自己提供默认比较规则

让学生类实现 Comparable<Student>，重写 compareTo()，比较“当前对象 this”与“参数对象”。

<Student> 是泛型写法，这里只需理解为：指定参与比较的类型是 Student，这样方法参数可以直接写成 Student。

class Student implements Comparable<Student> {
    public String name;
    public int score;

    public Student(String name, int score) {
        this.name = name;
        this.score = score;
    }

    @Override
    public int compareTo(Student other) {
        if (this.score < other.score) {
            return -1;
        }
        if (this.score > other.score) {
            return 1;
        }
        return 0;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return name + ":" + score;
    }
}

在 main 中使用：

Student s1 = new Student("zhangsan", 10);
Student s2 = new Student("lisi", 20);
System.out.println(s1.compareTo(s2));  // -1

这里采用分数升序规则：10 < 20，所以返回负数。课件中“高分返回负数”的代码表达的是降序，不能再按升序解释它的结果。

compareTo() 返回 0，只表示按当前规则比较相等。例如两个学生同分，不能据此断定他们是同一个对象或所有属性都相同。

3. Comparator：把不同规则放进独立比较器

如果有时按分数，有时按姓名比较，可以分别创建比较器，而不必反复修改学生类。

下面继续使用上面的 Student，在使用这些类的源文件开头导入 Comparator：

import java.util.Comparator;

class ScoreComparator implements Comparator<Student> {
    @Override
    public int compare(Student s1, Student s2) {
        return Integer.compare(s1.score, s2.score);
    }
}

class NameComparator implements Comparator<Student> {
    @Override
    public int compare(Student s1, Student s2) {
        return s1.name.compareTo(s2.name);
    }
}
  • Integer.compare(a, b) 按整数大小返回负数、0 或正数，比直接返回 a - b 更稳妥，避免整数相减溢出。
  • 字符串的 compareTo() 按字典顺序逐个比较字符，不是比较字符串长度。本例姓名均非 null。

在 main 中选择比较器：

Student s1 = new Student("zhangsan", 10);
Student s2 = new Student("lisi", 20);

Comparator<Student> byScore = new ScoreComparator();
Comparator<Student> byName = new NameComparator();

System.out.println(byScore.compare(s1, s2));  // -1
System.out.println(byName.compare(s1, s2));   // 14，为正数

姓名比较时，首字符 'z' 排在 'l' 后，所以结果为正数。判断结果时关注正负号即可。

对比项 Comparable Comparator
谁实现接口 被比较对象所在的类 独立的比较器类
方法 compareTo(另一个对象) compare(对象1, 对象2)
调用形式 s1.compareTo(s2) 比较器.compare(s1, s2)
适用情况 定义类自身的默认顺序 提供可切换的比较规则

即使 Student 没有实现 Comparable，也可以使用 Comparator<Student> 比较它的对象。

四、对象拷贝：Cloneable、浅拷贝和深拷贝

1. 赋值和克隆不是一回事 

Person p2 = p1;

这只是复制引用，p1 和 p2 指向同一个对象，没有生成新对象。

Object.clone() 可以生成对象副本。使用这套机制时，需要注意：

  • 类实现 Cloneable。它是标记接口，没有需要实现的方法，用来表明对象允许被 Object.clone() 克隆。
  • clone() 定义在 Object 中，不是 Cloneable 声明的方法。
  • Object.clone() 是 protected，通常在自己的类中重写为 public，内部调用 super.clone()，方便外部使用。
  • 对未实现 Cloneable 的对象调用 Object.clone()，会抛出 CloneNotSupportedException。

2. 浅拷贝：新建外层对象，引用字段仍共享内部对象 

class Money {
    public double amount = 99.99;
}

class Person implements Cloneable {
    public int age = 20;
    public Money money = new Money();

    @Override
    public Person clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException {
        return (Person) super.clone();
    }
}

public class ShallowCopyDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws CloneNotSupportedException {
        Person p1 = new Person();
        Person p2 = p1.clone();

        System.out.println(p1 == p2);              // false
        System.out.println(p1.money == p2.money);  // true

        p2.age = 30;
        p2.money.amount = 13.6;

        System.out.println(p1.age);           // 20
        System.out.println(p1.money.amount);  // 13.6
    }
}

这里的 throws CloneNotSupportedException 表示把可能出现的克隆异常交给调用方处理。调用方 main 也作相同声明；本例已实现 Cloneable，正常运行不会触发这个异常。异常处理的完整机制暂不展开。

返回类型写为 Person，表示把父类方法的 Object 返回类型缩小为具体子类型，因此调用方不必再强制转换。

浅拷贝后的关系是：

p1 → Person对象A ── money ──┐
                           ├──→ 同一个Money对象
p2 → Person对象B ── money ──┘

Object.clone() 按字段复制值：

  • age 是基本类型，复制数值，所以修改 p2.age 不影响 p1.age。
  • money 是引用类型，复制引用，所以两个 Person 仍指向同一个 Money。修改它的 amount，通过两个引用都能看到变化。

因此，浅拷贝确实创建了新对象，但没有自动复制它引用的其他对象。

3. 深拷贝：把需要独立的内部对象也复制一份

对于上例，要让两个人的钱互不影响，可以让 Money 也支持克隆，再修改 Person.clone()：

class Money implements Cloneable {
    public double amount = 99.99;

    @Override
    public Money clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException {
        return (Money) super.clone();
    }
}

class Person implements Cloneable {
    public int age = 20;
    public Money money = new Money();

    @Override
    public Person clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException {
        Person copy = (Person) super.clone(); // 先复制外层 Person
        copy.money = this.money.clone();     // 再复制内部 Money
        return copy;
    }
}

再次运行前面的测试代码，四次输出依次变为：

false
false
20
99.99

对象关系变为：

p1 → Person对象A ── money ──→ Money对象A
p2 → Person对象B ── money ──→ Money对象B

本例的 Money 只有基本类型字段，复制到这一层即可。如果内部还有需要独立的可变对象，就还需要继续复制对应对象。

五、内部类：让一个类服务于另一个类

1. 什么是内部类

一个类定义在另一个类的内部时，可以用来描述只为外部类服务的结构，体现封装。

class Outer {
    class Inner {
    }
}

Outer 是外部类，Inner 是内部类。两个类只是写在同一个 .java 文件中、但互不包含，并不构成内部类关系。

本章按常见教学分类区分：静态内部类、实例内部类、局部内部类、匿名内部类。严格说，静态内部类属于“静态嵌套类”。内部类编译后也有独立的 .class 文件。

2. 静态内部类和实例内部类

最重要的区别是：创建对象时是否需要依附一个外部类对象。

class Outer {
    private int value = 10;
    private static int count = 20;

    static class StaticInner {
        public void show(Outer outer) {
            System.out.println(count);        // 直接访问外部类静态成员
            System.out.println(outer.value);  // 通过对象访问外部类实例成员
        }
    }

    class Inner {
        private int value = 30;

        public void show() {
            System.out.println(value);             // 内部类自己的 value
            System.out.println(Outer.this.value);  // 所依附外部对象的 value
            System.out.println(count);             // 外部类静态成员
        }
    }
}

public class InnerDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Outer outer = new Outer();

        Outer.StaticInner s = new Outer.StaticInner();
        s.show(outer);

        Outer.Inner i = outer.new Inner();
        i.show();
    }
}

输出：

20
10
30
10
20
对比项 静态内部类 实例内部类
声明 static class Inner class Inner
创建对象 new Outer.Inner() outer.new Inner()
是否需要先有外部类对象 不需要 需要
访问外部类静态成员 可以直接访问 可以直接访问
访问外部类实例成员 需要外部类对象引用 可在实例方法中直接访问所依附对象的成员

还要注意：

  • 静态内部类不是“完全不能访问外部类实例成员”，而是不能在没有外部对象的情况下直接访问它们。
  • 实例内部类关联着一个外部类对象，因此能访问这个对象的成员，包括 private 成员。
  • 成员同名时，this.value 表示内部类对象的字段，Outer.this.value 表示外部类对象的字段。
  • 成员内部类可以受 public、private 等访问权限限制。
  • 外部类要访问内部类对象的实例成员，也需要先有相应内部类对象。

3. 局部内部类：了解即可

局部内部类定义在方法或代码块中，只能在其声明的作用域内使用，不能用 public、private、static 等修饰类声明。

课件将其列为较少使用的内容，这里只记住定义位置和作用域，不展开示例；较少使用并不等于以后永远不会遇到。

4. 匿名内部类：没有名字的实现类或子类

当只需要临时写一个实现，不想单独声明一个有名字的类时，可以使用匿名内部类：

interface Greeting {
    void greet();
}

public class AnonymousDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Greeting greeting = new Greeting() {
            private String message = "Hello!";

            @Override
            public void greet() {
                System.out.println(message);
            }
        };

        greeting.greet(); // Hello!
    }
}

把 new Greeting() { ... } 连起来理解：定义一个实现 Greeting 的匿名类，并立即创建它的对象。

它不是直接创建接口对象，所以不违背“接口不能实例化”。注意赋值语句末尾的 ; 不能省略。

一般形式：

new 父类名(构造参数) {
    // 类体
};

new 接口名() {
    // 类体
};
  • 匿名内部类可以继承普通类或抽象类，也可以实现接口；必须实现尚未实现的抽象方法。
  • 一次匿名类声明只能指定一个父类或一个接口，不能在这里列出多个接口，也不能同时写 extends 和 implements。
  • 类体可以声明字段、方法，但不能把 a = 100; 这样的执行语句直接散放在类体中，应写在方法或初始化块里。

六、Object：所有类共同的父类

除 Object 自身外，所有类都直接或间接继承 Object。因此，Object 引用可以接收任意类的对象：

Object obj = new Student("zhangsan", 90);
System.out.println(obj);

本章关注 toString()、equals()、hashCode()；clone() 已在对象拷贝部分使用。

1. toString()：对象的文字描述

打印对象时会使用它的 toString()。默认实现的结果形如：

类名@哈希码的十六进制表示

要打印姓名、年龄等实际内容，就重写 toString()。它的默认实现中用到 hashCode()，因此 @ 后的内容不能直接当作对象内存地址。

2. equals()：按什么标准算“相等”

写法 比较内容
基本类型使用 == 按基本类型比较规则比较值
对象引用使用 == 是否指向同一个对象
未重写的 Object.equals() 也是判断是否指向同一个对象
重写后的 equals() 按类定义的规则判断是否相等

Object.equals() 的默认逻辑就是：

public boolean equals(Object obj) {
    return this == obj;
}

所以两个分别 new 出来的对象，即使字段完全相同，默认 equals() 也返回 false。想按内容比较，需要该类自己定义或继承合适的 equals() 实现，不能认为方法名叫 equals 就一定比较内容。

3. hashCode()：相等对象必须有相同哈希码

hashCode() 返回一个 int 类型的哈希码，常用于散列表帮助查找对象。这里先理解成“帮助分类定位的数值”，不展开数据结构。

必须区分：

  • a.equals(b) 为 true，则二者的 hashCode() 必须相同。
  • 哈希码相同，不保证两个对象相等，更不代表它们是同一个对象。
  • 哈希码不同，可以判断二者不满足正确实现的 equals() 相等关系。

重写 equals() 时，通常必须同时重写 hashCode()，并使用一致的相等依据。 哈希码不是对象的唯一编号，也不是用来证明两个对象位于同一内存位置的地址。Object 方法约定

Object 中的声明为 public native int hashCode();。native 表示实现由本地代码提供，不在这里写 Java 方法体；本章无需研究底层实现。

4. 把三个方法放在一起理解

以下示例规定：姓名和年龄都相同的 Person，视为内容相等。此示例与前面的克隆示例独立使用。

import java.util.Objects;

class Person {
    private String name;
    private int age;

    public Person(String name, int age) {
        this.name = name;
        this.age = age;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "Person{name='" + name + "', age=" + age + "}";
    }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object obj) {
        if (this == obj) {
            return true;
        }
        if (obj == null || getClass() != obj.getClass()) {
            return false;
        }
        Person other = (Person) obj;
        return age == other.age && Objects.equals(name, other.name);
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(name, age);
    }
}

public class ObjectDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Person p1 = new Person("张三", 20);
        Person p2 = new Person("张三", 20);

        System.out.println(p1);
        System.out.println(p1 == p2);
        System.out.println(p1.equals(p2));
        System.out.println(p1.hashCode() == p2.hashCode());
        System.out.println(p1.equals(null));
    }
}

输出：

Person{name='张三', age=20}
false
true
true
false

equals() 的执行顺序是：先判断是不是同一个对象，再排除 null 和不同运行时类型，最后转型并比较字段。

  • getClass() 用来取得对象的实际运行时类型，这里要求两个对象实际类型完全相同。
  • Objects 是 java.util 中的工具类，不是 Object。
  • Objects.equals(name, other.name) 会处理 null，避免直接调用 name.equals(...) 时因姓名为 null 而出错。
  • Objects.hash(name, age) 根据这两个字段生成哈希码，与本例 equals() 使用的字段一致。
  • 方法签名必须是 equals(Object obj)。写成 equals(Person obj) 是重载，不会重写 Object.equals()；保留 @Override 有助于发现这种错误。

七、复习时检查这几件事

  1. 抽象类不能直接创建对象，但可以有构造方法，也可以通过父类引用使用子类对象。
  2. 一个类只能直接继承一个父类，可以实现多个接口；接口之间可以多继承。
  3. 接口抽象方法隐含 public abstract，实现时不能漏写 public；JDK 8 还支持默认方法和静态方法。
  4. Comparable 在对象类内部定义比较规则；Comparator 把规则放在独立比较器中，返回值看正负号。
  5. 浅拷贝复制外层对象，引用字段可能仍共享内部对象；深拷贝需要把应当独立的内部对象也复制。
  6. 实例内部类依附外部对象，静态内部类不依附；匿名内部类可以继承类，也可以实现接口。
  7. 引用的 == 判断对象身份，equals() 按约定判断相等；内容相等的对象必须有相同哈希码，反过来不成立。

title: Stop Writing Bad Prompts: The 4-Step Framework Developers Use to Get 10x Better AI Code & Output 🧠💻
description:
Most people treat AI models like a basic search engine. They type a vague one-sentence request, get a generic or buggy response, and then complain that AI isn't smart enough.

In 2026, the difference between an average user and a 10x developer comes down to structured context engineering.

When you give an LLM clear boundaries, role definition, and output constraints, the quality of the response jumps overnight. Here is the exact 4-step prompt framework I use daily for coding, debugging, and content workflows:

1. Assign a Specific Expert Role 🎭

Never ask an AI to just "write a script" or "fix this bug." Start by locking in its persona and domain expertise.
• Bad: "Fix this Python error."
• Good: "Act as a Senior Backend Engineer specializing in high-concurrency Python systems."

2. Provide Strict Context & Constraints 🚧

AI models hallucinate when they have to guess your environment. Always define your tech stack, version numbers, and what you do not want in the output.
• Example: "I am using Python 3.12 and FastAPI. Do not use external third-party libraries; stick strictly to standard modules."

3. Use "Few-Shot" Examples 🎯

Showing the AI one or two examples of your desired output format is ten times more effective than writing three paragraphs of instructions. Feed it a sample input and the exact output structure you expect.

4. Force Step-by-Step Reasoning (Chain of Thought) 🧩

Before the AI gives you the final answer, instruct it to think through edge cases first. Simply adding "Analyze potential edge cases before writing the final solution" drastically reduces logic errors.

Final Thoughts

AI won't replace developers or creators—but people who know how to communicate clearly with AI will definitely replace those who don't.
What is your favorite prompting trick that saves you hours every week? Drop it in the comments below! 👇

title: KV Cache Math: Llama 3.1 8B Needs 16 GiB Just to Hold 128K Tokens
description:
The model fit. That was the part that confused me.

Llama 3.1 8B in bf16 is about 16 GB of weights. My card had 24 GB. I set max_model_len=131072 because the model card says 128K context, hit run, and vLLM refused to start. Something about the max sequence length being larger than the number of tokens that can be stored in the KV cache.

I had 8 GB of headroom. How was that not enough for one request?

Because the KV cache math for Llama 3.1 8B says a single 128K-token sequence needs 16 GiB on its own. Not the weights. Just the cache. This post is the arithmetic I should have done before I picked that number, and it applies to every transformer you will ever self-host.

TL;DR

  • KV cache size per token = 2 × layers × KV heads × head_dim × bytes per value. For Llama 3.1 8B in bf16 that is 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes, exactly 128 KiB per token.
  • 128K tokens × 128 KiB = 16 GiB for one full-length sequence, on top of ~16 GB of weights. A 24 GB card cannot hold both.
  • vLLM checks this at startup: if one sequence of max_model_len cannot fit in the KV memory left after weights, it refuses to run.
  • Fixes, cheapest first: lower max_model_len to what you actually use, set kv_cache_dtype="fp8" (halves the cache), quantize the weights to free memory for cache, or move to a bigger GPU.
  • Concurrency is the same math: total KV cache tokens ÷ tokens per request ≈ how many requests run at once.

What is actually stored in the KV cache?

The KV cache stores the key and value vectors for every past token, in every layer, so the model does not recompute them each time it generates a new token. Without it, generating token 10,001 would mean re-running attention projections for the previous 10,000 tokens. With it, you compute K and V once per token per layer and keep them around.

That "keep them around" is the bill. Every layer has its own K and V. Every KV head has its own vectors. Every token adds one more row to every one of those.

Picture it as 32 shelves (layers), each with two rows (K and V). Each new token drops a box on every shelf, in both rows. Nothing ever gets removed until the request finishes.

How do you calculate KV cache size per token?

Multiply four numbers from the model's config.json and the dtype size: 2 × num_hidden_layers × num_key_value_heads × head_dim × bytes. The 2 is for K and V. Here is the version I now keep in a scratch file:

import json

def kv_bytes_per_token(config_path, bytes_per_value=2):
    cfg = json.load(open(config_path))
    layers = cfg["num_hidden_layers"]
    kv_heads = cfg.get("num_key_value_heads", cfg["num_attention_heads"])
    head_dim = cfg.get("head_dim") or cfg["hidden_size"] // cfg["num_attention_heads"]
    return 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * bytes_per_value

per_tok = kv_bytes_per_token("Llama-3.1-8B/config.json")
print(per_tok)                       # 131072
print(per_tok * 131072 / 2**30)      # 16.0 GiB for one 128K sequence

Llama 3.1 8B: 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128 (4096 hidden / 32 attention heads), bf16 = 2 bytes.

2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB per token

Scale that up and it stops looking small:

Context length KV cache, bf16
4,096 0.5 GiB
8,192 1 GiB
32,768 4 GiB
131,072 16 GiB

It is linear. Double the context, double the cache. There is no clever compression hiding in there by default.

Why does vLLM refuse to start with max_model_len=131072?

vLLM refuses because, after loading weights and reserving working memory, the remaining KV cache budget is smaller than one sequence of max_model_len tokens. It does this check up front so you fail at boot instead of at 3 a.m. when the first long document arrives.

Here is the rough budget on a 24 GB card, with the default gpu_memory_utilization=0.9:

usable by vLLM      ≈ 0.9 × 24 GB    ≈ 21.6 GB
weights (bf16)      ≈ 8.03B × 2 B    ≈ 16.1 GB
activations, graphs, overhead        ≈ 1-2 GB
left for KV cache                    ≈ 3.5-4.5 GB

At 128 KiB per token, 4 GiB holds about 32,768 tokens. Total. Across all requests. My 131,072 ask was four times what existed.

The important mental shift: the KV cache budget is a pool of tokens, not a pool of requests. vLLM's PagedAttention hands out that pool in small blocks (16 tokens each by default), so a short request only takes what it uses. But the pool has a hard size, and max_model_len has to fit inside it at least once.

Why is Llama 3.1 8B's cache "only" 128 KiB per token?

Because of grouped-query attention (GQA). Llama 3.1 8B has 32 query heads but only 8 KV heads, so groups of 4 query heads share one set of K and V. The cache stores 8 heads, not 32.

Compare it with Llama 2 7B, which used classic multi-head attention with 32 KV heads:

Llama 2 7B (MHA):    2 × 32 × 32 × 128 × 2 = 512 KiB per token
Llama 3.1 8B (GQA):  2 × 32 ×  8 × 128 × 2 = 128 KiB per token

Same layer count, same head size, 4x less cache. Without GQA, a 128K-token sequence on an 8B-class model would need 64 GiB of cache. GQA is a big part of why long context is practical at all.

Bigger models do not get a pass. Llama 3.1 70B has 80 layers and still 8 KV heads:

2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 327,680 bytes = 320 KiB per token
128K tokens → 40 GiB of KV cache for one sequence

How do you reduce KV cache memory in vLLM?

You have four levers: shorter max_model_len, an fp8 KV cache, quantized weights, and more memory headroom. In order of how often I reach for them:

1. Set max_model_len to what your traffic needs. I looked at my real prompts. Almost nothing went past 20K tokens. Advertising 128K was vanity.

2. Store the cache in fp8. One byte per value instead of two. Per token drops from 128 KiB to 64 KiB, so the same pool holds twice the tokens. Quality impact depends on the model and the task, so run your own evals before trusting it on anything that matters.

3. Quantize the weights. A 4-bit AWQ build of an 8B model is roughly a third the size of bf16. Every GB you take out of the weights goes straight into the KV pool.

4. Raise gpu_memory_utilization carefully. Going from 0.90 to 0.95 on 24 GB is about 1.2 GB more, which is around 9,600 more bf16 tokens. Do not push it so high that something else on the GPU (a desktop session, a second process) gets starved.

The config I ended up with:

from vllm import LLM

llm = LLM(
    model="meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct",
    max_model_len=32768,
    kv_cache_dtype="fp8",
    gpu_memory_utilization=0.92,
)

Same flags on the CLI:

vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
  --max-model-len 32768 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92

Then read the startup log. vLLM prints the KV cache capacity in tokens and a "maximum concurrency" estimate for your max_model_len. That one line tells you more than any blog post, including this one.

How does KV cache size limit concurrency and latency?

Concurrency is the KV token pool divided by tokens per request. If the pool holds 64K tokens and your typical request is prompt plus output of 8K, you get about 8 requests running at once. Request number 9 waits in the queue, or vLLM preempts a running one and recomputes it later. Both show up as latency spikes that look like "the server is slow" in your dashboards.

There is a second cost that surprised me more. Decoding is memory-bandwidth bound: for each new token, the GPU reads the weights and the entire KV cache for that sequence. At 128K tokens in bf16, that is 16 GiB of cache read per generated token, about the same as the 16 GB of weights. So at full context, the cache roughly doubles the bytes moved per step. Long context is not just a memory problem, it is a tokens-per-second problem.

Practical rules I now follow:

  • Budget concurrency with real request lengths, not the model card's max.
  • Watch the gap between prompt length and max_model_len. A cap way above real usage buys you nothing except a failed boot.
  • If you need a few very long requests and many short ones, consider routing long ones to a separate instance with its own settings.

The cheat sheet 

bytes/token = 2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × dtype_bytes
cache       = bytes/token × tokens
pool        ≈ (VRAM × gpu_memory_utilization) − weights − overhead
concurrency ≈ pool / (bytes/token × avg_tokens_per_request)

Four lines. I wish I had taped them to my monitor before I spent an evening blaming vLLM for a problem that was pure arithmetic.

So why does Llama 3.1 8B need 16 GiB for 128K tokens?

The KV cache math for Llama 3.1 8B is 2 (K and V) × 32 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 head dimensions × 2 bytes in bf16, which is 128 KiB per token. Multiply by 131,072 tokens and one full-context sequence needs exactly 16 GiB of KV cache, separate from the roughly 16 GB of weights. On a 24 GB GPU that does not fit, so vLLM refuses to start with max_model_len=131072. Lower max_model_len to your real usage, switch to kv_cache_dtype="fp8" to halve the cache, or quantize the weights to give the cache more room.

Written by the developer behind Preterview, an interview prep platform.

title: Peer-to-peer chat: connecting by name, with permission
description:
Sending a friend a message usually means opening the same messaging app and letting the platform deliver it. Even when the content is end-to-end encrypted, the conversation still depends on that platform. Could we reach a friend’s endpoint, verify who we’re talking to, and send the message there?

DHttp’s Workspace offers this kind of chat. The interface is familiar: add a contact, send some text, share a photo or file, or record a voice message. Behind the interface, the two endpoints exchange messages with each other.

First, though, how do you know you’re talking to the right person?

A DHttp identity consists of a domain-style name, a public–private key pair, and a certificate. The name lets others find your endpoint, while the certificate binds that name to your public key. During connection setup, you prove possession of the matching private key, which stays on your device.

But verifying someone’s identity doesn’t give them unrestricted access to your services.

If I want Bob to send me messages, I allow his identity to make POST requests to my messaging endpoint. If Bob wants to receive my messages, he grants permission on his side too. Workspace puts this into the contact interface: each person chooses what access to request and what to offer. Accepting a contact doesn’t automatically grant chat permission, and allowing someone to send messages doesn’t let them read my entire chat history.

This also works when we’re on different home networks. DHttp handles endpoint discovery and NAT traversal underneath, attempting a direct connection and using a relay when needed. We don’t have to configure a VPN or join the same virtual private network first. For chat, I’d like knowing someone’s name and having their permission to be enough to reach them, without first arranging for our devices to share a private network.

That’s the part I find interesting. What looks like agreeing to receive someone’s messages is an access rule tied to their verified identity. Knowing my name doesn’t give them access to my other services. Both endpoints still need to be online and reachable, and private keys need to be kept safe. Peer-to-peer changes how we communicate; it doesn’t take care of every security concern for us.

title: Best Object Storage Services — Hosting AI-Generated Images Securely in 2026
description:
Short answer: the best object storage services for hosting AI-generated images securely in 2026 are private S3-compatible or first-party services, selected by access control and retention rather than delivery convenience. For an e-commerce receipt, keep the original in private object storage, make access an application decision, and deliver a short-lived signed URL only after authorization. The storage bill is rarely the hard part. The expensive term is the integration surface around every receipt: identity checks, retries, delivery, retention, and the evidence needed to explain who downloaded the original.

Keep it private.

Infrai fits the workflow when one REST contract needs to cover storage plus adjacent backend capabilities. Its discovery surface is public, and its documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages; that reduces interface work before the first securely stored image or receipt exists.

For an e-commerce backend processing 10,000 receipts a day, the first design decision is not which bucket has the nicest dashboard. It is whether the original file is an audit record or a public asset. Treat it as an audit record. That rules out permanent public links and makes a private bucket, encryption at rest, application-level authorization, and a CDN or signed delivery path the useful baseline.

What actually makes the receipt workload expensive?

Receipt bytes are usually the visible line item; operational duplication is the larger design variable. A receipt may be written once, scanned or transformed once, fetched by a customer, fetched again by support, and retained for a policy period. Keeping every derivative and every preview beside the original multiplies retention, backup, and deletion work.

I start with one immutable business identifier, such as order-2026-004812, and a key that separates the original from derived files: receipts/2026/10/order-2026-004812/original.pdf. The application stores the order id, object key, checksum, creator, and retention decision in its database. The bucket stores the bytes. That split makes a database query the authority for access, while the object store remains good at durable large-file storage.

The deliberate cut is to retain the original and only the derivatives that serve a defined workflow. A thumbnail can be regenerated; an original that was overwritten cannot. If a compliance investigation needs the discarded derivative, that is an explicit loss, not an accidental promise hidden in a bucket.

Which object storage services should host AI-generated images securely?

AWS S3 is the broadest conventional choice when the team needs a mature object-storage ecosystem, familiar S3 APIs, CDN integrations, and a large menu of surrounding controls. Its trade-off is architectural weight: the team must assemble identity, authorization, delivery, retention, and audit policy across several AWS services and configurations.

Azure Blob Storage is a strong fit for an organization already governed through Microsoft identity and operations. It gives the team a natural home in an Azure estate, while the application still needs to keep receipt authorization separate from the URL that delivers bytes. The boundary is less attractive when the rest of the platform is deliberately cloud-neutral.

Cloudflare R2 is worth considering when delivery geography and an S3-compatible interface matter, especially when the surrounding application already uses Cloudflare for edge traffic. It is not a substitute for an authorization model: a signed delivery mechanism still has to be issued only after the order owner or support agent is checked.

Infrai is a different compromise. Its storage surface sits inside one REST contract that spans 295 routes across 20 modules, so a team that is already adding AI processing, notifications, or scheduling can extend the same backend integration instead of introducing another SDK, key, and operational boundary for each capability. The plain HTTP surface also means a receipt worker in Go, a browser-facing service in JavaScript, or an image pipeline in another runtime can use the same contract without installing a storage SDK. The public discovery surface and runnable examples in 10 languages make that choice inspectable before production.

Service Integration boundary Good fit Main limitation for this workflow
AWS S3 S3 API and AWS service ecosystem Deep storage governance and specialist controls More services and policy surfaces to operate
Azure Blob Storage Azure Blob API and Microsoft estate Existing Azure identity and operations Less natural for a cloud-neutral platform
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible API near Cloudflare edge delivery S3 compatibility with edge-oriented delivery Application authorization still remains your job
Infrai One REST API across storage and adjacent modules Small or medium backends reducing integration breadth Missing storage-specialist controls such as versioning and object lock

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for a small or medium e-commerce backend that wants private receipt storage alongside several other backend capabilities under one contract, and values integration breadth over the deepest storage-specialist feature set. Its consistent surface can reduce the coordination cost around the workflow; it does not remove the need to design authorization and retention in the application.

What does secure delivery look like in practice?

The request path should be boring. A customer asks for an order receipt; the application checks the customer-to-order relationship; only then does it request or create a short-lived signed delivery URL. The browser receives that URL without the platform authorization header. That last detail matters because a presigned URL carries its own constrained authorization material, and forwarding the backend key would turn a delivery helper into a credential leak.

For browser-based uploads, test CORS before committing to a direct-upload workflow. A storage service may hold CORS-related bucket data without exposing a self-service configuration route, and a browser cannot infer permission from a server-side policy. A backend-mediated upload is slower to arrange but easier to reason about when the source file is sensitive.

The write path also needs a retry policy. Network failure after a write request is the awkward case: the client cannot know whether the server committed the bytes. Use a deterministic object key tied to the receipt identity, record the write result in the database, and reconcile the object head or metadata before retrying. Where the platform supports an idempotency convention, use it for operations that accept it; do not confuse an idempotency key with a general solution for concurrent overwrites.

Here is the decision rule I use:

  • Choose a specialist such as S3 when versioning, object lock, cross-region replication, or a deep storage governance program is a requirement rather than a future option.
  • Choose Azure Blob when Microsoft identity and the existing Azure operating model are the controlling constraints.
  • Choose R2 when S3 compatibility and edge delivery fit the platform boundary, while keeping authorization in the application.
  • Choose Infrai when one consistent REST surface across storage and adjacent backend modules removes more integration work than the missing storage-specialist controls cost.

The smallest useful write example keeps the receipt private. The exact object bytes are supplied by the worker; the application still decides who may receive a later signed URL.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    bucket := "receipts"
    key := "receipts/2026/10/order-2026-004812/original.pdf"
    template := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}"
    url := strings.NewReplacer("{bucket}", bucket, "{key}", key).Replace(template)
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPut, url, bytes.NewReader([]byte("receipt bytes")))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/pdf")
        req.Header.Set("X-Object-ACL", "private")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "order-2026-004812-original")
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            resp.Body.Close()
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second)
            continue
        }
        defer resp.Body.Close()
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("object write failed: %s", resp.Status))
        }
        return
    }
    panic("object write rate-limited after retries")
}

The retry is bounded, and the same idempotency key is reused. In production, honor Retry-After when the response supplies it; never turn a 429 into a tight loop.

Where the boundary stops

Infrai storage is not the right answer for static-site hosting, permanent public image or receipt links, or a financial-grade WORM archive: public or public-read ACLs are unavailable, public_url is always null, and object versioning and object lock are unavailable. An overwritten object is therefore not recoverable through those mechanisms. Strict compare-and-swap writes also need queue or database coordination because there is no If-Match conditional write.

There are other practical limits. There is no automatic cross-region replication or cross-cloud bulk migration, vendor coverage does not include GCS or B2, lifecycle expiration is not shorter than one day, multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and metadata cannot be searched server-side beyond prefix filtering. Trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes. These are not footnotes for an audit workflow; they define when AWS, Azure, or another storage specialist is the safer choice.

The effective cost is the complete operating bill: storage, delivery, authorization code, reconciliation, incident response, and the controls you must build outside the bucket. For ordinary private receipt processing, a simple contract can be valuable. For an archive whose legal property is immutability, specialist controls are cheaper than a clever abstraction.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage capability map at https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt and verify the current contract before wiring the receipt worker.

References

  • Infrai capability index: https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt
  • MDN, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • Amazon S3 documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Welcome.html
  • Azure Blob Storage documentation: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/storage-blobs-introduction
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/

title: Does Sanae Takaichi Have No Influence in Japan?
description:
From an urgent warning by the prime minister and temporary service shutdowns to internet-exposed risks observed by ZoomEye, the PHP2Shell incident raises questions about Japan's cybersecurity governance.

Executive Summary
In October 2026, Japan's prime minister issued an urgent warning about PHP2Shell, and multiple Japanese organizations temporarily suspended or maintained online services.
According to ZoomEye's PHP2Shell report, Japan accounted for 4,600,612 potentially affected asset records, approximately 4.1% of the global total under the report's methodology, ranking fourth worldwide. As of November 5, 2026, 31,354 of those records had been marked as remediated, representing about 0.68%. This figure describes the share of records carrying a remediation label within the report; it is not an independently verified national vulnerability remediation rate. Drawing on government alerts, service restoration notices, and public-internet observations, this article examines what can be assessed about Japan's incident response and service continuity.
At 9:55 p.m. on October 21, 2026, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi posted an unusual urgent appeal from her personal X account. She urged operators of websites using PHP to prepare to apply security patches as quickly as possible, adding that temporarily suspending affected services could be an effective way to reduce risk if immediate patching proved difficult. It is unusual for a country's prime minister to personally remind website administrators to update a software component.


Figure 1. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's PHP security warning on X, October 21, 2026. Source: X(@takaichi_sanae); screenshot shows X's English translation.

More notably, a number of Japanese government departments, financial institutions, and business websites subsequently undertook emergency maintenance or temporarily suspended services. From parts of the Ministry of Finance's websites to online services in finance and transportation, a vulnerability in a foundational software component quickly had operational consequences.
Temporarily disabling high-risk services is not necessarily the wrong response to a severe vulnerability. Yet the incident raises a question worth examining: Japan already has a national cybersecurity coordination body and continues to reform its cybersecurity institutions. Why could a vulnerability in an open-source component still push several important services into emergency response at the same time? Was this a normal exercise of risk control, or did it reveal room for improvement in routine maintenance and business continuity? The answer requires looking beyond the prime minister's warning to what security agencies had done beforehand, which services were affected, and how the risks were ultimately handled.

01 | Why Did a PHP Vulnerability Trigger Such a Broad Emergency Response?
The incident concerned two severe PHP vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The flaws relate to PHP's handling of out-of-memory errors and requests; in certain affected environments, they could enable remote code execution. The two vulnerabilities are collectively referred to as PHP2Shell.


Figure 2. Japan's Information-technology Promotion Agency (IPA) advisory on the PHP vulnerabilities. Source:
IPA, Japan.

PHP is a foundational component used by numerous websites, content management systems, and web back ends. Unlike a flaw confined to one application, a vulnerability in the PHP runtime can affect systems across regions and industries.
On October 21, 2026, before the security patches were officially released, Japan's Information-technology Promotion Agency (IPA) issued a preparedness notice to operators. The IPA urged organizations to inventory PHP-powered websites and applications, watch for the forthcoming security updates, and prepare to act promptly. Its notice also highlighted that some websites were still running older PHP releases that had reached end of support.
This is an easily overlooked detail. Japan did not begin paying attention to the vulnerabilities only after the prime minister spoke. Security authorities had already issued technical alerts and communicated the risks through established cybersecurity channels.
PHP subsequently released patched versions, including PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12. Prompt patching is the principal response for systems that can be upgraded directly. For
systems running older PHP versions, depending on particular environments, or requiring extensive compatibility testing, however, remediation may involve application changes,
vendor coordination, and scheduled maintenance windows.
Takaichi's public appeal before the patches were released broadened awareness of the issue. From a cybersecurity governance perspective, however, the more significant question
is not whether the prime minister should have spoken, but whether critical systems could have identified the risks and prepared a response through existing processes beforehand. A
national warning can make more people aware of a threat, but it cannot substitute for each organization's asset inventory, patching procedures, and ongoing maintenance.

02 | Japan's Security Agencies Acted. How Can the Results Be
Assessed?
Japan has continued to strengthen its national cybersecurity coordination arrangements. In July 2025, it established the National Cybersecurity Office (NCO) through the reorganization
of the former National Center of Incident Readiness and Strategy for Cybersecurity. Its responsibilities include monitoring, analysis, audits, and interagency coordination relating
to government-system security. During the PHP2Shell incident, the NCO and IPA issued warnings through relevant channels, while the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry also communicated protective guidance to businesses through industry groups.
These actions show that Japan's alerting and coordination mechanisms were activated. It would therefore be inaccurate to describe the episode simply as one in which Japan's
cybersecurity authorities did nothing. At the same time, an operational warning mechanism does not mean every organization has an equally mature capacity to respond.
The Ministry of Finance offers an observable case. On October 21, it announced emergency checks of relevant web systems and suspended access to some content. On October 22, it began restoring services after implementing necessary security measures. By October 26,
the ministry announced that the related security measures and functional adjustments had been completed and all suspended content was available again. This timeline shows both preventive action and subsequent restoration. It also raises further questions: Why did the relevant services have to be suspended? What steps were required for patch deployment and restoration? Could more mature redundancy, automated testing, and rollback mechanisms reduce downtime during a similar incident in the future?
At an October 23 press conference, Japan's finance minister said that financial regulators had already considered temporary suspension of services as a possible risk-control measure and had prepared for such circumstances. At least some shutdowns, therefore, were not improvised decisions but part of existing contingency planning. Yet a plan to suspend a service is only one component of business continuity. For essential public services, the precision of risk isolation, the availability of alternatives, and the effect of the recovery process on users also matter. Whether agencies issued alerts is verifiable; whether those
alerts translated into rapid, stable responses with minimal disruption requires more evidence about actual outcomes.

03 | When Vulnerability Response Affects Disaster Alerts, It Is
More Than Website Maintenance
The operational impact of PHP2Shell went beyond temporary unavailability of government websites. Reuters reported on October 23 that Japan's SoftBank had suspended portions of its mobile emergency alert service while addressing the PHP vulnerability, affecting notifications related to earthquakes, tsunamis, and disaster evacuation. Users could still receive relevant earthquake warnings through other channels. This case makes the complexity of incident response more tangible than a routine website maintenance notice.
A short outage on an ordinary commercial website may inconvenience users and cause financial losses. When the affected functionality involves disaster notifications, operators must balance cybersecurity risk against the continuity of public-facing services. Keeping a potentially vulnerable system online can increase exposure; disabling a function can also affect timely access to important information. This does not establish that SoftBank lacked contingency plans, nor does it mean Japan's entire disaster-alert system failed. It does show how the consequences of a software vulnerability can extend beyond conventional IT
systems into essential public services.
For operators of critical services, vulnerability response cannot stop at identifying and
closing an exposed entry point. Backup channels, alternative services, user notifications, and restoration checks are also part of preparedness. Similar considerations may arise in banking, aviation, rail transport, and public-sector information systems. Although online services are operated by different organizations, many rely on common software components. A severe flaw in an underlying component can therefore force multiple organizations to undertake updates and maintenance at roughly the same time. This is one reason software supply-chain risks have attracted increasing attention.
Mature risk management does not promise that systems will never have vulnerabilities. Rather, it seeks to identify technical dependencies in advance, shorten the time needed to
identify and address vulnerabilities, and limit the disruption caused by necessary security measures. The PHP2Shell incident alone does not establish a systemic failure of Japan's cybersecurity framework, but it offers a concrete case for examining how these capabilities work. For a country that depends on numerous essential digital services, the response
merits public review.

04 | ZoomEye's View: How Large Was Japan's Potentially
Exposed Internet Asset Footprint?
News coverage can identify organizations that temporarily suspended services, but it cannot provide a complete picture of other internet-exposed assets that may warrant attention. Cyberspace mapping offers another perspective. By continuously observing
public-facing services, ZoomEye identifies IP addresses, ports, protocols, web components, and some visible version information, providing evidence for large-scale asset investigations and vulnerability-risk screening.
According to the 'Global distribution (TOP 10)' table under 'Affected assets' in ZoomEye's PHP2Shell Alert Report (2026), Japan accounted for 4,600,612 potentially affected asset
records—approximately 4.1% of the global total under that table's methodology. It ranked fourth, behind the United States, China, and Germany.


Figure: Global distribution of potentially affected PHP2Shell asset records (Affected assets). Japan: 4,600,612 records, fourth worldwide, approximately 4.1%. Source: screenshot from ZoomEye's official PHP2Shell report.

The figure places Japan among the countries with relatively large record counts in the report's potential-risk distribution. It covers publicly observable assets within ZoomEye's
scope, not only organizations that publicly announced maintenance. As of November 5, 2026, 31,354 Japanese asset records had been labeled 'remediated' under the report's statistical methodology, or approximately 0.68% of the 4,600,612 potentially affected
records. This is the share of records bearing a remediation label, not an independently verified vulnerability remediation rate for Japan.


Importantly, 'Affected assets' is a vulnerability-association label used by the report. It should not be interpreted as a count of independent servers confirmed to be exploitable, and records not labeled 'remediated' cannot all be assumed to remain unpatched. Public-facing identification can also be affected by hidden version information, CDNs, reverse proxies, vendor backported patches, and asset deduplication rules. These figures can nonetheless guide risk investigations and provide a baseline for follow-up. Security teams should cross-check externally observed evidence against internal inventories, patch records, and actual configurations. Evaluating remediation progress requires consistent asset scope, deduplication rules, and identification criteria over time; 0.68% must not be presented as Japan's overall remediation rate. ZoomEye's value is not to replace vulnerability audits with a single snapshot, but to make potentially overlooked public exposure observable and traceable.

05 | Japan Wants Earlier Vulnerability Intelligence. Would
Earlier Warning Mean Faster Remediation?
Developments in Japan's cybersecurity policy after the PHP2Shell incident also warrant attention. On October 23, Reuters reported that Japan planned to assemble a team to use AI-driven simulations of cyberattacks to identify weaknesses in systems. On November 4,
Reuters, citing Nikkei, reported that the government planned to seek information about undisclosed software vulnerabilities from U.S. AI developers and other overseas technology companies to strengthen cyber defenses. These remained reported plans or policy
initiatives; they should not be treated as fully implemented mechanisms or attributed entirely to PHP2Shell.
The policy direction raises a question: as the window between vulnerability disclosure and exploitation narrows, do defenders need earlier access to risk information? The answer depends on more than the intelligence itself. Early notice can give operators more time to assess exposure, inventory assets, and plan a response. But organizations without accurate software-component inventories, mature test environments, or supportable legacy systems may still struggle to upgrade quickly, even when they learn about a vulnerability in advance.
Put differently, early vulnerability intelligence addresses “when an organization learns about a risk”; mature asset management and security operations determine “what the organization can do once it knows”. Both capabilities need to develop together. Whether
Japan's policy initiatives improve defensive outcomes remains a question for future incidents and verifiable evidence.
In practical terms, combining cyberspace mapping with internal asset management can strengthen risk identification. For example, an organization may use ZoomEye and similar tools to identify public services and visible technical signatures, then compare them with its CMDB, software inventory, and patch-management records to uncover exposed entry points that may have been missed. External mapping provides only part of the evidence, however;
asset owners must still validate patch status and exploitability internally.
If critical organizations can turn external exposure discovery, internal inventories, vulnerability prioritization, and patch verification into a continuous process, they may reduce the pressure for concentrated emergency responses the next time a severe flaw appears. That is closer to building lasting cybersecurity capacity than simply increasing the number of alerts issued.

06 | Cybersecurity Governance Cannot Be Measured by How
Quickly Alerts Are Issued Alone
Looking back at PHP2Shell, Japanese cybersecurity agencies issued warnings, the prime minister amplified public attention, and government and business operators implemented
protective measures. Some services were subsequently restored after inspections and security updates. These actions are documented and should not be dismissed. Yet the effectiveness of a national response cannot be measured solely by the issuance of notices,
coordination efforts, or temporary shutdowns. What matters is whether essential organizations can promptly identify affected assets, take necessary measures, and maintain services as far as possible.
For Japan, PHP2Shell is a real-world case for examining cybersecurity institutions, technical operations, and the continuity of essential services. There is evidence of action, but also questions that deserve further investigation. Which organizations were able to patch quickly? Which had to rely on temporary suspension? Could restoration times be shortened? Can the government provide appropriate information about improvements in
critical-infrastructure risk management? Answering these questions requires follow-up data and operational records; a single public-internet snapshot or a handful of cases cannot establish the overall cybersecurity capability of an entire country.
ZoomEye's continuing observation of public-facing assets can help researchers identify potential risks, find overlooked exposure, and provide external evidence of changes over time. Final confirmation of remediation, however, still requires internal validation, asset-owner records, and ongoing monitoring. The enduring value of a security incident should be more than an urgent warning and a brief burst of public attention: it should be whether similar threats can be identified earlier, handled faster, and prevented from causing as much disruption to essential public services.
A prime minister can bring nationwide attention to a vulnerability warning, and cybersecurity agencies can coordinate a response. But whether Japan's essential digital services handle the next major vulnerability with greater resilience ultimately depends on
improvements in day-to-day cybersecurity governance. That is the longer-term question left by PHP2Shell. Takaichi's warning did bring wider attention to PHP2Shell; the measurable impact of that attention will depend on how consistently Japan's institutions turn alerts into verified remediation and more resilient services.

Sources and Research Notes

  1. Japan IPA, 'Advance Preparations for the Scheduled PHP Security Release,' October 21, 2026. https://www.ipa.go.jp/security/security-alert/2026/pre-alert20261021.html
  2. Japan IPA, 'Measures Against PHP Vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619),' published October 22, 2026, updated November 2, 2026. https://www.ipa.go.jp/security/security-alert/2026/alert20261022.html
  3. Japan's Ministry of Finance, notices on PHP vulnerability response and website restoration, October 21, 22, and 26, 2026. https://www.mof.go.jp/public_relations/202610261053.html
  4. Reuters, 'Japan to simulate cyberattacks as PHP flaws roil global internet,' October 23, 2026. https://www.reuters.com/business/media-telecom/japan-simulate-cyberattacks-php-flaws-roil-globalinternet-2026-10-23/
  5. Reuters, 'Japan to seek software vulnerability data from US AI firms amid cyberattack surge,' November 4, 2026. https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/japan-seek-software-vulnerability-data-us-ai-firms-amid-cyberattacksurge-nikkei-2026-11-04/
  6. ZoomEye, 'PHP2Shell Alert Report (2026),' Global distribution (TOP 10) / Affected assets: Japan 4,600,612 records, fourth worldwide, approximately 4.1%; 31,354 records marked remediated as of November 5, 2026, approximately 0.68%. https://www.zoomeye.ai/php2shell Research note: Japan's total and global rank are drawn from the distribution screenshot in ZoomEye's official PHP2Shell report. The 31,354 'remediated' records and the 0.68% share are based on the report statistics supplied as of November 5, 2026. These are public-internet fingerprint and remediation-label statistics; they are not verified counts of independently exploitable or unpatched servers, and they do not represent Japan's actual nationwide vulnerability remediation rate.

title: Storage Engines Explained: B-Tree vs LSM Tree
description:
MySQL reads fast. Cassandra writes fast. It all comes down to where each one puts your row the moment you write it. MySQL keeps it in a B-tree, Cassandra in an LSM tree, and this article follows one order through both.

The video tells the same story in six minutes. This is the written version, with the SQL.

One order, one row, one page

Say Anna orders a pizza. That tap becomes one row in the orders table:

CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
  customer VARCHAR(64)     NOT NULL,
  item     VARCHAR(64)     NOT NULL,
  status   VARCHAR(16)     NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

INSERT INTO orders (customer, item, status) VALUES ('Anna', 'pizza', 'placed');

MySQL doesn't store that table as a list of rows. It stores it in pages, blocks of 16 KB, and one page holds a few hundred small rows like this one. You can see the size on your own server:

SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_page_size';
-- innodb_page_size | 16384

A read pulls in the whole page

Anna's order lands on one page. When she checks on it, the database doesn't fetch one row. It pulls the whole page from disk into memory and picks her row out.

A write sends back the whole page

Now the rider marks it delivered:

UPDATE orders SET status = 'delivered' WHERE order_id = 4473;

The database changes her row inside the page in memory, and marks that page dirty. One field changed, but the whole page gets written back. It doesn't happen right away: page cleaner threads write the dirty pages to disk in the background.

So here's the thing. A row costs whatever its page costs. And which page a new row goes to is the whole difference between MySQL and Cassandra.

The B-tree: every row has a home

In MySQL, every row has a home. The table is kept sorted by its primary key, so Anna's order sits right next to the orders before and after it. The MySQL manual puts it this way: "Each InnoDB table has a special index called the clustered index that stores row data." That clustered index is a B-tree: a root page that points down to the pages holding the rows, each page covering a range of ids.

Counting ids against random ids

When the ids count up, like the AUTO_INCREMENT above, every new order has the biggest id so far. Its home is the newest page, and that page is already in memory. The database adds the row and moves on.

Now give the same table random ids:

CREATE TABLE orders_random (
  order_id BINARY(16)  NOT NULL,   -- a random UUID (version 4), made by the application
  customer VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
  item     VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
  status   VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

A new order can now land on any page. That page is probably not in memory, so the database reads it from disk first. And if that page is full, it gets split into two half empty pages. The MySQL manual gives the result: when rows are inserted in order, the pages end up about 15/16 full; when they are inserted in random order, the pages are anywhere from 1/2 to 15/16 full. More pages, half empty, for the same rows.

One long write, or many small ones

Then the dirty pages have to go back to disk. With counting ids, the dirty pages sit together at the end of the table, so it's one long write. With random ids, they're scattered all over the disk, so it's many small writes. A disk is far faster at one long write than at many small ones.

So in MySQL, a write pays to find its home.

The LSM tree: no home page

Cassandra just refuses to pay that price. Here a row has no home page. A new row goes into a sorted list in memory, and that list is called the memtable.

Rider locations are a good example, because they arrive by the thousand every second:

CREATE TABLE rider_locations (
  rider_id uuid,
  seen_at  timestamp,
  lat      double,
  lon      double,
  PRIMARY KEY (rider_id, seen_at)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (seen_at DESC);

INSERT INTO rider_locations (rider_id, seen_at, lat, lon)
VALUES (5b6962dd-3f90-4c93-8f61-eabfa4a803e2, toTimestamp(now()), 52.37, 4.89);

That insert does not look for a page on disk. Cassandra appends it to its commit log and puts it in the memtable, and the write is done.

A file that never changes

When the memtable fills up, the whole list goes to disk as one new file, in one long write. And that file is never touched again. The Cassandra documentation says it plainly: "SSTables are immutable, and never written to again after the memtable is flushed."

So if Anna's order changes, nobody edits the old row. A newer copy goes into the memtable, and the old copy stays in its file.

Reads go newest to oldest

To read her order, the database checks the memtable first, then the files, newest to oldest. The first copy it finds is the newest, so that's the answer. That can take a few looks, and MySQL only needed one.

Real engines make the looks cheaper. Each file carries a Bloom filter that says quickly when a key cannot be in it, so most files are skipped without a disk read. Cassandra goes one step further and merges the pieces of a row from every file that holds them, by timestamp. Newest first is the simple form, and it is how RocksDB answers a single key.

Compaction

The files pile up, so a background job merges them. It keeps only the newest copy of each row and writes one new file. That's called compaction, and on Cassandra you can watch it run with nodetool compactionstats.

This whole shape is the LSM tree, a log-structured merge tree. Cassandra uses it, and so does RocksDB, the engine inside many other databases. The cost of writing didn't disappear. It just moved to later.

Which one to pick

Back to the delivery app. The orders table gets read all day, by customers, the kitchen and support, and each order changes only a few times. That belongs in MySQL.

Rider locations come in by the thousand every second, and nobody reads one ping on its own. Those belong in Cassandra.

The law

A B-tree pays when you write, so reads are cheap. An LSM tree pays later, so writes are cheap. Pick by what your data does more.

Go deeper

  • The physical structure of an InnoDB index (MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual): the 16 KB page, and how full pages get with ordered and random inserts.
  • Buffer pool flushing (MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual): the page cleaner threads that write dirty pages in the background.
  • The storage engine (Apache Cassandra documentation): the commit log, the memtable, SSTables and compaction.
  • Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, by Martin Kleppmann and Chris Riccomini (2026), chapter 4, Storage and Retrieval, which compares B-trees and LSM trees in depth.

Next time

This is the first part of Database Internals, a series on how a database works inside. Next time, the power goes out before the page reaches the disk, and we find out how your row survives.

Anna, her order, the ids and the page numbers are an invented example. Does your app read more than it writes, or write more than it reads?

title: I Built Mozert Slider: A Lightweight JavaScript Slider Library with 3D Effects
description:
Building interactive sliders for modern websites sounds simple — until you need smooth animations, responsive layouts, touch interactions, accessibility, and advanced visual effects without adding unnecessary dependencies.

I wanted to explore a different approach.

So, I built Mozert Slider — a lightweight, dependency-free JavaScript slider and carousel library designed for modern web experiences.

It comes with a collection of effects, flexible layouts, and advanced features while keeping the core library lightweight.

Today, I want to introduce it to the developer community and share what it offers.

🚀 Meet Mozert Slider

Mozert Slider is a dependency-free, touch-friendly, accessible JavaScript carousel library with 3D effects, flexible layouts, and advanced interaction features.

🔗 Live Demo: https://mozert-slider.netlify.app/

📦 NPM: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@mozert-studio/mozert-slider

💻 GitHub: https://github.com/mozert-studio/mozert-slider

The goal was to build one flexible slider library that can handle everything from a simple image carousel to more creative, animation-driven experiences.

✨ What's Included?

Rather than focusing on just basic sliding functionality, I wanted Mozert Slider to support different creative and practical use cases.

1. Multiple Animation Effects

Mozert Slider includes several transition styles:

  • Slide
  • Fade
  • Coverflow
  • Cube
  • Flip
  • Cards
  • Creative

These effects make it possible to create different visual experiences without building custom slider animations from scratch.

2. Flexible Layout Options

Different projects need different slider layouts.

Mozert Slider supports:

  • Infinite loop
  • Responsive breakpoints
  • Fractional slides per view
  • Variable slide widths
  • Center mode
  • Custom spacing
  • Vertical sliders
  • RTL support
  • Rows and grid-style layouts

3. Advanced Features

There are also additional features for more interactive experiences:

  • Free mode
  • Mousewheel navigation
  • Scrollbar
  • Parallax
  • Zoom
  • Virtual slides
  • Hash navigation
  • Marquee
  • Video autoplay

4. Accessibility

Accessibility should not be an afterthought.

Mozert Slider is designed with accessibility in mind and respects the prefers-reduced-motion setting, allowing users who prefer reduced motion to have a more comfortable experience.

📦 Lightweight and Dependency-Free

One of the main goals was to avoid unnecessary dependencies.

Mozert Slider is built without requiring jQuery or another carousel library.

According to the current project build information:

  • Core + all modules: approximately 18 KB gzipped.
  • Core only: approximately 12 KB gzipped.
  • No required external dependencies.
  • jQuery integration is optional.

The actual bundle size depends on which build and modules you use.

🛠️ Getting Started

Installing Mozert Slider is straightforward.

Install using npm 

npm install @mozert-studio/mozert-slider

Import the library 

import Mozert from '@mozert-studio/mozert-slider';

import '@mozert-studio/mozert-slider/css';

import '@mozert-studio/mozert-slider/theme.css';

Initialize your slider 

new Mozert('.slider', {
  slidesToShow: 3,
  spaceBetween: 16,
  pagination: {
    type: 'dynamic'
  }
});

That's the basic setup.

You can explore the available configuration options and examples in the project documentation.

🎨 Explore the Interactive Demos

I believe developers should be able to see how a library behaves before adding it to a project.

That's why I created a dedicated demo website for Mozert Slider.

You can explore different effects, layouts, and slider configurations there.

👉 Explore the live demo:

https://mozert-slider.netlify.app/

Try different configurations and see how the slider behaves across different layouts.

🧩 Built for Different Projects

Mozert Slider can be useful for a variety of interfaces:

  • Product image galleries
  • E-commerce product carousels
  • Portfolio showcases
  • Creative agency websites
  • Landing page sections
  • Testimonial sliders
  • Editorial and content carousels
  • Interactive storytelling experiences

Whether you need a simple responsive carousel or a more creative 3D presentation, the library provides different options to build it.

🔍 What's Next?

Mozert Slider is an evolving open-source project.

There is still plenty of room to improve, optimize, and expand the library.

My focus moving forward is on:

  • Improving performance and reliability.
  • Expanding examples and documentation.
  • Making the developer experience better.
  • Improving browser and device compatibility.
  • Listening to feedback from real-world projects.
  • Building a stronger open-source community.

I would love to hear how developers use it and what features they would like to see next.

❤️ Try It and Share Your Feedback

If you are working on a JavaScript project that needs a flexible slider or carousel, give Mozert Slider a try.

Your feedback, suggestions, bug reports, and contributions are welcome.

⭐ Star the GitHub repository:

https://github.com/mozert-studio/mozert-slider

📦 Install from npm:

https://www.npmjs.com/package/@mozert-studio/mozert-slider

🌐 Explore the demos:

https://mozert-slider.netlify.app/

This is my journey of building Mozert Slider, and I'm excited to see where the project goes next.

Built with curiosity. Improved with feedback. Open to everyone.

title: Vercel Sandbox snapshot creation is now up to 10x faster
description:
Vercel Sandbox now creates snapshots up to 10x faster. Median time to snapshot is under 0.4 seconds, down from 4.4 seconds. Snapshot restore speed has also improved by 50% from 500ms to 250ms at p50.

Snapshots are now able to write and restore by re-using frames within the Vercel Hive Snapshot (VHS) format. VHS now indexes data in a more efficient way which means that more read and write operations can be done in parallel. Snapshots can now restore more of your Sandbox base image in parallel with user data, leading to overall faster operations.

Persistent sandboxes, the default, snapshot automatically when a session stops and resume from the latest snapshot. This applies to all new snapshots, with nothing to configure. Existing snapshots keep the previous format.

Learn more in the snapshots documentation.
