title: Importing Etsy reviews into Shopify or Judge.me: what's free, what's legal, what breaks
description:
Moving an Etsy shop to Shopify is the easy half. The reviews are where people get stuck — not because the data is hard to move, but because there are three different routes with different coverage, and one of them is illegal if you do it wrong.

This is the practical version: which route to try first, what each one actually carries over, and where the FTC line sits.

Route 1 — Judge.me's free Etsy sync (try this first if you use Judge.me)

If Judge.me is your review app, they ship a native Etsy import on the free plan. You connect the shop, it pulls reviews over, and it keeps syncing on a schedule.

This is the right answer for most people, and it costs nothing. Two things to check before you rely on it:

  • Coverage. A sync typically covers your active listings with written reviews. Rating-only reviews, reviews on deactivated or deleted listings, and reviews on listings you've since restructured often fall outside it.
  • Portability. A sync puts the reviews inside Judge.me. It doesn't hand you a file. If you later switch review apps, or want an offline archive, you're back to square one.

So: free, fast, and good — as long as your shop is simple and you're staying on Judge.me.

Route 2 — Etsy's own review download (free, undocumented fields)

Etsy does let sellers download their reviews. It's buried:

Shop Manager → Settings → Options → Download Data
  → Take your data with you → Download Your Reviews

Most sellers don't know it exists, which is why "Etsy won't give you your reviews" is such a common (and wrong) claim online.

The catch is that Etsy's help article doesn't publish the column list. You get a file; you don't get a schema. So open it in a spreadsheet before you build anything on top of it, and verify four things:

  1. The review body and date — the obvious ones.
  2. Your seller replies — these are conversational context, and they're usually the first thing lost in a migration.
  3. The original full-resolution buyer photo URLs — not thumbnails. Thumbnail URLs are usually resized derivatives and look bad on a storefront.
  4. The listing each review belongs to — a listing ID or URL you can map to a Shopify product handle.

If all four are there, you may not need any tool. If one is missing, you need a different source for that column, because you cannot reconstruct a seller reply or an original photo URL after the fact.

Route 3 — a structured CSV you generate yourself

The manual version: collect rating, date, reviewer name, body, listing URL and photo URLs into a spreadsheet, then import.

The reason people build tools for this is that the last two columns are the annoying ones — photo URLs are often only present in the page's rendered markup, and listing URLs need normalising to something you can join on.

However you get there, the import is the same shape: one row per review, joined to a product on a stable key.

review_date, rating, reviewer_name, body, picture_urls, product_handle, seller_reply
2026-03-14,  5,      @someone,      "Arrived...", https://i.etsystatic.com/.../il_fullxfull.123.jpg, silk-scarf-no-7, "Thank you!"

Map product_handle (or product_id) to your Shopify handle, not the product title. Titles get edited; handles are what the storefront resolves. If you match on title, a rename silently drops the review.

Where the legal line is

This part gets skipped in most tutorials, and it's the part that can actually cost you.

The FTC's Rule on Consumer Reviews and Testimonials (16 CFR Part 465, in force since October 2024) targets fake and deceptive reviews. Two provisions matter when you migrate:

  • Reviews have to be for the same product. You can bring your own reviews with you when you move the same product to a new storefront. You cannot take reviews written about product A and display them on product B — even if you made both, even if they're similar.
  • Reviews have to come from your own customers. Displaying another seller's reviews as if they were yours is a misrepresentation, whether you scraped them, imported them, or a supplier handed them to you.

The practical rule for a migration: import reviews product-by-product, from your own shop, and don't merge variants that are meaningfully different products. If you consolidated five Etsy listings into one Shopify product, that's usually fine (same items, different packaging). If you folded a sticker listing's reviews into a mug listing because "it's all my shop", that's the fact pattern the rule is aimed at.

Two more things people get wrong:

  • Don't filter to only 5-star reviews. Selective display that misrepresents the overall rating is a separate problem from fake reviews.
  • Public review data is for research, not for your storefront. Ranking a competitor's bestsellers by review volume is legitimate market research. Copying their buyers' words onto your product page is not.

A short checklist

  1. Using Judge.me? Try the free Etsy sync first — then check whether rating-only and inactive-listing reviews came across.
  2. Want a file you own? Use Etsy's official download, and inspect the columns before planning around them.
  3. Either way, verify seller replies, original photo URLs and listing identifiers survived.
  4. Import per product, join on handle, keep your own reviews only.
  5. Keep an offline copy. Review history is the one asset you can't re-earn retroactively.

Disclosure: I build Etsy Review Studio, a Chrome extension that exports your own Etsy reviews to a CSV with a documented 13-column schema and generates it locally on your machine. Free tier covers 40 reviews. It's independent and not affiliated with Etsy, Shopify, Judge.me or Loox — and if the free options above cover your case, use them instead.

title: Will AWS Emulator Replace the AWS Blocks Mocks? What Running Both Revealed About a Third Testing Layer
description:
On November 11, 2026 (US time), AWS released AWS Emulator. It is a tool that receives your AWS SDK and AWS CLI calls on your own machine instead of in the cloud, and answers them with the same shape of response that AWS would return.

  • AWS Emulator on GitHub

When I saw the announcement, the first thing that came to mind was this:

Do the AWS Blocks mocks still have a reason to exist?

I have been making small contributions to AWS Blocks since it entered public preview. In a previous post, I looked at how Blocks differs from Amplify and App Studio.

One of the defining features of Blocks is that npm run dev runs the whole application on your machine without an AWS account. That works because every Block ships its own local implementation, in other words a mock. Now AWS itself has released a tool that reproduces AWS locally, so I wanted to know whether the two collide or fit together.

This post looks at the source code of both repositories, the raw data behind the fidelity scores that AWS Emulator publishes, and the results of running the same operations against the Blocks mocks and against AWS Emulator. It is one user and contributor's reading, not an official AWS position or roadmap.

The short answer: not a replacement, but a third layer

Here is where things stand today.

  • The two tools replace AWS at different layers. Blocks swaps in its mock at import time. AWS Emulator answers at the AWS API boundary.
  • The Blocks documentation states that no emulator is needed, and the AWS SDK is never loaded during local development. There is no place for AWS Emulator in today's Blocks developer experience.
  • At the same time, Blocks has no layer of tests that checks how AWS responds to what its AWS implementations send. Each Block's design document (DESIGN.md) lists many differences between the mock and AWS, and many of them are left to be verified in a sandbox (a temporary environment deployed to real AWS).
  • AWS Emulator publishes how closely it matches AWS as a "fidelity score". Taking only the operations that Blocks actually calls, data reads and writes (DynamoDB, S3, SQS and others) matched AWS 80 to 100 percent of the time. Realtime delivery to browsers, email sending, and sign-in flows still score low.
  • I started AWS Emulator on GitHub Actions and pointed the Blocks AWS implementations at it without changing any code. KVStore returned the same results as the mock, and FileBucket returned exactly the S3 behavior described in DESIGN.md (lowercased metadata keys and delete-marker handling).
  • IAM, data operations on the database (PostgreSQL), throttling, and eventual consistency remain gaps that AWS Emulator does not close.

So the most I can say today is that AWS Emulator does not replace the mocks, but has room to sit between the mocks and the sandbox as a third layer. On top of that, the place where it felt most useful first was not the developer's machine but the Blocks project's own tests.

A quick recap of AWS Blocks

AWS Blocks is an open-source framework that entered public preview in June 2026. It lets you build backends on AWS in TypeScript.

  • AWS Blocks on GitHub

Its building unit is the "Block". There is KVStore for key-value data, FileBucket for files, AsyncJob for background work, Realtime for pushing updates to browsers, several Auth Blocks for sign-in, and more. Each one is distributed as an npm package.

A Block bundles three things: the infrastructure definition for AWS (AWS CDK), the implementation that calls AWS services (AWS SDK), and a local implementation for running on your machine. All three share the same typed API, so your application code does not change between them.

In your backend code, you define a Block like this:

import { Scope, KVStore } from '@aws-blocks/blocks';

const scope = new Scope('my-app');
const sessions = new KVStore<string>(scope, 'sessions');
// Inside an API, call sessions.put('user-1', 'hello') or sessions.get('user-1')

There is no DynamoDB table name and no SDK call in this code. When you deploy, KVStore becomes a DynamoDB table, and Blocks also sets up the permissions that let your Lambda functions read and write it.

A Blocks application can run in three ways, and this post depends on keeping them apart.

Mode Command Summary
Local development npm run dev Every Block runs its local implementation. No AWS account needed
Sandbox npm run sandbox Deploys a temporary, per-developer backend to real AWS and runs on real services
Deployment npm run deploy Deploys the whole application to AWS with CDK (CloudFormation)

The CLI reference covers the commands in detail.

In this post, "mock" means the local implementation from the first row, and "sandbox" means the temporary environment on real AWS from the second row.

What AWS Emulator is

AWS Emulator reproduces the AWS APIs on your machine. You don't need an AWS account, and your requests go to the emulator instead of AWS. There is no additional service fee.

You start the emulator and point the AWS CLI or an AWS SDK at its local endpoint. Your application and test code stay the same, and they read and write resources that live inside the emulator. The state is kept in memory and disappears when you stop the emulator.

It ships as RPM and Debian packages for Linux, and as a Dockerfile for macOS and Windows. There is also an embedded mode for Rust tests that runs an isolated emulator per test, and a skill for AI coding agents so you can let your agent handle the setup.

The service definitions are generated from the same API models that the AWS SDKs are built from. For any service whose API model is published, the shape of requests and responses lines up with AWS. When AWS adds a service or an API, it appears in the emulator, and its behavior is filled in release by release. Operations whose behavior is not implemented yet return 501 Not Implemented.

What stands out most in this release is how the emulator was built. According to the AWS senior principal engineer who started the effort, the code was written entirely by autonomous AI agents. The team has not written or reviewed any of it.

  • How we built the agents that built AWS Emulator

The starting prompt had three steps: write tests with the AWS CLI, iterate on them until they pass against real AWS, then build an in-memory implementation that passes the same tests.

Tests that have been confirmed against real AWS become the reference, and the agents keep fixing the implementation against them. These reference tests are called fidelity tests, and their results are published with every release as fidelity scores. According to the official explanation, the emulator matches AWS most closely today for control plane APIs, such as creating and deleting resources. Fidelity for the data plane (the main function of a service, such as reading and writing data), and support for CloudFormation and the AWS CDK, varies by service. The analysis later in this post uses the raw data behind these scores.

The repository is open source, but it does not accept pull requests. CONTRIBUTING.md explains that AI agents keep the emulator up to date with AWS, and asks for issues instead.

AWS also states its limits clearly. The README says not to use the emulator for production workloads or to test security. The security page adds that it does not evaluate IAM policies or resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator, and the reverse can also happen.

Tools that reproduce AWS locally are not new. The AWS SAM CLI can run Lambda functions and API Gateway locally, and the third-party LocalStack has been around for a long time. In 2025, AWS itself added LocalStack integration to the AWS Toolkit for VS Code.

What is new about AWS Emulator is that it is official, that it generates nearly every service mechanically from the API models, and that it keeps publishing how closely it matches AWS as a score.

Two kinds of "local"

Both tools run locally, but they replace AWS at very different points.

AWS Blocks switches implementations with Node.js conditional exports. You list a file for each condition under exports in package.json, and Node.js picks the file that matches the current context. Here is what the KVStore package.json contains:

"exports": {
  ".": {
    "browser": "./dist/index.browser.js",
    "cdk": { "default": "./dist/index.cdk.js" },
    "aws-runtime": "./dist/index.aws.js",
    "default": "./dist/index.mock.js"
  }
}

By default you get the mock. During CDK synthesis you get the CDK construct. Only when the backend is bundled for Lambda does the aws-runtime condition load the implementation that uses the AWS SDK. The local development guide says that each Block ships a local implementation with the same typed API as production, so no emulator or additional tooling is required. It also says the AWS SDK is never loaded during local development.

AWS Emulator works one layer below. As described above, it receives the SDK calls themselves and returns the same shape of responses and errors as AWS.

Here is how the two relate:

Application code (new KVStore(...))
  │
  ├─ npm run dev (default) ──→ Blocks mock          … reproduces the Blocks API
  │
  └─ aws-runtime condition ──→ Blocks AWS implementation
                                  │
                                  └─ AWS SDK
                                       │
                                       ├─ AWS_ENDPOINT_URL ──→ AWS Emulator  … reproduces the AWS API
                                       │
                                       └─ AWS

The two also reproduce different things.

The Blocks mock reproduces the Blocks APIs, such as KVStore and FileBucket. When you write a value to KVStore, the mock stores it directly in local files or memory without going through DynamoDB. No DynamoDB request or response appears anywhere.

AWS Emulator reproduces the AWS APIs, such as DynamoDB and S3. It answers the requests that arrive from an SDK or the CLI in the same shape that DynamoDB or S3 would.

Because they reproduce different things, AWS Emulator has no place in today's Blocks developer experience. npm run dev never calls the SDK, so there is nothing to point at the emulator in the first place.

Neither repository mentions the other. The only hit for "emulator" in the Blocks repository is a pull request about the Android emulator.

The gap in how Blocks tests itself

Does that mean AWS Emulator has nothing to offer Blocks? Not quite. What caught my attention was how Blocks tests its AWS implementations.

KVStore has parity tests that keep the mock and the AWS implementation behaving the same way. Here is how the AWS implementation is exercised:

/**
 * Capture what the AWS runtime would send to DynamoDB and control what it reads
 * back, without touching the network. Real `KVStore`, real `PutCommand`.
 */
function captureAws(id: string, respond: () => any = () => ({})) {
  const store = new AwsKVStore<string>({ id: 'root' } as any, id);
  const sent: any[] = [];
  (store as any).docClient.middlewareStack.add(
    (_next: any) => async (args: any) => {
      sent.push(args.input);
      return { output: respond() };
    },
    { step: 'initialize', name: 'kv-parity-intercept', override: true },
  );
  return { store, items: () => sent };
}

The code does exactly what the comment says, in three steps.

First, it creates the real AWS implementation of KVStore (AwsKVStore). Next, it adds a middleware to the DynamoDB client inside it. Middleware in the AWS SDK for JavaScript v3 lets you run code before and after a request is sent. This middleware records the request in sent, never sends it to DynamoDB, and returns whatever respond() returns as the response.

In other words, the DynamoDB response the test receives is a value the test author prepared in respond. Real DynamoDB is never called from start to finish.

So this approach can verify what the AWS implementation sends, and nothing more. How DynamoDB responds stays within what the test author assumed.

The same gap shows up in each Block's DESIGN.md. Many Blocks have a "Mock vs AWS Behavior Differences" table that honestly lists where the mock and AWS behave differently, and "verify in a sandbox" appears again and again in the mitigation column. For FileBucket, the differences include how S3 handles delete markers, lowercased user metadata keys, and the error codes returned for an unknown versionId.

There is also one telling pull request. PR #999, merged in October, checks the CDK bootstrap status before deploying. Its verification notes say the maintainer pointed AWS_ENDPOINT_URL at a hand-made fake STS/SSM endpoint to exercise the real SDK clients and error handling without an AWS account.

The maintainers needed a way to reproduce AWS responses locally and built one on the spot. That is exactly where AWS Emulator could fit.

Running the same operations against the mock and the emulator

To see what this gap looks like in practice, I wrote a small script that runs the same operations against both the Blocks mock and the Blocks AWS implementation pointed at AWS Emulator. As I explain later, the place where AWS Emulator felt most useful first was testing in CI. So instead of my own machine, I started the emulator on a GitHub Actions Linux runner.

Setting up the emulator was just a matter of installing the published RPM and starting it. On startup it writes three files to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/: config with the endpoint and certificate location, emulator_credentials with the credentials, and the self-signed certificate ca.pem. To run the AWS implementation, I set these environment variables and loaded the Block with the aws-runtime condition:

D=~/.aws/emulator/9297
export AWS_CONFIG_FILE=$D/config
export AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE=$D/emulator_credentials
export NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=$D/ca.pem   # make Node.js trust the self-signed certificate
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=https://127.0.0.1:9297
node --conditions=aws-runtime --import tsx probe.ts --aws

I did not touch the Blocks AWS implementation code. Neither KVStore nor FileBucket hard-codes an endpoint when creating its SDK client, so the environment variables alone were enough to redirect them.

The table and bucket did have to exist beforehand, though. They are normally created by CDK at deploy time, so I created them directly with the SDK. A DynamoDB table starts in the CREATING state, and writing to it right away returns ResourceNotFoundException. That matches real DynamoDB, and I had to wait about three seconds before the table was usable. The mock never has this wait.

I used AWS Emulator 1.0.322 and the latest Blocks packages on npm (blocks 0.9.0, bb-kv-store 0.4.0, bb-file-bucket 0.4.0). For KVStore and FileBucket, I picked operations that DESIGN.md lists as differences.

Operation Blocks mock AWS implementation + AWS Emulator
Write to KVStore and read it back The written value The written value
Write to an existing key with ifNotExists ConditionalCheckFailedException ConditionalCheckFailedException
Write with an expired TTL, then read null null
Write a 450 KB value ItemTooLargeException ItemTooLargeException
Write to FileBucket with metadata Owner, then read Key stays Owner Key becomes owner
Read with an unknown versionId null null
Restore an unknown versionId NoSuchVersion NoSuchVersion
Overwrite across a delete marker, permanently delete the current version, then read replacement null

The four KVStore rows returned the same results from the mock and from the emulator. The behavior that DESIGN.md describes as aligned between the mock and AWS came back the same way through the AWS implementation.

The differences appeared in two FileBucket rows.

Metadata keys came back unchanged from the mock and lowercased from the emulator. DESIGN.md explains that S3 lowercases user metadata keys, so code that reads metadata.Owner works locally and gets undefined on AWS. The emulator reproduced that S3 behavior. A difference that DESIGN.md could only describe in words became visible as a test result.

The last row is easier to follow with S3 versioning in mind. A bucket with versioning enabled keeps past versions when you overwrite or delete an object. Deleting by key alone does not remove data. Instead, a "delete marker" is stacked on top as the latest version, and reads then see the object as deleted. Only deleting a specific version (by versionId) removes that version permanently.

The steps follow the DESIGN.md table exactly:

put('old')
delete()               ← versioning is on, so a delete marker is added
put('replacement')
delete(current versionId) ← permanently deletes replacement
get()

DESIGN.md says the mock returns old here, while S3 makes the earlier delete marker current and treats the key as deleted. The emulator returned null, exactly as described for S3.

The latest mock on npm, however, returned replacement, the version that had just been permanently deleted, not old. It turns out this mismatch was already fixed by PR #693, merged the day after 0.4.0 was published. The fix replaces the local current copy with the next version when the current version is permanently deleted. Reading the code on main, the mock should now return old as DESIGN.md says. The fix has not been released yet, so the npm version still shows the old behavior.

That leaves three different answers to the same steps: null from the emulator reproducing S3, old from the mock on main, and replacement from the published mock. The difference between old and null is documented in DESIGN.md as a known gap.

This is not something you are likely to hit in day-to-day development. Still, it shows the nature of the gap well. Even with a table of mock-versus-AWS differences and tests of what the AWS implementation sends, this kind of drift cannot be caught by any single test unless there is a layer that checks how AWS actually responds. You only find it by laying the mock, DESIGN.md, and real AWS behavior side by side. Doing that check with AWS Emulator confirmed that the S3 behavior written in DESIGN.md comes back exactly as described.

The ItemTooLargeException row for KVStore deserves a mention too. The KVStore AWS implementation checks whether the message of a ValidationException from DynamoDB contains "size has exceeded" with a regular expression, and turns it into ItemTooLargeException. The conversion depends on the wording of the message, not the error type. It worked against the emulator because the emulator's DynamoDB implementation defines the message "Item size has exceeded the maximum allowed size" as a constant that matches AWS.

Being generated from API models only means the shape of requests and responses matches AWS. The source shows that AWS Emulator also tries to match the wording of error messages. For a library like Blocks that reinterprets errors based on their wording, this makes a real difference.

Gaps AWS Emulator can and cannot close

So how much of what Blocks calls does AWS Emulator reproduce today?

AWS Emulator publishes fidelity scores with every release. The v1.0.322 release attaches the raw evaluation data as scores.json.gz. It records, for each short scenario (a sequence of calls such as creating, reading, and deleting a resource), whether the emulator's responses matched the ones recorded on AWS.

At the service level, DynamoDB, S3, and SQS pass roughly 60 to 70 percent. That number is not very useful for Blocks, though, because Blocks calls only a small subset of each service's operations.

So I listed the SDK clients that each Block's AWS implementation imports, narrowed the data down to the operations they actually call, and recomputed the match rate per step within each scenario.


Built from scores.json.gz in aws/aws-emulator v1.0.322

A few caveats apply. Only the tests classified as "wire" in scores.json carry per-step detail, and they make up about a quarter of the total. Operations with single-digit step counts are too few to read even a trend. The official documentation also explains that adding tests can surface differences that were already there as new failures, so a score should be read as a snapshot. What you see here is a trend at one point in time.

Even so, the split between operations that are already reproduced and those that are not is clear.

The operations called by the data-oriented Blocks (KVStore, DistributedTable, FileBucket, enqueuing in AsyncJob, Secret, AppSetting) have high match rates. Among the differences that DESIGN.md says to check in a sandbox, those about the shape of DynamoDB and S3 responses or their error codes are candidates for checking with AWS Emulator instead.

On the other hand, Realtime delivery to browsers, email sending in EmailClient, and the sign-in flow in AuthCognito do not look ready to be verified with the emulator yet.

And regardless of the scores, some gaps remain that AWS Emulator does not close.

The first is IAM. The DESIGN.md files of several Blocks, including KVStore, FileBucket, and AsyncJob, list "No IAM enforcement" as a difference, and the AWS Emulator README also says not to use it for security testing. According to the official security page, some services evaluate the policies of IAM users and roles that you create inside the emulator, but not the same way AWS does. Requests signed with the emulator's own keys are never denied. Blocks wires permissions automatically through CDK grants, and for now the only place to check that they are correct is a sandbox.

The second is the database. The Database and DistributedDatabase Blocks connect to PostgreSQL-family databases on AWS, such as Aurora Serverless v2 and Aurora DSQL. AWS Emulator does have an Aurora DSQL service, but it implements only management operations such as creating and deleting clusters. The path that runs SQL is not an AWS API, so it belongs to PGlite in the Blocks mock or to a sandbox, not to the emulator.

The third is behavior that depends on timing and scale, such as throttling and eventual consistency. Blocks itself treats these as inherently non-deterministic in DESIGN.md and offers no mitigation, and it is hard to expect the emulator to cover them either.

One more thing worth noting is that CloudFormation scores only around 20 percent at the service level. The official documentation also says that support for CloudFormation and the AWS CDK varies by service. Since a Blocks application is a CDK application, deploying a Blocks template to the emulator as-is to run the whole AWS implementation does not look practical yet.

Blocks testing in three layers

Putting this together, Blocks testing can be thought of in three layers.

Blocks mock                 AWS Emulator                 Sandbox (real AWS)
types, logic, usage   ··>   API responses and errors ··>  IAM, performance,
                                                          eventual consistency
      │                                                          ▲
      └──────── bridged today by the DESIGN.md difference tables ┘
Layer What it can verify What it cannot verify
Blocks mock Types, business logic, how Blocks are used, the feel during development How AWS responds
AWS Emulator The requests the AWS implementation sends, and the shape of the AWS API responses and errors IAM, PostgreSQL data operations, timing and scale
Sandbox (real AWS) Real behavior, including permissions, performance, and eventual consistency Speed and convenience

Today, Blocks has the first and third layers. The DESIGN.md difference tables bridge the space between them in prose. With AWS Emulator in between, some rows of those tables might move from "be careful" in prose to "verified" by tests. The metadata and delete-marker rows in this post are examples of exactly that.

What I expect for AWS Emulator and Blocks

From here on, this is my own expectation based on public information. It is not something AWS or the Blocks maintainers have said.

The first thing I expect is AWS Emulator showing up in the Blocks project's own tests. The parity tests' captureAws returns hand-written DynamoDB responses. Replace that with responses from the emulator, and the tests could check not only what the AWS implementation sends but also how AWS responds, inside CI and without an AWS account. There would be no need to hand-build fake endpoints for each verification, as in PR #999.

Use on developers' machines would likely come next. For example, a mode separate from npm run dev that runs the AWS implementations against the emulator. As the run above showed, loading the Blocks with the aws-runtime condition and pointing the SDK at the emulator through environment variables was enough to run the AWS implementations without an account. The foundation already exists.

There are two challenges before that happens.

The first is who creates the resources. The AWS implementations assume that the tables and buckets created by CDK already exist. In my run, I created the table and bucket with the SDK by hand and wrote the code to wait for the table to become usable. Judging by the CloudFormation scores, deploying the template to the emulator is not practical yet, so Blocks would need a separate way to prepare resources for the emulator.

The second is keeping the simplicity that Blocks local development promises. Blocks local development needs no AWS account, no internet connection, and no running container daemon. AWS Emulator, on the other hand, installs as a package on Linux but needs Docker on macOS and Windows. Requiring the emulator would give up the "nothing to set up" simplicity.

That is why I don't think the mocks will go away. There are gaps the emulator cannot close, such as PostgreSQL data operations and IAM. And the experience of running everything with just npm run dev is at the heart of what Blocks offers. With both in mind, it seems natural to position AWS Emulator not as a replacement for the mocks, but as an option that sits between the mocks and the sandbox.

Why "AWS Emulator makes the mocks unnecessary" doesn't hold yet

There is an opposing view. If an official emulator returns the same responses as AWS, wouldn't it be cleaner for Blocks to rely on it than to keep writing and maintaining a mock for every service?

The cost of maintaining the mocks is certainly not small. The DESIGN.md difference tables are long for every Block, and as the FileBucket drift in this post shows, the tables and the implementation can fall out of sync. AWS Emulator, by contrast, is maintained by AI agents that keep running fidelity tests and fixing the implementation, and the issues/ directory in its repository shows fixes accumulating over time.

Still, there are two reasons to be careful about replacing the mocks right away.

The first is that the mocks and the emulator reproduce different things. The Blocks mocks reproduce the types and error contracts of Blocks. The emulator reproduces the AWS APIs, so even with the emulator you still need the Blocks AWS implementations, which means more moving parts on your machine.

The second is the set of challenges above: Docker, preparing resources, and the database and IAM gaps. Putting those on users would move Blocks away from its experience of not having to think about AWS. In my previous post, I described Blocks as letting you be aware of the infrastructure without requiring you to be. Testing is the same: AWS Emulator fits the Blocks philosophy best as a layer that people who want that awareness can step down into.

Closing thoughts

When I learned about AWS Emulator, the first question that came to mind was whether the Blocks mocks were about to become unnecessary.

Reading the source of both projects, though, the two replace AWS at different layers to begin with. The Blocks mocks reproduce the API that Blocks exposes to its users. AWS Emulator reproduces the AWS APIs underneath it.

And between those two layers sits a gap that Blocks testing cannot yet cover: the DESIGN.md difference tables, the parity tests built on hand-written responses, and the fake endpoint a maintainer built by hand. That is where AWS Emulator fits most naturally.

AWS Blocks is still in public preview, and AWS Emulator has only just been released. Both are open source, so where the two meet should become visible by following their repositories. I'm looking forward to seeing whether the first point of contact shows up in the Blocks project's own tests or on developers' machines.

title: Enterprise Kubernetes Autoscaling: VPA, KEDA, and Karpenter Strategies
description:
Originally published on the HostingPodium Enterprise Engineering Blog.

Free SRE & Developer Diagnostics: Test your stack live with our DMARC Record Checker, Generator & SPF/DKIM Validator, Free Website Speed & Core Web Vitals Checker, or explore all 9 Free Webmaster & Cloud Engineering Tools.

A deep engineering guide covering production configurations and operational strategies for KEDA, VPA, and Karpenter autoscaling in Kubernetes.

Architectural Foundations of Elastic Infrastructure

Modern cloud-native platforms demand dynamic resource allocation mechanisms that operate without human intervention. Static over-provisioning wastes capital expenditure, while under-provisioning violates latency SLOs during traffic spikes. The convergence of Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (HPA), Vertical Pod Autoscaling (VPA), Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling (KEDA), and AWS Karpenter establishes an execution layer that responds to application telemetry, queue depth, and memory pressure in milliseconds.

Designing this control plane requires reconciling conflicting scheduling primitives. For instance, native HPA evaluates CPU and memory metrics via the Metrics Server every 15 seconds by default. When scaling stateful consumers or event-driven workers, polling resource utilization introduces unacceptable latency. KEDA bypasses this limitation by querying external telemetry sources directly, converting queue depth metrics into custom Prometheus metrics that trigger HPA scaling events before resource saturation occurs.

Core Autoscaling Subsystems Comparison

Subsystem Primary Trigger Scaling Mechanism Latency Profile Primary Failure Mode
HPA CPU, Memory, Custom Metrics Pod Replica Count 15 - 60 seconds Metric lag leading to cascading throttling
VPA Resource Utilization History Container CPU/RAM Limits 1 - 24 hours (Recommender) Pod eviction during in-place resizing
KEDA External Event Sources (Kafka, SQS) Pod Replica Count (0 to N) < 5 seconds (External Scaler) Connection pool exhaustion on scaling spikes
Karpenter Unscheduled Pods & Bin-packing EC2 Instance Provisioning 30 - 90 seconds Cloud Provider API rate limiting

Configuring KEDA for Event-Driven Zero-to-N Scaling

Standard HPA falls short when scaling workloads driven by asynchronous event queues. If an Apache Kafka topic accumulates 50,000 unread messages, CPU utilization metrics might remain near zero if the consumer pods are throttled or waiting for network I/O. KEDA solves this by deploying a custom metrics adapter that communicates directly with external event sources.

Below is a production-grade ScaledObject manifest configured to scale an enterprise event processor consuming from an Apache Kafka cluster based on lag per replica.

apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
 name: kafka-consumer-scaledobject
 namespace: production
spec:
 scaleTargetRef:
 apiVersion: apps/v1
 kind: Deployment
 name: event-processor-worker
 minReplicaCount: 0
 maxReplicaCount: 150
 cooldownPeriod: 300
 pollingInterval: 15
 advanced:
 horizontalPodAutoscalerConfig:
 behavior:
 scaleDown:
 stabilizationWindowSeconds: 600
 policies:
 - type: Percent
 value: 10
 periodSeconds: 60
 scaleUp:
 stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
 policies:
 - type: Percent
 value: 100
 periodSeconds: 15
 - type: Pods
 value: 16
 periodSeconds: 15
 selectPolicy: Max
 triggers:
 - type: kafka
 metadata:
 bootstrapServers: kafka-bootstrap.streaming.svc:9092
 consumerGroup: event-processor-group
 topic: transactions.incoming
 lagThreshold: "20"
 activationLagThreshold: "5"
 offsetResetPolicy: latest
 allowIdleConsumers: "true"

In this architecture, the scaling behavior block enforces aggressive scale-up parameters while damping scale-down operations. The activationLagThreshold parameter ensures that scale-from-zero triggers only when unread messages exceed 5 per partition, preventing spurious pod instantiation from heartbeat chatter.

Right-Sizing Workloads with VPA and Prometheus Integration

Vertical Pod Autoscaling (VPA) adjusts container CPU and memory requests and limits dynamically. However, running VPA in automatic mode alongside HPA creates scheduling instability, because the VPA eviction loop terminates pods to apply resource updates, which triggers false alarms in the HPA metrics pipeline. Production environments should deploy VPA in Off mode (recommendation-only) combined with Prometheus custom metrics exporters, or leverage in-place vertical scaling features where supported by the underlying Linux kernel and container runtime.

To capture accurate utilization baselines without relying solely on the default VPA recommender, operators scrape cgroups metrics directly through Prometheus using the following PromQL query for peak memory tracking:

max_over_time(container_memory_working_set_bytes{container!="", container!="POD"}[24h])

VPA Custom Resource Definition for Recommender Policies 

apiVersion: autoscaling.k8s.io/v1
kind: VerticalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
 name: api-gateway-vpa
 namespace: production
spec:
 targetRef:
 apiVersion: apps/v1
 kind: Deployment
 name: api-gateway
 updatePolicy:
 updateMode: "Off"
 resourcePolicy:
 containerPolicies:
 - containerName: '*'
 minAllowed:
 cpu: 100m
 memory: 128Mi
 maxAllowed:
 cpu: 4000m
 memory: 8Gi
 controlledResources: ["cpu", "memory"]

Infrastructure Provisioning and Bin-Packing with Karpenter

Traditional cluster autoscalers evaluate node groups and manage auto-scaling groups based on ASG heuristics, resulting in slow provisioning times (3 to 5 minutes) and suboptimal bin-packing. Karpenter replaces the cluster autoscaler by watching unscheduled pods directly and provisioning purpose-built EC2 instances within seconds.

Karpenter interacts directly with the AWS EC2 Fleet API, selecting instance types that optimize cost and availability based on requirements defined in the NodePool and NodeClass specifications.

apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1beta1
kind: NodePool
metadata:
 name: default
spec:
 template:
 spec:
 nodeClassRef:
 group: karpenter.k8s.aws
 kind: EC2NodeClass
 name: default
 requirements:
 - key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type
 operator: In
 values: ["spot", "on-demand"]
 - key: kubernetes.io/arch
 operator: In
 values: ["amd64"]
 - key: node.kubernetes.io/instance-type
 operator: In
 values: ["c6i.xlarge", "c6i.2xlarge", "m6i.xlarge", "m6i.2xlarge"]
 expireAfter: 720h
 limits:
 cpu: "1000"
 memory: 1000Gi
 disruption:
 consolidationPolicy: WhenUnderutilized
 consolidateAfter: 30s

The consolidation engine continuously analyzes cluster workloads. When pods can be repacked onto fewer nodes due to natural scaling down, Karpenter drains the underutilized nodes gracefully, enforcing pod disruption budgets (PDBs) to maintain service availability.

Observability and Runbook for Metric Discrepancies

Operating a multi-layered autoscaling stack requires comprehensive telemetry. When diagnosing scaling failures, platform engineers must inspect the custom metrics API registration and verify KEDA operator logs for authentication failures against external data planes.

  • Verify custom metrics availability: kubectl get --raw /apis/custom.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1
  • Inspect KEDA scaler metrics output: kubectl get scaledobject kafka-consumer-scaledobject -n production -o yaml
  • Check Karpenter controller reconciliation loops: kubectl logs -n kube-namespace -l app.kubernetes.io/name=karpenter --tail=100

By enforcing strict boundary conditions between event-driven replica scaling via KEDA, container resource right-sizing via VPA recommendations, and underlying node bin-packing via Karpenter, enterprise engineering organizations eliminate provisioning latency and resource waste.

Production Verification Checklist & Operational Runbook: Kubernetes Vertical & Horizontal Pod Autoscaling: VPA, KEDA Event-Driven Scaling & Karpenter

Before promoting any Kubernetes Vertical & Horizontal Pod Autoscaling: VPA, KEDA Event-Driven Scaling & Karpenter deployment into production traffic, senior platform and SRE teams validate deterministic failure handling, kernel resource ceilings, and observability telemetry across keda event-driven autoscaling kubernetes, vpa hpa cpu memory right-sizing, bin-packing node consolidation, prometheus custom metrics autoscaler. Unlike lab prototypes, production clusters must survive upstream network partitions, sudden concurrency bursts, and rolling node maintenance without dropping in-flight client transactions.

Pre-Cutover Acceptance Gates

  • Synthetic Load & Tail-Latency Benchmarking: Execute sustained concurrency tests against staging endpoints for Kubernetes Vertical & Horizontal Pod Autoscaling: VPA, KEDA Event-Driven Scaling & Karpenter, verifying that p95 and p99 response latencies remain within contractual SLO boundaries under 3x peak projected load.

  • Fault Injection & Chaos Verification: Simulate primary worker termination, AZ link degradation, and storage IOPS saturation to confirm automated failover and circuit-breaker recovery complete within sub-second thresholds.

  • Telemetry & Alert Routing Validation: Confirm Prometheus scrape targets, structured JSON log pipelines, and OpenTelemetry trace propagation emit actionable metrics for kubernetes-vpa-keda-event-driven-autoscaling-karpenter before live traffic cutover.

  • Immutable Rollback Readiness: Verify that declarative GitOps manifests, database migration snapshots, and previous container image digests can restore the prior production state in under 120 seconds.

# Production Readiness Verification Probe (kubernetes-vpa-keda-event-driven-autoscaling-karpenter)
systemctl is-active --quiet prometheus-node-exporter && echo "TELEMETRY_OK"
sysctl net.core.somaxconn net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse vm.swappiness
curl -fsSL -o /dev/null -w "http_code=%{http_code} ttfb=%{time_starttransfer}s
" http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz

By enforcing these pre-cutover verification gates alongside Multi-master control plane quorum, 99.99% ingress uptime, and sub-minute node replacement automation, engineering teams ensure Kubernetes Vertical & Horizontal Pod Autoscaling: VPA, KEDA Event-Driven Scaling & Karpenter operates with predictable throughput, cryptographic isolation, and continuous audit compliance across PCI-DSS segmentation, container image vulnerability scanning via Trivy/Clair, and immutable audit trails.

title: LAN, Tailscale or cloud? Working out which route a phone connected over from the socket address and the headers a tunnel adds
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of Bolo, and this post is published from my account. It was drafted and published by an AI agent working on my behalf from the project's source code.

Bolo AI lets you speak into your phone and have the text typed at the cursor on your PC. The PC side is a small Node.js server that the phone reaches over one of three routes: the home or office LAN, Tailscale, or a Cloudflare tunnel when neither is reachable. The window on the PC shows each paired phone and which route it is using, and that needs the server to answer a plain question for every connection: how did this one arrive?

It is a 10-line function. Here is why each line is there.

What the server can see

All connections end up as a WebSocket on the same port, so the only evidence is the socket's remote address and the request headers:

function routeOf(req) {
    const h = req.headers || {};
    if (h['cf-connecting-ip'] || h['cf-ray']) return 'Cloud';
    const ip = String(req.socket?.remoteAddress || '').replace(/^::ffff:/, '');
    if (ip === '::1' || ip === '127.0.0.1') return 'Cloud'; // cloudflared connects from localhost
    if (/^fd7a:115c:a1e0:/i.test(ip)) return 'Tailscale';
    const m = ip.match(/^100\.(\d+)\./);
    if (m && +m[1] >= 64 && +m[1] <= 127) return 'Tailscale';
    return 'LAN';
}

Line by line

Tunnel headers first. Cloudflare adds cf-connecting-ip and cf-ray. If either is present, the request came through the tunnel, whatever the socket says.

Loopback means the tunnel. The tunnel client (cloudflared) runs on the same PC and connects to the server from 127.0.0.1. So from the server's point of view a cloud connection has a local address. A naive "private address means LAN" test would label every tunnelled phone as LAN. The loopback check is the second guard in case the headers are ever stripped.

Strip the IPv4-mapped prefix. Node on a dual-stack socket reports IPv4 peers as ::ffff:192.168.1.20. Without the replace, none of the dotted-quad tests below would ever match.

Tailscale has two address families. IPv4 addresses are in the CGNAT range 100.64.0.0/10, which is 100.64.x.x through 100.127.x.x. Matching just ^100\. would also catch other 100.x addresses outside that range, so the second octet is range-checked. IPv6 addresses sit under the fd7a:115c:a1e0::/48 prefix.

Everything else is LAN. The fall-through is a deliberate default: if it was not a tunnel and not Tailscale, it reached the PC directly.

Where the answer is stored

The result is saved on the paired-device record as lastRoute, and kept in the in-memory map of live connections as route. A phone that switches from Wi-Fi to mobile data shows up as a new connection with a new route, and the window lists every route a phone currently has open.

A limit worth knowing

This is a label for the user's information, not an access-control decision. Headers can be set by anyone who can reach the port directly, so a client on the LAN could send cf-ray and be labelled Cloud. Authentication is by a per-phone token, checked separately; the route only decides what the window displays. If you ever want to gate behaviour on the route, trust only the socket address.

Dictated text stays out of it

The same module keeps a short history of recent dictations so the window can show them. It is held in memory only (the last 30, gone when the app exits), and the log records lengths, never the text. That rule was set before the history existed, so the history is built around it rather than an exception to it.

Source: src/devices.js in the PC server.

title: Buffalo Grain Elevator: A Five-Stage Toolchain and What Broke
description:
This one started with a call from a preservation group in Buffalo. They had a 1910s concrete grain elevator complex on the lake, thirty-eight silos in two rows, a marine leg tower, and a rail yard that still connects to a live line. The question was whether part of it could hold a fabrication shop, a small events floor, and a public walk at the top. Before anyone talked about membranes or budgets, I needed a model I could test against.

Stage 1 — base geometry from CADMapper

CADMapper brought in the parcel, the rail alignments, and the nearest streets. The silo complex itself was not in the open data at usable detail, so I traced the outer walls from a survey the group had scanned and used the export only for context and scale. That split matters. Context from the map, dimensions from the survey. When I mixed the two, the rail alignment drifted about two feet against the property line.

Stage 2 — parcel logic with Cityweft

The complex sits inside one legal parcel with three separate owners of record, which is a mess nobody had drawn. Cityweft let me weave a working subdivision inside the boundary so we could talk about phases instead of one building. The version we kept separated the silo block, the marine leg, and the rail yard into three parcels with a shared service spine. That one drawing did more for the conversation than any rendering.

Stage 3 — rules in CityEngine

CityEngine was the right place to test the zoning envelope on the waterfront edge. I wrote rules for height, setback from the rail, and a required public access strip, then generated massing variants for the two infill sites between the silos. The rules made a bad assumption visible early: the height limit measured from the street side lets a much taller building sit behind the silos than the waterfront plan intended. That is a code issue, not a design issue, and it is now in the meeting notes.

Stage 4 — massing inserts with Archshaper

Archshaper handled the shop and the events floor. I gave it the silo block footprint and tested a low shed against a taller box tucked between the bins. The low shed keeps the silo silhouette intact from the water. The taller box gets daylight into the shop but eats the public walk. We kept the low shed and moved the walk to the roof of the connecting gallery, which is a better idea than anything I drew by hand.

Stage 5 — quick volume checks with GenAnywhere

GenAnywhere is the fast pass. Drag a rectangle over the map, and it hands back building volumes for that rectangle. I boxed the rail yard and the two empty pads and generated options for a future phase, mostly to see how much floor area could fit without touching the silos. The numbers came back close to my hand estimate, which is the point. It took four minutes and confirmed that the yard is worth more as a yard.

What broke

• CADMapper exports the rail as a centerline, not a corridor. Buffers need to be drawn by hand.
• CityEngine rules failed on two silo footprints that were not closed. Cleaning the polygon in CAD fixed it.
• Archshaper assumes floor-to-floor heights. The silo block does not have them, so I had to fake levels and label them.
• GenAnywhere returns volumes without structure. Every option needs a manual check against the bin walls.
• Cityweft will happily weave parcels across a rail easement. I had to lock that strip before every run.

What I would keep

The stage order. Base context, parcel logic, rules, massing, then quick volume tests. Each stage produced one decision, and the decisions survived the meeting. I also kept every stage in its own file with the date in the name, because the group will ask for the version from three weeks ago and nobody will remember which one had the corrected rail easement.
Two days of work produced four ruled-out options and one plan. The model was never the deliverable. The list of things we could stop arguing about was.

title: Why Great Websites Need More Than Good Development
description:
A website can look impressive in a design presentation and still fail when real people start using it.

Maybe the navigation is confusing. Maybe the mobile layout feels cramped. Perhaps the pages take too long to load, or visitors cannot figure out what the business actually offers.

These problems often happen when website design and development are treated as two separate activities rather than parts of the same process.

Building a successful website requires more than writing clean code or choosing an attractive color palette. It requires a balance between user experience, visual communication, technical performance, and business goals.

  1. Start With the Purpose, Not the Layout

One common mistake in website projects is jumping straight into the visual design.

Before opening a design tool or writing components, understand what the website needs to accomplish.

Ask a few basic questions:

Who is the intended audience?

What problem does the website solve?

What should visitors do after landing on the homepage?

Which information matters most to potential customers?

How will success be measured?

These answers help establish the website's structure and content priorities.

For example, a SaaS company might need visitors to explore product features and request a demo. An ecommerce business needs clear product categories, useful product pages, and a straightforward checkout experience.

The design should support these objectives instead of competing with them.

  1. User Experience Should Guide Visual Decisions

Good design is not simply about making a website look modern.

It is about making information easier to understand and actions easier to complete.

A few principles make a significant difference:

Clear navigation: Visitors should understand where to find important information without having to search through multiple menus.

Readable typography: Font sizes, spacing, and contrast should make content comfortable to read across different devices.

Consistent components: Buttons, cards, headings, and forms should follow a recognizable visual system.

Meaningful calls to action: Every important page should guide visitors toward a relevant next step.

A visually attractive interface is valuable, but usability is what makes people comfortable interacting with it.

  1. Design and Development Should Work Together

A common challenge in website projects is the handoff between designers and developers.

A design might include animations, complex layouts, or interactive elements that are difficult to implement within the project's technical constraints.

When development starts too late, teams may discover these problems after significant design work has already been completed.

A better approach is collaboration from the beginning.

Designers should understand the technical possibilities, while developers should understand the reasoning behind the interface.

This helps teams make practical decisions about:

Responsive layouts

Component architecture

Animation and interactions

Content management systems

Accessibility requirements

Future maintenance

Businesses looking for professional web design and development services should consider whether the team can manage both the creative and technical sides of the project.

Combining these disciplines helps reduce unnecessary revisions and creates a more consistent final product.

  1. Website Performance Is Part of the User Experience

Even a beautifully designed website can lose visitors if it performs poorly.

Performance should be considered throughout the development process, not treated as a final optimization task.

Some important areas include:

Image optimization: Use appropriately sized images and modern formats where supported.

Efficient code: Avoid unnecessary JavaScript and remove unused dependencies.

Responsive implementation: Make sure layouts work across mobile phones, tablets, and desktop screens.

Core Web Vitals: Monitor loading performance, visual stability, and interaction responsiveness.

Accessibility: Use semantic HTML, keyboard-friendly navigation, and sufficient color contrast.

These improvements help create websites that are easier to use and maintain.

  1. Build With Future Growth in Mind

A website should not become difficult to update every time a business launches a new service or changes its messaging.

This is why maintainability matters.

Reusable components, a sensible page structure, and an appropriate content management setup can make future updates much easier.

For development teams, this means thinking beyond the immediate launch.

Consider whether the website can support:

Additional landing pages

New product or service sections

Updated brand guidelines

Marketing campaigns

Third-party integrations

Growing content requirements

A flexible foundation reduces the need for expensive rebuilds as the business evolves.

  1. Test the Website Before Launch

A successful launch requires more than checking whether the homepage loads.

Testing should cover the complete experience.

A practical pre-launch checklist includes:

Test navigation links and buttons.

Check forms and submission confirmations.

Review mobile and tablet layouts.

Test pages across major browsers.

Check image loading and broken links.

Review page titles and meta descriptions.

Validate accessibility basics.

Measure page performance.

Check redirects and important URLs.

It is also useful to ask someone unfamiliar with the project to navigate the website. They may notice usability problems that the development team has overlooked.

Final Thoughts

Great websites are created when design decisions and technical decisions support the same purpose.

A good visual system helps communicate a brand. Thoughtful development makes the experience reliable. Performance and accessibility make the website more usable, while a flexible architecture allows it to grow alongside the business.

For businesses planning a new website or improving an existing one, the goal should not simply be to launch something that looks good.

It should be to build something that works well for the people using it and continues to serve the business over time.

That is the difference between creating a website and creating a useful digital experience.

title: CSS Units Cheat Sheet: px, em, rem, vh, and When to Use Each
description:
Originally published on DevToolsHub — free, privacy-first online tools for developers.

CSS units can be confusing. Should you use px or rem? When does vw make sense? What about ch and ex? Picking the right unit makes the difference between a layout that breaks and one that gracefully adapts to every screen size.

This reference breaks CSS units into two categories — absolute and relative — with clear examples of when to use each. Bookmark this page for your next responsive design project.

💡 Quick Rule of Thumb

Use rem for font sizes, px for borders/shadows, % for widths, vw/vh for full-screen sections, and em for spacing relative to the current font size.

Absolute Units

Absolute units are fixed-length values. They don't scale with the viewport, parent element, or font size. Use them for print stylesheets, borders, and situations where precision matters regardless of screen size.

Unit Name Relative to Best For
px Pixel 1px = 1/96th of 1 inch (screen) Borders, shadows, small precise spacing, images
pt Point 1pt = 1/72nd of 1 inch Print stylesheets, traditional typography
pc Pica 1pc = 12pt = 1/6th of 1 inch Print layouts (rarely used on web)
cm Centimeter 1cm = 37.8px (approx) Print stylesheets, physical measurements
mm Millimeter 1mm = 1/10th of 1cm Print stylesheets
in Inch 1in = 96px Print stylesheets
Q Quarter-millimeter 1Q = 1/40th of 1cm Print, Japanese/CJK layouts

⚠️ When Not to Use px

Avoid px for font sizes in modern responsive design. Users who change their browser's default font size will see no change in pixel-sized text, which creates accessibility issues. Use rem instead — it respects the user's font size preference.

Relative Units

Relative units scale based on the context — the viewport, parent element, or root font size. They are the foundation of responsive and accessible design.

Font-Relative Units

Unit Name Relative to Best For
em Em Font size of the parent element Spacing, padding, margins relative to text size
rem Root Em Font size of the root (<html>) element Font sizes, spacing (accessibility-friendly)
ch Character Width of the '0' character in current font Input widths, line length constraints
ex X-height Height of the 'x' character in current font Vertical alignment, inline spacing
ic Ideograph Width of CJK ideograph character Chinese/Japanese/Korean text layouts
lh Line height Computed line-height of the element Vertical rhythm, consistent spacing
rlh Root line height Computed line-height of the root element Global vertical rhythm

Viewport-Relative Units

Unit Name Relative to Best For
vw Viewport Width 1% of viewport width Full-width elements, hero sections, fluid typography
vh Viewport Height 1% of viewport height Full-height sections, modal overlays, sticky elements
vmin Viewport Minimum 1% of the smaller viewport dimension (width or height) Responsive square elements, safe sizing for all orientations
vmax Viewport Maximum 1% of the larger viewport dimension (width or height) Full-screen backgrounds, decorative elements
svw / svh Small Viewport Viewport size excluding dynamic browser chrome Mobile-safe full-screen layouts
lvw / lvh Large Viewport Viewport size including potential browser chrome When you want the full device screen regardless of UI
dvw / dvh Dynamic Viewport Dynamically updates as browser chrome shows/hides Works like 100vh but handles mobile toolbar changes

⚠️ Viewport Unit Gotcha on Mobile

On iOS Safari, 100vh includes the browser toolbar height, which collapses when scrolling. This causes content to be taller than expected. Use 100dvh (dynamic viewport height) or 100svh (small viewport height) for reliable full-height sections on mobile.

Percentage Unit

Unit Name Relative to Best For
% Percentage Depends on property: width → parent width, height → parent height, font-size → parent font-size, padding/margin → parent width (even for vertical padding) Fluid layouts, responsive widths, aspect ratios

💡 Percentage Padding Quirk

When using padding-top: 50% or padding-bottom: 50%, the percentage is calculated from the parent's width, not height. This is actually useful for creating fixed-aspect-ratio boxes (like a 16:9 container) without JavaScript.

When to Use Each Unit

The table below maps common CSS properties to their recommended units.

Property Recommended Unit Why
font-size rem Respects user's browser font size setting. Avoids compounding issues of em.
padding / margin rem Consistent spacing regardless of nested font sizes.
width / max-width % or rem % for fluid layouts, rem for fixed content widths (e.g., article max-width).
height auto (avoid fixed) Let content determine height. Use min-height with vh for full-screen sections.
border-width px Borders should be crisp and not scale with text size.
border-radius px or rem px for small radii, rem for larger rounded corners that should scale.
box-shadow px Shadow blur and spread should stay crisp.
line-height unitless (e.g., 1.5) Unitless values scale proportionally with font-size changes.
gap rem Grid/flexbox gaps should scale with content size.
hero / full-screen dvh Dynamic viewport handles mobile browser toolbar correctly.
fluid typography clamp() Combine rem + vw with min/max bounds (e.g., clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 2rem)).
icon sizing em Icon scales with surrounding text size automatically.

Practical Examples

Fluid Typography with clamp()

The clamp() CSS function lets you set a font size that scales between a minimum and maximum value. This is the modern way to do responsive typography without media queries.

/* Fluid heading: scales from 1.5rem to 3rem between 320px and 1200px viewports */
h1 {
  font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 1rem + 2.5vw, 3rem);
  line-height: 1.1;
}

/* Fluid body text */
p {
  font-size: clamp(0.875rem, 0.75rem + 0.5vw, 1.125rem);
  line-height: 1.6;
}

Full-Height Hero Section (Mobile-Safe) 

.hero {
  /* dvh = dynamic viewport height — handles mobile browser toolbar */
  min-height: 100dvh;
  /* Fallback for older browsers */
  min-height: 100vh;
  min-height: 100svh;
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
}

Consistent Spacing with rem 

:root {
  /* Set root font size. Browser default is 16px = 1rem */
  font-size: 100%; /* Respects user preferences */
}

.card {
  padding: 1.5rem;    /* = 24px at default font size */
  margin-bottom: 1rem; /* = 16px */
  border-radius: 0.5rem; /* = 8px */
  gap: 0.75rem;       /* = 12px grid gap */
}

h2 {
  font-size: 1.25rem; /* = 20px */
  margin-bottom: 0.5em; /* relative to h2 font size */
}

16:9 Aspect Ratio Box 

.aspect-16-9 {
  /* Padding % is calculated from parent width */
  /* 9/16 = 56.25% */
  width: 100%;
  padding-bottom: 56.25%;
  position: relative;
  overflow: hidden;
}

.aspect-16-9 > * {
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  width: 100%;
  height: 100%;
  object-fit: cover;
}

Perfectly Centered Modal 

.modal-overlay {
  position: fixed;
  inset: 0;
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  background: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5);
}

.modal {
  width: min(90vw, 600px);  /* 90% of viewport width, max 600px */
  max-height: 90dvh;        /* 90% of dynamic viewport height */
  overflow-y: auto;
  padding: 2rem;
  background: #fff;
  border-radius: 0.75rem;
}

calc() in Practice

The calc() function lets you mix units freely. It's extremely useful for fluid layouts where you need arithmetic operations on CSS values.

/* Sidebar + main: 250px sidebar, rest is main */
.main-layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 250px 1fr;
  gap: 2rem;
}

/* Full-width container with fixed gutters */
.container {
  width: calc(100% - 3rem);
  max-width: 1200px;
  margin-inline: auto;
}

/* Fluid typography alternative */
h1 {
  font-size: calc(1.5rem + 2vw);
}

/* Height minus header */
.content {
  min-height: calc(100dvh - 4rem);
}

/* Background that extends beyond content area */
.hero {
  width: 100vw;
  margin-left: calc(-50vw + 50%);
}

Unit Comparison Table

A quick comparison of how different units behave at different scales. Assumes root font size of 16px and a 1200px wide viewport.

Value px rem em (parent 16px) vw (1200px) %
Small 8px 0.5rem 0.5em 0.67vw 0.67%
Body 16px 1rem 1em 1.33vw 1.33%
Medium 24px 1.5rem 1.5em 2vw 2%
Large 32px 2rem 2em 2.67vw 2.67%
Heading 48px 3rem 3em 4vw 4%

🎯 Summary: Unit Decision Flow

  • font-size → rem (or clamp() for fluid scaling)
  • spacing (padding, margin, gap) → rem (consistent everywhere)
  • widths → % (fluid), rem (fixed content), min() (max bound)
  • heights → auto (preferred), dvh (full-screen)
  • borders / shadows → px (keep them crisp)
  • icon sizes → em (scale with text)
  • line-height → unitless number (always)
  • fluid typography → clamp() with rem and vw
  • full viewport sections → 100dvh (dynamic) or 100svh (small)
  • mixed calculations → calc()

Common Mistakes & How to Avoid Them

CSS units seem simple until a layout breaks. These are the mistakes developers make most often — and the fixes that prevent them.

1. Using px for Font Sizes Hurts Accessibility

px font sizes ignore the user's browser font-size setting, so users who increase their default font size (often for vision reasons) see no change on your site. Use rem for font sizes — it scales with the root font size — and reserve px for borders, shadows, and 1px hairline rules that should stay crisp.

2. Confusing em with rem

rem is always relative to the root element font size (usually 16px), so it is predictable anywhere in the tree. em is relative to the current element's font size, and because it compounds, nested elements can produce surprising sizes: a 1.5em padding inside a 1.5em font becomes 2.25em of effective spacing. Use rem for global spacing and typography; use em deliberately when a component should scale with its own font size (icons, button padding).

3. Using 100vh for Mobile Full-Height Sections

On mobile browsers, 100vh refers to the largest viewport, which includes the area hidden behind the URL bar — so a 100vh section gets cut off or causes scroll jumps when the bar collapses. Use 100dvh (dynamic viewport height) for mobile full-height layouts, with 100svh as a fallback for older browsers.

4. Using vw for Font Sizes Without clamp()

A headline set to 4vw looks great on desktop but becomes unreadably small on phones and comically huge on ultrawide monitors. Wrap viewport units in clamp() with rem bounds: font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 4vw, 3rem). This gives you fluid scaling without ever crossing accessibility limits.

5. Expecting Percentage Heights to "Just Work"

height: 50% only works when the parent has an explicit height (not auto). A common trap is setting a child to 100% inside a parent whose height comes from content — the percentage resolves to auto and the layout collapses. If the parent's height is content-driven, use flexbox/grid stretch, min-height, or viewport units instead of percentages.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between px and rem?

px is an absolute unit — 1px is 1/96th of an inch on screen — so it never changes regardless of browser settings. rem is relative to the root element font size (usually 16px, so 1rem = 16px). Because rem scales when users change their browser's default font size, it is the recommended unit for font sizes, padding, and margin. Use px for borders and shadows that must stay visually identical at any zoom level.

What is the difference between em and rem?

rem is relative to the root element font size, so 1rem is the same everywhere in the document. em is relative to the current element's font size, and it compounds through nesting — a 2em margin inside a 1.5em font resolves to 3em. This makes em great for components that should scale with their own text (icon sizes, button padding) and rem better for site-wide spacing and typography.

When should I use vw and vh?

vw and vh are 1% of the viewport width and height. Use them for full-screen hero sections, overlays, and fluid typography inside clamp(). Avoid raw vh for mobile heights — the URL bar changes the visible viewport, so use 100dvh (dynamic) or 100svh (small) instead. For widths, prefer % when the size should relate to a container rather than the whole viewport.

Should I use px or rem for font sizes?

Use rem. Because rem is relative to the root font size, it respects the user's browser font-size preference — a core accessibility requirement. px ignores that setting, which can make your text impossible to resize for users with low vision. A common pattern is setting the root font size in rem (or leaving it at the default 16px) and sizing everything else in rem, with clamp() for fluid type.

What is the difference between vh, svh, lvh, and dvh?

These are the four viewport-height units. vh equals 1% of the largest viewport — on mobile that includes the area hidden behind the browser UI. svh is the small viewport (visible area when the URL bar is shown), lvh is the large viewport (URL bar hidden), and dvh is the dynamic viewport, which updates live as the browser UI expands and collapses. For mobile full-height sections, 100dvh gives the smoothest behavior, with 100svh as a fallback.

Try It Yourself

If this cheat sheet helped you clean up your CSS, try the free developer tools on DevToolsHub. The Color Converter is handy when you're writing CSS that mixes hex, rgb(), and hsl() values alongside your unit choices, and the JSON Formatter is a quick way to tidy up the design tokens and theme config files where your spacing and typography scales live. Both run entirely in your browser — no sign-up, no tracking.

title: Draw the idea, not the topic
description:
Think of the last ten blog posts you opened. I'd bet at least half had the same kind of header image: a laptop on a wooden desk, a rocket for a launch, a lightbulb for an idea, a magnifying glass for anything about search.

Here's a quick test for any of them. Cover the title and look only at the picture. Can you tell what the article claims? Not what it's about, what it says. Usually you can't. The picture shows the topic. It tells you nothing about the idea.

That gap, between drawing the topic and drawing the idea, is the one thing that shapes how we think about illustration more than anything else.

Decorative pictures aren't neutral

It's tempting to think a decorative image is harmless: at worst it takes up some space. The research on learning says otherwise.

Shannon Harp and Richard Mayer called them seductive details: material that is interesting and loosely related to the topic, but doesn't carry the point. In their 1998 study ("How seductive details do their damage", Journal of Educational Psychology), adding that kind of material to a science lesson made people understand the lesson worse, not better. Highlighting the important parts didn't fix it. Moving the seductive details to the end weakened the damage; putting them first made it worse.

Mayer later folded this into what he calls the coherence principle: people learn better when extraneous material is left out rather than included. The reason is simple. Attention and working memory are limited, and an irrelevant picture still has to be looked at, decoded and set aside. It competes with the thing you actually wanted the reader to get. The effect seems strongest for exactly the people most articles are written for: readers who are new to the subject.

So the useful question isn't "does this page need an image?" It's "what is this image doing?"

An illustration is a metaphor you can see

The picture that helps is almost always a metaphor: one thing understood in terms of another. That's not a designer's trick. In Metaphors We Live By (1980), George Lakoff and Mark Johnson argued that metaphor is how we think about abstract things in the first place. We spend time, waste it, save it, because we understand time through money.

Maggie Appleton, who has drawn a lot of explanations of programming concepts, puts this to work in her case study How to Draw Invisible Programming Concepts. She maps a source (something physical and familiar) onto a target (the abstract idea), so that the qualities they share carry over. Her examples: CSS selectors as painting different parts of a house, a router as a metro map.

The part I find most useful is her point that a metaphor hides and highlights. Every metaphor shows some properties of the idea and leaves others out of the frame. Picking a metaphor is really choosing which part of the idea matters most for this reader, right now.

How we look for one

None of this needs drawing skill. It needs a sentence and a list.

1. Write the one sentence the reader should leave with. Not the title. The claim. "Retrying a request is safe if the endpoint is idempotent" is a claim. "Idempotency" is a topic.

2. List what's true about the idea. For idempotency: doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once; the extra attempts are harmless; the system remembers the first one.

3. Look for a physical thing with the same shape. The lift button: you press it, the lift is called; you press it five more times out of impatience, still one lift. Everyone has done this. The metaphor carries the whole claim in one object.

4. Check what it hides. The lift button says nothing about how the system remembers the first press, or what happens if the lift breaks halfway. If your article is about that, you need a different picture.

5. Run the swap test. Put the image next to the title of a different article. If it still fits, it hasn't said anything yet. A laptop fits every article about software. A lift button fits one.

A few more that pass the test:

  • Rate limiting as a bouncer at a club door: not a wall that keeps everyone out, a person letting people in at a pace the room can take.
  • Technical debt as interest on a loan: the problem isn't the shortcut, it's that you keep paying for it every month you don't fix it.
  • A cache as the fridge next to the cooker: the shop has everything, the fridge has what you'll need in the next ten minutes, and sometimes the milk in it has gone off.

That last one shows the "hides and highlights" point well. The fridge highlights speed and staleness. It hides eviction rules completely. For a post about cache invalidation, it's perfect. For one about LRU, it's the wrong picture.

One object is usually enough

When a metaphor works, it rarely needs company. One lift button, drawn large, with space around it, does more than a lift button surrounded by servers, arrows, clouds and a small potted plant. The extra objects are the seductive details again: they make the image look busier and the idea harder to find.

This is also why we try to keep every image on the same paper as the text around it, without frames or shadows. A framed picture reads as a separate thing to look at. An object on the page reads as part of the explanation.

When not to illustrate

Sometimes the honest answer to "what is this image doing?" is "nothing". A short reference page, a changelog, a list of settings: these don't have one idea to carry, and a picture there is decoration by definition. Leaving it out is a design decision too.

The rule we keep coming back to is short. Draw the idea, not the topic. If you can't say the idea in one sentence yet, the picture isn't the problem.

Sources

  • Harp, S. F., & Mayer, R. E. (1998). How seductive details do their damage: A theory of cognitive interest in science learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 90(3), 414–434.
  • Mayer, R. E. Multimedia Learning, chapter on the coherence principle (Cambridge University Press).
  • Lakoff, G., & Johnson, M. (1980). Metaphors We Live By. University of Chicago Press.
  • Maggie Appleton, How to Draw Invisible Programming Concepts: Part I and Metaphors We Web By.
