Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.26

We've released version 6.26 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Scheduled callback for IVR overcapacity

Scheduled callback is now available as an overcapacity deflection option for IVR queues. When a queue is over capacity, callers can choose to schedule a callback. Google Cloud CCaaS then hands the call to your configured virtual agent, which books the callback through the Callback call API. Administrators choose the virtual agent, an optional greeting, and the data parameters to pass at the global or queue level. Reporting shows whether each caller submitted a callback or left without one.

Administrators: You can configure scheduled callback for overcapacity deflection globally at Settings > Call > Overcapacity Deflection, or per queue at Settings > Queue > IVR (Interactive Voice Response) > Edit / View > [QUEUE] > Overcapacity Deflection > Configure.

For more information, see Overcapacity deflection per-queue and Callback call API.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Salesforce: PKCE and refresh token rotation support

You can now connect Google Cloud CCaaS to Salesforce apps that require Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) and refresh token rotation. Salesforce turns both settings on automatically for newly created connected apps and external client apps. Google Cloud CCaaS uses PKCE when authorizing Salesforce administrator and agent connections. It also saves replacement refresh tokens returned by Salesforce, keeping connections working across subsequent token refreshes. Salesforce apps that don't use these settings keep working as before. This update adds no new configuration steps in Google Cloud CCaaS.

For more information, see Salesforce integration guide.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Branded caller ID label was truncated in the Outbound Number selector when the agent application language was set to French Canadian.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls experienced significant delays in connecting after being assigned to an agent.

  • Fixed an issue where whisper announcements played more than once and the call panel was slow to load in the agent desktop.

  • Fixed an issue where Salesforce case creation was delayed until the end of a call for inbound callers without a matching contact record.

  • Fixed an issue where callbacks to Norwegian, Danish, and Swedish landline numbers were incorrectly dialed with a +1 prefix, causing the calls to fail.

  • Fixed an issue where merged call recordings incorrectly reported only the duration of the first segment in the Calls API.

  • Salesforce account linking now completes only in the browser that started it. An authorization link opened in another browser or an incognito window is refused and can't be reused afterwards, and an administrator's Link New User action must be finished by the same signed-in administrator. Android and iOS agent apps link as before. This behavior is off by default and can be enabled per instance.

  • Fixed an issue that affected call connection stability during active calls for instances using Agent Assist.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent callback calls incorrectly required manual acceptance even when queues were configured for Auto-Answer.

  • Fixed an issue where Telnyx and Twilio virtual agent calls remained stuck in a connected state for an extended period if the carrier didn't send a terminal status callback.

  • Fixed an issue where SMS replies to auto-dismissed chats were incorrectly recorded as an agent timeout instead of an end-user timeout.

  • Fixed an issue where the Unanswered Transferred Call Expiration setting wasn't enforced for calls parked in an overcapacity deflection state.

  • Fixed an issue that affected connection stability and prevented calls from being accurately recorded as end-user hangups when callers hung up while waiting in a queue.

  • Fixed an issue where the external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) new call event payload was missing the queue service level field.

  • Fixed an issue where callers were disconnected when an agent finished their wrap-up following a queue transfer to a virtual agent.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls escalated from a virtual agent to a human agent reported inaccurate call-level queue and wait durations in reporting and data exports.

  • Fixed an issue where unrecorded voicemails incorrectly created Salesforce cases even when the Create CRM records for abandoned calls setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where activating a new language in the CCaaS portal caused the Languages & Messages page to crash or display an infinite loading spinner.

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata files were duplicated across different day folders in external storage when re-uploads occurred after midnight.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls became permanently stuck in a queued status without reaching a terminal state.

  • Fixed an issue where active agents were incorrectly signed out due to inactivity because the system didn't recognize activity outside the embedded call panel.

  • Fixed an issue where a permanent loading spinner appeared in the agent desktop top bar for instances with the email channel disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound keypad (DTMF) entries didn't reach the virtual agent during periods of stream instability or reconnection.

  • Fixed an issue where the external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) new call event payload was missing required parameters.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls involving a virtual agent didn't record an end time and duration when deflected to an overcapacity queue.

  • Fixed an issue where call recordings weren't fetched or saved when CRM ticket creation failed.

  • Fixed an issue where after-hours phone deflections didn't appear in the Deflections dashboard if the outbound dial timed out or failed.

  • Fixed an issue where scheduled phone number obfuscation caused degraded performance for live calls.

  • Fixed an issue where CRM ticket assignees weren't consistently updated following an agent's pickup of a chat.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls became stuck in a queued state after a caller selected a callback during a cold transfer to a specific agent.

  • Fixed an issue where Smart Disposition suggestions weren't pre-selected on the wrap-up screen, causing the disposition field to remain empty after a call ended.

  • Fixed an issue where calls were incorrectly routed to agents even when the minimum available agent floor wasn't met.

  • Fixed an issue where cold transfers to a direct agent extension didn't trigger overcapacity deflection, leaving callers on hold until they disconnected.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent replies were cut off or silenced when using bidirectional streaming with barge-in disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where JSON chat transcripts in external storage contained unredacted message text even when the setting to store unredacted transcripts was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where the Keep Waiting label in the overcapacity deflection screen displayed an inconsistent font style compared to other menu options.

title: What to Keep in Mind for a Cloud Migration
description:
I have led a couple of platform migrations, from on-premises to AWS and from one AWS account structure to another. Each time my job was to coordinate the application, database, DevOps and network teams from scoping to cutover.

This is the list I would want you to keep in mind before you start one. It is grouped into seven categories. Under each I say what to think about and, where it helps, what we did.

1. Scope: decide what changes and what waits

A migration is a chance to modernize, and it is also the easiest place to over-engineer. Start from the rules of the target environment. Ours were no static credentials, TLS on database connections, nothing public by default, autoscaling, and tags on every resource so cost splits by application.

Then list every improvement someone wants and make a call on each one.

Area Think about What we did
Database Move to a managed engine? Upgrade the major version in the same move? Moved to Aurora with an engine upgrade and TLS
Runtime Can VMs, ECS and EKS collapse into one? Consolidated on EKS
Secrets Use a secrets manager and take passwords out of code and config files Secrets moved into AWS
Configuration Externalize parameters so the same build deploys to every environment Config maps
Logging Send application logs to a central store instead of local disk Central search cluster
Access Use roles between services and drop long-lived keys Role-based access
Pipeline Can one pipeline deploy everything? Is GitOps in reach? One CI server in a shared account. GitOps came later, once the runtime was standard
Search and loaders Upgrade or rewrite now, or carry them over as they are? Deferred. Both needed application code changes
Backups Does going live need a new backup design? Deferred. Snapshots were enough

Two columns in the task tracker kept this honest: "key project goal" and "blocker for the first environment". A task with a no in both waited.

2. Discovery: get the complete picture

Get a complete application architecture diagram before anyone builds. Expect the first version to be partial, and keep asking. A platform that has run for years has connections nobody wrote down.

Build an inventory for every environment:

  • Which component runs where, and why it runs there.
  • Every DNS name, with its zone, load balancer, protocol, target group and the resource behind it.
  • Every inbound caller and every outbound dependency.
  • Every loader, job and script that reads or writes the data.

Check your assumptions two and three times, including the convenient ones. We worried that bucket names were stored in the database, which would have made renaming buckets painful. We checked, and they were in a properties file. We also assumed a transit gateway would cover traffic between accounts, and we needed VPC peering as well.

Compare the environments against each other. Production and non-production are rarely built the same way, and the differences are where the cutover steps change.

Even with all of this, three things found us late: another product's web client that read our object storage directly, a data warehouse job that read a logging table we planned to retire, and a monitoring script that counted documents in the old search cluster. Leave room in the plan for your own version of these.

3. People and calendar: one scrum, one plan

Each team has its own backlog, its own way of working and other projects competing for the same people. Someone has to keep those plans moving as one.

  • Run one scrum across all teams. Ours started weekly, went to twice a week to clear blockers, and became daily near the first cutover.
  • Ask every team the same three questions. What are you working on, and what is the estimate? What is blocked or likely to slip, and what is the alternative? What still has to happen for the next environment to cut over on its date?
  • Keep one board. One epic, with each team's own tickets linked in.
  • Spell out requirements early. When one team settles on a solution, share what it needs from the others the same day.
  • Post outcomes in the shared channel. Two-person working sessions are fine, but the result belongs where every team sees it.
  • Follow up instead of waiting. It never hurts to over-communicate.
  • Plan around the calendar. Change freezes, public holidays and time off for key people all punch holes in a quarter. Keep a tab for who is out and when, and set each environment window around it.

Dates will still move, and ours did on the first environment. Build slack around the known gaps so one slip does not push every later window.

4. Data: the part that decides the cutover

Compute can be redeployed. Data has to be moved, kept in sync and proven correct, so it shapes the whole cutover. There is no single right method, only questions you have to answer.

Can you take downtime? Decide this first, with the product owner. A short window removes a whole class of design. We could take one.

One direction or two? Bidirectional replication buys an easy rollback and costs you conflict handling and weeks of testing. We tested replicating back from the upgraded engine to the old one and hit problems. We chose one direction: seed the new database from a shared snapshot, replicate old to new with native replication, and roll back by export and import. That rollback carries downtime, so tell the product team before they agree.

Native or heterogeneous tooling? Every engine has its own replication. Tools such as AWS DMS or Oracle GoldenGate cover moves across engines. Pick the option with the fewest steps to script and test. For us that was native.

Where else does the data live? Rarely in one place. Ours was in three, each with its own method:

Store How it moved Rollback
Relational database Snapshot seed, then one-way native replication Export and import
Search cluster Snapshot to a shared bucket and restore, then a remote reindex of the current day during the window Reindex back
Object storage Bidirectional bucket replication, left on for days after cutover Files already in both accounts

What feeds it and what reads it? List every inbound loader and every downstream reader. We stopped the loaders before the window and repointed them after. The downstream warehouse stayed on the old database for one more day.

What can testing break? Readiness tests that write to the new database while replication is running can break the replication. Plan which tests write, and when.

5. Network and edges: where it usually breaks

The application and the database get the attention. The surprises come from DNS, load balancers and allowlists.

DNS. If the domain's hosting moves too, stage it so a rollback never touches the registrar. We moved ours into Route 53 like this:

  1. Create the new hosted zone as an empty shell. Not live, and no records created early.
  2. Add temporary names in the old zone that point at the new load balancers, so the new stack can be tested before cutover.
  3. At cutover, repoint the old zone's records to the new load balancers.
  4. The next day, sync the records into the new zone.
  5. After 24 hours, publish the new name servers at the registrar next to the old ones.
  6. After another 24 hours, remove the old name servers and watch the URL monitors.

Load balancers. Decide where TLS terminates, what the listener rules are, and whether each endpoint gets its own load balancer or shares one with host and path routing. Have services call each other through a load balancer or a DNS name, not through the cluster's internal networking.

Allowlists. A new account means new outbound addresses. Every partner and internal service that allowlisted the old ones needs the new ones before cutover. Give every outbound call (email delivery, analytics, partner APIs) its own line in the inventory. Check inbound routes too, such as loaders that still run on-premises.

Object storage. If browser or mobile clients read buckets directly, the CORS rules move with the buckets. If bucket names change, find every place a name is stored.

Edge protection. Check what sits in front of production that the lower environments lack. One of our APIs was behind a web application firewall only in production, and a deployment that rewrote its DNS record would have broken it.

6. Cutover: rehearse it the same way every time

Cut over the lowest environment exactly the way you will cut over production. People will ask why QA needs this much ceremony. QA is the only rehearsal production gets.

  • Use one runbook format for every environment. Ours had a preparation tab, a cutover tab, a rollback tab and a DNS tab. Every row had a date, time, duration, team, owner and status.
  • Write the application test cases before the first environment. Run the same set in every environment.
  • Get a sign-off from each team. Once before the window and again after it.
  • Script every cutover and rollback command. Store the scripts before the night.
  • Say ahead of time what a lower environment cannot prove. A production-only firewall, a registrar change and a disaster-recovery copy are typical.
  • Give cleanup its own change request. We had two people present for every bucket deletion.

Our rehearsals showed that deployments had to finish before the window, that published DNS had to be checked against expected results, and that the cutover needed an application redeploy. Each of those would have been a surprise in production.

For a sense of scale, our production runbook budgeted about forty minutes from cutting traffic to sign-off.

7. Monitoring, retention and cost: decide early

Monitoring. Set up monitoring and central logging in the new environment before the cutover. Put full coverage of databases and application URLs on the production readiness list. Stay on one approved logging path. If the cluster auto-instruments applications, a new service comes up already covered.

Retention. Autoscaling without retention is a bill that grows quietly. Set retention at every layer as it is built: log indices, database logging tables, buckets and container images. We left some of these until after cutover, and I would not do that again.

Cost. The cost lessons are mostly about deciding early:

  • Pick instance classes before the build, so reserved capacity can be planned.
  • Run the consolidated cluster on reserved instances.
  • Create temporary instances with volumes that delete on termination.
  • Question any design that copies data between accounts more than it needs to.
  • Ask whether every log line is needed before paying to ship and store it.

My take

A migration is mostly coverage. Know what you have, decide what changes now and what waits, move the data with a rollback you have tested, and rehearse the cutover in every environment. In my experience the hard moments come from things nobody wrote down far more often than from the technology.

It is also never one person's work. Application, database, DevOps and network engineers build it. The lead's job is to keep the scope honest, the plan visible and the teams talking to each other.

With a clear scope, a complete architecture diagram, a regular scrum and a firm timeline, and with AI tools to speed up the inventory and runbook work, three to five months is a fair plan for most platform migrations.

title: Making AI-Generated Websites Match Your Brand: Structure, Style, and Local Edits
description:
Originally published on We0 on November 11, 2026. This English edition was adapted with AI assistance.

Brand style depends on more than a color palette. Define page structure, spacing, typography, content, and editing rules so that AI-generated pages can evolve without losing their identity.

Conclusion first: whether they look alike depends on how deeply you can edit after generation

Let us answer the two questions directly.

First, AI-generated websites do show obvious homogeneity: many tools by default follow a 'template library + one-shot generation' path, and when the same requirement is put into different tools, the layout rhythm, whitespace ratio, and section order are often highly similar. Second, similarity is not inevitable. When a tool has an independent style layer, an editable design canvas, and element-level and multi-select editing capabilities, the same requirement can produce very different pages, and they can be adjusted repeatedly after launch without being torn down and rebuilt.

In other words, 'AI-made websites all look the same' describes the default way most tools work, not the ceiling of AI website building. What really determines the final result is how deeply you can intervene after generation. The next thing to judge is whether your team needs 'a presentable page launched in three minutes' or 'an official website that carries the brand and must be iterated over the long term.' These two things have completely different requirements for tools.

Why do many AI-generated websites look very similar

Similarity comes from four specific mechanisms, not a vague explanation such as 'AI has bad taste.'

  1. Template libraries set the ceiling. The generation of many tools is essentially 'pick a preset template, then replace the copy and images.' The available structures are limited, and style variation can only stay at this layer.
  2. Prompts do not carry enough information. If you only write 'help me make a company website,' AI can only apply the default aesthetic average: a centered large headline, three-column features, gray-white colors, and card-based cases.
  3. Generation is one-shot, and edits are page-wide. Changing one sentence of copy carries the risk of reflowing the whole page. Users often end up not changing it at all, and homogeneity is preserved.
  4. The content itself is repetitive. Placeholder copy, generic stock images, and a lack of brand-specific cases and data make sites read like the same batch even when the structure differs.

Cross-sectional reviews show the direct consequences of this mechanism. A 2026 AI website builder review, when testing local service sites, pointed out that test sites generated by Durable 'all look like they come from the same template family, just with different colors,' and positioned it as a transition option for fast launch rather than a long-term platform (Nubia Magazine review).

The implication for businesses is direct: the cost of homogeneity is not at the moment of building the site, but in brand recognition and conversion afterward. An official website that does not show industry attributes or brand personality is hard for visitors to remember, and even harder to be cited by AI search as a representative answer in a field.

Can AI choose different design styles based on brand positioning

Yes, but you need to distinguish two kinds of 'style.'

One is just reskinning: change the primary color, change a background image, change a set of default fonts. There is a visual difference, but structurally it is still the same template, and visitors can feel familiarity after scrolling two screens.

The other is structural-level difference: the hero format, the choice and order of sections, the presentation of cases and testimonials, whitespace density, and the closing method all change with brand tone. A brand website cares more about company background and trust building; a marketing page emphasizes focused selling points and a conversion path; a portfolio values visual rhythm and project ordering. The difference must happen at the structure and content organization layer to count as a real style distinction.

The judgment standard is therefore simple: if a tool's 'style' appears only in colors and fonts, it is still giving you a template; if it can change section combinations and content rhythm, you have a chance to make a page that does not look like a template.

Colors, fonts, layout, page structure: to which layer can you specify

Customization granularity is roughly divided into four layers; the deeper you go, the closer you get to actually doing design.

Layer How to describe it to AI Typical failure of doing only half a layer
Visual layer Primary color, secondary color, neutral color, accent color and usage ratios; font family and type scale; corner radius and shadows Changing only the primary color without changing hierarchy is just a skin change
Typography layer Grid columns, container width, section spacing, whitespace density, text-image ratio Changing only colors without changing whitespace leaves the page crowded
Structural layer Page list, section order on each page, sections to explicitly avoid Without a defined list, extra pages are generated or pages are missing
Semantic layer Target customers, core selling points, facts that must appear, and FAQs The copy is all adjectives and lacks citable information

Most complaints that 'AI websites all look the same' are actually stuck at the third layer: users only give first-layer instructions, and tools only open first-layer edits. Raise the description to the structural and semantic layers, and the output difference will immediately become larger. For example, for a finance and tax SaaS aimed at small and medium-sized businesses, you can prompt like this: dark ink green as the primary color with a warm white background and a single high-brightness accent color, no gradients; content area width controlled, section spacing on the larger side, cards no more than two columns; the homepage is fixed as hero + customer pain points + three capabilities + two cases + pricing + FAQ + closing CTA, no carousel; the copy must include the company entity, implementation cycle range, and five FAQs. This passage costs very little, yet it determines whether AI is filling in a template or organizing a page.

If I only want to change one module, do I need to regenerate the whole page?

It depends on whether the tool provides element-level editing. The ideal state is to change it yourself: change one headline, replace one image, adjust one paragraph of description, and only that place moves while the rest of the layout stays unchanged. This kind of interaction is a basic capability in design tools, but in AI website builders it is a key dividing line: tools that support element-level editing turn changes into a matter of seconds, while tools that do not require regenerating the whole page every time and accepting uncontrollable reflow.

When batch adjustments are needed, the gap is even more obvious: unify button copy across the site, lower all card headline font sizes by one step, unify case image ratios, replace a certain type of accent color globally. The value of multi-select editing is not speed, but consistency: changing items one by one is easy to miss and easy to cause style drift; after multi-selecting and submitting one unified change, similar elements change together. There are two things to note when using it: before batch editing, confirm that element types are consistent—one button and one text link usually differ in style, and mixed selection will deform the result; after batch editing, spot-check non-target sections, because a unified font-size adjustment may cause line-break misalignment in a dense section.

Operationally, judge in this order:

  1. First distinguish whether the change is content-level (copy, images, links) or structural-level (adding sections, changing layout).
  2. Content-level changes go through element-level editing and should not trigger regeneration.
  3. Structural-level changes are made by adjusting sections on the canvas, or by targeted redoing of a single section, rather than redoing the whole page.
  4. Only when the overall style needs a new direction is it worth regenerating the whole page.

How to check desktop and mobile effects separately

Typography that looks restrained on desktop often becomes a hero that takes two screens to finish on mobile. It is recommended to fix the checking order:

  1. First look at the overall rhythm on desktop: whether the hero information is fully communicated within the hero, and whether whitespace between sections is even.
  2. Then switch to mobile: whether the hero is squeezed, whether buttons are easy to tap, and whether tables and code blocks overflow horizontally.
  3. Confirm breakpoint behavior page by page: whether card columns drop to a single column as expected, and whether navigation collapses into a menu.
  4. Check long text and mixed Chinese-English typesetting: whether the type scale breaks, and whether line height is compressed.
  5. Recheck on real devices, at least one iOS and one Android device, not just simulators.

Test case: the same requirement, three brand styles

Fix the same content draft—a finance and tax SaaS official website for small and medium-sized businesses, with the same page list (homepage, product capabilities, cases, pricing, FAQ, contact)—and change only the style instructions to generate three versions.

  • Tech brand style: dark background with monochrome highlights; the hero uses a capability-oriented claim; the product capability section is arranged in three columns; cases are presented as data metric cards.
  • Minimal business style: warm white background with dark ink green; the hero keeps only one value proposition and one CTA; section spacing is noticeably increased; cases change to two-column text and images; decorative graphics are removed.
  • Creative design style: asymmetric grid; headline font-size range is larger; cases change to a large-image waterfall layout; FAQ uses two-column accordions.

The biggest difference is not color, but hero information density, section order, and whitespace ratio. When these three change, the same content reads as three brands.

Then do a local modification comparison: before the change, the hero subtitle was a three-line industry description, and on mobile users had to scroll two screens to see the CTA; after the change, the subtitle was compressed into a one-sentence description of just over ten words, and the CTA was moved below the hero, while the other sections stayed unchanged. The result is complete hero information without triggering a full-page reflow—this is exactly the difference between element-level editing and full-page regeneration.

Cross-sectional testing from a designer's perspective also confirms that the gap mainly comes from whether the site can be changed after generation. When the same requirement was given to Squarespace Blueprint AI, Wix AI, Lovable, Webflow AI, and Framer AI for generation, design item scores ranged from 1/5 for Framer to 4/5 for Wix and Webflow; Webflow's output was considered the best designed, but the editor users then enter would deter most business owners (Design by Ency test).

Purchase and acceptance checklist: judging whether an AI website builder can be changed

Use the following checklist during the trial phase; it is much more reliable than watching demo videos.

Check item Specific question Pass standard
Generation method Template replacement or section composition Can specify page list and section order
Style control Can you specify colors, fonts, grid, whitespace Can produce structural-level differences, not just reskinning
Local editing Does changing one piece of copy trigger full-page regeneration Element-level editing, with the rest of the layout unchanged
Batch editing Can multiple elements be selected and adjusted together Supports multi-select and maintains visual consistency
Multi-device acceptance Can you switch device views for checking Desktop, tablet, and mobile can be checked separately
Iteration continuity Is the original design preserved after changes The baseline can continue and can be rolled back
Launch and operations Does it support domain deployment, content management, and SEO/GEO basics Content can be continuously updated after launch

If two or more of the first five items fail, the tool is more suitable for temporary pages than for a long-term official website that carries the brand. After choosing a tool, three more things need to be added: write 'can it be changed' into the selection criteria, not just generation speed; organize brand guidelines into a reusable constraint list (primary color and usage ratio, type scale, corner radius and shadow rules, hero information limit, image style, prohibited elements), and give it to AI together with the requirement each time, so style drift will be significantly reduced; establish a content draft—company entity information, service scope, case data, and FAQs—which serve both visitors and AI search citations.

How we0 supports this 'editable' chain

Generation is not the endpoint. In the three-step process—describe the requirement, multi-Agent real-time building, adjust in the visual canvas and publish to your own domain—adjustment is a default step, not a remedy. Multi-style design turns sections such as hero, advantages, introduction, features, cases, pricing, FAQ, and CTA into a composable page system, with style differences reflected in section selection and page rhythm; the editable design canvas supports element-level editing of text and images, multi-select editing, and switching between device views, so local adjustments do not require redoing the whole page (capability description: we0 official website).

It should be noted that these capabilities solve the efficiency problem of customizability and iterability; they do not promise rankings, traffic, or deal outcomes—those depend on content quality, industry competition, and operational investment.

FAQ

Do AI-generated websites all look the same?
The default output of most tools is indeed similar because they follow a template-library plus one-shot generation path. When a tool supports section composition, style parameters, and element-level editing, the same requirement can produce noticeably different results.

Can I specify colors, fonts, and layout?
Yes, but describe them by layer: colors and type scale at the visual layer, grid and whitespace at the typography layer, page list and section order at the structural layer. If you only give visual-layer instructions, the output usually still looks like a template.

If I only want to change one module, do I need to regenerate the entire page?
No, provided the tool has element-level editing capabilities. Text and image elements can be edited directly on the canvas without affecting the rest of the layout; only a complete style change requires regeneration.

How do I confirm the mobile effect?
Check in a fixed order: desktop hero and section rhythm, mobile hero information volume, breakpoint behavior (card columns, navigation collapse), mixed Chinese-English typesetting and long text, and finally recheck on real devices.

Related Tools

  • We0: an AI intelligent website building and lead growth workspace, covering natural language website building, editable design canvas, content management, and SEO/GEO optimization.
  • Squarespace Blueprint AI, Wix AI, Framer AI, Webflow AI: mainstream AI website builders that appeared in this comparison, which can be used to verify style controllability.

Related Links

  • we0 official website
  • Top 10 Best AI Website Builders In The World 2026 · Nubia Magazine
  • Best AI Website Builders 2026: 5 Tested by a Designer · Design by Ency

Summary

AI-generated websites look similar because template libraries set the structural ceiling, prompts do not carry enough information, one-shot generation cannot be edited locally, and content assets are repetitive—not because of the ceiling of AI capability. Move brand requirements from colors and fonts to section order, page lists, and a citable information layer, and the same content can read as three styles; changing one module does not require regenerating the whole page if the tool has element-level editing; changing multiple places depends on multi-select editing for consistency; desktop and mobile must be accepted separately. we0 uses a composable multi-style page system and an editable design canvas to support the adjustment stage after generation, allowing the official website to iterate continuously while retaining the original design.

title: Building a Merchant-to-Category Learning Pipeline That Runs Entirely on Your Phone
description:
When you review your monthly spending, you do not want to see a raw list of bank reference codes like UPI/CR/429810291/SWG*BLR.

You want to see:

  • Food & Dining: Rs. 12,450
  • Groceries: Rs. 8,200
  • Fuel: Rs. 4,100
  • Utilities: Rs. 3,500

To make transaction tracking effortless, an expense tracker must automatically map messy merchant strings into human-readable categories.

Commercial apps solve this by harvesting merchant data in the cloud. Every time millions of users swipe their cards, the app uploads the merchant strings to central servers, where crowdsourced tags categorize the business.

The privacy cost is immense: central servers track which coffee shops you frequent, which pharmacies you visit, and which fitness centers you attend.

Here is how FinLedger architected an on-device merchant-to-category learning pipeline (LocalCategoryIntelligenceEngine.kt, commit e4b4df2) that learns your personal categorization preferences entirely offline.

The Merchant Normalization Challenge

Before a system can categorize a merchant, it must normalize the messy strings generated by payment processors.

Consider how the same merchant appears across different banks and payment channels:

  • "SWIGGY BANGALORE IND"
  • "UPI-SWIGGY-swiggy.payu@icici-429182"
  • "POS 491029 SWIGGY FOODS"
  • "BUNDL TECHNOLOGIES PVT LTD" 
flowchart TD
    RawStrings["Raw Bank SMS Merchant Strings:
    'SWIGGY BANGALORE IND'
    'UPI-SWIGGY-swiggy.payu@icici'
    'POS 491029 SWIGGY FOODS'"] --> Normalizer["Deterministic String Normalizer:
    1. Strip payment rail prefixes (UPI-, POS, NEFT)
    2. Strip VPA handles (@icici, @okhdfc)
    3. Strip terminal IDs and location suffixes"]

    Normalizer --> CleanKey["Normalized Merchant Key:
    'SWIGGY'"]

    CleanKey --> Pipeline["Local Category Engine"]

FinLedger's normalizer strips transaction prefixes (POS, UPI, IMPS, ACH), removes VPA routing handles (@oksbi, .payu@icici), and discards dynamic terminal codes.

This extracts a clean, stable merchant root key—such as SWIGGY, ZOMATO, SHELL, or UBER—in less than 20 microseconds.

The Multi-Tiered On-Device Pipeline

Once the merchant key is normalized, the engine evaluates categorization through a prioritized three-tier hierarchy:

flowchart TD
    CleanKey["Normalized Merchant Key"] --> Tier1{"Tier 1:
    User Personal Overrides
    (Learned Local Relational Map)"}

    Tier1 -->|Found Exact Match| Result1["Apply User Learned Category
    (Confidence: 100%)"]

    Tier1 -->|Not Found| Tier2{"Tier 2:
    Pure Kotlin ML Model
    (TF-IDF + Logistic Regression)"}

    Tier2 -->|Confidence > 75%| Result2["Apply ML Inferred Category
    (Confidence: High)"]

    Tier2 -->|Uncertain| Tier3["Tier 3:
    Default Fallback
    (Flag for Review / Other)"]

Tier 1: The Local Relational Feedback Loop

The user is always the ultimate authority. If a user buys office supplies at a department store and categorizes it under Work & Business, that preference belongs to them, regardless of what a general dictionary says.

In FinLedger, whenever a user edits or confirms a transaction's category:

  1. The app updates an internal Room SQLite entity: merchant_category_preferences.
  2. The record maps the normalized merchant key (normalized_merchant) to the selected category ID (category_id), along with an incremented usage counter and last-updated timestamp.
  3. The next time an SMS arrives with that merchant key, Tier 1 intercepts it immediately. The app applies the user's custom choice with 100% confidence.

Tier 2: The Lightweight Inference Engine

For merchants the user has never encountered before, Tier 2 evaluates the normalized string and surrounding SMS context using FinLedger's pure Kotlin machine learning engine (LocalSmsIntelligenceEngine.kt).

Using sublinear TF-IDF and logistic regression, the engine detects semantic markers:

  • Keywords like "Fuel", "Petrol", "HPCL", or "IOCL" yield Transportation & Fuel.
  • Keywords like "Hospital", "Pharmacy", "Clinic", or "Medicals" yield Healthcare.
  • Keywords like "Supermarket", "Grocery", or "Mart" yield Groceries.

If the top predicted category has a calibrated Softmax probability exceeding 75%, it is assigned as the default suggestion.

Tier 3: The "Never Guess" Fallback

If the merchant is novel and the ML model is uncertain (e.g., an unfamiliar regional shop name like "Guptha & Sons"), the pipeline refuses to guess.

The transaction is assigned to General / Uncategorized and highlighted in the pending review tray with a prompt inviting the user to pick a category. The moment the user picks a category, Tier 1 learns it permanently for all future visits.

Memory and Storage Footprint

Because everything runs on SQLite and in-memory caches:

  • The local merchant dictionary occupies less than 200 KB of encrypted SQLite storage for a typical user over two years.
  • Lookup queries execute against indexed columns in less than 0.3 milliseconds.
  • No background network daemons exist; the database never syncs merchant names to external cloud servers.

Key Takeaway

A smart personal finance app does not need to send your shopping habits to the cloud to understand where you spend your money.

By combining deterministic string normalization, a local relational feedback loop, and a lightweight on-device ML engine, FinLedger creates a categorization pipeline that gets smarter with every transaction you log—without sacrificing your privacy.

FinLedger is a privacy-first, offline-first personal finance application for Android that models bank accounts, credit cards, and cash without double-counting.

Explore FinLedger on Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.devanshufinance.app

title: November 09, 2026
description:
AI Hypercomputer

Feature

Generally available: Pathways on Cloud is now generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Major features include the following:

  • Single-controller execution model: Coordinate multi-slice and multi-host Cloud TPU workloads from a single Python client process. Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and centralized scheduling to support both Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) and Multiple Program, Multiple Data (MPMD) workloads. For example, training and reinforcement learning (RL) loops.
  • Resilient and elastic training: Keep training jobs running across hardware interruptions with resilient training, including the following capabilities:
    • Elastic training: Dynamically scale down to healthy Cloud TPU slices during unplanned hardware failures and scale back up when replacement slices rejoin without restarting the entire job.
    • Suspend-resume: Automatically save and restore high-bandwidth memory (HBM) state to Cloud Storage during planned GKE preemption events.
    • Hot-swapping: Remap interrupted workloads onto standby or lower-priority Cloud TPU slices.
  • Colocated Python sidecar containers: Run custom Python code directly on Cloud TPU host VMs alongside Pathways workers. For example, multi-host data loading with Grain or RemoteIterator, and distributed asynchronous checkpointing with Orbax.
  • Interactive mode and Shared Pathways Service: Run, inspect, and debug JAX workloads interactively from a notebook or terminal using interactive mode, or share a long-running pool of Cloud TPU slices on demand across multiple users and jobs with the Shared Pathways Service.
  • Cluster Director, Cluster Toolkit, and GKE integration: Launch JAX workloads on the Pathways runtime using Cluster Director or Cluster Toolkit (gcluster with --pathways and --pathways-headless), or by deploying Kubernetes JobSet manifests on GKE.
  • pathwaysutils utility package: Use the pathwaysutils Python package for advanced features such as the Shared Pathways Service, elasticity, and experimental.reshard for device-side data transfers across hosts over Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) or Data Center Network (DCN).
  • Standard libtpu.so layering and custom libtpu.so support: Pathways is layered over the standard libtpu.so shared library and provides a way to dynamically link in a user-provided libtpu.so at runtime using PathwaysJobSet.with_custom_libtpu in pathwaysutils.
  • Single-process profiling, observability, and compilation cache: Capture end-to-end JAX profiler traces across the client, proxy, resource manager, and Cloud TPU hosts from a single process. Reuse compiled XLA modules with a persistent compilation cache on Cloud Storage, and view Pathways control and data plane metrics in Cloud Monitoring.
  • Agentic workload debugging: Troubleshoot failed, crashing, or stalled Pathways workloads on GKE using the pathways-workload agent skill. With this skill, AI agents can inspect Cloud Logging container logs, node kernel logs, and GKE events to help identify root causes and fixes.
  • Supported Cloud TPU versions, JAX versions, and container images: Supports TPU7x (Ironwood), TPU v6e (Trillium), TPU v5p, and TPU v5e for JAX versions 0.12.0.1, 0.12.0, 0.11.2, 0.11.1, 0.11.0, 0.10.2, and 0.10.1, with container images published in Artifact Registry:
    • Image locations:
      • Pathways resource manager and worker: us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways/server:TAG
      • IFRT proxy server: us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways/proxy_server:TAG
      • Colocated Python sidecar: us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways/colocated_python_sidecar:TAG
    • Image tags: Replace TAG with one of the following tags, which are created automatically when a Pathways build passes qualification tests and is promoted to production:
      • YYYYMMDD-jax_JAX_VERSION: Pinned tag created by combining the UTC promotion date (YYYYMMDD) with -jax_ and the verified JAX version (JAX_VERSION) after per-version qualification tests pass. For example, 20261108-jax_0.12.0.1.
      • jax-JAX_VERSION: Rolling tag updated after per-version qualification tests pass to point to the most recent verified image for that JAX release. For example, jax-0.12.0.1 or jax-0.12.0.
      • latest: Rolling tag updated when a build passes qualification tests against the most recent supported JAX release.

For more information, see Introduction to Pathways on Cloud.

Smart batching automatically batches and offloads eligible AI operations for asynchronous evaluation. It improves query execution speed without requiring you to rewrite queries into complex array structures. In PostgreSQL 18 and later, this feature is enabled by default. For more information, see Accelerate performance for queries with AI functions.

  • Sentiment analysis: the ai.analyze_sentiment function is generally available on AlloyDB clusters running PostgreSQL 17 and later. This built-in function classifies the sentiment of text as positive, negative, or neutral directly within SQL queries in real time. For more information, see Analyze text sentiment.

Meta Muse models in Preview

Muse Wonder from Meta (meta/muse-wonder-1.0), Muse Ember from Meta (meta/muse-ember-1.0), and Muse Spark 1.3 from Meta (meta/muse-spark-1.3) are available in Preview on the global endpoint through the OpenAI-compatible Responses API. Muse Wonder and Muse Spark 1.3 accept text, image, and PDF inputs, and Muse Ember accepts text and image inputs. All three models support reasoning, function calling, structured output, and a 1M-token context window.

For more information, see Muse models from Meta.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Feature

GKE Gateway now supports Server Name Indication (SNI)-based routing with TLS passthrough. You can use TLS protocol-specific rules to route incoming TLS streams from the Gateway to Kubernetes Services based on SNI without terminating TLS at the GKE Gateway load balancer. Application developers can create TLSRoute resources to expose secure TLS traffic to applications that run in the GKE cluster.

Creating TLSRoute resources requires the Gateway API version 1.5.0 or later CRDs (Standard channel), which are installed in GKE version 1.35.2-gke.1842000 or later.

This feature supports single-cluster and multi-cluster GKE Gateway load balancers by using the following GatewayClass resources:

  • gke-l7-rilb
  • gke-l7-regional-external-managed
  • gke-l7-rilb-mc
  • gke-l7-regional-external-managed-mc
  • gke-l7-cross-regional-internal-managed-mc

For more information, see Deploy a TLS passthrough Gateway.

Feature

Agent Substrate on GKE is now Generally Available (GA) for GKE Standard clusters running version 1.37 or later.

Agent Substrate is an infrastructure layer designed for large-scale, high-density AI agent workloads, such as personal assistants and coding agents. Because interactive agents often remain idle while waiting for user input, running them on traditional microservice infrastructure can underutilize CPU and memory resources. Agent Substrate uses a lightweight control plane that bypasses standard Kubernetes Pod scheduling limits to provide fast sandbox provisioning and efficient suspend-and-resume capabilities.

For more information, see About Agent Substrate on GKE.

Managed Service for Apache Spark

Announcement

Managed Service for Apache Spark (formerly Google Cloud Serverless for Apache Spark): Runtime version 4.0 is generally available (GA). This version includes the following components:

  • Apache Spark 4.2.0
  • BigQuery Connector 0.46.0
  • Cloud Storage Connector 4.0.7
  • Java 25
  • Python 3.13
  • Scala 2.13.17

Runtime 4.0 also introduces the following changes:

  • Batch workloads run in the premium tier and use Lightning Engine by default.
  • Memory shapes determine the memory of drivers and executors. The default highmem memory shape provides 7.75 GiB of memory per vCPU.
  • Premium tier workloads that use the default driver configuration are eligible to run the driver on a fast-startup VM, which reduces startup time.
  • The Lakehouse runtime catalog is the default Spark catalog for batch workloads and interactive sessions.
  • Workloads that don't use GPUs consume the Data Compute Units quota instead of Compute Engine CPU and disk quotas.

Runtime 4.0 doesn't support some features of earlier runtimes, such as SparkR batches, Jupyter sessions, and the Persistent History Server. For more information, see Unsupported functionality and behavior changes.

Memorystore for Redis

Feature

Memorystore for Redis supports the CLIENT command and the following subcommands:

  • CLIENT | CACHING
  • CLIENT | GETNAME
  • CLIENT | GETREDIR
  • CLIENT | HELP
  • CLIENT | ID
  • CLIENT | INFO
  • CLIENT | KILL
  • CLIENT | LIST
  • CLIENT | NO-TOUCH
  • CLIENT | REPLY
  • CLIENT | SETNAME
  • CLIENT | TRACKING
  • CLIENT | TRACKINGINFO

For more information about the CLIENT command and its supported subcommands, see Supported and blocked commands. This feature is generally available (GA).

SAP on Google Cloud

Announcement

Google Cloud's Agent for SAP version 3.16

Version 3.16 of Google Cloud's Agent for SAP is generally available (GA). This version introduces enhancements for the agent's configureinstance command and some framework level updates.

For more information, see What's new with Google Cloud's Agent for SAP.

Security Command Center

Feature

Security Command Center predefined roles are modified. For information about the changes and how to migrate your custom roles, see Migrating custom roles.

Feature

Preview: Security Command Center Vulnerability Assessment for Google Cloud helps you detect vulnerabilities and exposed secrets in the container images of your Cloud Run services, jobs, and worker pools with Vulnerability Assessment for Cloud Run (Preview).

For more information, see Enable and use Vulnerability Assessment for Google Cloud.

Virtual Private Cloud

Feature

General Availability: You can create an internal range with the INTERNAL_ADDRESS purpose to allocate global internal IPv4 addresses for Private Service Connect endpoints that access global Google APIs.

For more information, see Internal ranges for Private Service Connect endpoints.

title: SOMS: Building Federated Chat for Self-Hosted Servers
description:
SOMS (Simple Open Messaging Service) is an MIT-licensed, self-hosted chat platform with cross-server messaging, group conversations, rich media, and one-to-one WebRTC audio/video calls. Its backend uses NestJS, Fastify, and PostgreSQL; native clients use Tauri and a shared Rust runtime.

The design centers on a practical self-hosting problem: independent servers go offline. A personal server might restart, lose connectivity, or move behind a different network address.

How can peers catch up without making successful delivery of every notification a correctness requirement?

SOMS addresses that with advisory notifications, pull-based synchronization, and durable deletion facts. This article explains those choices, along with the PostgreSQL task system and native-client architecture.

Status: SOMS 0.1.0-alpha.2 and SOMFP v1.0.0-draft.2 are technical previews. Stable operation and upgrade compatibility are not guaranteed before beta. APIs, federation contracts, and storage formats may change incompatibly. Use isolated deployments with disposable data, not production or critical communications.

Want to see the interface first? Open the SOMS Playground. It runs a simulation in browser memory without an account or backend. It is a UI demo, not a live federation or call-interoperability test.

What SOMS includes

  • Messaging: direct and group conversations, rich text, replies, mentions, and link previews.
  • Media: images, video, and voice messages, with SHA-256 verification for federated resource transfers.
  • Federation: authenticated server-to-server HTTP APIs, cursor-based catch-up, and separate deletion queries.
  • Calls and realtime updates: one-to-one WebRTC voice/video calling, cross-server signaling, and Server-Sent Events for client updates.
  • Administration: role-based access control, quotas, content reports, and moderation tools.
  • Clients: an Angular web/PWA interface and native clients using Tauri, Rust, and platform adapters.

SOMS servers federate using SOMFP (Simple Open Messaging Federation Protocol), a separate protocol from Matrix and XMPP. It connects independently operated domains without a global coordinator or shared database. Individual resources still have defined authorities, such as the origin server of a group.

1. Push to notify, pull to synchronize

A push-based system can be reliable, but it needs explicit rules for offline delivery, retry limits, and reconciliation. SOMFP instead keeps notification delivery out of the authoritative synchronization path.

A signed POST /somfp/v1/feed-heads tells a peer that newer feed bounds are available. The hint is advisory: receiving it does not mean the receiver has synchronized, and missing it must not lose the underlying state. Consumers need catch-up and reconciliation independently of hint delivery.

SOMFP separates change discovery from content retrieval, rather than putting every kind of change into one append-only event log:

  1. State Feed — GET /somfp/v1/state-feed: a per-peer, compacted feed of relationship facts and content-head projections. A thread content head advertises message and tombstone bounds, not the message bodies themselves.
  2. Message Query — GET /somfp/v1/messages: retrieves messages for a thread using message-sequence coordinates.
  3. Tombstone Query — GET /somfp/v1/message-tombstones: retrieves deletion facts using an independent thread-local deletionSeq cursor.

A simplified exchange looks like this:

Hints announce changes. Pull queries retrieve authoritative state and content.

This is a conceptual flow, not a requirement to drain all messages before deletions. Each query has its own coordinates and authorization rules. Message sequences, deletion sequences, and State Feed IDs are not interchangeable, and monotonic does not mean contiguous.

The benefit is recoverable progress: a consumer can continue from persisted cursors rather than depend on replaying every wakeup notification. Recovery depends on durable storage, retained authoritative data, and valid authorization.

2. Deletions are durable facts

Deleting only the publisher's message row would leave an offline replica without a reliable way to discover the deletion. SOMFP therefore exposes authoritative tombstones separately from messages.

The protocol defines this structure:

interface MessageTombstone {
  deletionSeq: ThreadSequence;
  thread: ThreadAddress;
  messageSeq: ThreadSequence;
  type: 'USER_RETRACTION' | 'MODERATION_REMOVAL';
  deletedAt: EpochMilliseconds;
}

deletionSeq orders deletion facts. messageSeq identifies the target in the publisher's message-coordinate space. Neither is a globally interchangeable message identifier. For example, a group origin republishes an accepted deletion using its own target-message coordinate rather than blindly forwarding the previous hop's sequence.

Authoritative tombstones are retained permanently by the protocol. A conforming consumer authenticates the publisher, validates its authority over the target, and applies the deletion according to the synchronization rules. Local moderation of a replica does not automatically grant authority to delete that content on every server.

Separate deletion cursors make offline catch-up explicit. They do not imply that every deletion is delivered in a single total order with subsequent messages, nor can they force an uncooperative server to erase backups, exports, or independently retained copies.

3. Trust starts with HTTPS; continuity comes from pinned keys

Public discovery metadata is served at GET /somfp/discovery.

Initial peer trust comes from hostname-validated HTTPS. After recognition, a peer pins a root public key and authenticates requests using Ed25519 HTTP Message Signatures in the RFC 9421 wire format.

The key roles are distinct:

  • Root keys anchor a peer's identity.
  • Signing-key certificates authorize HTTP signing keys under a root.
  • HTTP request signatures bind the request method, path, query, authority, date, and content digest.

A newly fetched discovery document does not silently replace a pinned root. Ordinary signing-key rotation remains under that root; root changes use the protocol's explicit recognition and rotation process, subject to local adoption policy.

Ordinary JSON responses are protected by hostname-validated TLS, not by an independent signature on every returned event. Request authentication, response transport integrity, and resource-digest verification serve different purposes.

Security boundary: these mechanisms authenticate federation traffic and protect it in transit. They are not end-to-end message encryption between chat participants.

4. PostgreSQL instead of an external message broker

The backend combines NestJS and Fastify with PostgreSQL and Drizzle. A Caddy edge can provide TLS termination, reverse proxying, and static assets. Direct backend HTTP/2 is available when backend TLS is configured; a TLS-terminating proxy can use HTTP/1.1 on the upstream connection.

Background work uses a PostgreSQL-backed durable task system rather than requiring Redis or RabbitMQ:

  • Persistent task state: queued work and execution progress live in the database.
  • Retry and recovery: the dispatcher can revisit unfinished work after a process restart, subject to each task's retry and checkpoint semantics.
  • Domain-owned behavior: generic scheduling lives in src/durable-task/; task handlers and business rules remain with their owning domains.

Database locking is part of that design. Non-key read-modify-write operations prefer FOR NO KEY UPDATE to avoid unnecessary conflicts with foreign-key checks, alongside consistent lock ordering to manage contention.

The trade-off is operational: fewer services simplify deployment, while task traffic and application traffic share PostgreSQL. Database health, workload, backups, and recovery remain central to running an instance.

5. Shared Rust policy, native platform capabilities

The Angular interface runs in browser and native environments. Native clients share a Rust runtime; the browser uses its own runtime.

For native clients, Rust is the shared owner of business rules and cross-platform runtime orchestration. Platform adapters expose OS capabilities:

Share native policy in Rust; keep OS capabilities in platform adapters.

The boundary is intentionally strict:

  1. Adapters report facts. Lifecycle changes, connectivity observations, notification interactions, and permission results become inputs to Rust.
  2. Rust owns decisions. Connection policy, session/account generations, synchronization, and notification/call decisions belong in shared native code rather than parallel Kotlin and Rust state machines.
  3. Adapters execute OS actions. Notification rendering, secure-storage access, audio routing, and platform media APIs remain platform responsibilities.
  4. Async results are validated. Cancellation and session-generation checks prevent stale work from publishing into a newer session.

The native architecture keeps blocking I/O and long-running work off the UI thread, while OS APIs that require the main thread run there. Native persistence includes local caches and platform-backed credential storage; protecting credentials is separate from encrypting message or media caches.

6. Try the interface or deploy a test instance

The SOMS Playground demonstrates conversations, group interactions, and media/calling interfaces using an in-memory simulation. No backend setup is needed.

For an isolated self-hosting trial, the Docker Compose configuration generator helps prepare a deployment configuration. Treat generated credentials as secrets, and use disposable data during the technical preview.

Web/PWA, Android, macOS, and Linux clients are available in alpha. Check the release assets for the installation packages actually published for a particular version; source/build support is not the same as an available download.

  • GitHub repository
  • Release assets
  • SOMFP specification and schemas

The most useful feedback at this stage is concrete: try two test servers, interrupt connectivity, restore it, and inspect message catch-up and deletion propagation. Reports that include the versions, topology, and reproduction steps will help test whether these architectural choices hold up outside the development environment.

title: Running hundreds of Telegram bots on one Node.js server: 8 lessons from production
description:
Most Telegram bot tutorials end at "it works for one bot". Our platform runs a few hundred merchant bots (shops, paid channels, AI assistants) from one Node.js cluster, and almost every hard bug we hit only appeared at that scale. Here are the lessons, in the order they hurt.

1. One process cannot own every bot: shard by bot

A single Node process runs out of event-loop headroom long before it runs out of memory. We run one primary process plus a pool of worker processes, and each bot belongs to exactly one worker. The reverse proxy routes every webhook request to the worker that owns that bot (a stable hash of the bot id), so a bot's updates are always handled in one place, in order, with its in-memory state.

The rule that keeps this sane: anything that must happen once (schedulers, reminders, cleanup jobs) runs only on the primary, and every worker checks "do I own this bot?" before acting.

2. Start bots slowly, or Telegram will rate-limit all of them

On boot, the naive code calls getMe and setWebhook for every bot at once. With hundreds of bots that is a burst of thousands of requests, and Telegram answers with 429 Too Many Requests and a retry_after that can lock bots out for minutes. Every restart degraded every bot.

Fixes that worked:

  • Cache getMe results in the database and only refresh them in the background.
  • Check getWebhookInfo first and call setWebhook only when the URL or settings are actually wrong.
  • Spread the remaining calls over time with a small queue, and honour retry_after when it is short. Give up and retry later when it is long.

3. Answer the webhook fast and do the work after

Telegram waits for your HTTP response. If your handler awaits a database call, an AI model or a file upload before answering, slow requests pile up and Telegram starts retrying, so you get the same update twice.

Reply 200 as soon as the update is validated and queued, then process it. The exception is payments: save a pre_checkout_query or a successful payment durably before you answer, because that is the one place where losing an update costs real money.

4. Deduplicate updates by update_id

Retries, restarts and proxy hiccups all produce duplicates. Keep the last few thousand update_ids per bot (an LRU in memory is enough for most of them) and drop repeats before any handler runs. For anything that moves money, add a second, durable "processed" table keyed by the callback or payment id, so a duplicate can never pay out twice even across a restart.

5. Use secret_token on every webhook

setWebhook accepts a secret_token, and Telegram sends it back in the X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token header on every request. Check it, and reject requests without it. Also keep the bot token out of the webhook URL: URLs end up in proxy access logs, monitoring tools and error reports. Use an opaque id in the path instead.

6. Be careful what shutdown does

A classic trap is a "clean" shutdown handler that deletes each bot's webhook on SIGTERM. It looks tidy, but a routine restart then unregisters every bot the process owned. Shutdown handlers should stop taking new work and flush queues. They should not change anything on Telegram's side.

Related: wrap startup code so that one bad module cannot crash the process on load. With a cluster, a crash on load is a silent total outage, because every worker dies the same way.

7. Rate-limit per user and per bot

One user tapping a button 50 times a second, or one bot being flooded, should not slow every other bot down. A sliding window per (bot, user) and per bot, checked before any handler, keeps the noise out. Escalate repeat offenders to temporary bans rather than answering every request.

8. Your bot library will silently drop new update types

Telegram keeps adding update types. In November 2026 Bot API 10.4 added widget_query for interactive widget cards. Older libraries only dispatch the types they know, so new ones vanish without an error. If you rely on a library, check how it handles unknown updates, and handle new types yourself before the library's dispatcher. (I wrote up the widget case here: Telegram widgets: interactive cards inside chat messages.)

Also remember allowed_updates: if you ever set an explicit list, new types are not delivered until you add them.

The short version

  • Shard bots across workers, one owner per bot.
  • Run schedulers on one process only.
  • Start slowly and cache getMe.
  • Answer fast, but save payments first.
  • Dedupe by update_id, and durably for money.
  • Use secret_token and keep tokens out of URLs.
  • Make shutdown boring.
  • Rate-limit per user and per bot.
  • Watch for new update types.

These lessons come from building TeleCrow, a no-code platform for Telegram shop bots, paid-channel bots and AI assistants. If you run many bots yourself, I hope this saves you a few late nights.

Disclosure: I work on TeleCrow.
