title: Verify Boba, Soneium and World Chain IDs with a JSON-RPC batch
description:
Before using an RPC endpoint, check that it serves the network you intended. A successful HTTP response alone cannot tell you that. For Boba, Soneium and World Chain mainnet, the expected chain IDs are 288, 1868 and 480 respectively.

This example checks each network with one JSON-RPC batch containing eth_chainId and eth_blockNumber. The code uses the built-in fetch in Node.js 22 and was verified offline on Node.js 22.22.0; there are no dependencies, models, accounts or API keys to configure. The requests only read data. They do not sign or broadcast transactions.

The endpoints come from the public chain catalog. Its saved November 12 snapshot permits both methods and batches of up to ten items on these three public endpoints. Each batch below contains two items. Public method, range and rate-limit policies still apply; this is not a promise that every RPC method is available anonymously.

Run the check

Save the following as example.mjs, then run:

node example.mjs

The script processes networks sequentially. It rejects redirects, requires HTTP 200 and validates both response IDs without depending on their order. Each result must be a nonnegative hexadecimal JSON-RPC quantity. A mismatched chain ID, RPC error, malformed response or request failure stops the script before the next network and sets a nonzero exit status. There are no retries or fallback providers.

const networks = [
  ['Boba', 288n, 'https://api.blockvectra.com/v1/boba_mainnet/public'],
  ['Soneium', 1868n, 'https://api.blockvectra.com/v1/soneium_mainnet/public'],
  ['World Chain', 480n, 'https://api.blockvectra.com/v1/world_mainnet/public'],
];
const quantity = value => {
  if (typeof value !== 'string' || !/^0x(?:0|[1-9a-fA-F][0-9a-fA-F]*)$/.test(value)) {
    throw new Error('Invalid hexadecimal quantity');
  }
  return BigInt(value);
};

try {
  for (const [name, expected, url] of networks) {
    const controller = new AbortController();
    const timer = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 10_000);
    try {
      const response = await fetch(url, {
        method: 'POST',
        redirect: 'error',
        signal: controller.signal,
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
        body: JSON.stringify([
          { jsonrpc: '2.0', id: 'chain-id', method: 'eth_chainId', params: [] },
          { jsonrpc: '2.0', id: 'block-number', method: 'eth_blockNumber', params: [] },
        ]),
      });
      if (response.status !== 200) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
      const batch = await response.json();
      if (!Array.isArray(batch) || batch.length !== 2) throw new Error('Invalid batch');
      const results = new Map();
      for (const item of batch) {
        if (!item || typeof item !== 'object' || Array.isArray(item)
          || item.jsonrpc !== '2.0' || Object.hasOwn(item, 'error')
          || !['chain-id', 'block-number'].includes(item.id) || results.has(item.id)) {
          throw new Error('Invalid response ID, version, or RPC error');
        }
        results.set(item.id, quantity(item.result));
      }
      if (results.size !== 2 || results.get('chain-id') !== expected) {
        throw new Error(`${name}: chain ID mismatch`);
      }
      console.log(`${name}: chainId=${expected}, blockNumber=${results.get('block-number')}`);
    } finally {
      clearTimeout(timer);
    }
  }
} catch (error) {
  console.error(error instanceof Error ? error.message : 'Request failed');
  process.exitCode = 1;
}

Read the output narrowly

Captured responses at 2026-11-12 07:01 UTC:

Boba: chainId=288, blockNumber=41731014
Soneium: chainId=1868, blockNumber=30666059
World Chain: chainId=480, blockNumber=37565615

Those block numbers are a dated output example, not values to assert in your application. Your run will usually return different heights. A valid height is not an independent freshness or canonical-chain check.

For an Agent or a larger application, treat a nonzero exit as a reason to stop and inspect the error before proceeding. Do not silently continue on another network, and do not turn this identity check into a transaction-sending step.

These two reads do not verify WebSocket subscriptions, indexed Data API availability or historical completeness. For the next read-only steps and authentication distinctions, see the developer quickstart.

title: AUTO CDC Deletes Stop at Bronze in a Multi-Hop Pipeline
description:
Why deletes reach bronze but never reach silver when every hop runs in one Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipeline, how I found the cause, and a small change that makes them flow all the way to gold.

A colleague sent me a message on Slack.

They had a multi-hop pipeline: landing, bronze, silver. Every hop used AUTO CDC, and every table had Change Data Feed (CDF) turned on.

Updates worked everywhere. Deletes went from landing to bronze. The bronze change feed even showed the delete.

But silver never deleted the row.

They also found a community thread with the same problem. A Databricks employee answered that it is supported, and listed the usual checks. The author checked all of them on a recent runtime, and it still failed. The thread ends with "it seems to work for single-hop only".

I wanted to understand why, so I built the smallest pipeline that shows the problem.

This guide walks you through what I found. We build the pipeline, we watch the delete disappear, we find where it goes, and then I show you the workaround that works for me.

I may be wrong about some internal details. If you know more, please tell me in the comments.

The pipeline

Everything in this guide uses one pipeline with four tables:

landing  ->  bronze  ->  silver  ->  gold
                    \->  silver_naive

landing is a plain Delta table. I only append rows to it. Each row says what happened to a key:

column meaning
id the key
name the data
op UPSERT or DELETE
seq the order of events for one key

bronze reads landing with AUTO CDC:

from pyspark import pipelines as dp
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, expr

@dp.temporary_view(name="landing_feed")
def landing_feed():
    return spark.readStream.table("landing")

dp.create_streaming_table("bronze", table_properties={"delta.enableChangeDataFeed": "true"})
dp.create_auto_cdc_flow(
    target="bronze",
    source="landing_feed",
    keys=["id"],
    sequence_by=col("seq"),
    apply_as_deletes=expr("op = 'DELETE'"),
    except_column_list=["op"],
    stored_as_scd_type=1,
)

silver_naive reads the bronze change feed with the pattern you find in the docs and in most answers online. It drops update_preimage rows, and it deletes when _change_type = 'delete':

@dp.temporary_view(name="bronze_cdf_naive")
def bronze_cdf_naive():
    return (
        spark.readStream.option("readChangeFeed", "true")
        .table("bronze")
        .filter("_change_type != 'update_preimage'")
    )

dp.create_streaming_table("silver_naive")
dp.create_auto_cdc_flow(
    target="silver_naive",
    source="bronze_cdf_naive",
    keys=["id"],
    sequence_by=col("_commit_version"),
    apply_as_deletes=expr("_change_type = 'delete'"),
    except_column_list=["_change_type", "_commit_version", "_commit_timestamp"],
    stored_as_scd_type=1,
)

silver and gold use the workaround. We get to it later.

Watching the delete disappear

I ran three steps. After each step I ran the pipeline and listed the rows in every table.

step bronze silver_naive
insert alice, bob, carol 1, 2, 3 1, 2, 3
delete bob, update carol 1, 3 v2 1, 2, 3 v2
insert bob again, delete alice 2 v3, 3 v2 1, 2 v3, 3 v2

Bronze is correct. silver_naive got carol's update, but it kept bob after the delete, and it kept alice after the second delete.

This is the exact problem from the thread.

So far, nothing new. Now let us find where the delete goes.

Looking at the change feed from outside

First, I read the bronze change feed with SQL, from a notebook:

SELECT _change_type, _commit_version, id, name
FROM table_changes('my_catalog.my_schema.bronze', 1)
ORDER BY _commit_version

The result for the delete of bob:

delete   4   2   bob

This looks perfect. There is a delete row. So the problem must be in silver... right?

Looking at the change feed from inside

Then I added one more table to the pipeline. It does nothing smart. It only saves the bronze change feed, exactly as a flow inside the pipeline reads it:

@dp.table(name="bronze_cdf_seen_from_inside")
def bronze_cdf_seen_from_inside():
    return spark.readStream.option("readChangeFeed", "true").table("bronze")

The result for the same delete of bob:

update_preimage   4   2   bob

No delete row. Only one update_preimage row, and no update_postimage row after it.

The same commit, read from two places, gives two different answers:

reader what the delete looks like
SQL table_changes delete
a second pipeline delete
a flow in the same pipeline update_preimage, nothing else

I also checked the silver MERGE in DESCRIBE HISTORY. For that commit, numSourceRows was 1. Only carol's update reached the MERGE. The delete was lost in the read, before AUTO CDC could do anything.

Why this happens

This is my understanding. I could not find it in the docs, so please read it as my best guess.

AUTO CDC does a soft delete. It does not remove the row from the table at once. It marks the row with a hidden tombstone, so it can handle events that arrive out of order. You can see this in DESCRIBE HISTORY bronze: the MERGE uses a column called __DeleteVersion, and later a separate DELETE cleans up old tombstones.

A reader outside the pipeline gets a clean view. Databricks turns the tombstone into a delete row.

A flow inside the same pipeline sees the change as an update of the row: the live row becomes a tombstone row. The pipeline hides the tombstone row, so the update_postimage disappears. Only the update_preimage is left.

And the usual pattern drops every update_preimage row.

So the delete is lost.

This also explains the comment in the thread. With a single hop, the reader is a different pipeline, so it gets a real delete row.

The workaround

The idea is simple: inside the same pipeline, an update_preimage with no update_postimage is a delete.

I do not want state or joins to find "a preimage with no postimage". AUTO CDC can do it for me if I give it the right order.

I change three things:

usual pattern workaround
rows to keep drop update_preimage keep all rows
what is a delete _change_type = 'delete' _change_type IN ('delete', 'update_preimage')
sequence_by _commit_version struct(_commit_version, 0 for delete, 1 for upsert)

Here is silver:

IS_DELETE = "_change_type IN ('delete', 'update_preimage')"

@dp.temporary_view(name="bronze_cdf_for_silver")
def bronze_cdf_for_silver():
    return spark.readStream.option("readChangeFeed", "true").table("bronze")  # keep all rows

dp.create_streaming_table("silver", table_properties={"delta.enableChangeDataFeed": "true"})
dp.create_auto_cdc_flow(
    target="silver",
    source="bronze_cdf_for_silver",
    keys=["id"],
    sequence_by=expr(f"struct(_commit_version, CASE WHEN {IS_DELETE} THEN 0 ELSE 1 END)"),
    apply_as_deletes=expr(IS_DELETE),
    except_column_list=["_change_type", "_commit_version", "_commit_timestamp"],
    stored_as_scd_type=1,
)

Gold reads silver in the same way.

Why it works:

  1. A real update has an update_preimage and an update_postimage in the same commit. The preimage gets order (version, 0) and the postimage gets (version, 1). AUTO CDC keeps the latest event for a key, so the upsert wins. Nothing is lost.
  2. A soft delete has only the update_preimage. It is the latest event for that key, so AUTO CDC deletes the row.
  3. A real delete row is still a delete. If Databricks changes this behaviour in the future, the workaround keeps working.

The same three steps, now with every table:

step bronze silver gold silver_naive
insert alice, bob, carol 1, 2, 3 1, 2, 3 1, 2, 3 1, 2, 3
delete bob, update carol 1, 3 v2 1, 3 v2 1, 3 v2 1, 2, 3 v2
insert bob again, delete alice 2 v3, 3 v2 2 v3, 3 v2 2 v3, 3 v2 1, 2 v3, 3 v2

Silver and gold now match bronze, including a key that comes back after a delete.

Positives

  • One pipeline. No extra pipelines, no state, no joins.
  • Updates and deletes both flow through every hop.
  • It also accepts real delete rows, so it does not depend on the bug staying.

Negatives

  • It depends on behaviour that I could not find in the docs. A runtime upgrade can change it.
  • You must keep update_preimage rows in the view. If someone adds the usual filter back, deletes break again, and nothing fails loudly.
  • Every upstream update becomes a removal plus an upsert downstream, so each hop does more work per change.
  • I only tested SCD type 1. I did not test SCD type 2.

The other option: one pipeline per hop

If you prefer to stay on the documented pattern, put each hop in its own pipeline. Then silver reads bronze from outside, and it gets real delete rows.

Positives

  • The documented pattern works as written.
  • No special rules in your code.

Negatives

  • More pipelines to deploy, schedule, and monitor.
  • You need to order the runs, so bronze finishes before silver starts.

Two things the workaround does not cover

Tombstone purge. AUTO CDC keeps a tombstone for about 48 hours after a delete. Then a separate DELETE in the table history purges it. Setting pipelines.cdc.tombstoneGCThresholdInSeconds as a table property does not make the purge run sooner, so the purge needs a long-running test. Nobody has shown yet what the in-pipeline stream delivers at purge time.

Physical erasure. A delete removes the row from the table, not from the files. Older data files and change feed files keep the row until the retention period ends and VACUUM runs. If you build this for GDPR, design the file retention and VACUUM schedule as a separate step.

What I tested, and what I did not

I tested a small example on serverless, CURRENT channel, in November 2026: insert, update, delete, and a delete followed by an insert of the same key, through bronze, silver, and gold.

I did not test classic compute, large volumes, SCD type 2, or the tombstone purge.

Wrapping up

When a delete stops between two hops, do not trust only table_changes(...). It shows you what an outside reader sees, not what your flow sees.

Add a debug table that saves the change feed inside the pipeline, and look at it. Then check numSourceRows on the MERGE in DESCRIBE HISTORY.

If you see an update_preimage with no update_postimage, try the workaround above, and run your delete test again after every runtime upgrade.

If someone from Databricks reads this: is this the expected behaviour? I would love to know the official way to do it.

title: Five Bugs Hiding in a URL Shortener (and the Fix for Each)
description:
"Design a URL shortener" is one of the most common system design questions. The usual answer draws three boxes: an API, a database and a cache. That answer is fine until real traffic touches it.

I spent a week building the version that survives production, as a runnable system in the interview-traps repo: one design lesson, five traps and a rollup. Each trap has the naive code, the fix and a test that proves both, against a real Postgres database with 50 concurrent users. You can read each lesson in the browser, starting with the design lesson.

This post is the short version: what each bug is, why it ships, and the one-line rule that prevents it.

Start with the numbers

Before drawing anything, the design lesson fixes the numbers every later decision depends on. These are the assumptions I used for the exercise, not measurements:

  • New links: about 100 million a month, roughly 40 writes a second.
  • Redirects: about 4,000 a second on average, ten times that at peak. That is 100 reads for every write.
  • Stored links: about 6 billion rows over five years.
  • Redirect budget: under 50 ms, because it sits in front of every click.

The ratio matters most. A system with 100 reads per write should have its redirect optimised first, and everything below follows from that.

Bug 1: the ID collision

A common first version creates the next short code with SELECT MAX(id) + 1. It works for a single user. Under concurrent creates, many requests read the same maximum and every one of them gets the same code.

Nothing errors. All fifty users are told their link was created. In the trap run, one code was handed out repeatedly, and every user after the first owned a link that pointed at somebody else's destination.

Fix: let the database hand out the value. A sequence (nextval) or an identity column is unique by construction, with no retry loop, and a UNIQUE constraint on the code column is the safety net.

Bug 2: the stale redirect

The owner edits a link's destination. The code updates Postgres and stops there. The redirect path reads from Redis, so visitors keep going to the old page until the cache entry expires.

In the trap, the database said the new destination while all 50 visitors after the edit still reached the old, dead page.

Fix: delete the cache key in the same code path as the database write. And redirect with 302, not 301, for any link that can be edited: browsers cache a 301, so repeat visitors never come back to your server to see the change.

Bug 3: analytics on the hot path

The owner wants a click count, so the redirect runs UPDATE links SET clicks = clicks + 1. The count is right. The cost is that your fastest endpoint now writes to a database row on every click, and every click writes the same row.

Postgres lets one transaction update a row at a time, so click number 50 waits for 49 commits ahead of it. Waiting clicks also hold pool connections, which can starve every other endpoint.

In the rollup run, the slowest redirect with the counter on the hot path waited 42.7 ms. With the count moved off the hot path, it took 0.8 ms. Exact timings move between runs and machines, so read these as a demonstration of the shape, not a benchmark.

Fix: count in memory (Redis INCR) and flush to the database in batches. The trade-off to say out loud: counts lag by a few seconds. If a lost batch matters, use a durable queue instead.

Bug 4: the vanity alias race

Two users both want /launch. A common version checks whether the alias is free, then runs an upsert "so retries don't error". Everyone passes the check, the upsert silently overwrites the previous owner, and everyone is told the alias is theirs.

In the trap run, 49 users were told /launch was theirs, and the other 48 were sharing a link that sent their clicks to one user's destination.

Fix: make the database decide, in one statement: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING. Zero rows returned means the alias is taken. A retry from the same owner can be treated as success.

Bug 5: cleanup at scale

A nightly job runs DELETE FROM links WHERE expires_at < now(). It is correct SQL, and on a staging table with a few thousand rows it works.

At scale it is one transaction. If it runs past the statement timeout, or past the next deploy, Postgres rolls back all of it. Not half done: zero deleted. The table only grows, so tomorrow's run is longer, and the job fails every night while the table keeps filling.

Fix: delete in short batches over the primary key, so each batch is its own tiny transaction and progress survives a crash. At real scale, partition by month and drop whole partitions.

One caveat from the repo: the demo scales the statement timeout down to fit a laptop. Production would be something like a 30-second timeout against billions of rows. In the demo, 300,000 expired links stayed in place in the bug run, and the batched fix deleted all of them and left 30,000 live links untouched. Treat those as a demonstration, not a benchmark.

The pattern behind two of the five

Bugs 1 and 4 share one shape: read, decide, write, with a gap in between. It is the same shape as the double-booked seat, where two users book the same seat. Once you learn to look for the gap, you will see it in signup flows, coupon codes, inventory and invitations as well.

The other three have their own rules:

  • A cache is a second copy of the truth, so every write path must invalidate it.
  • The hot path should do only what the user is waiting for.
  • Never delete millions of rows in one statement.

The scoreboard

When I run all five traps with npm run shortener:all, the output ends with: "5/5 naive versions broke. 5/5 fixes held." Each trap uses 50 concurrent users on a real Postgres. Races are races, so exact counts move a little between runs; the verdicts do not.

What this does not cover

The week left gaps on purpose: id generation across regions, abuse and malicious-link scanning, rate limiting link creation, a real click-event pipeline instead of a counter, and multi-region redirects. Each of those is its own topic. If an interviewer pushes past the five bugs, say so rather than bluffing.

When internal work is enough, and when to get help

If your product has one Postgres database and one cache, you can check each of these five spots in an afternoon. Search for MAX( used to build ids, edits that skip cache invalidation, counters updated inside request handlers, check-then-upsert code and unbatched deletes.

It gets harder when the same problems are spread across services, queues and third-party APIs. That is where a structured review, like the one in what to audit in a vibe-coded MVP, saves time.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should a URL shortener redirect with 301 or 302?

Use 302 when the destination can be edited or clicks must be counted. A 301 is cached by browsers, so edits are not seen by repeat visitors and repeat clicks never reach your server.

Why not generate short codes with SELECT MAX(id) + 1?

Two concurrent requests can read the same maximum and hand out the same code. A database sequence gives each request a unique value by construction, and a UNIQUE constraint on the code column is the safety net.

Related Reading

  • The Double-Booked Seat: Fixing a Booking Race Condition in Postgres
  • Why I Prefer Boring Architecture for SaaS
  • Reducing Latency Without Rewrites
  • Cron, Queue, or Workflow? A SaaS Background Jobs Guide

Next Step

Run the traps yourself: clone the interview-traps repo, then run npm run shortener:bug -- id-collision and the matching shortener:fix, or everything at once with npm run shortener:all. The individual lessons are on the Labs traps page.

If you are running a SaaS with hot paths, caches, counters or nightly jobs and want these failure shapes checked before they show up in production, that is the focus of my production readiness upgrade. Bring a description of your redirect or checkout path and your background jobs, and we can work out where the gaps are.

Originally published at somanathkhadanga.com.

title: CQRS & Event-Driven Thinking: Commands, Queries, Domain Events & the Outbox Pattern Explained 📨
description:
📨 CQRS & Event-Driven Thinking: Let's Learn from ZERO!

These are important backend architecture concepts, especially with FastAPI, PostgreSQL, SQLAlchemy, repositories, services and a social media app. We'll cover:

  • 🔀 What Command-Query Separation (CQS) means
  • 🧩 What CQRS is and how it differs from CQS
  • ⚔️ Commands vs queries
  • 📣 What domain events are
  • 🌐 How event-driven architecture works
  • 🏢 Real examples using an Instagram-like app
  • ✅ Advantages, disadvantages, use cases and interview questions

We'll start simple and gradually move towards real backend code. 🚀

1. 🤔 First, Understand the Problem

You're building an Instagram-like app. A user can:

  1. Create a post
  2. Like a post
  3. Comment on a post
  4. Follow another user
  5. View their home feed
  6. Search for posts
  7. View someone's profile

All of these touch the database. But are they all doing the same kind of work? No! There are two fundamentally different kinds of operations:

Kind Examples Effect
✍️ Writing / changing data Create a post, like a post, delete a comment, follow a user Changes the database
👀 Reading / retrieving data Get all posts, view comments, get a profile, search posts Retrieves information without changing it

This distinction is the foundation of Command-Query Separation.

2. 🔀 Command-Query Separation (CQS)

  • Command: an instruction to perform an action
  • Query: a request to retrieve information
  • Separation: keeping these two responsibilities apart

📌 Command-Query Separation means separating operations that change data from operations that only read data. A command changes the state of the system. A query returns information but does not change the state.

State means the current stored condition of your application. For example, a post:

{
  "id": 101,
  "caption": "My first post",
  "likes_count": 10
}

Its current state: the post has 10 likes.

2.1 ✍️ Command example: like a post

The frontend sends POST /posts/101/like. The backend:

  1. Identifies the logged-in user
  2. Checks the post exists
  3. Checks the user hasn't already liked it
  4. Inserts a like record
  5. Updates the like count, if your design stores one 
Before:  { "id": 101, "likes_count": 10 }
After:   { "id": 101, "likes_count": 11 }

The database state changed, so this is a Command.

2.2 👀 Query example: get post details

The frontend sends GET /posts/101. The backend finds the post, retrieves its caption, author and like count, and returns:

{
  "id": 101,
  "caption": "My first post",
  "likes_count": 11
}

Did we change anything? No. So this is a Query.

2.3 📊 Visual comparison

✍️ COMMAND (write) 👀 QUERY (read)
Changes application state Does not change application state
Create, Update, Delete, Like Get, List, Search, Retrieve

🧠 Command = change something. Query = ask for something.

2.4 📋 More examples

Operation Type Reason
Create post Command Inserts data
Edit caption Command Updates data
Delete post Command Removes data
Like post Command Changes like state
Follow user Command Changes follow relationship
Get profile Query Reads data
Get feed Query Retrieves posts
Search users Query Reads matching records
Get comments Query Retrieves comments

📝 A query can have internal work such as logging or caching, but its purpose must not be to change the business data being queried.

3. 🤷 Why Do We Need CQS?

Imagine this function:

def get_post(post_id):
    post = database.get_post(post_id)

    if post.likes_count == 0:
        post.likes_count = 1
        database.save(post)

    return post

What's wrong? It's named get_post(), so we expect it to retrieve a post. But it also changes the database! Someone calling get_post() might accidentally modify application data. A better design:

def get_post(post_id):
    return database.get_post(post_id)


def like_post(post_id):
    post = database.get_post(post_id)
    post.likes_count += 1
    database.save(post)
    return post
  • get_post() → Query
  • like_post() → Command

✅ Main benefit: your code becomes easier to understand, maintain, test and debug.

4. 🧩 What is CQRS?

📌 CQRS = Command Query Responsibility Segregation. It's an architectural pattern based on the same idea as CQS.

  • CQS is a principle about separating read and write operations
  • CQRS takes that further by letting the read and write sides have different models, responsibilities, and sometimes different data stores

4.1 🏛️ Traditional architecture 

Frontend (React)
     ▼
Backend API (FastAPI)
     ▼
PostgreSQL Database   ← same database for reading and writing

Writing means insert/update/delete, reading means select. This is completely valid and works very well for many apps. But if your app becomes extremely popular (1 million users, 10 million posts, millions of feed requests, thousands of new posts and likes every minute) the database must handle heavy reads and writes together. That's where CQRS can become useful.

4.2 🧱 CQRS architecture 

                    Frontend (React)
                 ┌────────┴────────┐
              Command            Query
          (write request)    (read request)
                 ▼                  ▼
         Command Handler      Query Handler
   (validates and processes   (processes read
            writes)              requests)
                 ▼                  ▼
          Write Model          Read Model
          (PostgreSQL)    (optimized for retrieval)

(Conceptual. Read and write models may use the same database or different ones.)

Write side: handles commands, validates business rules, changes application state, saves data.

Read side: handles queries, retrieves information, returns data in a format suitable for the frontend, and can be optimized for fast reads.

4.3 🗄️ Does CQRS require two databases?

No! A very important interview question. There are two common implementations:

Option A: same database, separate models. Command and query logic are separate, but they share the same underlying database. For example, the command handler uses the SQLAlchemy ORM to create a post, while the query handler uses optimized SQL to retrieve posts.

Option B: separate read and write databases. Write model: PostgreSQL. Read model: Redis, Elasticsearch, or a separate PostgreSQL database. The read database may hold precomputed or denormalized information for faster retrieval. Use this when you need independent scaling or specialized read storage.

4.4 📖 What is a Read Model?

📌 A read model is a representation of data designed specifically for reading.

Suppose your database has:

users:

id username
1 deepika
2 arjun

posts:

id user_id caption
101 1 My first post
102 2 Weekend vibes

likes:

id post_id user_id
1 101 2
2 101 1

To display a feed you may need to join several tables and count likes. Your frontend wants:

[
  {
    "post_id": 101,
    "username": "deepika",
    "caption": "My first post",
    "likes_count": 2
  }
]

This combined structure is a read model. It's shaped for the frontend's needs rather than matching your original tables. Instead of repeating expensive joins and calculations on every feed request, you can maintain a read-optimized representation, for example a precomputed like count or a denormalized feed projection.

4.5 ✍️ What is a Write Model?

The write model is the representation used to perform and enforce changes. When a user likes a post, the write side must ensure the post exists, the user exists, the user hasn't already liked it, and the like is stored correctly. It maintains business rules and data integrity.

Write Model Read Model
Handles changes Handles retrieval
Processes commands Processes queries
Enforces business rules Optimizes presentation
Focuses on consistency Focuses on efficient reads

4.6 📍 When should we use CQRS?

  1. Read-heavy apps: millions of users frequently retrieve information
  2. Complex queries: many joins, aggregations and calculations
  3. Different scaling needs: read and write traffic scale independently
  4. Different data representations: the frontend needs data structured differently from the normalized write database
  5. Complex business workflows: many operations and rules affect the same domain

When should you avoid it? For a small CRUD app, CQRS adds unnecessary complexity. You'd maintain two models, command handlers, query handlers, event processing, synchronization, and error handling for failed projections. A normal layered FastAPI app is often enough.

⚠️ CQRS is an architectural choice, not a requirement for every backend.

5. 📣 What is Event-Driven Thinking?

A user creates a post and the backend saves it. After that, several other things may need to happen:

  1. The post should appear in the user's feed
  2. Followers may receive notifications
  3. The profile's post count may increase
  4. Analytics may record the new post
  5. An image-processing service may generate thumbnails

Should the post-creation function directly perform all of these? It could, but if the notification service is slow or temporarily unavailable, should the user wait for it before their request finishes? Probably not. That's where event-driven thinking helps.

5.1 📌 What is an Event?

📌 An event represents something that has already happened.

Examples: UserRegistered, PostCreated, PostLiked, CommentAdded, UserFollowed, OrderPlaced, PaymentCompleted.

Notice the past tense. An event is a completed fact. PostCreated means a post has already been created. It doesn't mean someone is requesting creation. That distinction is extremely important.

5.2 ⚔️ Command vs Event

✍️ Command 📣 Event
CreatePost: "Please create a new post." PostCreated: "A new post has been successfully created."
An instruction that requests something happen A fact that announces something happened
Command Event
RegisterUser UserRegistered
CreatePost PostCreated
LikePost PostLiked
AddComment CommentAdded
FollowUser UserFollowed
PlaceOrder OrderPlaced
MakePayment PaymentCompleted

🧠 Command = request to do something. Event = notification that something has happened.

5.3 🌐 How does event-driven architecture work? 

1. User creates a post          → React frontend
        ▼
2. CreatePost command           → backend receives the instruction
        ▼
3. Command Handler              → validates and saves the post
        ▼
4. PostCreated event            → a fact is published after successful creation
        ▼
5. Event Bus / Event Broker     → distributes the event to interested consumers
        ├── 🔔 Notifications
        ├── 🖼️ Media
        └── 📊 Analytics

One event can trigger several independent reactions.

A. Event Producer: the component that creates and publishes an event. Here, the post creation service saves the post and publishes PostCreated.

B. Event: carries information about what happened:

{
  "event_id": "evt_001",
  "event_type": "PostCreated",
  "post_id": 101,
  "user_id": 1,
  "created_at": "2026-11-12T10:30:00Z"
}

(An illustrative payload.) It tells other components which event occurred, which post was created, which user created it and when. An event should contain enough information for consumers to do their work, without unnecessarily exposing private data.

C. Event Bus / Event Broker: a communication system that receives events from producers and delivers them to interested consumers. Technologies include RabbitMQ, Apache Kafka, Redis Streams, AWS EventBridge. For a small app you can even use a simple in-process event dispatcher with no broker at all.

D. Event Consumer: a component that receives and reacts to an event. When PostCreated occurs, the notification consumer sends notifications, the analytics consumer records the activity, and the media consumer processes images. Each has its own responsibility.

🔗 The event producer doesn't need to know the internal implementation of every consumer, which reduces coupling.

6. 🏷️ What are Domain Events?

📌 A domain event is an event that represents something meaningful that happened in the application's business domain.

A domain is the business area or problem your app is built to handle:

Application Domain
Instagram-like app Social networking
Banking app Banking
E-commerce app Online shopping
Hospital app Healthcare management
Food delivery app Food ordering and delivery

In a social media app the domain includes users, posts, comments, likes, follows and notifications. When a user follows another user and the operation succeeds, we can represent that important business fact as the domain event UserFollowed.

6.1 📋 Examples of domain events

Social media:

Domain Event Meaning
UserRegistered A new account was registered
ProfileUpdated A profile was updated
PostCreated A new post was created
PostDeleted A post was deleted
PostLiked A user liked a post
CommentAdded A comment was added
UserFollowed A user followed another user
UserUnfollowed A user unfollowed another user

E-commerce:

Domain Event Meaning
ProductAddedToCart A product was added
OrderPlaced An order was placed
PaymentCompleted Payment succeeded
OrderCancelled An order was cancelled
ItemShipped An item was shipped

6.2 ⚖️ Domain event vs command vs query

Concept Meaning Example
Command Request to perform an action LikePost
Query Request to retrieve data GetPost
Domain Event Something meaningful happened PostLiked

A complete sequence:

  1. A user clicks Like
  2. The backend receives LikePost
  3. The backend checks the rules
  4. The backend saves the like
  5. The backend generates PostLiked
  6. Other components react to PostLiked 
LikePost (Command)
     ▼
Business logic + database write
     ▼
PostLiked (Domain Event)
     ▼
Event consumers: 🔔 Notification · 📊 Analytics

The command asks the system to do something. The event records that the system successfully did it.

6.3 🤔 Are domain events always published to Kafka or RabbitMQ?

No. A domain event is a concept. It can exist entirely inside your application. For example, your Python app can create a PostCreated event object and pass it to an internal event dispatcher. You only need Kafka, RabbitMQ or another broker when your architecture requires the capabilities they provide.

7. ⏳ Synchronous vs Asynchronous Event Processing

7.1 🐢 Synchronous processing

The caller waits for the operation to finish before continuing:

def create_post(post_data):
    post = save_post(post_data)
    send_notification(post)
    update_analytics(post)
    return post
  1. Save post
  2. Wait for notification
  3. Wait for analytics
  4. Return response

If notification takes 3 seconds and analytics takes 2, the request may take about 5 seconds longer than the database save itself. The user waits for all of it.

7.2 🐇 Asynchronous event processing 

def create_post(post_data):
    post = save_post(post_data)

    publish_event(
        "PostCreated",
        {"post_id": post.id},
    )

    return post

Event consumers process their tasks independently (notifications, analytics, image processing), and the request doesn't have to wait for them.

Synchronous:   Save post → Send notification → Update analytics → Return response (after all)

Asynchronous:  Save post → Publish event → Return response
                              ├── Notification
                              └── Analytics   (processed independently)

📝 Asynchronous doesn't automatically mean a separate server or message broker. Python background tasks, queues and distributed brokers are different implementation options. For reliable processing across services, a durable message broker is often preferable to an in-memory background task.

7.3 🕐 What is Eventual Consistency?

A user creates a post. The write database saves it immediately, but your separate read database or feed projection may take a moment to receive and process PostCreated. For a brief moment the write database says the post exists, while the read database hasn't caught up. After the event is processed, both agree.

Time T1 (write completed)   Write DB: Post exists (ID 101)   Read DB: Post not yet visible
Time T2 (event processed)   Write DB: Post exists (ID 101)   Read DB: Post exists (ID 101)

📌 Eventual consistency: the system may temporarily show slightly outdated information, but if processing succeeds and continues, the read side eventually catches up.

For analytics, recommendation updates and notification delivery, a small delay is often acceptable. But for critical operations such as checking an account balance before a withdrawal, you generally need strong consistency at the point of decision.

8. 💥 What Happens If Event Processing Fails?

Your app saves a post in PostgreSQL, then tries to publish PostCreated to RabbitMQ, but RabbitMQ is temporarily down. The post exists, yet the event was never published, so the notification service may never learn about it. That's a reliability problem. One important solution is the Transactional Outbox Pattern.

8.1 📤 Transactional Outbox Pattern

Instead of saving business data and publishing the event as two unrelated operations, save both the business data and an event record in the same database transaction.

posts:

id caption
101 My first post

outbox_events:

id event_type payload published
1 PostCreated post_id:101 false

The process:

  1. Start a database transaction
  2. Insert the post
  3. Insert the PostCreated event into the outbox table
  4. Commit the transaction
  5. A background worker reads unpublished events
  6. The worker publishes them to the broker
  7. The worker marks them as published after successful delivery 
BEGIN TRANSACTION
  Insert post
  Insert event
COMMIT              ← both records saved together
     ▼
Background Worker
     ▼
Message Broker

Even if the broker is down, the event remains safely stored in PostgreSQL and can be published later.

⚠️ Caveat: a worker can publish an event and crash before marking it as published, so the event may be delivered again. That's why consumers should be idempotent.

8.2 🔁 What is Idempotency?

📌 Idempotency means performing the same operation multiple times produces the same intended result as performing it once.

Suppose PostLiked is delivered twice. If your consumer blindly increments the like count each time, the count goes up twice. That's wrong. A safer design:

  • Store processed event IDs
  • Check whether an event was already processed
  • If yes, skip it
  • If not, process it and record its ID

9. ⚡ How Does This Fit into FastAPI Architecture?

9.1 🥞 Traditional layered architecture

For POST /posts:

frontend → FastAPI Router → Post Service → Post Repository → PostgreSQL

The router receives the request, the service implements business logic, and the repository handles database operations.

9.2 🧩 Introducing CQRS

Separate the write and read responsibilities:

                     FastAPI
              ┌─────────┴─────────┐
        Command Router       Query Router
              ▼                   ▼
       Command Handler       Query Handler
              ▼                   ▼
       Write Repository      Read Repository
              ▼                   ▼
          Database            Database

Command handler:

class CreatePostCommand:
    def __init__(self, user_id, caption):
        self.user_id = user_id
        self.caption = caption


def handle_create_post(command, repository):
    post = repository.create(
        user_id=command.user_id,
        caption=command.caption,
    )

    return post

Query handler:

def handle_get_post(post_id, repository):
    return repository.get_by_id(post_id)

(Simplified examples, not a complete production implementation.)

  • CreatePostCommand represents the instruction
  • handle_create_post() processes the write
  • handle_get_post() retrieves information

You can have separate command and query handlers even when both use the same SQLAlchemy session and PostgreSQL database.

9.3 📣 Introducing domain events

Extend the command handler:

def handle_create_post(command, repository, event_publisher):
    post = repository.create(
        user_id=command.user_id,
        caption=command.caption,
    )

    event = {
        "event_type": "PostCreated",
        "post_id": post.id,
        "user_id": command.user_id,
    }

    event_publisher.publish(event)

    return post

CreatePost Command
     ▼
Command Handler
     ▼
Post Repository
     ▼
PostgreSQL
     ▼
PostCreated Event
     ▼
Event Publisher
     ▼
Event Consumers

⚠️ For production reliability, you'd normally use the transactional outbox pattern instead of relying on a direct database-write-then-publish sequence.

10. 🆚 Domain Events vs Integration Events

Related, but not identical.

Domain event: represents an important business fact inside a particular domain. It might be used by your app's internal business logic.

PostCreated(
    post_id=101,
    user_id=1,
)

Integration event: communicates something that happened to another system or independent service. It might be published through RabbitMQ or Kafka so another service can consume it.

{
  "event_type": "PostCreated",
  "post_id": 101,
  "user_id": 1
}
Domain Event Integration Event
Internal to a domain Shared across service boundaries
Represents business facts Communicates business facts to other systems
Can be an internal Python object Usually has a serialized message format
May never leave the application Intended for external consumers

A domain event can lead to an integration event, but not every domain event needs to be published externally.

11. ⚔️ CQRS vs Event-Driven Architecture vs Event Sourcing

These three are often discussed together but solve different problems.

🅰️ CQRS. Separate reading and writing responsibilities. CreatePost → command, GetPost → query. Focus: how your app handles reads and writes.

🅱️ Event-Driven Architecture (EDA). Components communicate and react to events. PostCreated triggers notifications, analytics and image processing. Focus: how components communicate and respond to changes.

🅲 Event Sourcing. A different concept. Don't confuse it with EDA. Normally your database stores the current state:

{
  "account_id": 1,
  "balance": 700
}

With event sourcing, instead of treating current state as the primary record, you store the sequence of events that produced it:

Event Amount
AccountCreated 0
MoneyDeposited +1000
MoneyWithdrawn -200
MoneyWithdrawn -100

The balance is calculated by replaying the events: 1000 − 200 − 100 = 700.

Traditional database:  Current balance = ₹700
Event sourcing:        Deposited ₹1,000 → Withdrawn ₹200 → Withdrawn ₹100 → Current balance = ₹700

Why use it? Complete history of changes, ability to reconstruct previous states, audit trails, and understanding exactly how a value changed over time.

But it adds complexity: event versioning, event replay, data migration, handling duplicate events and maintaining projections. You don't need event sourcing just because you're using events.

Concept Main responsibility
CQS Separate reads and writes at the operation level
CQRS Separate read and write models/responsibilities
Event-Driven Architecture Communicate through events
Domain Events Represent important business facts
Event Sourcing Store state changes as an event history

🎯 Very important: CQRS and EDA can be used together, but neither requires Event Sourcing.

12. 🧵 Practical Example: A Social Media App

Imagine Deepika likes Arjun's post.

Step 1: the frontend sends a command

POST /posts/101/like
Authorization: Bearer access_token

Step 2: FastAPI receives the request

@router.post("/posts/{post_id}/like")
async def like_post(
    post_id: int,
    current_user=Depends(get_current_user),
):
    return await service.like_post(
        post_id,
        current_user.id,
    )

Step 3: the service processes the command. It checks the post exists, checks whether the user already liked it, applies business rules, and creates the like record.

Step 4: the database saves the change

likes
id | post_id | user_id
1  | 101     | 1

Step 5: a domain event is generated

{
  "event_type": "PostLiked",
  "post_id": 101,
  "user_id": 1
}

Step 6: event consumers react. The notification service informs the post owner, analytics records the interaction, and a read projection updates the like count, if the app maintains one.

Step 7: the user retrieves the post

GET /posts/101

This is a Query. The query handler returns:

{
  "post_id": 101,
  "caption": "My first post",
  "likes_count": 15,
  "liked_by_me": true
}

This one example demonstrates CQS, CQRS, domain events, event-driven architecture, event consumers and eventual consistency.

📝 If liked_by_me must update immediately, read it from the authoritative write-side data, or otherwise ensure the response reflects the successful write. Don't assume an asynchronously updated read model is immediately current.

13. 📖 Important Terms

Term Beginner-friendly meaning
Command Handler Processes a command
Query Handler Processes a query
Write Model Handles data modifications
Read Model Represents data for retrieval
Event Producer Creates and publishes events
Event Consumer Receives and processes events
Event Bus Distributes events
Event Broker Messaging infrastructure for event delivery
Domain Event Important business occurrence
Event Payload Data contained in an event
Eventual Consistency Different data representations become consistent over time
Idempotency Repeating an operation doesn't produce duplicate effects
Event Sourcing Stores events as the primary history of state changes
Transactional Outbox Reliably stores events alongside database changes
Message Queue Holds messages until consumers process them

14. 🧭 When Do These Concepts Work Together?

Situation Useful concept
Separating get_post() and create_post() CQS
Different read and write models CQRS
Sending notifications after a post is created Event-driven architecture
Representing a successful follow action Domain events
Updating a read database asynchronously CQRS + events
Keeping event publication reliable Transactional outbox
Preventing duplicate message processing Idempotency
Keeping complete historical state changes Event sourcing

15. 🎤 Interview Questions and Answers

Q1. What is Command-Query Separation?
A design principle that separates operations into Commands, which modify application state, and Queries, which retrieve information without modifying business state.

Q2. What is CQRS?
Command Query Responsibility Segregation: an architectural pattern that separates read and write responsibilities, potentially using different models and data stores.

Q3. What's the difference between CQS and CQRS?
CQS is a principle applied at the operation or method level. CQRS is an architectural pattern that applies the separation more broadly to the application's read and write models.

Q4. What is a Domain Event?
Something important that has already happened in the business domain, such as PostCreated, PaymentCompleted or UserRegistered.

Q5. What's the difference between a Command and an Event?
A Command requests an action. An Event represents a fact that the action has happened.

Q6. What is Event-Driven Architecture?
An approach in which components communicate by publishing and consuming events. It helps decouple components and allows independent processing.

Q7. What is an Event Broker?
Infrastructure that receives and distributes messages between producers and consumers, such as RabbitMQ and Kafka.

Q8. What is Eventual Consistency?
Different data representations may temporarily contain different information but eventually become consistent after updates are processed.

Q9. What is the Transactional Outbox Pattern?
A reliability pattern that stores business data and the corresponding event record in the same database transaction. A background worker later publishes the event.

Q10. Does CQRS require two databases?
No. CQRS can use the same database with separate read and write models. Separate databases are optional.

Q11. Is Event-Driven Architecture the same as Event Sourcing?
No. EDA uses events for communication between components. Event sourcing stores events as the primary record of state changes.

Q12. What are the disadvantages of CQRS?
Architectural complexity, additional code, synchronization challenges, potential eventual consistency, and more difficult debugging.

16. 🧪 Test Your Understanding!

Try these before peeking at the answers! ❤️

  1. A user requests their profile details. What is this?

    • A) Command
    • B) Query
    • C) Domain Event

  2. A user clicks the Like button. What is the incoming instruction?

    • A) PostLiked
    • B) LikePost
    • C) GetPost

  3. The backend successfully saves a post. What event can represent this?

    • A) CreatePost
    • B) GetPost
    • C) PostCreated

  4. A post creation event triggers notifications and analytics independently. Which architecture is this?

    • A) Event-Driven Architecture
    • B) Event Sourcing
    • C) Normalization

  5. Does CQRS always require two databases?

    • A) Yes
    • B) No

  6. What helps reliably publish events after a database transaction?

    • A) B-tree index
    • B) Transactional Outbox
    • C) JWT

  7. What does Eventual Consistency mean?

    • A) Data never changes
    • B) All systems update at exactly the same time
    • C) Data representations may temporarily differ but eventually catch up

👀 Click to reveal answers
  1. B: Query. It reads data without changing it
  2. B: LikePost is the command. PostLiked is the event that follows
  3. C: PostCreated. Events are past-tense facts
  4. A: Event-Driven Architecture
  5. B: No. The same database with separate models is a valid CQRS implementation
  6. B: Transactional Outbox
  7. C: Representations may temporarily differ but eventually catch up

17. 🏁 Remember These Five Things

  1. 🔀 CQS = separate reading and writing operations
  2. 🧩 CQRS = separate read and write responsibilities/models
  3. ✍️ Command = an instruction to perform an action
  4. 📣 Domain Event = something meaningful that happened
  5. 🌐 EDA = components react to events and communicate through them

If this post helped you, drop a ❤️ or 🦄 and share it with a friend learning backend architecture. Happy coding! 👩‍💻✨

title: What counts as a breaking change in an OpenAPI spec
description:
A breaking change depends on which way the data flows. Requests may loosen and responses may tighten; the reverse breaks clients. A field guide with examples.

A breaking change is any edit to an API description after which a client written against the old description stops working against the new one. Every other edit is safe. That sounds obvious, but in practice people sort changes by how big they look: a removed endpoint feels dangerous, a new enum value feels harmless. The better question is which way the data travels. A client sends requests and reads responses, so the same edit can be safe on one side and harmful on the other. Below you will find the direction rule, the edits that are most often misjudged, and a short routine for reviewing pull requests.

Read the full report on AISkills402: https://aiskills402.com/blog/openapi-breaking-changes?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social

title: Vercel MCP now supports MCP events
description:
Vercel MCP now publishes events, so agents can subscribe to Vercel platform events like deployment.succeeded and deployment.error and react to what happens on your projects instead of polling for changes.

An agent subscribes once, filtering by team, project, and environment, and Vercel MCP manages an ordinary expiring Vercel webhook behind it. title: GitHub Find: A Model Family Built to Be Small Enough to Own
description:
I found jaredpalmer/kev while scrolling trending repos: a small family of decision models built on Qwen3.5, designed to be trained and run on your own hardware instead of called through an API. I haven't tested it, and I'm not going to pretend I have. This isn't a review, it's a case for why the idea deserves attention before anyone opens the code.

Here's the actual point. Most of the model conversation right now is about scale, bigger context windows, bigger parameter counts, bigger bills. Kev bets on the opposite: models small enough that you own them outright. Not "call an API and hope the vendor doesn't change the pricing tier next quarter", something you fine-tune on your own data and keep running when the network is down.

"Decision model" is the phrase worth sitting with. If this means classification-style output, pick an action from a bounded set, route a request, approve or deny, score a lead, that's a different design target than a chat model entirely. You don't need a massive general-purpose model to decide which of five support queues a ticket belongs in. You need something fast, cheap per inference, and predictable enough that you can write tests against its output distribution. Starting from Qwen3.5 instead of pretraining from scratch is the sane move if that's the actual goal.

Who benefits if the idea holds up: anyone running high-volume, low-latency classification or routing behind an API, where a full LLM call is overkill and the cost compounds fast. Teams that need to fine-tune on proprietary decision data and can't ship that data to a third-party endpoint. And agent orchestration generally, a layer of small, cheap "decide what happens next" models sitting in front of one expensive general-purpose model is a pattern that's going to show up more, because it's the only way the economics work once you're running agents at any real volume.

The real test is calibration, not size. "Tiny" plus "trainable on your own data" pushes the burden onto you to prove it isn't just confidently wrong. That's not a flaw in the idea, it's the question anyone should answer before putting a model like this near a production decision path.

Worth tracking if small, ownable models are on your radar: https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev

title: Claude Fable 5.2 now available on AI Gateway
description:
Claude Fable 5.2 from Anthropic is now available on AI Gateway.

Fable 5.2 is built for open-ended technical work and improves on earlier Fable models in coding, reasoning, and vision. It can run long, ambiguous tasks unattended, and works as an orchestrator that hands simpler tasks to smaller models, or as an advisor that other Claude models consult on harder problems. It also communicates more clearly and generates output faster than earlier Fable models. Effort runs from low to max, with high as the API default.

Fable 5.2 has cybersecurity and biology safety classifiers enabled. Access to Claude Fable 5.2 requires data retention. Anthropic does not support Zero Data Retention for the model. Prompts and completions are retained for 30 days and are not used to train Claude. If your team has ZDR turned on, AI Gateway returns an error instead of sending the request to Fable 5.2.

To keep requests served when a classifier is triggered, use model fallbacks. Add a models array to providerOptions.gateway, and AI Gateway tries each model in order when the cybersecurity classifier declines a request.

Call it through the AI SDK, the Chat Completions, Responses, and Anthropic Messages APIs, or a coding agent connected to AI Gateway. Use anthropic/claude-fable-5.2 as the model name:

This request falls back to Opus 5.5, then Sonnet 5.5, if the cybersecurity classifier declines it. The models option works the same way on every AI Gateway API format.

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Try Claude Fable 5.2 in the model playground.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

You can view all language models available on AI Gateway.

title: Can You Render JSX on Windows Without a Browser? I Built an Engine to Find Out.
description:
Can You Render JSX on Windows Without a Browser? I Built an Engine to Find Out.

A while ago, we shared an update mentioning that LeveloJS was rethinking its architectural foundation.

As the founder and lead developer of the project, I asked myself a question that felt unreasonable for a small setup:

Can we write regular JavaScript and JSX, yet render it directly onto an operating system window with zero Chromium, zero V8, and zero WebView?

I wasn’t interested in wrapping another browser inside an .exe. I wanted to find out what happens when you treat standard JSX as the direct blueprint for native, hardware-accelerated 2D graphics.

Today, I had one of those moments where I just sat back and stared at my monitor.

I ran the exact same JSX component on Google Chrome and inside the newly engineered LeveloJS Windows Native Host (levelo-windows).

I placed the two windows side by side.

The typography hierarchies (h1 through h6), the CSS Flexbox alignments, the dynamic button paddings, and the character measurements looked identical.

If you didn’t look at the title bar of the window, you honestly couldn't tell which one was the browser and which one was running directly on bare native pixels.

This Is Not an Official Release

Let me be completely transparent from the start: this is not a production release.

I haven't solved everything yet. Text input fields still need more platform wiring, complex scrolling is in the pipeline, and I still have edge-case node cleanups to refine.

This is an early engineering milestone. It is practical proof that our hypothesis—which felt like an impossible risk when we started—actually works.

Why I Refused the Existing Choices

When web developers want to target the desktop, they are usually forced into two paths:

  1. The WebView / Chromium Path (Electron, Tauri): You ship an entire browser or hook into the OS webview. It works, but your app inherits the massive complexity, startup lag, and memory footprint of a web browser.

  2. The New Vocabulary Path (React Native): You keep JSX, but you lose the web primitives you know. You cannot simply drop in a button, h1, or div—you have to relearn layout models around platform-specific components like View and Text.

I wanted a third path.

What if a developer could keep their familiar web-style primitives, but the engine underneath stripped away the browser entirely and spoke directly to the operating system?

What Is Actually Happening Under the Hood?

The architecture is broken into four distinct layers:

  1. QuickJS (The Embedded Runtime): Instead of pulling in hundreds of megabytes of V8 or Node.js runtime, I embedded QuickJS. It gives us standard ES2023 compliance, instant startup, and runs on a fraction of the memory.

  2. Zero-Copy OpCode Bridge: When a component updates, there is no Virtual DOM tree diffing. LeveloJS emits direct atomic operation codes (CreateElement, SetStyle, AppendChild) directly over a low-overhead FFI boundary into Rust.

  3. Taffy (The Layout Engine): Emulating browser layout by guessing coordinates is a trap. I wired the W3C Flexbox specification using Taffy. Every container, child, margin, and alignment calculation is solved natively by Rust according to true CSS standards.

  4. Skia (The Drawing Engine)*: Once Taffy computes the spatial bounds, pixels are blitted directly to the native OS window using Skia—the exact same high-performance 2D graphics engine that powers Google Chrome and Flutter.

Because the Web target and Native target are completely decoupled, a web application never loads or ships a single byte of native Rust binaries, and a native application never runs an embedded browser.

The Collaboration Behind the Journey

While I architected the core LeveloJS foundation, designed the CLI toolchain, and built the levelo-windows host from scratch, LeveloJS is also growing through collaboration.

My contributor, Joseph Nicholas Aburu—an experienced developer with over a decade of programming background—joined this journey to help explore what a truly multi-platform architecture can become. Having his insights and collaboration on optimization, ideas, and architecture reviews has been an invaluable asset in shaping the project's evolution.

Open source is built on shared passion, and LeveloJS reflects that spirit.

How I Actually Fixed the Rendering Parity

Getting rectangles to draw on a canvas is easy. Getting a native engine to match the nuanced typography, auto-sizing dynamic buttons, and hit-testing behavior of a modern web browser is brutal.

I spent weeks fighting alignment offsets, layout trees, and coordinate bugs. There were moments when my brain stopped working, the layout fell apart, and building my own engine felt like an overwhelming mistake.

It didn't magically fix itself. I had to tear down the rendering pipeline, isolate the Skia rendering logic from the layout calculations, and audit every single file step by step to trace where the coordinates were drifting.

By letting Taffy handle pure CSS Flexbox constraints and stripping away manual layout hacks from the Skia canvas layer, the pieces finally aligned through deliberate debugging:

  • Dynamic buttons began sizing and wrapping cleanly around their text content.
  • The Flexbox engine centered elements exactly where Chrome centered them.
  • Mouse events mapped directly to native event handlers, triggering real-time reactive state updates without lag.

I proved that you don't need a full browser engine just to render modern declarative UI.

What’s Next?

I am taking this step by step.

The next engineering priorities include:

  • Completing remaining tree-cleanup and lifecycle edge cases.
  • Expanding form controls and text inputs.
  • Researching the pipeline for Android and other platforms.

We don't claim to have all the answers, and we know there is a long road ahead. But building software is about having the courage to explore problems that others avoid.

I put my trust in Allah, we did the work, and the foundation is now alive and running.

LeveloJS is built and maintained under Motion Mind X.

Founder & Lead Architect: MD Saiful Alom Siam (@MotionMind2007)

Contributor: Joseph Nicholas Aburu (@Joseph4sure)
