title: Optimizing Large-Scale MongoDB Aggregation Pipelines: From Execution Plans to Production Tuning
description:
Originally published on tamiz.pro.

Aggregation pipelines are MongoDB's most powerful query mechanism — and its most performance-sensitive one. A pipeline that runs in 200ms against a million documents can take 45 minutes against a hundred million, with no algorithmic change, only scale. The difference between those two outcomes usually lives in execution plan selection, index coverage, operator ordering, and shard distribution — not in the pipeline logic itself.

This deep-dive examines the MongoDB query engine's approach to aggregation, identifies the specific mechanisms that cause exponential performance degradation, and provides the optimization strategies that matter at scale. We'll trace from wire protocol through the execution engine, then work through concrete transformations that reduce pipeline latency by orders of magnitude.

Table of Contents

  • 1. The Aggregation Execution Engine
  • 2. Pipeline Operator Classification
  • 3. Index-Driven Optimization
  • 4. Operator Ordering and Materialization
  • 5. $lookup and Join Optimization
  • 6. Sharding-Aware Pipeline Design
  • 7. Execution Plan Analysis
  • 8. Data Modeling for Aggregation
  • 9. Production Monitoring and Alerting
  • 10. Comprehensive Optimization Checklist

1. The Aggregation Execution Engine

MongoDB's aggregation engine processes pipelines through a block-based execution model. Each $match, $group, $sort, $project, or other operator is compiled into an execution stage. These stages form a directed acyclic graph (DAG) when blocking operators like $group are present.

Blocking vs. Streaming Operators

The fundamental distinction in pipeline execution is between streaming and blocking operators:

// Streaming operators process documents one at a time (or in bounded batches)
// - $match: filters documents as they arrive
// - $project: transforms each document independently
// - $addFields: enriches each document
// - $sortByCount: wraps $group + $sort (blocking)

// Blocking operators must consume ALL input before producing output
// - $group: accumulates all matching documents into groups
// - $sort: must buffer enough documents to produce sorted output
// - $limit: buffers until enough documents are consumed
// - $skip: discards documents until offset is reached

The engine optimizes streaming pipelines aggressively — it can push $match stages down to the storage layer, enabling index-only scans. Blocking operators force materialization into memory or temporary files, which is where most large-scale pipeline failures originate.

Query Planning and Optimization Phases

When you submit an aggregation pipeline, MongoDB performs several optimization passes:

  1. Stage folding: Adjacent $project stages are merged into a single projection
  2. Match pushdown: Leading $match stages are converted to storage-level filters
  3. Sort optimization: $sort followed by $limit can use an index to avoid full sort
  4. Index selection: The planner evaluates candidate indexes for the first blocking or first stage

The planner's critical limitation: it optimizes the pipeline as a whole but cannot reorder operators across blocking boundaries. A $match that appears after a $group cannot be pushed below it, regardless of logical equivalence.

Wire Protocol and Batch Processing

The $collStats command and explain execution reveal that MongoDB processes aggregation in batches. For sharded clusters, the planning phase fans out to all shards, each shard plans independently, and results are merged at the mongos. This means:

  • Each shard may select different execution plans
  • Merge cost at mongos is proportional to the number of intermediate documents returned
  • Shard-local blocking operators duplicate memory pressure across all shards

2. Pipeline Operator Classification

Understanding which operators do what — and what they cost — is the foundation of optimization.

Cost Classification Matrix

Operator Blocking? Memory Intensive? Index-Usable? Parallelizable?
$match No No Yes (leading) Yes
$group Yes Yes No Yes (shard-local)
$sort Yes Yes Yes (leading + limit) Partially
$project No No No Yes
$addFields No No No Yes
$lookup No Yes Yes (foreign key) Yes
$unwind No No Yes (with $match) Yes
$facet Yes Yes Mixed No
$bucket Yes Yes No Partially
$bucketAuto Yes Yes No No
$sortByCount Yes Yes Yes (count field) Yes
$sample Yes No Yes (with $match) No
$out / $merge Yes No No No
$unionWith No No Depends No

The $group Accumulator Model

$group is the most common source of memory exhaustion. Each accumulator type has different memory characteristics:

// $sum: O(1) memory per group — accumulates into a single value
// $push: O(n) memory per group — stores all elements in an array
// $addToSet: O(k) memory per group where k = distinct values
// $first/$last: O(1) memory per group
// $avg: O(1) memory per group — maintains count + sum
// $min/$max: O(1) memory per group
// $stdDevPop/$stdDevSamp: O(1) memory per group — uses Welford's algorithm

// DANGEROUS AT SCALE:
{
  $group: {
    _id: "$customerId",  // If cardinality = 50M, this materializes 50M groups
    orders: { $push: "$orderData" },  // Each group holds ALL its orders in memory
    total: { $sum: "$amount" }
  }
}

The $push accumulator is the most dangerous at scale. A group with 10,000 documents each containing a 1KB nested object materializes 10MB for that single group. When group cardinality is high AND each group contains many documents, you hit the 100MB default memory limit immediately.

3. Index-Driven Optimization

Indexes are the single highest-impact optimization for aggregation pipelines. The rule: only the leading $match (before any blocking operator) benefits from index utilization.

Compound Index Design for Aggregation 

// Pipeline:
// db.orders.aggregate([
//   { $match: { status: "completed", region: "us-east", createdAt: { $gte: new Date("2024-01-01") } } },
//   { $sort: { amount: -1 } },
//   { $limit: 100 },
//   { $group: { _id: "$customerId", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } }
// ])

// OPTIMAL INDEX (supports $match + $sort + projection):
db.orders.createIndex(
  { status: 1, region: 1, createdAt: -1, amount: -1 },
  { name: "agg_status_region_date_amount" }
)

// This index allows:
// 1. Index range scan for status + region (equality)
// 2. Sorted traversal by createdAt (range)
// 3. Sorted traversal by amount within the range
// 4. Covering projection if all needed fields are in the index

Index-Only (Covering) Scans

A covering index eliminates collection document fetches entirely. The pipeline reads exclusively from the index B-tree:

// If the pipeline only needs fields present in the index:
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "completed", region: "us-east" } },
  { $group: { _id: "$customerId", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } },
  { $project: { _id: 1, total: 1 } }
]).explain("executionStats")

// Required covering index:
db.orders.createIndex(
  { status: 1, region: 1, customerId: 1, amount: 1 },
  { name: "agg_covering_status_region_cust_amount" }
)

// Verify with explain — look for "IXSCAN" with no "FETCH" stage

The executionStats output reveals whether the pipeline achieves an index-only scan. If you see stage: "FETCH" in the plan, the engine is reading full documents from the collection. Eliminating this stage can reduce I/O by 10-100x depending on document size.

Multikey Indexes and Array Fields

When grouping on array fields, MongoDB creates multikey indexes that expand the index entries:

// Document structure:
// { orderId: 123, tags: ["electronics", "premium", "sale"], amount: 99.99 }

// Multikey index on array field:
db.orders.createIndex({ tags: 1, amount: 1 })

// WARNING: Multikey indexes prevent index-only scans for $group.
// The engine cannot determine which index entry maps to which document
// without fetching the full document. This forces FETCH stage.

// Better approach: pre-compute a non-array grouping field
// or use $unwind + $match before $group

Partial Indexes for Aggregation

Partial indexes reduce index size and improve cache residency:

// Only index documents relevant to the aggregation
db.orders.createIndex(
  { customerId: 1, amount: 1 },
  {
    name: "agg_active_orders",
    partialFilterExpression: {
      status: { $in: ["completed", "refunded"] },
      amount: { $gt: 0 }
    }
  }
)

// Benefit: Smaller index = better B-tree depth = fewer disk pages in cache
// A 500MB index vs a 5GB index can be the difference between
// entirely in-memory scan vs repeated disk I/O

4. Operator Ordering and Materialization

The order of operators in a pipeline determines memory pressure, disk spilling, and execution time. The optimization principle: filter early, transform late.

The Filtering Cascade Pattern 

// ANTI-PATTERN: Group before filtering
// Materializes ALL groups, then discards most
[
  { $group: { _id: "$customerId", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } },
  { $match: { total: { $gte: 1000 } } },  // Too late — all groups already materialized
  { $sort: { total: -1 } },
  { $limit: 1000 }
]

// OPTIMIZED: Push filtering before grouping where possible
[
  { $match: { amount: { $gte: 1 } } },  // Pre-filter cheaply (uses index)
  { $group: { _id: "$customerId", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } },
  { $match: { total: { $gte: 1000 } } },  // Post-group filter (unavoidable)
  { $sort: { total: -1 } },
  { $limit: 1000 }
]

The $sort + $limit Optimization

$sort followed by $limit is a special pattern that MongoDB optimizes. Instead of sorting ALL documents, it maintains a bounded priority queue of size N (the limit). This is O(n log k) where k = limit:

// Pipeline: Get top 100 customers by order count in a specific category
// WITHOUT $sort+$limit: sorts ALL matching documents into memory
[
  { $match: { category: "electronics" } },
  { $group: { _id: "$customerId", count: { $sum: 1 } } },
  { $sort: { count: -1 } },  // Sorts ALL groups — potentially millions
  { $limit: 100 }
]

// The engine DOES optimize $sort + $limit into a top-N heap,
// but you can reduce input size further with pre-filtering:
[
  { $match: { category: "electronics", orderDate: { $gte: last30Days } } },
  { $group: { _id: "$customerId", count: { $sum: 1 } } },
  { $sort: { count: -1 } },
  { $limit: 100 }
]

$facet: Isolation at a Cost

$facet allows parallel sub-pipelines within a single document. It's powerful but forces materialization of ALL input into memory:

// $facet materializes ALL input documents before processing
// Only use when the input to $facet is already heavily filtered
[
  { $match: { region: "us-east", status: "completed" } },  // Heavy pre-filter
  { $facet: {
    revenueByMonth: [
      { $group: { _id: { $month: "$createdAt" }, revenue: { $sum: "$amount" } } },
      { $sort: { _id: 1 } }
    ],
    topProducts: [
      { $group: { _id: "$productId", count: { $sum: 1 } } },
      { $sort: { count: -1 } },
      { $limit: 10 }
    ],
    summary: [
      { $group: { _id: null, totalRevenue: { $sum: "$amount" }, orderCount: { $sum: 1 } } }
    ]
  }}
]

// Memory cost: ALL documents matching $match are held in memory simultaneously
// for ALL sub-pipelines. For 1M documents × 500 bytes = 500MB just for input buffering.

allowDiskUse: When and How

When materialization exceeds the 100MB in-memory limit, MongoDB can spill to disk:

// CRITICAL: allowDiskUse is NOT always safe
// It trades memory for disk I/O — potentially making things 10-100x slower

// Safe with allowDiskUse: predictable, bounded output
// - $group with known cardinality
// - $sort with known input size

// DANGEROUS with allowDiskUse: unpredictable output size
// - $push with unknown group sizes
// - $facet with multiple sub-pipelines on large input
// - $sort on high-cardinality data with no $limit

// Production pattern: set allowDiskUse with monitoring
[
  { $match: { status: "completed" } },
  { $group: { _id: "$region", revenue: { $sum: "$amount" } } },
  { $sort: { revenue: -1 } }
], { allowDiskUse: true }

5. $lookup and Join Optimization

$lookup is MongoDB's equi-join operator. At scale, it behaves like a hash join and can consume enormous memory.

$lookup Execution Models 

// Basic $lookup (hash join on foreign key)
db.orders.aggregate([
  {
    $lookup: {
      from: "customers",
      localField: "customerId",
      foreignField: "_id",
      as: "customer"
    }
  }
])

// The engine builds a hash index on the foreign collection's foreignField.
// For 50M customer documents, this hash index consumes ~2-4GB of RAM.
// This is the #1 cause of OOM in aggregation pipelines.

Optimized $lookup Patterns 

// PATTERN 1: Filter before lookup (reduce hash table size)
[
  { $match: { status: "completed" } },  // Reduce input documents
  {
    $lookup: {
      from: "customers",
      localField: "customerId",
      foreignField: "_id",
      as: "customer",
      // pipeline option allows filtering the foreign collection BEFORE hash build
      pipeline: [
        { $match: { active: true, region: "us-east" } },
        { $project: { name: 1, tier: 1 } }  // Project only needed fields
      ]
    }
  }
]

// PATTERN 2: Replace $lookup with pre-joined embedded data
// If the lookup field is rarely updated, embed it at write time:
// { orderId: 123, customerId: "c1", customerName: "Alice", customerTier: "gold" }
// Eliminates the join entirely — read-only, zero join cost

// PATTERN 3: Use $expr with $in for single-document lookups
// When you only need to verify existence:
{
  $match: {
    $expr: {
      $eq: ["$customerId", "$customerLookup"]  // Pre-resolved
    }
  }
}

Hash Join Memory Analysis 

// Memory consumed by $lookup hash table:
// Formula: numDocuments × (keySize + valueReferenceSize + overhead)
// For 50M customers with ObjectId keys:
//   = 50M × (12 bytes ObjectId + 8 bytes pointer + ~32 bytes overhead)
//   = 50M × 52 bytes ≈ 2.6 GB

// Mitigation: Use the pipeline option to reduce foreign collection size
// BEFORE hash table construction:
db.orders.aggregate([
  {
    $lookup: {
      from: "customers",
      localField: "customerId",
      foreignField: "_id",
      as: "customer",
      pipeline: [
        // This $match runs on the foreign collection BEFORE hash build
        { $match: { _id: { $in: topCustomerIds } } },  // If possible
        { $project: { name: 1, email: 1 } }  // Slim the documents
      ]
    }
  }
])

// Even better: If you know the set of customerIds in advance,
// pre-fetch customer data and use $addFields with $reduce/$arrayElemAt

6. Sharding-Aware Pipeline Design

In a sharded cluster, aggregation pipelines execute as a distributed plan. Understanding the fan-out and merge phases is essential for optimization.

Distributed Execution Model 

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        mongos                                │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │              Global Planning Phase                     │  │
│  │  1. Send pipeline to all shards for planning          │  │
│  │  2. Collect execution plans from each shard          │  │
│  │  3. Select merge strategy based on operator type      │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │              Fan-Out Execution Phase                   │  │
│  │  Send pipeline to Shard 1 → returns partial results    │  │
│  │  Send pipeline to Shard 2 → returns partial results    │  │
│  │  Send pipeline to Shard N → returns partial results    │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │              Merge Phase (at mongos)                   │  │
│  │  Merge all partial results into final output            │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Shard Key Alignment

The shard key determines whether a pipeline can execute entirely on a single shard (no fan-out):

// Sharded collection: orders
// Shard key: { customerId: "hashed" }

// Pipeline 1: SINGLE SHARD (no fan-out)
// $match on shard key routes to exactly one shard
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { customerId: "customer_12345" } },  // Routes to 1 shard
  { $group: { _id: "$category", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } }
])

// Pipeline 2: FULL FAN-OUT (all shards)
// No $match on shard key before first blocking operator
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $group: { _id: "$category", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } },  // ALL shards
  { $sort: { total: -1 } },
  { $limit: 10 }
])

// Pipeline 3: PARTIAL FAN-OUT
// $match on non-shard-key field fans out but reduces per-shard work
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "completed" } },  // All shards, but less data per shard
  { $group: { _id: "$region", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } },
  { $sort: { total: -1 } }
])

Merge Strategy by Operator

Different operators merge differently at mongos:

Operator Merge Strategy Cost
$group + $sum/$avg Two-phase: shard-local partial groups → global re-group O(shards × groups)
$group + $push/$addToSet Two-phase: shard-local arrays → global concat + dedup O(shards × groups × avgArraySize)
$sort + $limit Partial sort on each shard → merge top-N at mongos O(shards × log(limit))
$sort (no limit) Partial sort on each shard → merge all sorted streams O(totalDocuments)
$count Sum of shard counts O(shards)
$first/$last Cannot merge correctly across shards without global sort Requires special handling

Avoiding Two-Phase $group

The two-phase group merge (partial groups on shards, then global re-group) doubles the grouping work. You can avoid it:

// Two-phase group (default when group _id is not the shard key):
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $group: { _id: "$category", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } }
  // Phase 1: Each shard groups by category → returns partial results
  // Phase 2: mongos re-groups all partial results
  // If 10 shards × 50 categories = 500 intermediate docs to merge
])

// Single-phase group (when group _id IS the shard key):
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { customerId: { $in: allCustomerIds } } },  // Routes to specific shards
  { $group: { _id: "$customerId", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } }
  // Each shard handles its own customerId groups — no merge needed
])

// Alternative: Pre-aggregate in application layer
// Issue N separate queries (one per shard) and merge results in app code
// Gives you explicit control over merge logic and error handling

Zoned Sharding for Time-Series Aggregations 

// For time-series data, zoned sharding keeps date ranges on single shards
db.adminCommand({
  shardCollection: "analytics.events",
  uniqueIndex: {
    key: { timestamp: 1, service: 1 },
    partialFilterExpression: { timestamp: { $type: "date" } },
    shardKeyPattern: {
      timestamp: { $gte: new Date("2024-01-01"), $lt: new Date("2024-02-01") }
    }
  }
})

// Now: monthly aggregations hit a SINGLE shard
[
  { $match: { timestamp: { $gte: new Date("2024-01-01"), $lt: new Date("2024-02-01") } } },
  { $group: { _id: "$service", count: { $sum: 1 } } }
]
// No fan-out, no merge — single shard executes the entire pipeline

7. Execution Plan Analysis

The explain command is the primary diagnostic tool for pipeline optimization.

Reading Execution Plans 

const plan = db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "completed", createdAt: { $gte: new Date("2024-01-01") } } },
  { $group: { _id: "$region", revenue: { $sum: "$amount" } } },
  { $sort: { revenue: -1 } }
]).explain("executionStats")

// Key metrics to examine:
console.log(plan.stages)  // Execution stage tree
console.log(plan.executionStats.totalDocsExamined)  // Documents read
console.log(plan.executionStats.totalKeysExamined)  // Index entries scanned
console.log(plan.executionStats.allPlansExecution[0].stage)  // Selected stage type
console.log(plan.executionStats.executionTimeMillis)  // Wall clock time

Critical Metrics 

// The ratio of docsExamined to nReturned tells you pipeline efficiency:
// docsExamined / nReturned = 1.0 → perfect (index-only, no waste)
// docsExamined / nReturned = 1000 → reading 1000 docs to produce 1 result

// For aggregation pipelines:
const stats = plan.executionStats
const efficiency = stats.totalDocsExamined / Math.max(stats.nReturned, 1)

if (efficiency > 10) {
  console.log(`WARNING: Examining ${stats.totalDocsExamined} docs for ${stats.nReturned} results`)
  console.log("Consider: better index, earlier $match, or covering index")
}

// Check for COLLSCAN (full collection scan — almost always bad):
function hasCollectionScan(stages) {
  for (const stage of stages) {
    if (stage.stage === "COLLSCAN") return true
    if (stage.inputStages && hasCollectionScan(stage.inputStages)) return true
  }
  return false
}

if (hasCollectionScan(plan.stages)) {
  console.log("CRITICAL: Pipeline performs full collection scan")
}

// Check for blocking stages that could be eliminated:
function findBlockingStages(stages) {
  const blocking = new Set(["SORT", "GROUP_BY", "COUNT", "UNION_WITH" ])
  const results = []
  for (const stage of stages) {
    if (blocking.has(stage.stage)) results.push(stage)
    if (stage.inputStages) results.push(...findBlockingStages(stage.inputStages))
  }
  return results
}

The $planCache and plan stability

MongoDB caches execution plans in the plan cache. For aggregation, the cache key includes the pipeline's first operator and its arguments:

// Clear the plan cache for a collection (use sparingly in production):
db.orders.runCommand({ planCacheClear: "orders" })

// Lock a specific plan (MongoDB 5.0+):
db.orders.runCommand({
  planCacheSet: "orders",
  filters: [{
    type: "aggsPlan",
    query: { status: "completed" },
    indexName: "agg_status_region_date_amount"
  }],
  params: "locked"
})

// This prevents the planner from choosing a suboptimal plan
// after cache expiration or workload shift

8. Data Modeling for Aggregation

Sometimes the optimal optimization is not in the pipeline but in the data model.

Pre-Aggregation Pattern 

// Instead of aggregating 10M order documents on every query,
// maintain a pre-aggregated collection updated via triggers or scheduled jobs:

// orders_summary collection (updated every 5 minutes or via change streams):
// {
//   _id: { customerId: "c123", month: "2024-01" },
//   totalRevenue: 5000.00,
//   orderCount: 25,
//   avgOrderValue: 200.00,
//   lastOrderAt: ISODate("2024-01-28")
// }

// Query: instant read from pre-aggregated data
db.orders_summary.aggregate([
  { $match: { "_id.customerId": "c123" } },
  { $sort: { "_id.month": -1 } },
  { $limit: 12 }
])

// Update via change streams:
const changeStream = db.orders.watch([
  { $match: { "operationType": { $in: ["insert", "update", "delete"] } } }
])

changeStream.on("change", async (change) => {
  // Incrementally update orders_summary
  // This trades write amplification for read performance
})

Denormalization for Aggregation 

// ANTI-PATTERN: Join-heavy aggregation
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $lookup: { from: "customers", localField: "customerId", foreignField: "_id", as: "cust" } },
  { $unwind: "$cust" },
  { $lookup: { from: "products", localField: "productId", foreignField: "_id", as: "prod" } },
  { $unwind: "$prod" },
  { $group: { _id: "$cust.region", revenue: { $sum: "$amount" } } }
])
// Cost: 2 hash joins, potentially GB of memory

// OPTIMIZED: Denormalize frequently-joined fields
// Order document already contains:
// { orderId: 123, customerId: "c1", customerRegion: "us-east", productId: "p1", productName: "Widget", amount: 99.99 }

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { customerRegion: "us-east" } },
  { $group: { _id: "$customerRegion", revenue: { $sum: "$amount" } } }
])
// Cost: Single index scan, no joins

Rollup Hierarchies

For OLAP-style queries, maintain multiple rollup levels:

// orders_by_day: 1 document per (customer, day) — updated continuously
// orders_by_week: 1 document per (customer, week) — updated daily
// orders_by_month: 1 document per (customer, month) — updated monthly

// Query strategy: route based on time range
db.orders_by_month.aggregate([
  { $match: { "_id.customerId": "c123", "_id.month": { $gte: "2023-01", $lte: "2024-12" } } },
  { $sort: { "_id.month": -1 } }
])
// Returns 24 documents instead of aggregating 500,000 order documents

9. Production Monitoring and Alerting

Monitoring aggregation pipeline performance requires instrumentation at multiple levels.

Slow Query Log Configuration 

// Enable slow query logging for aggregation operations
db.adminCommand({
  profile: 2,  // Log ALL operations
  slowms: 100  // Threshold: 100ms
})

// In production, use threshold-based:
db.adminCommand({
  profile: 1,
  slowms: 2000  // Only log operations > 2 seconds
})

// Query the system.profile collection:
db.system.profile.aggregate([
  { $match: { op: "command", "command.aggregate": { $exists: true }, duration: { $gt: 5000 } } },
  { $sort: { duration: -1 } },
  { $limit: 20 }
])

Programmatic Pipeline Performance Monitoring 

// Wrapper that measures and logs aggregation performance
async function monitoredAggregate(collection, pipeline, options = {}) {
  const { timeout = 30000, alertThreshold = 5000, label = "pipeline" } = options

  const startTime = process.hrtime()
  const controller = new AbortController()
  const timeoutId = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), timeout)

  try {
    // Get execution stats
    const explainResult = await collection
      .aggregate(pipeline, { ...options, explain: "executionStats" })
      .toArray()

    const stats = explainResult[0]
    const execStats = stats.executionStats || stats.stages?.[0]?.executionStats

    const metrics = {
      label,
      executionTimeMs: execStats?.executionTimeMillis,
      docsExamined: execStats?.totalDocsExamined,
      keysExamined: execStats?.totalKeysExamined,
      nReturned: execStats?.nReturned,
      hasCollectionScan: JSON.stringify(stats.stages).includes('COLLSCAN'),
      memoryBytes: execStats?.memUsage
    }

    // Alert on degradation
    if (metrics.executionTimeMs > alertThreshold) {
      console.error(`[ALERT] Pipeline "${label}" exceeded threshold:`, metrics)
    }

    return metrics
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timeoutId)
  }
}

// Usage:
const stats = await monitoredAggregate(
  db.orders,
  [
    { $match: { status: "completed" } },
    { $group: { _id: "$region", revenue: { $sum: "$amount" } } }
  ],
  { label: "revenue_by_region", alertThreshold: 3000 }
)

Server Status Metrics for Aggregation 

// Current in-progress operations (detects stuck pipelines)
db.adminCommand({ currentOp: true, allOps: false }).inprog
  .filter(op => op.cmd?.aggregate)

// Detect operations exceeding threshold:
const slowOps = db.adminCommand({ currentOp: true, allOps: false }).inprog
  .filter(op => {
    if (!op.cmd?.aggregate) return false
    const elapsed = Date.now() - op.activeSince?.getTime()
    return elapsed > 60000  // Running for over 60 seconds
  })

// Kill a stuck aggregation:
db.adminCommand({ killCursors: "orders", cursors: [cursorId] })
// Or kill by operation:
db.adminCommand({ killOp: opId })

// Cluster-wide aggregation monitoring:
db.adminCommand({ serverStatus: 1 }).metrics.document
// {
//   insert: ...,  // document inserts
//   query: ...,   // document queries  
//   update: ...,  // document updates
//   delete: ...   // document deletes
// }

db.adminCommand({ serverStatus: 1 }).metrics.aggregate
// {
//   scans: ...,        // documents scanned by aggregation
//   resultSets: ...,  // documents returned by aggregation
//   yields: ...        // context switches during aggregation
// }

Alerting Rules 

// Example: Alert when aggregation scan ratio degrades
// scans / resultSets > 100 indicates inefficient pipeline
const aggregateMetrics = db.adminCommand({ serverStatus: 1 }).metrics.aggregate
const scanRatio = aggregateMetrics.scans / Math.max(aggregateMetrics.resultSets, 1)

if (scanRatio > 100) {
  // ALERT: Aggregation pipelines are scanning 100x more documents than returned
  // Action: Review recent pipeline changes, check for index drops
}

// Alert when ops control detects high aggregation load
const activeAggregations = db.adminCommand({ currentOp: true }).inprog
  .filter(op => op.cmd?.aggregate).length

if (activeAggregations > 10) {
  // ALERT: More than 10 concurrent aggregation operations
  // May indicate application bug or thundering herd
}

10. Comprehensive Optimization Checklist

Pre-Deployment Validation

  1. Index existence: Verify all leading $match fields have supporting indexes
  2. Index coverage: Confirm the index covers all projected fields (eliminate FETCH stage)
  3. Cardinality analysis: Measure $group _id cardinality — if > 10M, consider pre-aggregation
  4. Shard routing: Validate whether pipeline fans out or routes to single shard
  5. Memory estimation: Calculate worst-case memory for blocking operators
  6. explain validation: Run explain("executionStats") on representative data

Runtime Optimization

  1. Leading $match: Always place $match before blocking operators
  2. Covering indexes: Design indexes to eliminate collection document fetches
  3. $sort + $limit: Always pair expensive sorts with limits
  4. $lookup pipeline option: Filter foreign collection before hash build
  5. allowDiskUse monitoring: Enable but alert on disk spill events
  6. Plan cache locking: Lock optimal plans for critical pipelines

Architecture-Level Decisions

  1. Pre-aggregation: For sub-second latency requirements, maintain rollup collections
  2. Denormalization: Embed join fields for read-heavy workloads
  3. Shard key alignment: Design shard keys to match query patterns
  4. Read preferences: Route analytics queries to secondary nodes
  5. Query isolation: Use dedicated replica set members for heavy aggregations
  6. Connection pooling: Limit concurrent aggregation operations per node

Ongoing Maintenance

  1. Index rebuild schedule: Rebuild indexes after mass data ingestion
  2. Plan cache monitoring: Alert when plans change unexpectedly
  3. Workload analysis: Regularly review system.profile for regression
  4. Capacity planning: Model growth rates against memory limits
  5. Kill switch: Implement timeout-based circuit breakers for aggregation operations

The optimization landscape for MongoDB aggregation pipelines operates at the intersection of query planning, memory management, distributed execution, and data modeling. There is no single silver bullet — effective optimization requires understanding how the engine plans your specific pipeline, which operators force materialization, and how shard distribution affects the merge phase. The patterns above, applied systematically, routinely reduce pipeline latency from minutes to milliseconds at scale. For teams operating at petabyte scale, invest in execution plan monitoring and automated alerting as infrastructure — pipeline performance degradation is often the leading indicator of broader system issues.

For deeper exploration of query optimization patterns across database systems, see Tamiz's Insights for related deep-dives on distributed systems performance.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does my $group operator consume all available memory?

$group materializes one entry per distinct _id value in memory. If your grouping field has high cardinality (millions of distinct values), each entry's memory footprint accumulates. The fix is one of: (1) reduce cardinality by pre-filtering with $match before $group, (2) replace $push with bounded accumulators like $sum/$avg that use O(1) memory per group, (3) enable allowDiskUse: true to spill overflow to disk, or (4) redesign the query to avoid grouping on a high-cardinality field entirely.

How do I determine if my aggregation pipeline is using an index?

Run pipeline.explain("executionStats") and inspect the stage tree. Look for IXSCAN stages — these indicate index usage. If you see COLLSCAN, the pipeline is scanning the entire collection. The specific index used appears in the IXSCAN stage's pattern field. Additionally, check executionStats.totalKeysExamined — if it's significantly lower than totalDocsExamined, you're getting index benefits.

When should I use $facet vs. separate aggregation pipelines?

Use $facet when you need multiple aggregations over the SAME filtered dataset and want to avoid scanning the collection multiple times. However, $facet materializes ALL input documents in memory simultaneously for all sub-pipelines. If the input is already small (post-filter), $facet is ideal. If the input is large, prefer separate pipelines with individual $match stages — each can use its own optimal index and avoids holding all documents in memory at once.

title: Vercel Tracing is now generally available
description:
Vercel Tracing is now generally available on all plans. You can now search and inspect traces from the dashboard or the Vercel CLI, and new Next.js projects get tracing by default. Pricing is unchanged from the beta.

Browse and search traces in the dashboard

In beta, you could only open a trace per request from the Logs page. The new Traces page shows every trace and span in one place, for a project or your whole team. Switch between a Spans list and a Traces list, filter each, and search with Kibana Query Language (KQL). A Live mode streams new traces as they arrive. A query like span.name:db* AND span.duration > 500 narrows to slow database spans by name and duration.

Search traces from the CLI

The Traces page uses the same KQL as vercel traces search --query, so a query built in the dashboard runs in the CLI unchanged. Search covers every project in your team, or one project with the --project flag. Inspect a single trace with vercel traces inspect <request-id>, and manage a project's sampling rules with vercel traces config.

Automatic tracing for new Next.js projects

In beta, nothing was collected until you added a sampling rule. Starting with Next.js 16.5, new projects created on Vercel that include at least one Node.js function get tracing turned on after their first successful build. Vercel adds one sampling rule tracing 100% of requests in all environments and injects instrumentation at build time, so traces include Next.js framework spans with no setup. To opt out, remove all sampling rules in Settings → Tracing.

Longer retention

In beta, traces followed your runtime log retention. Hobby now keeps traces for 3 days instead of 1 hour, Pro for 14 days instead of 1 day, and Enterprise for 14 days instead of 3 days.

Read the Tracing documentation to learn more.

title: Fail closed on incoming Messages, wireless emergency alerts, and headphone safety warnings
description:
When narrative content drives a physical actuator, three interrupt paths look like "just restore state" until they are not: an incoming Messages / iMessage / RCS / SMS conversation or in-line reply composer mid-session, a Wireless Emergency Alert / Presidential / AMBER / earthquake / severe-weather government alert, and a headphone-safety / loud-sound-reduction / system volume-limit sheet. Each needs a default that fails closed — toward idle, toward re-arm only after a named beat, toward interrupt-clear ≠ motor authority.

on incoming_messages_thread_or_reply_composer_opened():
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on thread_dismissed_or_reply_sent():
        # messaging UI gone ≠ motor envelope restored
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

on wireless_emergency_alert_or_government_alert_opened():
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on alert_dismissed_or_acknowledged():
        # alert UI cleared ≠ motor authority
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

on headphone_safety_or_volume_limit_sheet_opened():
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on warning_dismissed_or_volume_lowered():
        # safety UI gone ≠ previous intensity restored
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

The incoming-Messages rule is easy to mix up with an incoming voice or video call, a tap-to-open push, a co-player progress notification, Notification Center, and a Contacts or Calendar picker. A call is a telephony interrupt. A push-open brings an app forward. A progress notification is not a conversation surface. Notification Center is a shade of history. A picker is a people-or-event sheet. A Messages thread is a conversation surface. Dismissing it or sending a reply clears that surface; it must not restore motor authority.

The Wireless Emergency Alert rule sits next to — but is not — a user-scheduled alarm or calendar notice, a tap-to-open push, Notification Center, Focus / Do Not Disturb, or a Live Activity / Dynamic Island. An alarm is user-scheduled. A push is opt-in app mail. Notification Center is a history shade. Focus can silence ordinary alerts; WEA can pierce it. Live Activity is a phone-side glance. A WEA is a government or carrier emergency alert. Acknowledge only clears that alert; it must not restore motor authority.

The headphone-safety rule is an OS hearing-safety dialog, not a Bluetooth audio-route change, not muting story audio, not a voice-assistant takeover, and not VoiceOver or a magnifier. Audio-route change is an already-paired headset connecting, disconnecting, or flipping to speaker. Mute is a playback control. A voice assistant takes over the session. VoiceOver is an accessibility surface. A volume-limit sheet is a safety warning. Dismissing it or turning the volume down only clears that warning; it must not restore motor authority.

Buyers can test two of the three without code: open a Messages thread or in-line reply mid-session and see whether dismissing it or sending a reply restarts intensity, and trigger a headphone safety or volume-limit warning then dismiss it. A Wireless Emergency Alert is harder to stage, but the acceptance question is the same: acknowledging the alert must not put motor authority back on. These map to questions like "how do AI stories control physical devices" and "Lovense alternative with AI stories."

This is the model CRAVE AI uses for story-controlled play on official devices: AI story-controlled vibrator. Principle write-up: narrative-to-device sync. Devices: AI sex toys.

title: What Is the Main Benefit of Continuous Integration in Testing?
description:
A developer merges a small change on Friday afternoon. Everything looks fine. On Monday morning, checkout is broken, three other features are failing, and nobody knows which of the last 40 commits caused it.

This is the exact problem continuous integration solves. So, what is the main benefit of continuous integration in testing? In one line

The main benefit of CI in testing is fast feedback bugs are caught within minutes of the commit that caused them, when they are cheapest and easiest to fix.

Everything else, like better code quality, safer releases and happier teams, follows from that one idea.

What is continuous integration?

Continuous integration (CI) is a development practice where every code change is automatically built and tested as soon as it is pushed to a shared repository. Instead of developers working alone for weeks and merging everything in one risky step, they integrate small changes many times a day, and an automated CI pipeline checks each one.

A typical CI pipeline does this on every push or pull request pulls the latest code, builds the application, runs automated tests (unit tests, integration tests, sometimes UI tests), and reports pass or fail to the team.

Why fast feedback is the biggest benefit

A bug found 10 minutes after you wrote it is a small fix. You still remember the code, the change is tiny, and only one commit is suspect. A bug found three weeks later is expensive the original developer may have moved on, the code has changed around it, and other features may already depend on the broken behaviour.

CI shrinks that gap. Because tests run automatically on every change, problems show up while the context is fresh. That is why teams that adopt continuous integration spend less time debugging and more time building.

Other benefits of continuous integration in testing

Fewer integration bugs: merging small changes often avoids the painful "merge hell" at the end of a sprint.

Automated regression testing: old features are re-tested on every change, so new code cannot quietly break what already worked.

Higher code quality: a failing build blocks bad code from reaching the main branch, and checks like linting and code coverage become routine.

Faster, safer releases: when the main branch is always tested and working, shipping becomes a routine event instead of a stressful one. This is also the foundation for CI/CD (continuous delivery and deployment).

Less manual testing: testers spend time on exploratory and usability testing instead of repeating the same checks by hand.

Team confidence: developers refactor and improve code without fear, because the tests will tell them quickly if something breaks.

These benefits do not end at launch. Once software is live, every patch, dependency update and security fix needs the same safety net, which is why reliable IT Support & Maintenance Services | Spark Tech pair ongoing monitoring with automated testing so that fixes never cause new outages.

A simple CI example

Here is a minimal GitHub Actions workflow that builds a .NET project and runs its tests on every push and pull request. The same idea works in Jenkins, GitLab CI, Azure DevOps and CircleCI

name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:

test:
runs-on: ubuntu-latest
steps:
- uses: actions/checkout@v4
- uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
with:
dotnet-version: 8.0.x
- run: dotnet restore
- run: dotnet build --no-restore
- run: dotnet test --no-build

If any test fails, the pipeline turns red and the pull request cannot be merged until it is fixed.

5 CI best practices for better testing

Commit small and often. Small changes are easier to test, review and fix.

Keep the build fast. Aim for results in about 10 minutes. If the pipeline is slow, developers stop waiting for it and start ignoring it.

Fix a broken build immediately. A red pipeline is the team's top priority, not something to deal with later.

Test at multiple levels. Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and a small number of end-to-end tests give the best balance of speed and coverage.

Avoid flaky tests. Tests that fail randomly destroy trust in the pipeline. Fix or remove them quickly.

Small businesses often skip this because they have no dedicated DevOps person. That is where outsourced IT support and maintenance services help someone else keeps the pipelines, servers, updates and backups healthy while your team focuses on features.

Common CI mistakes to avoid

Treating CI as only a build server and writing too few automated tests

Letting the main branch stay broken for days

Running every slow test on every commit instead of splitting fast and slow suites

Ignoring test results because the pipeline is noisy or flaky

Skipping CI for "small" hotfixes, which are often the riskiest changes

Is continuous integration worth it?

For almost every team, yes. Even a basic pipeline that builds the project and runs a handful of tests on each push will catch problems that manual testing misses. You can start small set up one workflow, add your most important tests, and grow from there.

If you do not have the time or skills in house, a trusted partner offering software maintenance and support can set up, monitor and maintain your testing and release process for you, so problems are caught early and your systems stay stable.

Final thoughts

The main benefit of continuous integration in testing is simple you find out about problems immediately, not after your customers do. Faster feedback means cheaper fixes, higher quality and calmer releases.

Do you already use CI in your projects? Which tool do you prefer GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI or something else? Share it in the comments.

title: Eight Voices Agreed, and That Is the Part That Fails
description:
Anton describes a system already running: he stopped blindly trusting one model, put Codex next to Claude Code to check it, and ended with a panel of 8 voices reviewing his code. His framing is sharper than the usual complaint: every output a model produces is a hallucination, and the only difference is whether it happened to be right.

Our panel ledger backs the benefit, and the number is high. On the node that keeps the log: 18 live panel calls, 17 of them returned a finding, across three rails, Gemini 7, Grok 6, Codex 5, with six separate pieces of work fanned out to all three at once. 94 percent of calls brought something back. So "each of them sees the world its own way" is not a feeling, it is what the ledger shows.

But the mechanism he credits is the one the research blames. He says that with several models judging each other they are more likely to find a consensus, "the hallucination that is acceptable to all of them". That sentence describes, almost word for word, what the literature calls correlated hallucination. The Council Mode paper attributes 19 percent of its failures to exactly that: every expert model confidently converging on the same wrong fact. Kim and colleagues report that LLM errors are more than 60 percent correlated, which puts a floor under what any naive ensemble can fix. And a 2026 result proves that under a standard belief model, debate between agents given identical inputs forms a martingale, so expected correctness does not improve across rounds at all.

The practical reading is the opposite of consensus: what breaks the correlation is difference, different vendors, different training, different information in front of each one. Our own log is the cleanest illustration. In August the three rails reviewed one fix and produced three different lists, and one of Gemini's findings was disproved by reading the code rather than by a vote. The value came from the spread and from a human arbiter at the end, not from three of them agreeing.

"You can argue with it and win" has a measured rate. The Stanford SycEval study pushed back against models on 500 algebra problems and 500 medical questions, and in 14.66 percent of cases a model abandoned a correct answer for a wrong one under pressure. Pushing in the right direction worked 43.52 percent of the time. Once a model had caved, the new position held at 78.5 percent persistence. Pre-emptive objections broke models more often than objections raised mid-conversation, 61.75 against 56.52 percent. And the worst detail for code review: objections that cited a source produced the highest regressions of all. So yes, you can out-talk it, and the price is that your own panel can be talked into agreeing with you.

His central claim, that everything a model emits is a hallucination, matches where the field arrived by a different road. The September 2025 paper by Kalai, Nachum, Vempala and Zhang reviewed ten major benchmarks and found nine of them score answers in binary fashion, awarding zero for expressing uncertainty. Under that scoring, the expected score for guessing is always higher than for abstaining. The model is not occasionally inventing things; it was optimised in a regime where a guess scores and "I do not know" never does.

So the panel is exactly as useful as he says, for a reason he does not name. Eight voices help because they disagree, not because they converge, and the moment they converge is the moment you have lost your only instrument.

⚠️ Caveats. The panel ledger comes from one node and stops on 17 August 2026, 87 days before this post, so "94 percent of live calls returned a finding" describes 18 calls over 11 days and not the current system; the hub keeps its own rails and they are not counted here. The finding field records that text came back, not that the finding was correct. Engine self-tests account for 185 of the 203 records, so the aggregate 77 percent success is mostly a statement about its own test suite. The external figures are single studies: the 60 percent error correlation is reported second-hand, and the widely quoted 58.19 percent overall sycophancy rate could not be confirmed in SycEval's abstract, so it is excluded here.

The full story, in two versions:
📖 For humans, the longread: https://github.com/tonydzi/clawrush/blob/main/longreads/20261110.md
🤖 For machines, the devlog: https://github.com/tonydzi/clawrush/blob/main/devlog/20261110.md. Just hand this link to your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) and it will figure everything out: it is written for machines.

title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
description: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

title: ASEAN Cross-Border QR Payments in Spring Boot: EMVCo Router
description:
An ASEAN cross-border QR payment works like this: the payer's app parses the EMVCo QR text, checks its CRC16 checksum, detects which scheme (PayNow, DuitNow, PromptPay or QRIS) owns the code, locks an FX quote, and sends an idempotent instruction down the bilateral link to the merchant's country. This post shows how to build that router in Spring Boot.

The regional headlines are all about new links. By December 2025 the region had counted 29 QR and instant-payment linkages, Cambodia now has five bilateral links, and Singapore and Vietnam switched theirs on in July 2026. MAS and the Association of Banks in Singapore are studying a second generation of PayNow ahead of Singapore FinTech Festival on 18 to 20 November 2026. Each of those is a pairwise agreement between two scheme operators. None of them gives the sending bank a single thing to call.

That gap lands on whoever writes the payer-side code at a bank, wallet or acquirer. In practice the scheme operators run the pipes, and your institution runs the part that decides which pipe a given scan should use, what to quote, and what to do when the answer never comes back. This post walks through one scan in plain terms, then the design I would use for an EMVCo QR parser and corridor router in Spring Boot, and closes with the failure modes that generate pager alerts. If you have worked through PSD2 API development, the shape is familiar: several regulated rails and no common hand-off.

Part 1: One scan, end to end

A Thai customer, with a Thai banking app, stands in front of a Singapore stall that has a printed QR code. They scan it. The app reads the text, notices that the merchant template belongs to PayNow rather than PromptPay, and asks an FX service how many baht equal the stall's price in Singapore dollars. The service answers with a rate held for a short window, often around a minute. The customer sees the baht amount, confirms with a fingerprint, and the app sends an instruction into the Thailand to Singapore link. On the Singapore side it becomes a PayNow credit to the merchant. A confirmation travels back, the stall owner hears a chime, and the customer sees a green tick.

Three terms are all you need beyond that: an instant payment scheme is a national rail (PayNow in Singapore, PromptPay in Thailand, DuitNow in Malaysia, with QRIS as Indonesia's QR standard); a linkage is the bilateral connection between two of them; and FX is the conversion step in between.

What surprised me when I looked at the architecture is that there is no ASEAN-wide network. There is Thailand-Singapore, Malaysia-Singapore, Indonesia-Thailand and so on, each negotiated separately, each with its own message details, operating hours and definition of "completed". Mandate-style payments run into the same trap of rules that look uniform and are not, which I covered in Commercial VRP in Spring Boot: each rail's notion of consent, retry and finality differs, and your code has to absorb that difference rather than pretend it away.

My working thesis is that the QR text is standardised and the corridors are not. That is why the router exists. Who runs it? Usually the payer-side institution, or its processor, because that is the party holding the customer relationship, the FX exposure and the compliance obligation. Scheme operators will not run it for you: they connect two ends of one corridor and have no reason to model your customer's wallet balance or your FX margin.

Part 2: What the QR text contains

EMVCo, the body behind the common QR specification, defines the payload as a flat string of TLV records: a two-digit tag, a two-digit length, then the value. Some values contain a nested TLV string.

Here is a complete, valid example I use in tests, a dynamic PayNow-style code for S$4.50 at a made-up stall:

00020101021226370009SG.PAYNOW010120210201912345K0301052045812530370254044.505802SG5919LAU PA SAT STALL 126009Singapore63047598

Broken apart: 000201 (format 01), 010212 (dynamic), 2637... (template in tag 26, 37 characters long, holding sub-tag 00 SG.PAYNOW, a proxy type, the proxy value and an editable-amount flag), 52045812 (category 5812), 5303702 (SGD), 54044.50 (amount), 5802SG, 5919LAU PA SAT STALL 12, 6009Singapore, and 63047598 (CRC). The identifiers and sub-tag layout above are illustrative; real ones come from each scheme's specification.

The tags I rely on for routing:

Tag Meaning
00 Payload format indicator, always 01
01 Point of initiation: 11 static (reusable), 12 dynamic (one-off, usually carries an amount)
26 to 51 Merchant account information templates, one per scheme the merchant accepts
52 Merchant category code
53 Currency, ISO 4217 numeric (702 SGD, 764 THB, 458 MYR, 360 IDR)
54 Transaction amount, optional
58 Country code
59, 60 Merchant name and city
62 Additional data such as bill or reference numbers
63 CRC, a 4-hex-digit checksum

Tags 26 to 51 are the ones that matter for a router. One printed code can carry several templates, for example a PayNow template in one tag and a card-network template in another. Inside each, sub-tag 00 holds a globally unique identifier naming the owning scheme. Detect the scheme from that identifier, never from the tag number, because tag numbers are chosen by whoever generated the code and two merchants can put PayNow in different slots.

The identifier strings and sub-tag layouts must come from each scheme's current specification and your sponsor bank's onboarding pack. I keep them in configuration, and the values in the code below are placeholders that show shape only.

Step one: reject bad codes cheaply

The checksum in tag 63 is CRC-16 over the whole payload, up to and including the 6304 that introduces the field. The variant is CCITT-FALSE: polynomial 0x1021, initial value 0xFFFF, no reflection, no final XOR. A quick self-test is the string 123456789, which must produce 29B1; the sample payload above produces 7598. Validate before parsing anything else. A failed CRC is a damaged print, a camera misread, or a sticker pasted over a legitimate code, and in none of those cases do you want to burn an FX quote or a corridor call.

public final class EmvCrc16 {

    private EmvCrc16() {}

    public static int compute(String payloadUpToAndIncluding6304) {
        int crc = 0xFFFF;
        for (byte b : payloadUpToAndIncluding6304.getBytes(java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {
            crc ^= (b & 0xFF) << 8;
            for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
                crc = ((crc & 0x8000) != 0) ? (crc << 1) ^ 0x1021 : crc << 1;
                crc &= 0xFFFF;
            }
        }
        return crc;
    }

    public static boolean isValid(String payload) {
        if (payload == null || payload.length() < 8) return false;
        int cut = payload.length() - 4;
        if (!payload.startsWith("6304", cut - 4)) return false;
        String expected = String.format("%04X", compute(payload.substring(0, cut)));
        return expected.equalsIgnoreCase(payload.substring(cut));
    }
}

The CRC field must be last. I have seen generators append trailing whitespace or a newline, so input is trimmed at the edge and anything still failing the position check is refused. Do not "repair" payloads. An instrument that needs repair is one you decline.

Step two: a parser that does not trust lengths

The TLV walker bound-checks every length. A declared length running past the end of the string is exactly what a hostile input would contain. My parser returns an immutable map of tag to value and throws one typed exception, MalformedQrException, which the API maps to a 422 with a stable error code. Nested templates go through the same parser recursively, capped at depth two, since no scheme I have read about needs more.

Step three: scheme detection from tags 26 to 51

Detection walks every template in 26 to 51, parses sub-tag 00, and matches it against a registry. The result is a list, because a code can legitimately offer more than one scheme.

public record SchemeMatch(String schemeId, int templateTag, Map<String, String> fields) {}

@Component
public class SchemeDetector {

    private final Map<String, String> guidToScheme; // from configuration

    public SchemeDetector(SchemeRegistryProperties props) {
        this.guidToScheme = props.guidToScheme();
    }

    public List<SchemeMatch> detect(Map<String, String> tlv) {
        List<SchemeMatch> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int tag = 26; tag <= 51; tag++) {
            String raw = tlv.get(String.format("%02d", tag));
            if (raw == null) continue;
            Map<String, String> sub = TlvParser.parse(raw, 1);
            String guid = sub.get("00");
            if (guid == null) continue;
            String scheme = guidToScheme.get(guid.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT));
            if (scheme != null) out.add(new SchemeMatch(scheme, tag, sub));
        }
        return out;
    }
}

Unknown identifiers are skipped, not fatal. A Thai app will meet templates for schemes it cannot pay through, and the right move is to ignore them and use the one it supports. Once a scheme is chosen, the instruction has to survive retries and crashes, which is where the transactional outbox pattern in Spring Boot payment systems earns its place. For the settlement work queues, Kafka share groups in Spring Boot payment pipelines are worth a look.

Part 3: The router and the corridor model

Here is the system I would build, shown in the diagram.

I model a corridor as an ordered pair, source scheme and destination scheme, plus a bundle of properties: which adapter speaks to it, its operating hours and cut-off, per-transaction and daily limits, the currencies it supports, its timeout budget, and whether it returns a synchronous final answer or only an acknowledgement followed by a later status message. Direction matters. Thailand to Singapore and Singapore to Thailand are separate corridors that happen to share a diagram edge.

public record Corridor(
        String source,
        String destination,
        String adapterBean,
        LocalTime opensAt,
        LocalTime closesAt,
        ZoneId zone,
        BigDecimal perTxnLimit,
        Duration ackTimeout,
        boolean asyncFinality) {

    public boolean isOpen(Instant now) {
        LocalTime t = now.atZone(zone).toLocalTime();
        return !t.isBefore(opensAt) && t.isBefore(closesAt);
    }
}

Corridor definitions live in configuration and are reloaded without a deploy, because limits and windows change by circular, not by release cycle. Routing is then a lookup: given the payer's home scheme and the list of SchemeMatch entries, return the open corridors, ordered by a preference rule (cheapest FX, then highest recent success rate). If none are open, the user is told which window to retry in, which is kinder than a generic failure.

Locking FX without lying to the customer

The FX service returns a quote: pair, rate, an expiresAt, and a quote id. The router stores it with the payment attempt and shows the payer the converted amount. The rule I would enforce is that the corridor instruction carries the quote id and the exact converted amount the customer confirmed. If expiresAt has passed when the customer confirms, or by the time the message is built, the router discards the quote and asks again rather than quietly re-pricing. Silent re-pricing is how a customer approves 412 baht and is charged 418.

The rate-expiry race is real: the user dawdles on the confirm screen for 55 seconds of a 60-second window, the request takes 8 seconds to reach the adapter, and the quote dies in flight. The fix is to validate expiry with a safety margin equal to your p99 path latency, not at the moment of the tap.

Idempotent settlement

Every payment attempt gets a client-generated idempotency key that travels from the app through to the adapter. The API layer stores it in a unique-constrained table before doing anything else:

@Transactional
public PaymentAttempt accept(String idemKey, QrPayRequest req) {
    return attempts.findByIdemKey(idemKey)
        .orElseGet(() -> {
            PaymentAttempt a = PaymentAttempt.create(idemKey, req);
            attempts.saveAndFlush(a);          // unique index on idem_key
            outbox.enqueue("settlement.requested", a.id(), a.toInstruction());
            return a;
        });
}

A duplicate request returns the stored attempt and its current state; it does not create a second instruction. The outbox row and the attempt commit together, and a relay publishes to the Kafka topic settlement.requested, keyed by attempt id so that all events for one payment stay ordered on one partition. Concurrent duplicates race on the unique index; the loser catches the constraint violation and re-reads. I also pass the same key as the end-to-end reference in the corridor message wherever the scheme allows, so the destination side can detect a replay even if my side loses its own state.

Per-corridor adapters consume the topic and are the only components that know a scheme's message format. They translate the internal instruction to the corridor's wire format, call the link, and publish settlement.result events. An adapter must be a thin translator with no business rules, so that adding a corridor means adding one class and one configuration entry.

The state machine

I keep the attempt state deliberately small: RECEIVED, QUOTED, CONFIRMED, SENT, COMPLETED, FAILED, UNKNOWN. UNKNOWN is the important one. It means "we sent an instruction and do not know the outcome", and it is a first-class state with its own handling rather than a synonym for failed. Anything that times out after SENT goes there, never to FAILED.

Part 4: Compliance and data constraints

A router like this is a regulated activity before it is a technical one. Points that shape the design:

  • Data localisation and residency. Regulators in several of these markets, including the central banks of Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia and the Monetary Authority of Singapore, set expectations about where payment data may be stored and processed. Indonesia's rules in particular push toward domestic processing for domestic transactions. Do not assume one central cluster can hold everything; check with your compliance team early and design the storage layer so a corridor's records can live in-region.
  • Licensing. Operating on the payer side generally requires being a licensed bank or payment institution in your home market, and the destination scheme will onboard you through a sponsor or participant arrangement. Your adapter configuration is shaped by that contract.
  • AML and sanctions screening. Cross-border hops are where screening is strictest. Screen the beneficiary name and country from tags 58 and 59 before sending, and keep the screening result and list version on the attempt record. A screening hold needs its own state so that a manual review does not look like a timeout.
  • Amount and purpose reporting. Some corridors cap per-transaction amounts and require a purpose or merchant category, which is why tag 52 is retained, not discarded after parsing.

None of this is exotic, but each item adds a mandatory step in the hot path, and the added latency eats into the FX quote window described above.

Part 5: Failures that page people

These are the failure patterns I would design against, each of which has a recognisable shape in any system of this kind.

The timeout after SENT. The link takes your instruction, then the response never arrives. If you mark the payment failed and the customer retries, you may pay the merchant twice. If you mark it successful, you may have paid nobody. Treat it as UNKNOWN, query the corridor's status endpoint (or wait for the async status message) on a backoff, and only then resolve. Set an upper bound, for example 15 minutes, after which the case goes to a human operations queue rather than retrying forever.

The cut-off boundary. A corridor closes at its cut-off time. An instruction built at 23:59:58 and delivered at 00:00:03 lands in the next window, or is rejected. Check isOpen with a margin and, when close to the boundary, refuse and say when to retry. Include timezone in the corridor config: two schemes six hours apart do not share a day.

The reconciliation mismatch. Your records say 1,000 payments completed; the scheme's settlement file says 998. The two missing ones are usually UNKNOWN attempts that did not settle, and one or two settled attempts that you marked failed. Reconciliation should match on the end-to-end reference, produce three buckets (matched, only-ours, only-theirs), and auto-resolve only the ones with unambiguous evidence. A nightly job that quietly "fixes" differences hides the incidents you need to learn from.

The poison QR. One printed code with an off-spec template (a length field wrong by one) can throw in the parser and, if the consumer is not careful, stall a partition. Parsing happens at the API edge precisely so that malformed input is rejected with a 422 and never reaches Kafka. Anything that does get through to an adapter and fails should go to a dead-letter topic with the original payload, not retry in a tight loop.

Duplicate delivery. Kafka consumers are at-least-once. An adapter that receives the same settlement.requested twice must check the attempt state before calling the link. Combine that with the idempotency key in the wire message and a replay becomes a no-op on both sides.

Quote drift on retry. A retry of an UNKNOWN payment must reuse the original quote id and amount, not request a fresh one. Otherwise the customer is shown one price and settled at another.

What I would build first

Start with the CRC validator and parser with a test file of real-looking payloads, including broken ones; they are cheap and every later layer depends on them. Then a single corridor end to end against a sandbox, with the state machine and the UNKNOWN handling in place from day one, not bolted on after the first incident. Add the second corridor only when the first one's reconciliation runs clean. The QR format is the easy and well-documented part. The routing, FX discipline and failure handling are where your own engineering decisions show up, and they are what a bank or wallet actually has to own once the scheme links go live.

title: How Zapier turns ideas into working software in hours with Vercel
description:
Zapier on Vercel

  • Interactive partner demos in under two hours with v0, replacing a process that could take weeks

  • First versions of three internal applications, each built in one day

  • A shared daily briefing for more than 60 marketers, replacing individual efforts to assemble the same information

  • 3.3 million sandboxes created in one month, isolating the code execution behind Zapier’s AI workloads

Before the industry had a word for agents, Zapier was building them. Today Zapier is the AI orchestration platform connecting AI to the workflows, data, and systems businesses use every day.

Zapier has been a Vercel customer since they began using Vercel for web experiences several years ago. They stayed, and expanded, because every team that needed to ship quickly found the same answer: speed, with the security guardrails already in place. As they grew, so did their adoption of Vercel as more teams found new uses for the platform. Today, Vercel supports work across engineering, partnerships, and marketing, from customer-facing AI to interactive partner demos and internal applications.

The needs vary by team, but the priority is getting useful work into people’s hands quickly. A backend engineer can create an interactive demo of an integration inside a partner’s product. In marketing, a former product marketer with no prior deployment experience can share tools containing sensitive information through a company-approved environment and keep improving them as colleagues use them.

Zapier’s teams are moving faster and doing more than they could before. When the next launch comes around, building on Vercel is a given.

From weeks of prototype work to a demo in under two hours

Every partnership Zapier signs extends what its customers can automate. The Powered by Zapier team is how those partnerships become product, helping SaaS and AI companies embed Zapier’s automation capabilities directly into their own tools, so users can automate without ever leaving the partner’s app. The stakes are high, because Zapier relies on this team to make its platform the entry point to all the software in the world. The problem was speed: collaborating outside the organization took forever, with every prototype requiring screenshots, design time, and frontend resources, and weeks could pass before a partner saw anything clickable.

With v0, the team can create a fully interactive, multi-view prototype in under two hours, showing an embedded Zapier experience inside the partner’s own product.

Chu’s background is in backend development, not frontend engineering or design, but v0 lets her build these experiences without coordinating a separate design and frontend effort for every partner conversation. Partners can click through the flow and share it with colleagues, using the prototype as a blueprint for implementation alongside the API documentation.

Sharing sensitive internal data securely

In marketing, Joe Stych set out to make the team’s scattered knowledge easier to use. He had spent years in product marketing before becoming a agentic go-to-market engineer, but had never worked out of a Git repository or deployed an application.

At an internal hackathon, he built Marketing Hive, a shared source for positioning, messaging, personas, and competitive intelligence. Sharing his local prototype meant making sensitive information accessible to colleagues without exposing it to everyone else.

“The Hive holds our positioning, personas, and competitive intel, so I couldn't just send people a link. On Vercel it was behind our SSO from the first deploy, so I could share it without exposing it” says Joe Stych, Senior Lead, Agentic GTM at Zapier.

Zapier’s data and security teams had already endorsed Vercel. Stych deployed through the company’s approved internal tooling environment, with access gated behind Zapier’s single sign-on.

He develops in Cursor and keeps code and source material in GitLab, where changes trigger Vercel builds and deployments. If an update needs to be undone, he can roll back the deployment.

The first versions of three of his internal applications took about a day each. In roughly two months, a hackathon project had grown into production software used across marketing. It was built by someone who had never deployed anything before.

Internal apps for marketing and sales

Marketing Hive holds the knowledge. Marketing OS puts it to work. It gives more than 60 marketers a daily briefing in Slack and a dashboard with what changed across marketing, one update from each team, a win worth celebrating, and progress against goals. Each marketer can start from the briefing instead of assembling the same information from separate channels.

“The first five minutes of your day, you need to look at the Marketing OS update,” says Dan Slagen, Zapier’s CMO.

Readers mark what they found useful, helping Stych prioritize improvements. The briefings also spark discussions in a marketing channel open to everyone at the company.

Stych is building a sales coaching application that brings together account context and industry messaging before a call. Afterward, it reviews the Gong recording to highlight what worked and suggest changes to the talk track.

For the internal applications, he checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights. Decisions about positioning remain with people, and he says additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Model access and isolated code execution

Beyond Marketing OS, a separate team at Zapier uses AI Gateway to send requests to AI models on behalf of customers using Zapier products.

A common endpoint lets an application change or add models without maintaining a separate integration for each provider. Failover gives requests another route when a provider cannot serve them, while unified reporting lets a team see their usage across providers in once place.

What's next

Zapier’s relationship with Vercel began with web experiences and expanded as the company grew, with more teams finding uses for the platform as their needs changed. Today its role spans the software Zapier runs for customers and the tools its people build for one another, and every thread is still widening.

The clearest picture of where it leads is in marketing, where other teams are starting to borrow the pattern. The goal is more versions across the company, and perhaps a Revenue OS for Zapier’s customer-facing teams next, each built the way the first one was, by someone close to the problem. First comes trust. Stych still checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights, and additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Across all of it, Vercel helps Zapier put useful work into people’s hands and keep adapting it to the needs of the business.
