title: AI Skepticism Is Not Anti-Innovation—It Is How We Keep the Hype From Causing Harm
description:
TL;DR

AI skepticism is not the reflex to declare every new model useless, fraudulent, or dangerous. It is the obligation to demand evidence that a system improves an outcome without hiding costs, shifting risk, or making people less capable. The strongest AI products are already useful; the weakest habit is treating impressive demos as proof of dependable value. Healthy skepticism gives us a better way to identify which products deserve scale—and which deserve scrutiny.

The setup

AI has moved from research labs into hiring software, customer-service portals, coding environments, classrooms, and hospitals. ChatGPT reportedly reached 100 million monthly active users within two months of its release in November 2022, and the subsequent competition among OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, and others turned model quality into a consumer product and an industrial policy.

The conventional argument is straightforward: resistance to AI is like resistance to electricity or the spreadsheet. Early systems fail, institutions adapt, and productivity eventually follows. Under this view, early adopters who learn to use the tools will gain an advantage while skeptics accumulate obsolete skills.

That argument contains a truth and a dangerous omission. AI systems can produce large gains on specific tasks. The omission is that a task improvement is not the same thing as a better organization, a more valuable worker, or a more just economy.

The International Monetary Fund estimated in 2024 that generative AI could affect about 40% of jobs globally and 60% in advanced economies. But “expose” does not mean “replace,” and even the IMF’s own analysis said the effect would vary sharply by sector and country. The distinction matters. Exposure means questions are being asked about workflow, wages, managerial control, and the distribution of gains.

The important question is not whether AI is powerful. It is whether deploying it makes people and institutions better off after accounting for errors, displaced work, degraded skills, legal exposure, and concentration of power.

That is where skepticism becomes necessary.

The argument

1. A convincing demo is not a reliable system

AI companies are exceptionally good at showing what a model can do. They are less forthcoming about how often it fails, which failures matter, and what happens when a user does not know when to distrust the output.

The distinction became legally concrete in the 2024 Moffatt v. Air Canada decision. Air Canada’s website gave a customer incorrect information about bereavement-fare rules. The airline argued that it should not be responsible because the answer came from a separate chatbot. British Columbia’s Civil Resolution Tribunal rejected that argument and held the airline liable. The decision did not establish a broad chatbot doctrine, but it exposed a basic problem: organizations cannot outsource accountability to an interface while retaining the profits generated by automation.

Companies have learned to say “human in the loop.” That phrase is useful only when the human has enough context, time, authority, and incentive to intervene. A reviewer who sees dozens of generated documents per hour is not meaningfully supervising the system. They are rubber-stamping a queue.

Healthy skepticism therefore asks for more than a feature list. What is the error rate on ordinary inputs? What happens on unfamiliar inputs? Can the system recognize its own uncertainty? Who is liable when it is wrong? Does escalation to a human work, or merely appear in a product screenshot?

A model that can answer 90% of routine questions may be valuable if the remaining 10% is rare, detectable, and inexpensive to review. It may be reckless if the 10% contains medical, legal, financial, or safety-critical errors that users cannot identify.

The demo says what the system can do. Skepticism asks what it does when nobody is watching.

2. Productivity claims are real—and routinely overstated

Skeptics often dismiss AI productivity gains because they are bad at reading experimental evidence. That is its own failure.

In a well-known 2023 study published in Science, Harvard researchers Shakked Noy and Whitney Zhang assigned 453 college-educated professionals to write tasks such as product descriptions, press releases, and short reports. Generative AI reduced completion time by about 40% and improved evaluated quality by 18%. The average writing task fell from roughly 11 minutes to 6 minutes.

That is a substantial gain. Pretending otherwise is not skepticism; it is ideological denial.

But the result also demonstrates why “AI will raise productivity” is an incomplete claim. The experiment covered a bounded category of writing performed by experienced professionals. It did not measure a company’s total output, long-term skill development, coordination costs, customer satisfaction, or the time required to detect confidently wrong answers. It did not tell us whether a faster draft was easier to revise, whether workers became better at the underlying skill, or whether managers captured the savings through increased targets rather than higher wages.

A separate study of 5,179 customer-support agents found that AI assistance raised average productivity by about 14%, with gains of roughly 34% among the least-experienced workers. Again, the result is useful. Again, it does not prove that every support organization should replace people. Faster ticket resolution can mean better service—or fewer difficult cases receiving the attention they require.

Klarna’s announcement that its AI assistant could perform the work of 700 full-time customer-service agents became a symbol of AI-driven labor reduction in 2024. The company later moved to hire human agents amid complaints about service quality. The most defensible conclusion is not that Klarna’s automation failed. It is that a headcount-equivalence claim is not the same as evidence of customer satisfaction, lower costs, or equal service.

Healthy skepticism preserves the measured task-level gains while refusing to inflate them into claims about whole occupations.

3. The labor question is about power as much as unemployment

The public argument is usually framed as “AI replaces jobs.” The more plausible near-term mechanism is subtler: AI changes the tasks inside jobs, reduces the number of workers needed for existing output, and shifts bargaining power toward the organizations that own the models.

Anthropic’s Economic Index, released in 2025 after analyzing millions of Claude conversations, found that AI use was divided roughly 57% toward augmentation and 43% toward automation. It also found that about 36% of occupations used AI for at least a quarter of their tasks, while only 4% used it for at least three-quarters. That is evidence of broad penetration without mass displacement.

The index has limitations. Conversations with Claude are not a representative sample of every workplace, and usage is not the same as causal impact. But it offers a more useful picture than anecdotes. AI is entering many jobs without immediately eliminating them.

That can still be bad for workers. Consider customer support, legal research, software development, or graphic design. If AI compresses the output expected from each junior employee, companies may use fewer junior workers while continuing to demand senior-level output. The first people harmed are not necessarily the most productive; they are the workers who historically learned by doing repetitive work under supervision.

There is another cost: loss of institutional memory. An organization that lets a model produce answers without maintaining human expertise can become unable to audit the system. The worker still exists, but only as a reviewer of output generated from data the organization no longer fully understands.

This is why “AI as augmentation” is not automatically a labor-friendly answer. Who receives the extra output? Who learns the necessary skills? Does the employee get time to question the tool, or is the tool always right because refusal is treated as poor performance?

4. Skepticism matters most where truth has become a product

Education provides a clear example of what happens when society adopts AI faster than its ability to evaluate it. Universities moved from debating whether to allow ChatGPT to building detection systems, honor codes, and assessment redesigns.

The detection systems were not reliable. In a Stanford study of 61 TOEFL essays written by non-native English speakers, every essay was labeled as AI-generated by at least one of seven tested detectors. Such a high false-positive rate makes “AI detection” inappropriate for consequential punishment.

This does not mean students should be allowed to submit generated work as their own. It means institutions need assessment methods based on process, oral defense, in-class work, and transparent standards—not a statistical guess about stylistic patterns.

The same pattern appears in search, customer support, and professional advice: AI can create a plausible answer before anyone checks whether it exists. A fabricated case can be syntactically perfect. A plausible citation can point to a nonexistent paper. A confident summary can erase the exception that determines the legal or medical outcome.

Skepticism is therefore not merely an economic position. It is a defense of the human ability to distinguish reliable knowledge from fluent text.

What the conventional view gets wrong

The conventional view says skepticism has already been incorporated into “responsible AI” reviews, model cards, safety teams, and staged rollouts. Sometimes it has. More often, those practices become institutional decoration.

A model card describing training data does not establish whether the product is accurate in a particular workflow. A pilot with 50 users does not reveal behavior at 50,000. A disclaimer saying “AI can make mistakes” does not prevent a customer from acting on a confident mistake. Governance fails when organizations substitute documentation for measurement.

The opposite convention is also wrong: the assumption that falling model prices will automatically deliver shared prosperity. The Stanford AI Index reported that the inference cost for performance equivalent to GPT-3.5 fell more than 280-fold between November 2022 and October 2024. Lower costs expand access and make bad deployments affordable too. Cheap errors at scale remain errors.

There is a legitimate counterargument to skeptical positions: skepticism can delay beneficial tools and protect inefficient incumbents. AI-assisted coding, accessibility tools, scientific search, and protein analysis already create value. DeepMind’s AlphaFold database contains more than 200 million predicted protein structures and has been used by millions of researchers. A philosophy that treats every AI claim as suspect would miss these advances.

But “some applications work” does not justify “all deployments deserve trust.” The answer to real benefits is better evaluation, not surrender.

The implications

For builders

Builders should stop using benchmark scores as the main evidence of product value and start publishing task-specific evidence: accuracy, severe-error frequency, human-review time, user correction rates, and performance under real distribution shifts.

They should also make escalation operational. If a model is uncertain, the interface should identify the uncertainty, preserve the source material, and route the case to someone with authority. Logging, rollback, and incident review should be default capabilities rather than premium trust features.

The defensible moat will not simply be access to a model. It will be trustworthy integration into a valuable workflow.

For users

Users should treat AI as a fast junior colleague, not an oracle. That means using it to outline alternatives, generate drafts, and expose missing questions—but verifying consequential claims against primary sources.

We should also protect skills that make verification possible. A person who can no longer write, calculate, program, or evaluate an argument may use AI efficiently for a few months while becoming dependent on it for years.

For regulators

Regulation should focus on outcomes and evidence rather than declaring all AI good or bad. Consumer protection, employment, education, and healthcare need rules suited to their risks: incident reporting, documentation, audit access, and transparency about consequential automated decisions.

The EU AI Act is a useful test because it introduces risk tiers and enforcement dates rather than a blanket prohibition. Its general-purpose AI obligations began applying in 2025, with broader transparency requirements scheduled for August 2026. The real test is whether those rules produce measurable reductions in harm rather than expensive compliance documents for systems that never mattered.

For the industry

AI companies cannot rely on market enthusiasm indefinitely. Enterprise buyers will eventually ask whether lower labor costs or faster output compensate for review expense, liability, customer churn, and regulatory risk. The strongest vendors will be the ones capable of saying, with evidence, where the system should not be used.

What I'm watching next

First, I’m watching whether independent evaluations become tied to actual work rather than public leaderboards. Leaderboard saturation, benchmark contamination, and cherry-picked prompts make scores increasingly poor procurement tools. A bank, hospital, or software team needs an evaluation on its own tasks, including the ugly edge cases.

Second, I’m watching labor data for changes in task mix and entry-level hiring. Aggregate employment can remain stable while junior roles, apprenticeship paths, and wage ladders deteriorate. The signal will come from occupation-level hiring, hours, pay, and the share of work delegated to AI—not from how many companies announce an “AI strategy.”

Third, I’m watching the economics of agents. As models become cheaper and more capable, they will attempt actions rather than merely return text. The next major incidents may involve software agents making reversible mistakes, or irreversible ones. Systems that can send email, move money, modify code, or update medical records raise the standard from “does the answer sound right?” to “what damage can one wrong action cause?”

The bottom line

AI skepticism is not a prediction that the technology will fail. It is a refusal to confuse capability with value. Some systems already save time and improve real work. Others create legal exposure, weaken expertise, and conceal their true operating costs behind “augmentation.” The answer is not unconditional adoption or reflexive rejection. It is evidence: measured error rates, meaningful human oversight, transparent costs, and consequences for the people whose labor is being reorganized. We should be enthusiastic about useful tools and ruthless about unsupported claims. That is not anti-innovation. It is how innovation becomes something more than a fundraising story.

title: How to Create a Next.js App: Your First Project, Step by Step
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

To create a Next.js app, install Node.js, run one command, npx create-next-app@latest, answer a few simple setup questions, then run npm run dev and open localhost:3000 in your browser. That is the whole process. In the next ten minutes you will have a real project running on your own computer, ready to edit.

What You Need Before You Start

You do not need much, and you do not need to be an expert. You need three things: Node.js, a code editor, and some basic React knowledge.

First, install Node.js LTS, the stable long term support version, from the official Node.js website. Next.js needs a recent version, so update old installs now. Then check it in your terminal:

node -v
npm -v

If both print a version number, you are ready. If you see command not found, reopen the terminal or reinstall Node.

Second, install a code editor. Visual Studio Code is free and works well, but any editor is fine.

Third, you need basic React: components, JSX, and props at a simple level. If that feels new, work through this beginner React roadmap for learning React step by step first. An hour there makes this guide much easier.

The One Command That Creates Everything

Open your terminal, move to the folder where you keep your projects, and run this command:

npx create-next-app@latest my-first-app

In short: npx runs a tool without installing it permanently, create-next-app is the official starter, latest means use the newest version, and my-first-app is your folder name. Use lowercase letters and hyphens, not spaces.

The tool downloads what it needs, then asks a short list of questions. When it finishes, you will see a success message.

The full official instructions live in the Next.js installation guide on nextjs.org, which is worth bookmarking because it is updated whenever the setup process changes.

What Each Setup Question Really Means

Beginners often just press Enter repeatedly. The defaults are sensible, but it is better to know what you are agreeing to.

Setup question What it means Recommended for beginners
Would you like to use TypeScript? TypeScript adds type checks to JavaScript and helps catch mistakes early. Yes, if you know a little TypeScript. No is also fine while learning.
Which linter would you like to use? A linter checks your code style and spots common errors as you type. Choose the default option.
Would you like to use Tailwind CSS? Tailwind lets you style pages with small utility classes inside your markup. Yes. It pairs very well with Next.js and is easy to learn gradually.
Would you like your code inside a src/ directory? This puts your app code in a src folder to keep the project tidy. Either works. No keeps the structure simpler for a first project.
Would you like to use App Router? The App Router is the modern way to build Next.js apps, using the app folder. Yes. Always choose this for new projects.
Would you like to customise the import alias? An alias like @/ lets you write short import paths instead of long relative ones. Keep the default.

My advice: choose TypeScript only if you are comfortable with it, say yes to Tailwind and the App Router, and keep the defaults elsewhere. Every option can be added later.

The official Next.js documentation introduction (nextjs.org) — what Next.js is and how the docs are organised.

Run Your App and See It Live

Now move into your new folder and start the development server:

cd my-first-app
npm run dev

The terminal will print a local address, usually http://localhost:3000. Open that address in your browser. You should see the default Next.js starter page. Congratulations, your app is running.

While the dev server runs, every save updates the browser almost instantly. Leave the terminal open while you work, and press Control plus C to stop it. If port 3000 is busy, Next.js will use 3001 instead.

A Quick Tour of Your Project Folders

Open the project in your editor. You only need a few files on day one.

The app folder is where your pages live. This is where you will spend most of your time. Inside it, page.tsx is your home page, layout.tsx wraps every page with shared parts like a header, and globals.css holds your global styles.

The public folder holds static files like images. For example, public/logo.png appears at localhost:3000/logo.png.

The file package.json lists your dependencies and scripts, such as dev, build, and start. You will rarely edit it by hand at first.

Ignore the rest for now; files like next.config are already configured. If you are unsure what Next.js adds on top of React, this explanation of what React is and why it is used for building interfaces will fill in the background nicely.

Edit Your Home Page

Let us make the starter page yours. Open app/page.tsx, or app/page.js if you chose JavaScript, delete the starter content, and try something small like this:

export default function Home() {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Hello, this is my first Next.js app</h1>
      <p>I built this in about ten minutes.</p>
    </main>
  );
}

Save the file and check your browser. The page has already changed. A page is just a React component that returns markup, exported as the default export.

Try small changes next: another paragraph, a new heading, a list. Breaking things now is fine, it is how you learn.

Add a Second Page

A real website needs more than one page, and in Next.js adding a page is simply adding a folder. Inside the app folder, create a new folder called about, and inside it create a file called page.tsx:

export default function AboutPage() {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>About me</h1>
      <p>This is my second page. No router setup needed.</p>
    </main>
  );
}

Now visit localhost:3000/about. Your new page is live, with no configuration. The folder name becomes the URL. To understand this system properly, read how routing works in Next.js with folders and files when you are ready for links, layouts, and dynamic pages.

To link between pages, use the Link component from next/link. It preloads linked pages, so changes feel instant.

Your Next Steps After Day One

Keep your next steps small. Add a contact page and a projects page, build a shared header in your layout file, and add images from public with a little Tailwind styling.

When you feel comfortable, explore the official Next.js documentation a section at a time. Do not try to learn everything in one weekend. Build one tiny thing, finish it, then build the next.

One last tip: commit to Git early, even if it is messy. It gives you a safety net to return to a version that worked.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Next.js free to use?

Yes. Next.js is free and open source. Creating and running an app on your own computer costs nothing. You only pay if you later choose paid hosting or paid services.

Do I need to know React before Next.js?

You need the basics: components, JSX, and props. You do not need to be advanced. If you can build a small React page, you can start Next.js and learn the rest as you go.

Should I choose TypeScript or JavaScript?

Either is fine for a first project. JavaScript feels simpler at the start. TypeScript helps catch errors as projects grow, and most professional teams use it, so it is worth learning later.

What is the difference between npm run dev and npm run build?

The dev command runs your app for development, with instant updates when you save. The build command creates an optimised production version, ready to put online for real visitors.

Conclusion

Creating a Next.js app is really just three moves: install Node.js, run create-next-app, and start the dev server. Everything else, the folders, the pages, the styling, you can learn piece by piece inside a project that already works. Start today, keep the project small, and change one thing at a time. Your first app does not need to impress anyone. It just needs to exist.

title: How Mercor ships internal apps and billions of production tokens on one platform
description:
Mercor on Vercel

  • Batch jobs cut from 12 hours to 2 hours

  • 18M requests and 63B tokens routed through AI Gateway in 10 days

  • Expert access provisioned in seconds via Vercel Passport

  • Over 2,000 projects created by hundreds of internal builders

Mercor connects hundreds of thousands of domain experts with frontier AI labs, helping those labs generate the human data they need to train and evaluate leading models. It also runs large batches of automated grading jobs to evaluate models for labs and enterprises.

Demand arrives in bursts that can push model traffic to peak capacity for days, even as individual evaluation or labeling jobs carry 24-hour deadlines. With so little time to deliver, requests waiting on a provider’s rate limits can put a client’s deadline at risk.

Mercor’s business teams also need applications tailored to each engagement, giving experts a way to see their tasks and progress without waiting for changes to the core platform.

For Aaron Brown, Mercor’s Head of Security, enabling more people to build means making it easier to give them the access they need and keep track of how they use it. Mercor uses Vercel AI Gateway to manage model access and Vercel Passport to handle secure access to their applications.

When model capacity becomes a customer deadline

Mercor’s mix of direct integrations and third-party gateways could not provide enough token-per-minute capacity for its open-model workloads when demand surged. As requests hit provider limits and entered retry queues, time-sensitive batch jobs stretched beyond 12 hours, consuming more than half of a client’s 24-hour deadline.

AI Gateway provided more inference capacity and failover routing between providers when requests hit rate limits, helping batch work continue instead of waiting in retry queues. Mercor reports that those jobs now finish in 2 to 3 hours, leaving more time to complete the rest of the client’s work. In its first 10 days on Gateway, the team routed 18 million requests and 63 billion tokens, without hitting rate limits.

Mercor continues to use multiple gateways and vendors, valuing Vercel for its combination of model access, controls, and hands-on support when the team needs more capacity. Engineers also get one API for leading foundation model providers and a growing catalog of open models, so they can try a new model without building another provider integration.

Giving engineers room to experiment within limits

As model use grew, Mercor needed to understand where token spend was going, but its previous setup offered little visibility into usage by team and project. A single loop error in a script could exhaust the available budget.

Hundreds of Mercor engineers now use open models through AI Gateway with per-user keys that carry expiration dates, token limits, and spend limits. Security can give experimentation a budget and an end date, then use the usage records to see which user, project, and workload is driving consumption. Engineers can try different models through the same gateway under those controls, without managing another set of provider credentials each time.

Managing access as business teams build

A few hundred people across Mercor’s business teams now build applications on Vercel, where the company’s project count has grown from fewer than a dozen to roughly 2,000. Many of those projects are temporary environments for a specific client engagement.

One production use case gives experts detailed views of their project tasks and progress. Rather than ask engineering to add every engagement’s interface to the core platform, business teams build the interfaces themselves and share them with the experts doing the work.

To share those applications, teams need to control who can sign in without taking on a separate authentication setup for every project. Passport provides that common authentication layer, handling sign-in to Vercel deployments through an existing identity provider.

Mercor’s identity team built a product called Audiences, integrating Vercel Passport as a first class primitive, to automate access provisioning. Once a team selects the experts who need access, Audiences creates the IdP group, Vercel connection, and Passport configuration. With that workflow, Mercor reports provisioning access in seconds for audiences ranging from dozens of experts to tens of thousands. Offboarding works the same way in reverse. Because access is derived from the IdP group, removing the group at the end of an engagement removes access to the project, so no stale access is left behind.

Limiting what each agent can do

Alongside those applications, Mercor uses agents to answer questions from experts in its marketplace, automate HR workflows, and help employees navigate internal systems. Mercor’s approach is to give each agent narrow permissions suited to its job, rather than everything available to the person who invoked it.

For agents that use open models through AI Gateway, Mercor can also scope model access, set expiration dates, and cap spending. That governs their model use while Mercor separately determines which systems and actions each agent can access.

What’s next

Mercor expects more open models to power its internal agents and systems, and more teams outside engineering to build tools for experts. As that work grows, the company wants teams to spend less time setting up model integrations and application authentication so they can respond to client workloads with tight deadlines.

The aim is to make the secure path the fastest path, with shared model access and repeatable authentication workflows helping experts get the tools they need and labs get their work back on time. Mercor wants to support that growth without security work increasing at the same rate.

About Mercor: Mercor is an AI data company that organizes human intelligence for AI training and evaluation. Its network of more than 5M experts, from doctors to lawyers to engineers, powers benchmarks, enterprise evals, RL environments, post-training and agent deployments.

title: Get a second-opinion code review from Claude Code over MCP
description:
Your coding agent is good at reviewing code. It is less good at reviewing its own code: it reads the change with the same prompt, the same context and the same assumptions that produced it. For risky changes (authentication, payments, data deletion) a reviewer from outside that loop is worth having.

This post shows how to ask an independent AI agent for a review from inside Claude Code, using the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The steps below use Claude Code and a public pull request.

1. Add a remote MCP server

This walkthrough uses the read-only planning operation on the Speedbot.dev MCP server as its example. The same brief structure works with other review tools.

claude mcp add --transport http --scope user speedbot-hire "https://speedbot.dev/mcp/core"

Run /mcp in Claude Code to confirm the connection. No account is needed to request a plan.

2. Request a read-only plan

Ask Claude Code something like:

Use speedbot_hire with operation plan: one independent code review of the changes in PR #42 of my public repository. Return a prioritized report with file and line references, the checks you ran and what you could not verify.

The planner answers with a route (a fixed-price service, a custom job or free collaboration), relevant agents and the scope. Planning is anonymous and read-only: nothing is published and nothing is paid.

3. Write a brief a reviewer can finish

A good brief has four parts:

  • Where: the public repository and the exact pull request or commit.
  • What should happen: the expected behavior and the test command.
  • What counts as done: for example "every finding has a file and line reference" or "the new test fails before the patch and passes after it".
  • What not to send: secrets, private data or code you may not share.

4. Check before you accept

Run the test command from the report. Confirm high-impact findings at the referenced lines. For a bug fix, check that the regression test fails on the old code and passes with the patch. A finding without a reproducible check is a hypothesis, not a defect.

Compare the results

Run the same brief against the original review and the second review. Compare their findings against the same commit and test results. Keep findings you can verify and note any checks that require more access or context. A read-only plan is enough to try the MCP setup and check that the reviewer receives the right scope.

Disclosure: Speedbot.dev maintains the example MCP server. AI was used to draft this article.

title: Wrapping strings in t() was the easy part of translating my React app
description:
I tried getting an AI agent to internationalize a side project and spent longer checking its diff than it would have taken me to do it myself. It did the work. It also picked the languages, decided where the language files went, and chose Simplified Chinese without asking. None of that was wrong exactly, but I had to read every changed file to find out.

So I started doing it properly, and then I built a tool for it. This post is mostly the first part: the things that make i18n harder than "wrap every string in t()". The tool comes at the end.

The boring part

For a React app that wasn't built with translation in mind, the work looks like this, for every piece of text:

  1. Find the string in the JSX
  2. Make up a key for it
  3. Replace it with t('the_key')
  4. Add the key and the English text to en.json
  5. Get it translated into every other language file

Steps 1 to 4 are tedious but easy. Step 5 is where things break, and mostly not in ways you'd notice by looking at the translated text.

Plurals aren't "one or many"

English has two forms: 1 item, 2 items. So you write two keys and move on. Plenty of languages need more, and Russian shows the problem best: it has four. The form depends on the last digits of the number, so 1, 21 and 101 all use one form, 2 to 4 another, 5 to 20 a third. i18next handles this with suffixed keys, and the Russian file needs all of them:

{
  "items_one": "{{count}} товар",
  "items_few": "{{count}} товара",
  "items_many": "{{count}} товаров",
  "items_other": "{{count}} товара"
}

Arabic has six (_zero, _one, _two, _few, _many, _other). Chinese and Japanese have one.

If your Russian file only has items_one and items_other because that's what English had, nothing errors. For 5 items i18next looks for items_many, doesn't find it, and falls back: depending on your settings, Russian users get the English sentence or a missing-key string in the middle of the page.

Placeholders get translated too

"Hi {{name}}, you have {{count}} messages" contains two things that must come out exactly as they went in. Machine translation, and AI models especially, will sometimes translate the placeholder name along with the sentence: {{name}} becomes {{nombre}}. The JSON is still valid, and the app now shows an empty gap where the name should be.

The fix isn't a better prompt. It's checking every translation against the source: same placeholders, same count, and rejecting it if they differ.

Markup in the middle of a sentence 

<p>By signing up you agree to our <a href="/terms">Terms</a>.</p>

You can't translate "By signing up you agree to our" and "Terms" separately, because other languages put the link somewhere else in the sentence. In react-i18next this becomes <Trans>, and the translation file keeps the tag as a number:

"agree_terms": "By signing up you agree to our <1>Terms</1>."

Translators (human or not) can move <1>…</1> wherever the grammar needs it, as long as they don't drop or rename it. Another thing worth checking automatically.

Not every string is text

A lot of strings in a React codebase look like text and aren't: className="flex items-center", URLs, console.log messages, and product names like "GitHub" or "Markdown" that should stay as they are. Translate those and you get broken styling, or a German UI that talks about "Abschlag".

Choices nobody tells you you're making

  • zh isn't one language for this purpose. Simplified (mainland China, Singapore) and Traditional (Taiwan, Hong Kong) are written differently, and people notice.
  • Where the language files live (src/locales, public/locales) depends on how you load them.
  • If you use Next.js with the App Router, useTranslation() doesn't work in server components at all.

An agent will make these choices for you, quietly. They're all fine to make. I'd just rather make them myself.

What I ended up building

guided-i18n is a VS Code extension that does those five steps with a review in the middle:

  • A parser finds the strings locally and skips the ones that aren't text.
  • You get a checklist of every string and the key it'll get, before anything changes. Untick what should stay hardcoded.
  • It rewrites the code to t() or <Trans>, writes the JSON files, and translates them with your own API key (Anthropic, or anything OpenAI-compatible).
  • Every translation is checked for placeholders, tags and plural forms. A failure gets one retry, then it's reported instead of written.
  • Undo reverts the whole run, code and language files together.

Only the strings and a little context (file path, component name) go to the model, never whole files. A single file usually costs cents. The biggest project I tried it on was about 840 files and cost a few dollars.

Honest limits: React with react-i18next and JSON files only, for now. If you already use an AI agent and don't mind reviewing its diff, it will cover more odd cases than this does. This is for when you'd rather see every change before it happens.

It's free (you pay your AI provider directly), and it's on the VS Code Marketplace and on Open VSX for Cursor and Windsurf.

If you try it on your codebase, I'd like to hear where it gets things wrong: GitHub issues or the comments here.

title: Byg et før-og-efter billedværktøj med HTML, CSS og JavaScript
description:
Et billede fortæller ikke altid hele historien.

Men to billeder kan gøre en forskel.

Forestil dig en have, hvor et stort træ er blevet fældet. Ejeren vil gerne sammenligne området før og efter arbejdet.

Hvor meget lys er der kommet ind?

Hvordan ser haven ud uden den store krone?

Og hvilke dele af området er blevet ændret?

Det er et godt eksempel på en lille webfunktion, som kan være nyttig i mange forskellige projekter.

I denne guide bygger vi et før-og-efter-værktøj med HTML, CSS og JavaScript.

Brugeren vælger to billeder fra sin egen computer. Billederne bliver vist ved siden af hinanden i browseren.

Vi bruger ingen eksterne biblioteker og ingen backend.

Det betyder, at vores demo ikke uploader billederne til en server.

Hvad skal værktøjet kunne?

Vi holder kravene enkle.

Brugeren skal kunne:

  • Vælge et førbillede.
  • Vælge et efterbillede.
  • Se begge billeder på samme side.
  • Bruge værktøjet på mobil.
  • Fjerne billederne igen.

Derudover skal formularen være tilgængelig med tastatur.

Vi skal heller ikke gemme billederne permanent.

Det er et bevidst valg, fordi mange billeder fra private haver kan vise boliger, biler eller andre personlige oplysninger.

1. Opret projektets filer

Vi bruger tre filer:

index.html
style.css
script.js

Du behøver ikke et framework.

Åbn blot filerne i din foretrukne kodeeditor.

2. Byg HTML-strukturen

Vi begynder med en overskrift, to filfelter og to områder til billedvisning.

Gem dette som index.html.

<!doctype html>
<html lang="da">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport"
        content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

  <title>Før og efter - Billedsammenligning</title>

  <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
  <script src="script.js" defer></script>
</head>

<body>
  <main class="container">
    <header>
      <h1>Før og efter</h1>

      <p>
        Sammenlign to billeder direkte i browseren.
        Billederne sendes ikke til en server.
      </p>
    </header>

    <section aria-labelledby="uploadTitle">
      <h2 id="uploadTitle">Vælg billeder</h2>

      <div class="upload-grid">
        <div class="field">
          <label for="beforeInput">
            Billede før arbejdet
          </label>

          <input
            type="file"
            id="beforeInput"
            accept="image/*">
        </div>

        <div class="field">
          <label for="afterInput">
            Billede efter arbejdet
          </label>

          <input
            type="file"
            id="afterInput"
            accept="image/*">
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section aria-labelledby="resultTitle">
      <h2 id="resultTitle">Sammenligning</h2>

      <div class="comparison-grid">
        <figure>
          <img
            id="beforeImage"
            alt="Førbillede"
            hidden>

          <figcaption>Før</figcaption>
        </figure>

        <figure>
          <img
            id="afterImage"
            alt="Efterbillede"
            hidden>

          <figcaption>Efter</figcaption>
        </figure>
      </div>
    </section>

    <button type="button" id="resetButton">
      Fjern billeder
    </button>

    <p id="status"
       role="status"
       aria-live="polite"></p>
  </main>
</body>
</html>

Bemærk brugen af label og figure.

Hvert filfelt har en synlig label. Det gør det lettere at forstå, hvilket billede der skal vælges.

figure og figcaption giver en tydelig forbindelse mellem billedet og beskrivelsen.

Vi bruger også hidden, så tomme billedelementer ikke bliver vist, før brugeren vælger filer.

3. Lav et responsivt layout

Nu skal billederne placeres ved siden af hinanden på store skærme.

På mobil skal de stå under hinanden.

Gem følgende som style.css.

* {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

body {
  margin: 0;
  padding: 24px 16px;
  background: #f4f7f4;
  color: #26352b;
  font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
  line-height: 1.6;
}

.container {
  max-width: 1000px;
  margin: 0 auto;
  padding: 28px;
  background: #ffffff;
  border-radius: 16px;
}

h1,
h2 {
  line-height: 1.3;
}

h1 {
  color: #15573b;
}

.upload-grid,
.comparison-grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr));
  gap: 20px;
}

.field {
  margin: 12px 0 24px;
}

label {
  display: block;
  margin-bottom: 8px;
  font-weight: 700;
}

input[type="file"] {
  display: block;
  width: 100%;
  max-width: 100%;
  font: inherit;
}

figure {
  margin: 0;
  min-width: 0;
  padding: 12px;
  background: #eaf1eb;
  border-radius: 12px;
}

figure img:not([hidden]) {
  display: block;
  width: 100%;
  height: auto;
  max-height: 380px;
  object-fit: contain;
}

figcaption {
  padding-top: 12px;
  font-weight: 700;
  text-align: center;
}

button {
  margin-top: 24px;
  padding: 12px 20px;
  border: 0;
  border-radius: 8px;
  background: #15573b;
  color: #ffffff;
  font: inherit;
  font-weight: 700;
  cursor: pointer;
}

button:hover {
  background: #10442e;
}

button:focus-visible,
input:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #a35b13;
  outline-offset: 4px;
}

#status {
  min-height: 24px;
  margin-top: 18px;
}

@media (max-width: 650px) {
  .container {
    padding: 18px;
  }

  .upload-grid,
  .comparison-grid {
    grid-template-columns: 1fr;
  }
}

Her bruger vi CSS Grid.

To kolonner giver en enkel sammenligning på større skærme.

På mobil ændrer media query layoutet til én kolonne.

Vi bruger også object-fit: contain.

Det sikrer, at hele billedet kan ses, uden at vi automatisk beskærer det.

4. Vis billederne med JavaScript

Når en bruger vælger en fil, skal vi vise den i det rigtige billedelement.

Det kan vi gøre med URL.createObjectURL().

Metoden opretter en midlertidig objekt-URL, som browseren kan bruge til at vise den valgte fil.

Vi skal huske at frigive disse URL'er, når de ikke længere er nødvendige.

Gem følgende som script.js.

const beforeInput =
  document.querySelector("#beforeInput");

const afterInput =
  document.querySelector("#afterInput");

const beforeImage =
  document.querySelector("#beforeImage");

const afterImage =
  document.querySelector("#afterImage");

const resetButton =
  document.querySelector("#resetButton");

const status =
  document.querySelector("#status");

const imageUrls = {
  before: null,
  after: null
};

function removeImage(type) {
  const image = type === "before"
    ? beforeImage
    : afterImage;

  if (imageUrls[type]) {
    URL.revokeObjectURL(imageUrls[type]);
    imageUrls[type] = null;
  }

  image.removeAttribute("src");
  image.hidden = true;
}

function loadImage(file, type) {
  const image = type === "before"
    ? beforeImage
    : afterImage;

  removeImage(type);

  if (!file) {
    return;
  }

  if (!file.type.startsWith("image/")) {
    status.textContent =
      "Vælg venligst en billedfil.";
    return;
  }

  const url = URL.createObjectURL(file);

  imageUrls[type] = url;

  image.onload = () => {
    if (imageUrls[type] !== url) {
      return;
    }

    image.hidden = false;

    status.textContent =
      "Billedet er klar til visning.";
  };

  image.onerror = () => {
    if (imageUrls[type] !== url) {
      return;
    }

    removeImage(type);

    status.textContent =
      "Billedet kunne ikke åbnes.";
  };

  image.alt = type === "before"
    ? "Valgt billede før arbejdet"
    : "Valgt billede efter arbejdet";

  image.src = url;
}

beforeInput.addEventListener("change", () => {
  loadImage(beforeInput.files[0], "before");
});

afterInput.addEventListener("change", () => {
  loadImage(afterInput.files[0], "after");
});

resetButton.addEventListener("click", () => {
  beforeInput.value = "";
  afterInput.value = "";

  removeImage("before");
  removeImage("after");

  status.textContent =
    "Begge billeder er fjernet fra visningen.";
});

window.addEventListener("pagehide", () => {
  removeImage("before");
  removeImage("after");
});

Nu har vi en simpel billedvisning, som fungerer uden et eksternt bibliotek.

JavaScript kontrollerer først, om den valgte fil er en billedtype.

Derefter oprettes en midlertidig URL.

Når brugeren vælger et nyt billede eller trykker på nulstil, frigives den tidligere URL.

Det er især nyttigt, hvis brugeren prøver flere store billeder i samme session.

5. Hvorfor er løsningen mere privatlivsvenlig?

I vores eksempel bliver filerne håndteret direkte i browseren.

Der er ingen kode, som sender billederne til en server.

Vi bruger heller ikke lokal lagring eller en database.

Når siden lukkes, findes der derfor ingen gemt kopi i vores applikation.

Men det betyder ikke, at alle mulige privatlivsrisici automatisk er væk.

Hvis du senere tilføjer analyseværktøjer, tredjepartsscripts eller en backend, kan situationen ændre sig.

Derfor bør privatliv tænkes ind fra begyndelsen.

I en færdig applikation kan det også være nyttigt at informere brugeren om, hvordan billeder og metadata håndteres.

6. Test med forskellige billeder

Et værktøj kan se fint ud med ét testbillede og stadig fejle med andre billeder.

Prøv derfor flere scenarier.

Et stort landskabsbillede

Kontrollér, at billedet bliver skaleret korrekt.

Et billede i højformat

Undersøg, om det stadig kan ses uden at blive beskåret.

Kun ét billede

Brugeren skal kunne se et førbillede uden at vælge et efterbillede.

En fil, som ikke er et gyldigt billede

Værktøjet skal vise en forståelig besked.

Et nyt billede i samme felt

Kontrollér, at det gamle billede bliver erstattet.

Nulstil-knappen

Begge billeder skal forsvinde, og felterne skal blive tømt.

Det kan også være nyttigt at teste med tastatur alene.

Brugeren skal kunne vælge billeder og bruge knappen uden en mus.

7. Hvad mangler før produktion?

Dette er en læringsdemo.

Den viser billeder lokalt, men er ikke et færdigt dokumentationssystem.

Hvis du vil udvikle den videre, kan du overveje:

  • Begrænsning af filstørrelser.
  • Bedre fejlbeskeder.
  • Tastatur- og skærmlæsertest.
  • Mulighed for selv at skrive billedbeskrivelser.
  • Billedbehandling med passende hukommelsesstyring.
  • Klar information om eventuel databehandling.

Hvis løsningen skal understøtte professionelle arbejdsrapporter, skal der også være en plan for dokumentation, adgangskontrol og korrekt opbevaring.

En demo med to billeder kan være nyttig, men den bør ikke præsenteres som dokumentation for, at en opgave er udført sikkert eller korrekt.

Hvorfor bruge træfældning som eksempel?

Når et stort træ fjernes, kan området ændre sig tydeligt.

Der kan komme mere dagslys ind i haven. Udsigten kan ændre sig, og der kan blive plads til nye planter eller andre formål.

Derfor kan før- og efterbilleder være interessante for både haveejere og fagfolk.

Men billeder fortæller ikke alt.

De viser ikke nødvendigvis, hvordan træets tilstand var før arbejdet, eller hvilke sikkerhedsmæssige vurderinger der blev foretaget.

Fotografier bør derfor betragtes som visuel dokumentation, ikke som en selvstændig faglig vurdering.

Dansk Træpleje har base i Vejle og arbejder med blandt andet beskæring, træpleje og professionel træfældning.

Hvis du vil læse om den virkelige faglige kontekst, kan du se, hvordan virksomheden arbejder med at fælde træer i Vejle.

Værktøjet i denne guide er et selvstændigt kodeeksempel. Det er ikke en beskrivelse af en eksisterende funktion på virksomhedens hjemmeside.

Hvad har vi lært?

Vi har bygget et lille billedværktøj med tre almindelige webteknologier.

HTML giver strukturen.

CSS skaber et responsivt layout.

JavaScript læser de valgte filer og viser dem midlertidigt i browseren.

Vi har også brugt URL.revokeObjectURL() til at rydde op efter de midlertidige objekt-URL'er.

Det vigtigste er, at løsningen ikke kræver en stor teknisk platform for at være nyttig.

Nogle gange er en lille, tydelig funktion nok.

Og hvis brugeren forstår, hvad der sker med billederne, er vi allerede kommet et godt stykke med både brugeroplevelse og privatliv.

description:
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Announcement

The following AlloyDB AI functions and improvements are available in Preview:

  • The ai.extract function lets you extract structured data from unstructured text directly within your database queries without needing external extraction pipelines. For more information, see Extract structured data.

  • The ai.classify function lets you categorize unstructured text into predefined labels directly within your database queries. For more information, see Classify text.

  • Parameter names and signatures for AI query engine functions (ai.analyze_sentiment, ai.summarize, and ai.agg_summarize) are updated. For more information, see Model endpoint reference.

    • The prompt and prompts parameters are renamed to input and inputs in scalar and batch functions respectively.

    • An optional additional_instructions parameter is added to ai.summarize and ai.agg_summarize to provide custom instructions to guide summary formatting, length, and tone.

    • In cursor-based versions of ai.analyze_sentiment and ai.summarize, the prompt parameter is removed.

    • ai.agg_summarize supports multiple positional signatures, including passing optional additional instructions and specifying model IDs.

Apigee X

Feature

The Apigee API Health & Availability dashboard is now generally available in Cloud Monitoring to help you monitor the health, performance, and availability of your Apigee API proxies in real time:

  • Golden signal scorecards: track aggregate Traffic (requests per second), Error Rate (5xx), and Latency (p95) scorecards.
  • Status code and error trends: visualize the Request Rate by Status Code chart over time and identify problematic APIs using the dedicated 5xx Error Rate by Proxy and 4xx Error Rate by Proxy charts.
  • Granular filtering: filter telemetry by project_id, location, and proxy_name to troubleshoot specific regions or proxies.

For more information, see API Monitoring.

BigQuery

Feature

The Data Engineering Agent now integrates with Google Drive, letting you provide Google Sheets files, CSV, or JSONL files as input for your data engineering pipelines.

This feature is generally available (GA).

Feature

You can now use conversational analytics in Connected Sheets to ask questions and analyze your BigQuery data using natural language. The Gemini side panel can help you translate your questions into optimized SQL queries and execute them, summarize key trends, and insert live, refreshable database objects directly into your workbook.

This feature is generally available (GA).

Feature

The AI.COUNT_TOKENS function, which estimates the token count of a text string, is generally available (GA).

Bigtable

Feature

You can use Apache Avro schema bundles to query individual fields within Avro records stored as serialized bytes in Bigtable. You can query your Avro data using GoogleSQL for Bigtable, continuous materialized views, and logical views. This feature is in Preview.

Cloud DNS

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, CNAME chasing behavior will change so that Cloud DNS follows CNAME chains between public and private zones. If your private zones or response policies have overlapping domain names with public CNAME targets, queries might resolve to unintended internal IP addresses or return resolution errors.

The following table outlines the current and updated behaviors.

Source of CNAME answer Current behavior (until January 5, 2027) New behavior (starting January 5, 2027)
Cloud DNS public zone Subsequent queries search only public DNS zones and internal DNS. Private zones, forwarding zones, and response policies are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order: response policies, private zones, forwarding or peering zones, internal DNS, and public zones.
Cloud DNS private zone Subsequent queries search only authorized private zones. Public DNS zones are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in authorized private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.
Cloud DNS response policy zone Cloud DNS systems don't perform queries for CNAME answers received from response policy local data rules. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in response policies or private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.

Review your CNAME chasing needs before January 5, 2027. Test your DNS query paths using dig or nslookup to identify CNAME chasing scenarios.

  • Look for private-to-public CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from response policies or private zones that don't match any response policy or record in a private zone. Previously, these queries resulted in a NXDOMAIN answer but after January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a record in a public zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses.
  • Look for public-to-private CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from public zones that don't match any record in a public zone. Previously, these CNAME chasing scenarios would have resulted in a NXDOMAIN response. After January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a response policy or record in a private zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses if the private zone doesn't have the record.
  • For CNAME chasing scenarios under your control: As best practice, configure matching time-to-live (TTL) values for all records in the CNAME chain.

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, Cloud DNS will disable full responses to DNS queries of type ANY (QTYPE=ANY) in public authoritative zones. Instead, a single resource record will return for ANY queries, chosen from the existing resource record sets that match the query.

Standard traffic from web browsers, applications, and API traffic query specific record types directly and are therefore unaffected with no action required.

However, certain legacy scripts, automated health checkers, debugging commands (for example, dig example.com ANY), or custom third-party monitoring systems that explicitly query ANY records will receive the first available record instead of a full zone inventory. You must complete the following configuration updates before January 5, 2027:

  • Identify legacy queries: Review internal tools, deployment scripts, or third-party DNS monitoring configurations for commands or API calls that request the ANY record type. Cloud DNS logs in Cloud Logging can be helpful with this.
  • Transition to specific queries: Update the tools to query the specific, individual record types they require (for example, querying for A, AAAA, MX, or TXT records separately).
  • Retrieve full zone records: If you use ANY queries to retrieve all records in a zone, use the Cloud DNS REST API (resourceRecordSets.list), the gcloud CLI (gcloud dns record-sets list), or the Google Cloud Console instead.

Risks associated with not making these changes include the following:

  • False monitoring alarms: Automated uptime or DNS monitoring tools checking ANY responses may misinterpret the new response as a system failure and trigger false alerts.
  • Broken automation pipelines: Internal deployment or CI/CD scripts that rely on parsing a full zone dump with an ANY query will fail to retrieve the expected data payload and may crash.
  • Disrupted IT diagnostics: Network administrators running manual legacy troubleshooting commands will no longer see a quick summary of all domain records, which could delay active network incident diagnostics.

Cloud Load Balancing

Feature

Regular expression URL rewrites (regexRewrite) for route rules in URL maps are now generally available (GA) for Application Load Balancers. You can use regular expression pattern rewrite actions to rewrite URL paths by substituting or removing URL path components before forwarding requests to your backends.

This feature is available in:

  • Global external Application Load Balancers

  • Regional external Application Load Balancers

  • Cross-region internal Application Load Balancers

  • Regional internal Application Load Balancers

For more information, see Regular expression URL rewrites for route rules.

Cloud Workstations

Feature

Cloud Workstations supports configuring direct access ports on workstation clusters in Preview. Direct access ports let you connect directly to a workstation port using the standard https://WORKSTATION_NAME.CLUSTER_ID.cloudworkstations.dev:PORT URL format instead of encoding the port as a prefix in the URL.

To set direct access ports, use the --direct-access-ports flag with the gcloud beta workstations clusters create and gcloud beta workstations clusters update commands—for example, --direct-access-ports=80,8080.

Config Connector

Announcement

Config Connector version 1.160.0 is now available.

Feature

New Alpha Resources (Direct Reconciler):

  • CCInsightsAnalysisRule

    • Manage Customer Experience Insights analysis rules to define rules for analyzing conversational data.

  • ConfigDeploymentGroup

    • Manage Infrastructure Manager deployment groups to orchestrate and manage deployments collectively.

  • DataLineageProcess

    • Manage Knowledge Catalog data lineage processes to track data origin and movement.

  • DataplexDataProduct

    • Manage Knowledge Catalog data products to package and share data assets across an enterprise.

  • DialogflowKnowledgeBase

    • Manage Dialogflow ES knowledge bases to provide FAQs and articles for agent answers.

  • DiscoveryEngineSchema

    • Manage Agent Search schemas to define document structures and schemas for data stores.

  • DiscoveryEngineSession

    • Manage Agent Search sessions to maintain conversation context and history for search and recommendations.

  • DiscoveryEngineSitemap

    • Manage Agent Search sitemaps to crawl web pages for search data stores.

  • ManagedKafkaConnectCluster

    • Manage Managed Service for Apache Kafka Connect clusters to run connectors that integrate Apache Kafka with Google Cloud and external systems.

  • MigrationCenterPreferenceSet

    • Manage Migration Center preference sets to specify migration preferences and target cloud architecture assumptions.

  • MigrationCenterSource

    • Manage Migration Center sources to configure data sources for importing asset data.

  • NetAppActiveDirectory

    • Manage NetApp Volumes Active Directory configurations to enable SMB and NFS domain-joined authentication.

  • NetAppHostGroup

    • Manage NetApp Volumes host groups to group client hosts for volume access.

  • NetworkConnectivityTransport

    • Manage Network Connectivity transports for connecting network endpoints.

  • NetworkSecurityMirroringEndpointGroupAssociation

    • Manage Network Security Integration mirroring endpoint group associations to associate packet mirroring endpoint groups with Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks.

  • NetworkServicesLBEdgeExtension

    • Manage Service Extensions load balancing edge extensions to customize Cloud CDN and edge proxy traffic processing.

  • NetworkServicesLBTrafficExtension

    • Manage Service Extensions load balancing traffic extensions to customize request and response processing in Application Load Balancers.

  • NetworkServicesServiceLBPolicy

    • Manage Cloud Service Mesh service load balancing policies to configure fine-grained traffic distribution across backend services.

  • SaaSServiceMgmtUnit

    • Manage App Lifecycle Manager units to manage SaaS deployment units.

  • StorageInsightsReportConfig

    • Manage Storage Insights report configurations to generate inventory and audit reports for Cloud Storage buckets.

  • WorkloadManagerEvaluation

    • Manage Workload Manager evaluations to scan and evaluate workloads against best-practice rules.

Feature

New Fields:

  • BigtableTable

    • Added support for spec.columnFamily[].type.

  • MemorystoreInstance

    • Added support for spec.gcsSource.

  • MonitoringDashboard

    • Added support for timeSeriesQuery.opsAnalyticsQuery in dashboard widgets.

Feature

New Features:

  • Added support for a configurable maximum exponential backoff delay ceiling and retry halting for direct controllers by using the cnrm.cloud.google.com/backoff-max-delay-in-seconds annotation.
  • Updated resource actuation to halt delete operations when the cnrm.cloud.google.com/actuation-mode annotation is set to Paused on an individual resource.

Change

Reconciliation Improvements:

Added support for direct reconciliation to more resources, with opt-in behavior. The API is unchanged. To use the direct reconciler, add the alpha.cnrm.cloud.google.com/reconciler: direct annotation to the corresponding Config Connector object. The following resources now have direct reconciliation support:

  • ComputeNetworkFirewallPolicy

    • Added support for direct reconciliation (opt-in).

  • ComputeProjectMetadata

    • Added support for direct reconciliation (opt-in).

  • FirebaseHostingSite

    • Added support for direct reconciliation (opt-in).

  • NetworkServicesEdgeCacheService

    • Added support for direct reconciliation (opt-in).

  • OSLoginSSHPublicKey

    • Added support for direct reconciliation (opt-in).

  • SQLSSLCert

    • Added support for direct reconciliation (opt-in).

Fixed

Bug Fixes:

  • AlloyDBCluster (#13963)

    • Fixed false-positive diffs on labels, initialUser, and network during takeover and re-reconciliation in the direct controller.

  • ArtifactRegistryRepository (#13873)

    • Fixed migration diffs on cleanupPolicies and cleanupPolicyDryRun when switching from the Terraform-based controller to the direct controller.

    • Fixed creation default and deletion behavior mismatches between the direct controller and the legacy controller.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: VPC connectivity and static IP egress for custom MCP servers

You can configure Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) connectivity for custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) server data stores by routing outbound tool traffic through Agent Gateway (supported in us-central1 and europe-west1). You can host private MCP servers inside your VPC network by using Private Service Connect (PSC) network attachments and agent connectivity templates. You can also route traffic to public MCP servers through Cloud NAT with static external IP addresses for strict IP allowlists.

This feature is generally available (GA). For more information, see:

  • Prerequisites to set up a custom MCP server data store with VPC connectivity
  • Set up your custom MCP server data store

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Gemini Robotics ER 2 (Preview)

Gemini Robotics ER 2 (gemini-robotics-er-2-preview) is available in Preview. Gemini Robotics ER 2 is an embodied reasoning vision-language model built on Gemini 3.5 Flash for robotics applications, including spatial reasoning, agentic code execution, task orchestration, and video understanding.

Feature

xAI's Grok 4.7 is generally available

Grok 4.7 is now generally available (GA) for production use on the global endpoint and the US multi-region endpoint.

Google Cloud Armor

Feature

Cloud Armor supports advanced match conditions to include attributes for inspecting request body content and parameters. This lets you write custom CEL rules to filter traffic based on raw body content, structured data (JSON, Form Data, GraphQL), and query parameters. For more information, see Attributes in "Create and view Cloud Armor security policy rules." This feature is generally available (GA).

Google Cloud VMware Engine

Feature

VMware solution on Google Cloud is generally available (GA). VMware solution lets you deploy, configure, and manage VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) on dedicated bare-metal Compute Engine instances within your Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network under a Bring Your Own License (BYOL) model.

Key features include the following:

  • Provision dedicated bare-metal ESXi nodes (z3-highmem-192-highlssd-metal) directly in your project with deletion protection and Local SSD storage for vSAN.
  • Automate node preparation, Secret Manager credential storage, vSwitch and Dynamic NIC networking, Cloud DNS zone and record synchronization, vSAN storage initialization, and VCF installer appliance deployment by using Terraform and the VMware solution toolkit.
  • Distribute nodes across isolated availability domains by using spread placement policies to align with vSAN fault domains for high availability.
  • Connect ESXi nodes and VLAN-tagged Dynamic NICs directly to your VPC subnets without requiring private services access peering.

For more information, see VMware solution on Google Cloud overview and Compare VMware Engine models.

  • 1.34.300-gke.59

title: I built a local-first API client in Rust and Tauri
description:
At the start of this year I began building Flux, an open source alternative to Postman. The goal was simple: an API client that feels light, runs natively and keeps your work on your own machine.

I launched it in July, and as of today it has a little under 500 downloads, which is more than I expected when I started.

What it is

Flux is a native desktop API client built with Tauri 2, Rust and React. It uses under 30 MB of RAM and the installer is around 9 MB.

It's local-first: your collections and requests live on your machine, and cloud sync is optional, not a requirement.

Besides regular HTTP requests, it has a few things built in that I'd normally need separate tools for:

  • gRPC support
  • Load testing, so you can hit an endpoint hard without installing anything else
  • Mock servers, for when the backend isn't ready yet
  • AI helpers: generating test suites, diagnosing errors, autocomplete, and editing request bodies in plain language

Why Tauri instead of Electron

Electron ships a full copy of Chromium and runs a Node backend inside every app. Tauri takes a different route: it uses the operating system's own webview for the interface, and the backend is Rust. That's where most of the savings in memory and installer size come from.

For an app you leave open all day next to your editor, your browser and everything else, that difference adds up.

It's open source, and I'd love help

Flux is MIT-licensed, and I'm building it in public. If you want to contribute, there's plenty to do: bug fixes, new features, better docs, or just telling me what you'd want from an API client.

If you try it and something breaks, opening an issue helps a lot. And if you're curious how a Tauri app is put together, the code is a decent place to poke around.

  • Website and download: https://fluxapi.dev
  • Code: https://github.com/angeldevmobile/Flux-Post

If you've switched away from Postman or Insomnia, I'd like to know what made you do it, and what Flux would need for you to switch.

title: Make CI Automation Failures Explainable
description:
CI automation usually does not fail because there is no log. It fails because the useful evidence is scattered across a runner, a test inbox, a webhook provider, and three unrelated dashboards.

When a job turns red, the first question is rarely just “what command exited with code 1?” We want to know which test data was created, which message or event was expected, what actually arrived, and whether a retry changed the result. Without that chain, debugging becomes archaeology.

This article describes a small pattern I use for making automation failures easier to explain: give every run an evidence ledger and publish one compact receipt when the run ends. It works for email tests, browser checks, API workflows, and other developer tools.

The failure is not the log line

A normal CI log is a timeline of commands. That is useful, but it is not always a timeline of causes.

For example, a browser test may report that a verification link was missing. The real cause could be any of these:

  • The test created a fixture for the wrong run.
  • The application sent the event, but the worker retried it later.
  • The inbox query used a broad subject and selected an older message.
  • A cleanup step removed the message before the assertion ran.
  • The test passed locally because the local clock was a little different.

The log may contain clues for each case, but a developer has to manually join them. That is the expensive part. A receipt should make the joins explicit, even when the final status is failed.

Model each CI run as an evidence ledger

Start with a run identifier that is unique outside the CI provider too. A short commit SHA plus the CI attempt number works well, for example a81f2c7-attempt-2.

Every resource created for the test should carry that identifier:

  • test account or email fixture
  • outbound event ID
  • worker job ID
  • inbox message ID
  • assertion result
  • cleanup result

The ledger does not need a database on day one. A JSON file stored as a CI artifact is often enough. The important part is ownership: each record says which run created it and what happened next. This also keeps a test from accidentally reading another run's data, which is a common source of flaky results.

If your UI flow has several asynchronous states, define them before writing assertions. A test email state machine for React forms is a useful mental model: “created”, “sent”, “received”, “opened”, and “expired” are different facts, not one big “email worked” fact.

A small receipt format

Keep the receipt boring. Boring is good when somebody is staring at it during an incident. Here is a minimal shape:

{
  "run_id": "a81f2c7-attempt-2",
  "status": "failed",
  "started_at": "2026-11-12T05:00:14Z",
  "finished_at": "2026-11-12T05:01:03Z",
  "fixture": {
    "id": "fixture-a81f2c7",
    "owner": "checkout-verification"
  },
  "events": [
    {"name": "created", "id": "evt_91", "at": "2026-11-12T05:00:21Z"},
    {"name": "received", "id": "msg_44", "at": "2026-11-12T05:00:37Z"}
  ],
  "assertions": [
    {"name": "verification_link_present", "ok": false, "reason": "wrong host"}
  ],
  "cleanup": {"ok": true, "deleted": ["fixture-a81f2c7"]}
}

There is no need to make this format fancy at first. Use stable names, UTC timestamps, and IDs that can be searched in the other systems. If a field is unknown, write null or an explicit reason instead of silently leaving a gap. A missing value is itself useful evidence.

One small rule saves time: record the expected value beside the observed value. “Wrong host” is better than “link assertion failed,” but expected_host and observed_host is better still. It save a second trip through the application configuration.

Turn the receipt into a developer tool

An evidence ledger becomes valuable when the team can find it without learning a new ritual. Add three simple outputs to the CI job:

  1. Print a one-line summary with the run ID and the first failed assertion.
  2. Upload the full receipt as an artifact with a predictable filename.
  3. Add links from the job summary to the relevant event, message, and cleanup logs.

For pull requests, a small Markdown summary is enough:

Email verification: FAILED
Run: a81f2c7-attempt-2
First bad state: verification_link_present
Expected host: staging.example.test
Observed host: example.test
Receipt: artifacts/a81f2c7-attempt-2.json

This pattern also helps with privacy. The receipt can store opaque IDs and hashes instead of full message bodies or personal addresses. For teams handling test email, an audit trail for privacy-safe test email shows why retention and access rules belong in the design, not as a cleanup afterthought.

Do not over-collect. A receipt that copies every payload becomes a new security problem and is harder to read. Keep the minimum fields needed to reproduce the decision, then link to protected logs when more detail is required.

What to do about retries

Retries are where many automation reports become confusing. Treat every attempt as a child of one logical run, and include the attempt number in each resource key. The parent receipt can then say whether the second attempt reused data or created a clean fixture.

If a retry changes the result, report both outcomes. “Passed after retry” is not the same signal as “passed.” The distinction matters because a retry may hide a race, a delayed worker, or a flaky dependency. The failure ledger should make that visible, not smooth it away.

Also make cleanup idempotent. If the first attempt already deleted a fixture, the second cleanup should report “already absent” as an acceptable outcome. Otherwise the cleanup error can distract from the original failure.

Checklist before you ship the workflow

  • Does every created test resource include a run and attempt ID?
  • Can the receipt identify the first bad state, not only the last failed command?
  • Are expected and observed values recorded together?
  • Are retry outcomes kept distinct?
  • Can a developer open the artifact from the CI job summary?
  • Does cleanup run on success, failure, and cancellation?
  • Are private payloads excluded or protected?
  • Does the report remain useful when an external service is unavailable?

The goal is not another observability platform. It is a small shared contract between the test, the automation runner, and the person who has to fix the failure. Once that contract exists, noisy CI output starts to read like a story: what the run owned, what changed, where the first unexpected state appeared, and what was cleaned up. That is usually enough to get unstuck faster.

title: The fx adapter now runs the harness on the host
description:
The fx adapter for the AI SDK’s HarnessAgent now uses libfx, the TypeScript library for fx. The harness and model requests run in your application’s process, while built-in filesystem and shell operations remain isolated in the sandbox.

This simplifies sandbox setup: you no longer need to install fx inside the sandbox, run a sandbox bridge, or expose a sandbox port. Model credentials stay on the host, outside the environment where the agent runs commands.

The rewrite also adds:

  • Built-in tool filtering: choose which built-in tools the agent can use

  • Mid-turn steering: send new instructions while a turn is running

  • Structured output: generate responses that match a schema

  • Image tool results: return images to the model through toModelOutput()

Sessions can be saved and resumed in a new host process.

Update @ai-sdk/harness-fx to the latest version to use the new adapter. Learn more in the fx harness documentation.
