title: Your White-Label AI Portal Works. Now Make It Usable.
description:
Most white-label developer portals do not fail because the API is broken. They fail in the awkward space between “the endpoint works” and “a new user understands what to do next.”

That gap is easy to underestimate. The team has already spent weeks on model access, metering, and deployment, so changing a logo or rewriting a login screen feels cosmetic. Then the first real users arrive. They cannot tell which tool to open, the domain redirects strangely, the pricing units are ambiguous, and the documentation assumes they already know the product.

A branded AI portal is not just a reskinned dashboard. It is a small product with its own trust signals, information architecture, economics, and support burden. Treating configuration as product design makes the difference between a portal people can technically access and one they can actually use.

The first screen is an interface contract

A visitor should be able to answer three questions almost immediately: What is this site? What can I make here? What should I click first?

A short, specific promise usually works better than a wall of fashionable language. “Generate catalog images and ad variations” gives the visitor something concrete. “An intelligent, all-in-one creative ecosystem” could describe almost anything.

The same restraint helps with branding. A compact logo has to survive a small navigation bar, dark mode, mobile screens, and browser scaling. Fine lettering and elaborate illustrations may look impressive in the source file but turn into visual noise at 32 pixels. Test the exported asset in the actual interface rather than approving it on a design canvas.

This is also where naming matters. The product name should be easy to remember, type, and say aloud. If users have to explain the spelling every time they share it, the brand is creating friction before the application even loads.

Authentication should feel boring

Login is infrastructure from the operator's perspective, but it is a trust test from the user's perspective. People do not care which authentication flow is technically elegant. They care that the option is familiar, the redirect behaves normally, and they return to the page they intended to use.

Pick the default sign-in method around the audience, not around the engineering team's preferences. Then test it without an administrator session. A persistent admin cookie hides exactly the class of problems a first-time visitor will encounter: missing callbacks, unexpected account selection, broken redirects, and pages that silently assume an authenticated state.

A useful habit is to run the whole path in a private browser window. Start at the public homepage, create or access an account, open a tool, and sign out again. Repeat it on a phone. It sounds basic, but this short exercise catches more launch blockers than another hour inside the settings panel.

Your domain is part of the product

A custom domain does more than make a URL prettier. It gives support messages, documentation, and community posts a stable address. It also signals continuity: users are less likely to wonder whether they have been sent to an unrelated service.

Domain setup has two sides. The application needs to know which hostname belongs to the site, and DNS needs to direct that hostname to the platform. For an Ace Data Cloud subsite, the documented target is a CNAME pointing to platform-proxy.acedata.cloud.

A typical record looks like this:

Type:   CNAME
Name:   ai
Target: platform-proxy.acedata.cloud

That would normally make ai.example.com the user-facing hostname. Before adding it, check whether ai already has an A, AAAA, or CNAME record. Conflicting records are a common source of “it works for me” debugging because DNS caches do not all refresh at the same moment.

Do not stop after the DNS panel shows a green status. Open the public hostname, verify that it reaches the intended portal, inspect the TLS certificate, and follow the login flow. A domain is ready when the complete journey works over HTTPS, not when a record merely exists.

A homepage is a decision surface, not an inventory

AI platforms often accumulate capabilities faster than their navigation can explain them. Image generation, editing, chat, video, audio, and developer tools all compete for the same top-level space. Showing every feature may feel transparent, but it transfers the job of product strategy to the visitor.

The homepage should emphasize the jobs users came to perform. If most customers create product visuals, put generation and editing near the front. If the audience is building integrations, make API access and documentation easy to reach. Less common utilities can stay available without occupying the most valuable part of the page.

The hero banner deserves the same discipline. Give it one job. It can introduce the main use case, announce a genuinely important change, or direct newcomers to a starting point. Trying to fit the product pitch, feature matrix, discount, tutorial, and pricing message into one image produces a banner that nobody reads.

Text inside images is especially fragile. It may be cropped on mobile, become unreadable on high-density screens, or remain invisible to assistive technology. Keep critical meaning in HTML whenever possible, and preview the real page at narrow and wide breakpoints.

Pricing is an engineering problem with a copywriting layer

A price table can look polished while still being impossible to reason about. The usual problem is not the number itself; it is the missing unit. Per request, per generated image, per second of video, and per token are very different promises.

Start with the underlying cost model. Include failed-job behavior, retries, storage, support, payment fees, and any free usage you plan to offer. Then present the customer-facing unit in language that does not require knowledge of the upstream provider.

If a request can vary significantly in cost, a single flat label may be misleading. A short example is often more useful than another tooltip:

Standard image: 1 credit
High-resolution image: 2 credits
Ten-second video: 12 credits

These are illustrative units, not universal rates. The important part is that the interface and documentation use the same vocabulary. If the dashboard says “credits” while the help page explains “requests,” users will assume the conversion is being hidden from them.

Pricing changes also need a communication path. Quietly changing the amount after users have built habits around it may save a short announcement, but it creates a much longer trust problem.

Documentation should absorb predictable questions

You do not need a large documentation site on launch day. You need a small one that answers the questions people will actually ask.

A useful starting set covers account access, the first successful task, billing units, common errors, and a visible support route. Write each page in the order the user experiences the product. Screenshots help when they show the exact control being discussed, but they should support the instructions rather than replace them.

Error guidance deserves special attention. “Something went wrong” tells the user nothing. Even when the underlying provider returns a complex response, the portal can explain whether the user should retry, change an input, check their balance, or contact support with a request ID.

Documentation should grow from support evidence. When the same question appears repeatedly, the answer belongs in the product or the docs. This feedback loop is far more valuable than trying to predict every possible tutorial before anyone has used the site.

The quiet settings still shape trust

Analytics, referral rules, and privacy terms are easy to postpone because they are not part of the main creative workflow. They become painful later if they were configured casually.

Analytics should answer a small set of useful questions: where users leave, which tools they open, and whether an onboarding change improves activation. Collecting events without a decision attached to them creates data storage, not insight.

Referral programs need written definitions for attribution, eligibility, rewards, and settlement. Privacy language needs to match what the site actually collects and which third-party services it uses. Copying another company's policy without updating the business name, contact route, or data practices is not a shortcut; it is an inaccurate public statement.

Launch from the user's side of the glass

Before sharing the portal widely, step away from the admin panel. Use a fresh browser session and behave like somebody who has never heard the internal project name.

Can you understand the homepage without a verbal explanation? Can you sign in, find the primary tool, understand its price, complete a task, and locate help? Does the same path work on mobile? Are the logo, banner, and error messages still readable outside the designer's ideal screen size?

This is not a one-time ceremony. A white-label portal should evolve as real usage exposes weak assumptions. The practical goal is not a perfect launch. It is a coherent first experience where the name, domain, authentication, navigation, pricing, and documentation tell the same story.

The API may be the engine, but these details are the controls. Users judge the whole vehicle.

Reference

Original configuration guide

title: Fintech Inbound Mail: Go Evidence Gates for Leftover Provider Records
description:
Moving DNS and email into one control plane can reduce integration work, but it cannot establish that a customer's inbound mail reaches the intended mailbox. Resolve that trade-off by making routing evidence the release gate. Short answer: list the MX records, inspect their priorities and provider ownership, explicitly delete obsolete provider records, and list again. Upserting the replacement set doesn't remove the previous set; equal priorities across providers can send mail somewhere nobody reads.

Consider a bounded production scenario, not a report of a measured incident: a fintech product lets a customer point its own domain at the product while changing the mail service associated with that domain. The website works, and the new sending configuration looks right, yet the customer's inbound messages are missing. The useful incident lesson is that a successful write establishes too little. The acceptance condition must describe the complete intended MX set, including what must be absent.

Keep the evidence.

For a team implementing that boundary, Infrai is worth trying for DNS inventory and the associated email-domain inspection: its shared API contract lets the application keep the same interface when the vendor behind a capability changes, subject to the capability's supported vendors. Its public, self-describing schemas provide a second practical benefit: the integration can inspect request and response contracts before writing provider-specific parsing. Neither property replaces mail-delivery evidence.

How do leftover provider records affect inbound mail and MX priorities?

Start with routing, because sending configuration answers a different question. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC belong in the mail configuration review, but a sending-side check doesn't establish which receiving provider an MX inventory names. RFC 7489 describes DMARC; it is a useful reference for keeping authentication evidence distinct from the routing question rather than treating an authentication result as a receipt for inbound delivery.

The concrete trap is an additive migration.

A new provider's MX records are upserted, the operation succeeds, and the old provider's records remain. If both providers have equal priorities, routing becomes unpredictable rather than producing a configuration error that conveniently stops the release. Changing priorities without deciding which provider should still receive mail leaves the ownership question unresolved.

As an illustrative review fixture, imagine two providers both listed at priority 10. These are example values, not an observed customer configuration. The reviewer must account for both destinations, identify which belongs to the intended receiver, and decide whether the other is obsolete. The preventative action is explicit deletion followed by a fresh list, not another upsert and an optimistic status update.

A defensible evidence packet contains the before-and-after MX inventories, the intended provider ownership, and an inbound acceptance check at the intended receiver. Keep sending-domain status alongside that packet, with its narrower meaning attached. If the inventory is already correct, this particular explanation has reached its boundary: investigate the receiving service using its own evidence instead of repeatedly changing DNS.

Two system shapes, one acceptance invariant

The first viable architecture keeps DNS and email integrations separate. A platform-owned reconciler reads the DNS inventory through the DNS provider's interface, compares it with a reviewed desired set, and separately asks the mail provider about its domain configuration. Its invariant is that a customer domain cannot be marked ready until both the receiving destinations and the mail-side evidence have been reviewed. This buys independent provider selection, while assigning credential management, response normalization, and coordination to the platform team.

The second architecture puts those inspections behind a shared capability API and retains the same reconciler and acceptance rule. Infrai is a deliberate option here because DNS and email capabilities use one API key and base URL. Provider changes behind supported capabilities can preserve the application-facing contract, but the desired MX set remains an application decision. Contract stability doesn't mean arbitrary providers have identical behavior or that existing customer records should be deleted automatically.

For this fintech onboarding workflow, prefer the shared interface when the platform team wants to maintain one evidence-producing controller and the supported provider choices fit its requirements. Prefer direct integrations when a DNS or mail specialist's control surface is itself a requirement. The recommendation turns on evidence ownership and operating work; a shorter integration is valuable only if the release gate remains intact.

The combined approach also concentrates trust, billing, and the outage surface in one vendor.

Say that in the design review before choosing it.

The cross-capability benefit is particularly concrete during SPF or DKIM maintenance. With DNS records and the mail service available through one key, a controller can coordinate inspection instead of relying on a person to copy values between two dashboards and remember to re-check them after a DKIM rotation. This is an integration pattern to implement, not a claim that a shared key automatically reconciles records or proves deliverability.

Buy versus build depends on who owns the evidence

There are several credible stacks.

The table compares the integration boundaries the team would own, rather than asserting that one provider has better measured delivery. No comparative delivery benchmark is established here.

Stack What to buy What the platform still builds Appropriate boundary
Amazon Route 53 + Amazon SES Separate DNS and email service interfaces within AWS The mapping between DNS inventory, mail configuration, and a customer-domain acceptance decision A team deliberately choosing the AWS service boundary
Cloudflare DNS + Resend A DNS service and a separately selected email service Two-provider credential handling, record handoff, and evidence correlation A team that values independent DNS and email selection
Infrai DNS + email One capability interface and one key across the two groups Desired-state ownership, explicit obsolete-record decisions, and the delivery gate A team reducing integration surface while retaining its own acceptance controller

The Cloudflare-plus-Resend alternative requires two provider signups and two credential sets, along with glue that translates the mail service's requirements into DNS changes and correlates the later inspections. Route 53 plus SES can share an AWS account signup, but still introduces two service interfaces and their permission configuration; don't turn that into an inaccurate claim that two AWS accounts are required. Account count and integration count measure different work.

The specialist or direct-provider choice is better when the team's required control or evidence exists at that provider's interface and hasn't been established in a shared contract. Conversely, choosing an independent email service for its sending workflow doesn't, by itself, establish where inbound mail is received. Make receiving ownership explicit in every row of the implementation plan.

A Go gate that carries DNS evidence into the mail check

The preventative code path below is deliberately read-only. It lists DNS records, presents the actual response for review, and permits the email-domain inspection only after the operator has checked MX priorities and leftovers. The first response becomes the evidence input to the second stage; its digest is carried into the mail inspection output so the two cannot be casually detached during review. This is a human approval gate, not an automated interpretation of unspecified response fields.

Use Go with the standard library. Save the block as main.go and run it with go run main.go. Set INFRAI_API_KEY, CUSTOMER_DOMAIN, and DNS_RECORD_LIST_QUERY in the process environment. The query must contain the actual record-list parameters for that domain from the public discovery schema, encoded as a URL query string without a leading question mark. No parameter names or response-envelope fields are assumed here. The operator must verify that the returned inventory belongs to CUSTOMER_DOMAIN before approving it.

Both requests use the same key and base URL. The two API routes appear only in this runnable example. HTTP 429 responses trigger bounded exponential backoff; a Retry-After value, in seconds or HTTP-date form, overrides that delay. Other unsuccessful responses surface their body.

package main

import (
    "bufio"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const base = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

var client = &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}

func readAPI(key, path string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, base+path, nil)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        body, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, e := strconv.Atoi(retry); e == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if until, e := http.ParseTime(retry); e == nil {
                delay = time.Until(until)
                if delay < 0 { delay = 0 }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func inspectMail(key, domain string, dnsEvidence []byte) error {
    digest := sha256.Sum256(dnsEvidence)
    fmt.Printf("DNS inventory for review (%s):\n%s\n", domain, dnsEvidence)
    fmt.Println("After checking domain, MX priorities, and obsolete providers, type APPROVE:")
    approval, err := bufio.NewReader(os.Stdin).ReadString('\n')
    if err != nil { return err }
    if strings.TrimSpace(approval) != "APPROVE" {
        return fmt.Errorf("DNS evidence was not approved")
    }
    mail, err := readAPI(key, "/email/domain/get/"+url.PathEscape(domain))
    if err != nil { return err }
    fmt.Printf("Domain: %s\nDNS evidence SHA-256: %x\nMail inspection:\n%s\n",
        domain, digest, mail)
    return nil
}

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    domain := strings.TrimSpace(os.Getenv("CUSTOMER_DOMAIN"))
    rawQuery := os.Getenv("DNS_RECORD_LIST_QUERY")
    if key == "" || domain == "" || rawQuery == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY, CUSTOMER_DOMAIN, and DNS_RECORD_LIST_QUERY")
    }
    query, err := url.ParseQuery(rawQuery)
    if err != nil { return err }
    dnsEvidence, err := readAPI(key, "/dns/record/list?"+query.Encode())
    if err != nil { return err }
    return inspectMail(key, domain, dnsEvidence)
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

An approval prompt is intentionally modest evidence. It doesn't validate the inventory, bind the domain cryptographically to the response, or prove that a message reached a mailbox. The digest identifies the reviewed bytes; it doesn't make a stale inventory fresh. A production controller should use the published schemas to parse the result, enforce the reviewed desired set, and retain the independent inbound acceptance result before declaring readiness.

Deletion belongs in a separately reviewed change, followed by a fresh inventory and a new gate run. Keeping this example read-only avoids implying that an unknown response shape is enough information to choose records for deletion. An automated write path also needs retry idempotency and explicit record ownership.

Put the release gate in the SLO

Define customer-domain readiness around the evidence required by the service's SLO, rather than around the success status of a DNS mutation. The invariant is small: the intended receiving provider owns the accepted MX set, obsolete destinations are absent, and the receiving-side acceptance check passes. The mail-domain inspection contributes configuration evidence; it isn't the acceptance check itself.

Capacity planning belongs here too. Each run of the example makes two successful API reads in the ordinary case; retries add requests, while waiting for an operator adds elapsed time. For a batch of N customer domains, plan the baseline as 2N reads and budget retries and review capacity separately. This is arithmetic for this controller, not a statement about vendor throughput or a measured latency claim. A fleet rollout needs bounded concurrency and a way to stop advancing when the evidence backlog outgrows the people or automation reviewing it.

Don't apply this MX cleanup diagnosis to every missing message. It fits a migration with stale receiving destinations or conflicting provider priorities. If those conditions are absent, or a specialist exposes required receiving evidence that this integration doesn't cover, follow that evidence instead. The engineering win is a defensible readiness decision, not a larger pile of successful API calls.

Sources and References

References for the capability contract, authentication boundary, and the direct-service alternatives discussed above:

  • RFC 7489, DMARC
  • Amazon Route 53 documentation
  • Amazon SES documentation
  • Cloudflare DNS documentation
  • Resend documentation

If the shared-controller boundary fits your customer-domain workflow, start with the public schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
description: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. title: Your AI Agent Works Perfectly in Testing. So Why Does It Fail in Production?
description:
Your AI Agent Works Perfectly in Testing. So Why Does It Fail in Production?

An AI agent can pass every test you give it and still create serious problems after deployment.

It might select the wrong customer record, trigger an unnecessary workflow, call an API with incorrect parameters, or continue taking actions when it should have stopped and asked for human approval.

The frustrating part is that the agent may not actually be broken.

The problem is often the environment in which it operates.

During testing, developers usually provide controlled inputs, predictable data, limited permissions, and clearly defined tasks. Production environments are different. They contain incomplete information, unexpected user requests, changing data, API failures, and situations that were never included in the original test cases.

This creates an important engineering challenge:

Building an AI agent that works is not the same as building an AI agent that can be trusted in production.

Let's look at why these failures happen and what developers can do to prevent them.

1. Testing environments are usually too predictable

Consider an AI agent designed to process customer support requests.

In development, it might receive requests like:

  • Where is my order?
  • Can I update my delivery address?
  • I want to cancel my subscription.

The agent identifies the intent, retrieves the relevant information, and returns an appropriate response.

Everything works.

But real users rarely follow predictable patterns.

A customer might send an incomplete message, combine multiple requests, provide an incorrect order number, or ask for something outside the agent's permissions.

For example:

"Cancel my order, but only if it hasn't been shipped. Also, update my delivery address if cancellation isn't possible."

This request requires the agent to understand conditions, retrieve accurate information, and choose the correct action.

A simple happy-path test might never reveal whether the agent can handle this safely.

What developers should do:

Test realistic and difficult scenarios, not just successful ones.

Include:

  • Missing or incomplete information.
  • Conflicting instructions.
  • Unexpected user inputs.
  • Invalid API responses.
  • Network timeouts.
  • Duplicate requests.
  • Tasks outside the agent's scope.

The goal is not simply to prove that the agent can complete a task. It is to understand what happens when it cannot.

2. Giving an AI agent too much permission creates unnecessary risk

One common mistake is providing an agent with more access than it actually needs.

Imagine an agent responsible for managing customer records.

It needs permission to:

  • Read customer information.
  • Update contact details.
  • Add internal notes.

But it also receives permission to delete customer records, modify billing information, and change account ownership.

Even if the model is generally reliable, these additional permissions increase the consequences of a wrong decision.

A better approach is the principle of least privilege.

Give each agent only the permissions required for its assigned responsibilities.

For example:

Action Suggested control
Read customer record Allow
Add internal note Allow
Update contact details Validate before execution
Delete customer record Human approval
Change account ownership Human approval

The important distinction is that an AI agent should not automatically receive every permission available to the user or system account.

Its access should be designed around its actual role.

3. An incorrect decision can become a chain of incorrect actions

AI agents often use tools to complete multi-step tasks.

A typical workflow might look like this:

  1. Understand the request.
  2. Search a database.
  3. Retrieve relevant information.
  4. Decide what action is needed.
  5. Call an external API.
  6. Confirm the result.

The risk is that one incorrect decision early in the process can affect every step that follows.

For example, an agent might identify the wrong customer record. It then retrieves that customer's information and updates the wrong account.

The API call may succeed.

The workflow may even report that the task was completed successfully.

But the outcome is still incorrect.

This is why successful tool execution should never be treated as proof of a correct business outcome.

A useful engineering principle: validate important decisions before allowing them to trigger consequential actions.

Developers can introduce validation between steps:

def execute_customer_update(customer, changes):
    if not customer:
        return {
            "status": "rejected",
            "reason": "Customer not found"
        }

    if not validate_customer_changes(changes):
        return {
            "status": "rejected",
            "reason": "Invalid changes"
        }

    if changes_require_approval(changes):
        return {
            "status": "pending_approval",
            "changes": changes
        }

    return update_customer_record(customer, changes)

This is an illustrative control pattern. The validation, approval, and update functions must be implemented according to the application's actual data model and security requirements.

4. Human approval should be part of the architecture

There is a common assumption that automation becomes more valuable when humans are removed from every step.

That is not always true.

Some actions are low-risk and repetitive. Others can affect customer accounts, financial records, access permissions, or business operations.

A useful approach is to classify actions by their potential impact.

Low-risk actions

  • Searching information.
  • Categorizing requests.
  • Preparing summaries.
  • Drafting responses.

These may be suitable for automatic execution, depending on the application.

Medium-risk actions

  • Updating customer information.
  • Changing workflow status.
  • Sending routine notifications.

These should have appropriate validation and monitoring.

High-risk actions

  • Deleting records.
  • Issuing refunds.
  • Changing account permissions.
  • Making financial commitments.

These may require explicit human approval before execution.

The important point is that approval requirements should be determined by the consequences of an action, not simply by how confident the AI sounds.

5. Monitoring should continue after deployment

Many development teams focus heavily on pre-deployment testing.

But an AI agent's behavior can change when its environment changes.

For example:

  • An API introduces a new response format.
  • A database field changes.
  • A model version is updated.
  • A new tool is added.
  • Business rules are modified.
  • Users begin making requests that were not previously observed.

An agent that worked reliably last month may behave differently after these changes.

This makes continuous monitoring essential.

At minimum, developers should track:

Metric Why it matters
Task success rate Measures completed tasks
Tool-call failures Identifies integration problems
Invalid actions Reveals decision or validation issues
Human intervention rate Shows where automation needs assistance
Latency Helps identify performance problems
Repeated actions Helps detect duplicate execution
Escalation rate Measures when agents cannot safely proceed

Monitoring should also include enough context to investigate failures.

A useful event record might include:

{
  "agent_id": "support-agent-01",
  "task_id": "task-1042",
  "action": "update_customer_record",
  "approval_required": true,
  "approval_status": "pending",
  "execution_status": "not_executed"
}

Do not log sensitive information unnecessarily. Apply access controls, retention limits, and appropriate data protection measures to agent logs.

6. Build failure recovery into the workflow

No production system is completely immune to failure.

An external service may become unavailable. A request may time out. A tool may return incomplete data.

The important question is not whether a failure will happen, but what the system will do when it happens.

Consider an agent that sends a payment-related request to an external service.

The request times out.

Should the agent immediately send the same request again?

Not necessarily.

The original request may have succeeded even though the response never reached the application. Sending it again could create a duplicate transaction.

Developers should consider:

  • Idempotency keys for operations that must not execute twice.
  • Retry limits and exponential backoff.
  • Timeouts for external calls.
  • Clear failure states.
  • Duplicate-action detection.
  • Human escalation for uncertain outcomes.

For example:

def process_action(action, idempotency_key):
    existing = find_previous_action(idempotency_key)

    if existing:
        return existing

    try:
        result = execute_action(action)
        save_action_result(idempotency_key, result)
        return result

    except TimeoutError:
        return {
            "status": "unknown",
            "message": "Verify execution before retrying"
        }

This is a simplified illustration. In production, the idempotency record and business operation need appropriate atomicity and concurrency protection.

7. Test the entire system, not just the language model

An AI agent is more than a model.

It includes multiple components:

  • The model.
  • System instructions.
  • Tools and integrations.
  • APIs.
  • Databases.
  • Permissions.
  • Workflow logic.
  • Monitoring and logging.

Testing only the model's responses ignores many of the places where real failures occur.

A more complete testing strategy should include:

Unit testing: Test individual functions and validation rules.

Integration testing: Verify that tools, APIs, and databases communicate correctly.

Scenario testing: Test realistic user requests, including unusual and conflicting inputs.

Security testing: Check whether agents can access or modify resources beyond their permissions.

Regression testing: Repeat important tests whenever prompts, tools, models, or business rules change.

Failure testing: Simulate timeouts, unavailable services, malformed responses, and interrupted workflows.

A system should be evaluated based on its complete behavior, not just the quality of its generated text.

8. A practical pre-production checklist

Before deploying an AI agent, developers and engineering teams should be able to answer these questions:

  • [ ] Is the agent's purpose clearly defined?
  • [ ] Are its permissions limited to necessary actions?
  • [ ] Are important inputs validated?
  • [ ] Are high-impact actions protected by approval controls?
  • [ ] Are duplicate actions prevented?
  • [ ] Are API failures and timeouts handled?
  • [ ] Can developers trace important decisions and tool calls?
  • [ ] Are sensitive details protected in logs?
  • [ ] Have unexpected and conflicting inputs been tested?
  • [ ] Is there a process for stopping or disabling unsafe automation?
  • [ ] Are changes to prompts, models, tools, and workflows tested?
  • [ ] Can the system recover safely from uncertain outcomes?

If several answers are no, the system may need more engineering work before it is ready for production.

Final thoughts

AI agents are becoming increasingly capable, but capability alone does not make an automated system reliable.

Production readiness depends on the engineering surrounding the model: permissions, validation, monitoring, testing, failure recovery, and human oversight.

This is also an important consideration for organizations working in AI automation, including Octacer: automation should be evaluated not only by what an agent can accomplish, but also by whether its actions remain understandable, controlled, and accountable.

The best AI agent is not necessarily the one that performs the most actions without human involvement.

It is the one that knows what it is allowed to do, recognizes when something is uncertain, and stops when an action requires additional verification.

That is the difference between an AI agent that works in a demo and one that is ready for production.

Disclosure: This article was prepared with AI assistance and should be reviewed by the author before publication. The author is associated with Octacer; the company name is included for affiliation transparency, not as a product recommendation. The technical examples are illustrative rather than claims of personal production experience.

title: What 1,355 App Store reviews say people want from a Reels/Shorts blocker (2026 data)
description:
Of 1,355 App Store reviews of one Reels and Shorts blocking app (February 1 to September 6, 2026), 466 gave one to three stars. In those low ratings, the most common complaint was that the app was slow, heavy or crashed: 143 reviews, or 30.7%. The complaints most tied to a low rating were rarer: no way to switch between several accounts, Screen Time restrictions reaching unrelated websites, and login problems. In a wider set of 1,405 reviews, the most requested feature was posting Stories and making calls (110 of 266 reviews that asked for something).

I'm Ayumu Kitabayashi. I build a similar app, so I have an interest here; that is disclosed at the end. Below is the data, how I counted it, and what it can't tell you.

What was read

  • App: SocialLite – Block Reels&Shorts (iOS). It is one of the larger apps in this category, so it had enough written reviews to count. All numbers are about this one app.
  • Store: Apple App Store only, all countries in the export. US 600, Canada 148, UK 112, Australia 91, Germany 61, and 54 other countries (59 in all).
  • Period: February 1 to September 6, 2026. 1,355 reviews, no duplicate IDs, none deleted.
  • Stars: 5★ 671 / 4★ 218 / 3★ 166 / 2★ 105 / 1★ 195. Average 3.79.
  • Wishes: counted later on 1,405 reviews (the same 1,355 plus 50 from September 14 to 18).

Complaints in the 466 low ratings

I read all 466 one-to-three-star reviews in full and tagged each with every category that applied, so one review can count more than once. The last column compares how often a complaint shows up in low ratings with how often it shows up in four-and-five-star reviews. A high number means people who write it almost always rate low.

Complaint Reviews Share of low ratings Low vs high
Slow, heavy or crashes 143 30.7% 1.4×
The core job needs payment (e.g. hiding suggested posts) 51 10.9% 3.7×
Long, repeated or pushy onboarding 48 10.3% 5.7×
Too expensive, dislike of subscriptions 46 9.9% 8.8×
Things aren't hidden or slip through 41 8.8% 3.4×
Posting or other features break 36 7.7% 1.3×
Notifications don't arrive 25 5.4% 1.5×
Screen Time limits affect unrelated sites, or can't be removed 20 4.3% 19.1×
Account flagged, suspended or "suspicious login" 18 3.9% 8.6×
Can't log in, or logged out 15 3.2% 9.5×
No switching between multiple accounts 12 2.6% 22.9×
Asked to write a review before using the app 8 1.7% not in high ratings

Two things stand out.

Speed is the most common complaint, but it doesn't decide the rating on its own. At 1.4×, people who liked the app also mentioned it. One reviewer wrote: "Took 5 minutes to open instagram … I understand that the point is to slow down, but 5 minutes is excessive."

The rare complaints are the ones that come with one star. Account switching (22.9×), Screen Time side effects (19.1×) and login trouble (9.5×) are each under 5% of low ratings, but people who hit them rarely gave more than three stars. One reviewer described an unrelated website being blocked in their normal browser; another spent "an hour on the phone with an Apple Specialist" to get access back.

What is free also split the ratings. Low ratings said the free tier still let them scroll because suggested posts came up in the feed. In the later 50 reviews, several five-star reviews praised the opposite: that the main features worked for free.

What people asked for (1,405 reviews)

266 reviews (19%) contained a request. 65% of them came from four-and-five-star reviewers, so they read as "one more thing" rather than anger.

Request Reviews Share of the 266
Post Stories, make calls, send voice messages 110 41%
Notifications for DMs 61 23%
Sleep timer or background playback 27 10%
Dark mode 24 9%
More services (e.g. Pinterest) 19 7%
A one-time purchase instead of a subscription 17 6%
Multiple accounts 14 5%
Opening the official app sends you to the blocker 13 5%

The top two have the same cause: these apps open the web version of Instagram, which has no Stories posting, calls or push notifications. One four-star reviewer put the notification problem plainly: tapping an Instagram notification "opens instagram and not this app, then i start doomscrolling again."

In five-star reviews, the word "friends" appeared 99 times, 8.5 times the rate in one-and-two-star reviews. People don't want to leave social media. They want to keep their friends and lose the feed.

How it was counted

  • The reviews were exported from a review-tracking service as CSV, then merged and de-duplicated by review ID.
  • All 466 low ratings were read by one person. Keyword search was used to find candidates, and each was checked by reading. Keyword counting alone missed whole groups, such as the Screen Time cases.
  • Reviews in German, French, Italian and other languages (about 7%) were read in the original, not translated.
  • The "low vs high" ratio is the share of low ratings with the complaint divided by the share of high ratings with it.

Limitations

  • One app. Other apps in the category may have different problems.
  • Written reviews lean negative. On September 20 the app showed 4.76 stars from 7,317 ratings on the US store, while the written reviews averaged 3.79. Far more people tap a star than write a review.
  • One coder. The categories are my reading. I haven't published the per-review coding sheet, so the counts can't be checked line by line yet.
  • App Store only, iOS only. Nothing here is about Android.
  • Only low ratings were categorized for complaints. Request counts come from all stars.

Disclosure: what I do with this

I'm the developer of minulo, an iPhone app that opens Instagram, YouTube and other services with Reels, Shorts and suggested posts hidden. It is the same kind of app, so read this section with that in mind.

  • Hiding Reels, Shorts and suggested posts is free. Pro is optional ($9.99/month or $39.99/year in the US).
  • You sign in on each service's own page, so minulo never sees your password.
  • It shares the top request's limit: Stories posting, voice messages and calls don't work inside minulo. "Take a break" opens the official app for the minutes you choose.
  • Notifications: while minulo blocks an official app, that app's notifications don't arrive. Instagram DM notifications are a Pro beta exception.
  • It is also a web-view app, so speed is the complaint I watch most.

The full category table is on this page.

title: Solving Carpenter 1/16" Tape Rounding and IES Lighting Grids in Vanilla JS
description:
Floating-point math in JavaScript is straightforward until your output has to survive a real jobsite tape measure or a ceiling full of floor joists and garage door tracks.

While building two browser-based layout calculators for residential framing and ceiling lighting, I ran into three geometry problems where naive total / count math quietly fails in the real world. Here is how the underlying math works and how I implemented it in zero-dependency JavaScript.

1. Why "Step-Off" Rounding Ruins Railing Layouts

Under the 2024 International Residential Code (IRC R312.1.3), open guardrail balusters cannot allow a 4-inch sphere to pass through.

Suppose you have a 92" clear inside span between two deck posts using nominal 2x2 wood spindles (1.5" actual width):

export function solveLevelBalusters(clearSpanIn, balusterWidthIn = 1.5, maxClearGapIn = 4.0) {
  const minCount = Math.max(
    1,
    Math.floor((clearSpanIn - maxClearGapIn) / (balusterWidthIn + maxClearGapIn)) + 1
  );

  // If landing right on 4.000", add one spindle for lumber shrinkage margin
  let count = minCount;
  let exactGap = (clearSpanIn - count * balusterWidthIn) / (count + 1);
  if (exactGap >= maxClearGapIn - 0.02) {
    count += 1;
    exactGap = (clearSpanIn - count * balusterWidthIn) / (count + 1);
  }

  return { count, exactGap, onCenter: exactGap + balusterWidthIn };
}

For 92", 18 spindles give 19 equal gaps of 3.421" (4.921" on-center).

If you convert 4.921" to the nearest 1/16" (4-15/16", which is 4.9375") and tell a carpenter to step off a 4-15/16" spacer block 18 times down the rail, that tiny +0.0164" rounding error compounds across every spindle. By the last post, the final gap shrinks by nearly 5/16".

The fix is simple but critical: always compute cumulative positions in full floating-point from 0" (hooked on the inside face of Post A), and only snap to 1/16" at the display step:

export function formatSixteenths(inches) {
  const totalSixteenths = Math.round(inches * 16);
  const whole = Math.floor(totalSixteenths / 16);
  let num = totalSixteenths % 16;
  if (num === 0) return `${whole}"`;

  let den = 16;
  while (num % 2 === 0 && den > 1) {
    num /= 2;
    den /= 2;
  }
  return whole > 0 ? `${whole}-${num}/${den}"` : `${num}/${den}"`;
}

2. Stair Rake Projection (cos θ Trap)

Stair railings introduce a second trap. Plumb balusters stand vertically, which means the horizontal clear gap G is governed by level geometry, while carpenters hook their tape diagonally along the sloped bottom rail.

Given stair unit rise R and unit run T (for example, 7.5" rise over 10.5" run):

  1. Rake angle: θ = atan2(R, T) (≈ 35.54°)
  2. Horizontal span from sloped rail length Ls: Lh = Ls * cos(θ)
  3. Diagonal on-center step along the rail: S_sloped = (G + W) / cos(θ)

If someone marks 3-3/4" gaps directly along the 35.5° rail instead of projecting by cos(θ), the actual horizontal gap drops to 3.05", wasting spindles and crowding the stair run. And don't forget the triangular throat formed by the tread, riser, and bottom rail, where IRC R312.1.3 Exception 1 permits a 6-inch sphere (d = a + b - c incircle check on a right triangle).

I put the interactive 2D SVG/Canvas version of this cumulative tape schedule live at Baluster Spacing Calculator so you can test level runs, stair rake angles, and inline fence gate bays directly in the browser.

3. IES Zonal Cavity Lumen Method & Garage Door Shadows

On the electrical side, most "divide ceiling height by 2" rules of thumb fail in two rooms: low 7.5 ft basements (where wide-angle pancake wafers cause harsh glare) and high-bay garages (where open overhead garage doors block the front row of shop lights).

Instead of guessing fixture counts from raw floor square footage alone, the IES Zonal Cavity equation accounts for how much light is absorbed by walls above the 30" workplane:

export function solveZonalCavity({
  lengthFt,
  widthFt,
  ceilingHeightFt,
  workplaneFt = 2.5,
  targetFootcandles = 75,
  lumensPerFixture = 4500,
  llf = 0.85,
}) {
  const areaSqFt = lengthFt * widthFt;
  const hrc = Math.max(1, ceilingHeightFt - workplaneFt);

  // Room Cavity Ratio: tall narrow rooms lose more light to walls
  const rcr = (5 * hrc * (lengthFt + widthFt)) / areaSqFt;
  const cu = Math.max(0.42, Math.min(0.88, 0.88 - 0.066 * rcr));

  const rawFixtures = (areaSqFt * targetFootcandles) / (lumensPerFixture * cu * llf);
  return { areaSqFt, rcr: Number(rcr.toFixed(2)), cu: Number(cu.toFixed(3)), minFixtures: Math.ceil(rawFixtures) };
}

In a 24x24 workshop with a 10 ft ceiling aiming for 75 fc at bench height (RCR = 2.92, CU = 0.688), bare lumen division (43,200 lm / 4,500 lm = 10 lights) under-lights the bench by nearly 30%. Once cavity loss and light loss factors are included, you actually need 14 fixtures, and shifting the front row clear of the rolled-up overhead door tracks prevents dark hood shadows. You can test the live photometric heatmap and door-track clearance solver at Lighting Layout Calculator.

Open-Source Reference Equations

If you need the standalone ESM formulas for your own home-improvement scripts or CAD macros without pulling in UI dependencies, I published the reference implementations under MIT in kaiyilu/building-layout-math.

title: The Benjamin Manifesto: Zero-Drift Autonomous Dispatch, Typed Leases, and Swarm Supremacy
description:
The Benjamin Manifesto: Zero-Drift Autonomous Dispatch, Typed Leases, and Swarm Supremacy

A Declaration on Multi-Agent Coordination: Why Conversational Prompt Delegation is Broken, and How Project Benjamin Delivers Deterministic Routing, Pre-Flight Probes, and Absolute Goal Invariance.

Authored by Benni Alencar — Chief AI Systems Architect & Founder at Benni OS.

1. The Broken Telephone of Multi-Agent Systems

The technology industry has convinced itself that building multi-agent systems is simply a matter of having one LLM chat with another LLM.

In tutorial notebooks, this looks enchanting: a "Manager Agent" sends a paragraph of natural language to a "Coder Agent," which sends a paragraph to a "Tester Agent." Everyone nods. A venture capitalist writes a check.

Then the system is deployed against a complex, real-world enterprise mission:

  • By Step 3, the goal has mutated. The tester agent is testing a feature the human operator never requested, because natural language prompts degrade in semantic fidelity with every hop (the Broken Telephone catastrophe).
  • Capability Blindness strikes. A manager agent delegates a WebGL shader task or an Android APK build to a worker node that lacks GPU drivers or compilers. The worker hangs for forty minutes, burning tokens in confused retry loops.
  • Runaway Financial Burnout. An unmonitored agent encounters an unexpected exception, enters an infinite reflection loop, and spends $800 in API credits before a human notices.

The Benjamin Manifesto rejects conversational delegation entirely:

Natural language is an expressive interface for human thought; it is an atrocious, non-deterministic wire protocol for machine coordination. Autonomous multi-agent swarms must be coordinated through typed contracts, pre-flight capability probes, and cryptographic execution leases.

Project Benjamin (Skill 93 of Benni Master OS) is the supreme brain of autonomous dispatch.

2. The 4 Invariants of Benjamin Dispatch

Project Benjamin replaces loose conversational prompting with a formal Typed Work Packet (TWP) execution mesh:

flowchart TD
    subgraph Intent ["1. Mission Compilation"]
        Directive["Operator Intent / Strategic Directive"] --> IntentCompiler["Intent Compiler (Skill 90)"]
        IntentCompiler --> TWP["Typed Work Packet: Goal Vector g*, Token Budget, Invariants, SLAs"]
    end

    subgraph Probing ["2. Synchronous Pre-Flight Probe"]
        TWP --> NodeProbe{"Capability Probe: RAM, GPU Buffers, Binaries on PATH, Auth Leases"}
        NodeProbe -->|Pass| LeaseGrant["Issue Cryptographic Lease (Strict Token & Time Bounds)"]
        NodeProbe -->|Fail| AutoProvision["Auto-Provision or Dynamic Re-Route"]
    end

    subgraph Execution ["3. Sandboxed Swarm Execution"]
        LeaseGrant --> WorkerNode["Specialized Worker Agent (Isolated Workspace)"]
        WorkerNode --> ASTExecution["Local Bare-Metal Runtime / Tool Execution"]
        ASTExecution --> Telemetry["Real-Time Cosine Drift Telemetry D(s_t, g*)"]
    end

    subgraph Control ["4. Zero-Drift Enforcement & Settlement"]
        Telemetry --> DriftGate{"D(s_t, g*) <= 0.18?"}
        DriftGate -->|Aligned| RealityLock["Reality Lock Cryptographic Receipt (SHA-256)"]
        DriftGate -->|Divergent| Intercept["Semantic Intercept & Orthogonal Error Correction"]
        RealityLock --> RunLedger["Settled to Run Ledger Protocol (Skill 90c)"]
    end

3. Mathematical Foundations: Zero-Drift Angular Invariants

Let $\mathbf{g}^* \in \mathbb{R}^d$ represent the normalized semantic goal embedding vector established by the human operator. Let $\mathbf{s}_t \in \mathbb{R}^d$ represent the cumulative state embedding of a dispatched worker agent at execution step $t$.

The Semantic Drift Metric

We define instantaneous context drift $\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{s}_t, \mathbf{g}^*)$ as the angular distance in semantic latent space:

$$\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{s}_t, \mathbf{g}^) = 1 - \frac{\mathbf{s}_t \cdot \mathbf{g}^}{|\mathbf{s}_t| |\mathbf{g}^*|}$$

The Bounded Drift Invariant:

Project Benjamin enforces a strict upper bound across all execution trajectories:

$$\max_{t \in [0, T]} \mathcal{D}(\mathbf{s}t, \mathbf{g}^*) \le \Delta{\text{max}} \quad (\text{default: } \Delta_{\text{max}} = 0.18)$$

If at any point $\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{s}t, \mathbf{g}^*) > \Delta{\text{max}}$, the Benjamin Kernel executes an Immediate Semantic Intercept:

  1. Worker execution is suspended synchronously.
  2. An orthogonal error correction vector $\mathbf{e}_t = \mathbf{g}^* - \mathbf{s}_t$ is injected into the worker's active constraint layer.
  3. If the worker fails to re-converge within two micro-steps, the lease is revoked, the workspace is rolled back to its pre-dispatch checkpoint, and the task is re-routed to an alternate specialist node.

4. Pre-Flight Capability Probes: Zero LLM Burn on Broken Nodes

Before an agent consumes a single model token, Project Benjamin executes a synchronous, non-destructive Capability Probe:

  • Hardware Verification: Audits free system RAM, disk headroom, and GPU VRAM availability.
  • Binary Toolchains: Verifies that required compilers, runtimes (python, cargo, ffmpeg, node), and CLI tools exist on the system PATH.
  • Sovereign Auth Leases: Confirms that Nemesis Gateway (Skill 97) holds active, unexpired leases for all required enterprise connectors.

If any prerequisite fails, the model is never called. The failure is caught in sub-milliseconds at zero cost, eliminating the silent execution hangs that plague ordinary agent frameworks.

5. Cryptographic Leases and Anti-Loop Circuit Breakers

In Project Benjamin, no agent is granted open-ended execution authority. Every dispatch is bound by a signed Cryptographic Lease:

  • Hard Token Budget: Inviolable maximum token ceiling.
  • Tool Invocations Cap: Maximum discrete actions permitted.
  • Wall-Clock Lease: Hard execution timeout.
  • Workspace Isolation: File whitelist restricting write operations strictly to the sandboxed task directory.

Furthermore, Benjamin monitors the AST Action Hash Ring:

$$\text{ActionHash}_t = \text{SHA-256}(\text{ToolName} \parallel \text{CanonicalJSON}(\text{Arguments}))$$

If an agent repeats an identical action without state mutation in the workspace, the anti-loop circuit-breaker trips instantly, terminating the lease and rolling back the workspace.

6. The Sovereign Supremacy of Benjamin

Multi-agent coordination is an engineering problem, not a literary one.

With Project Benjamin governing your swarm:

  • Missions complete deterministically without human micromanagement.
  • Zero dollars are wasted on broken nodes or runaway hallucination loops.
  • Your enterprise achieves true swarm supremacy: dozens of specialized agents executing in perfect harmony under mathematical invariants.

Authored by Benni Alencar (@bennialencar) • Ecosystem Architect & Founder at Benni OS.

title: React Router: Pages That Change Without Reloading
description:
Open a shop site and click a product. The address bar changes, the page changes, and nothing reloads. Visitors expect that smooth switch now, and it is what makes a single-page app feel finished rather than half built. Without a router, the usual workaround is a pile of state: a variable holding the current view, a switch statement rendering one component or another, and links that are really buttons wearing a disguise. It works for two pages, then starts to creak. The address bar never changes, so a visitor cannot bookmark a product, share its link, or use the back button properly. React Router closes exactly that gap, and the question is when it is worth adding.

What I would check before using it

My first check is how many views the app really has. One page with a couple of panels does not need a router, and adding one just adds a dependency to keep updated. Three or more distinct views is where a router starts earning its place. Count the pages before reaching for the library.

My second check is whether the URLs need to mean anything. A shop lives on shareable links: a customer sends a product page to a friend, a search engine indexes it, a visitor bookmarks it. If the address bar never changes, none of that works, and the app is quietly broken for everyone who treats a URL as an address. If nobody shares or bookmarks a view, a router buys little.

My third check is the learning curve, and React Router is gentle here. The example below rests on four ideas: Routes and Route to map paths to components, Link to move between them, and useParams to read a value out of the URL. Anyone who knows React can read that code on the first pass. The cost is a dependency and a little setup.

My fourth check is the layout. Most apps repeat the same header and footer on every page, and React Router lets one layout component wrap the changing content instead of copying it into every view.

My verdict, as judgement: use React Router when an app has several views, when those views deserve real URLs, and when a shared layout would cut repetition. Skip it for a single view or a page that nobody links to. The recommendation flips when the page count drops to one, or the URLs stop mattering, because then the router is a dependency with no job to do.

One small shop, three routes, run end to end

The example is a small shop with three routes: the home page at /, a product list at /products, and a product detail page at /products/:id, where :id is a URL parameter read with useParams. The products are a canvas tote bag at $18, a ceramic mug at $14.50, and a notebook set at $9.25. Everything runs in plain Node with MemoryRouter and ReactDOMServer renderToString, so no browser and no build step are needed. MemoryRouter stands in for the BrowserRouter a real app would use, and every Link and useParams call sits inside it, because a Link rendered outside a router throws a cryptic error about a null context instead of rendering anything.

Here is the whole app:

const React = require("react");
const { renderToString } = require("react-dom/server");
const { MemoryRouter, Routes, Route, Link, useParams } = require("react-router");

const products = [
  { id: "1", name: "Canvas tote bag", price: 18.0 },
  { id: "2", name: "Ceramic mug", price: 14.5 },
  { id: "3", name: "Notebook set", price: 9.25 },
];

function Home() {
  return React.createElement("div", null,
    React.createElement("h1", null, "The Corner Shop"),
    React.createElement("p", null, "Three useful things, fairly priced."),
    React.createElement(Link, { to: "/products" }, "Browse products"));
}

function ProductList() {
  return React.createElement("div", null,
    React.createElement("h1", null, "Products"),
    React.createElement("ul", null,
      products.map((p) =>
        React.createElement("li", { key: p.id },
          React.createElement(Link, { to: "/products/" + p.id },
            p.name + " - $" + p.price.toFixed(2))))));
}

function ProductDetail() {
  const { id } = useParams();
  const product = products.find((p) => p.id === id);
  if (!product) {
    return React.createElement("div", null,
      React.createElement("h1", null, "Product not found"),
      React.createElement("p", null, "No product has id " + id + "."),
      React.createElement(Link, { to: "/products" }, "Back to products"));
  }
  return React.createElement("div", null,
    React.createElement("h1", null, product.name),
    React.createElement("p", null, "Price: $" + product.price.toFixed(2)),
    React.createElement(Link, { to: "/products" }, "Back to products"));
}

function NotFound() {
  return React.createElement("div", null,
    React.createElement("h1", null, "Page not found"),
    React.createElement(Link, { to: "/" }, "Back home"));
}

function App() {
  return React.createElement(Routes, null,
    React.createElement(Route, { path: "/", element: React.createElement(Home) }),
    React.createElement(Route, { path: "/products", element: React.createElement(ProductList) }),
    React.createElement(Route, { path: "/products/:id", element: React.createElement(ProductDetail) }),
    React.createElement(Route, { path: "*", element: React.createElement(NotFound) }));
}

for (const path of process.argv.slice(2)) {
  console.log("=== " + path + " ===");
  console.log(renderToString(
    React.createElement(MemoryRouter, { initialEntries: [path] },
      React.createElement(App))));
}

This is the real output from running it with Node, for the home page and the ceramic mug detail page:

=== / ===
<div><h1>The Corner Shop</h1><p>Three useful things, fairly priced.</p><a href="/products" data-discover="true">Browse products</a></div>
=== /products/2 ===
<div><h1>Ceramic mug</h1><p>Price: $14.50</p><a href="/products" data-discover="true">Back to products</a></div>

Two things are worth noticing. First, the URL parameter did real work: visiting /products/2 rendered the ceramic mug and its $14.50 price, pulled from the same products array as the list, so the list and the detail page can never disagree about a price. Second, the Link components rendered as ordinary anchor tags with the right href, which is why the back button and bookmarks keep working: the router is built on plain links, not on a trick.

The thing that went wrong came from the first version of this app, which had no catch-all route and no guard for a missing product. Visiting an unknown address rendered a blank page, with no error and no message, and visiting /products/999 crashed outright. Here is the real output from that broken run:

=== /nowhere ===

=== /products/999 ===
ERROR: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')

The blank page is the nastier of the two. The crash at least tells you something failed, but a blank page looks like the app loaded and chose to show nothing, so a visitor just leaves. The fix is two small additions: a route with path "*" that renders a "Page not found" message, and a guard in ProductDetail that checks whether the product exists before reading its name. After adding both, the same paths render properly, as the full run showed: /products/999 gives "Product not found" with a link back to the list, and /nowhere gives "Page not found" with a link home. Unknown URLs and unknown ids are normal traffic, not edge cases, so both guards belong in the app from the start.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

First, leaving out the catch-all route, as in the broken run above. The symptom is a blank page on any mistyped or outdated URL, with no error anywhere to point at. The fix is a Route with path "*" at the end of the Routes list, rendering a helpful not-found page with a link home.

Second, trusting the URL parameter without checking it. The symptom is a crash, "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')", when a visitor opens a product id that does not exist, because find returns undefined and the code reads a property off it. The fix is the guard shown above: look the product up, and if it is missing, render a not-found message instead of the detail view.

Third, using a plain anchor tag instead of Link for navigation inside the app. The symptom is a full page reload on every click, which throws away the app state and defeats the whole point of a router. The fix is to use Link for every in-app move, and save plain anchor tags for links that leave the site.

My call on React Router

React Router turns the address bar into a real part of the app instead of a decoration. The shop above needed four ideas, three routes, and two small guards, and every URL now leads somewhere sensible, including the wrong ones. That is the whole job, and the library does it without asking the app to change shape. Try it on a project with three or more views that people share links to, and watch the back button start behaving. If the app has one view and nobody links to it, skip the router and keep the code plain. The router is worth it when the URL matters, and not a moment sooner.

Further reading

  • React Router documentation, https://reactrouter.com/
  • React docs, Learn React, https://react.dev/learn
  • React docs, Adding Interactivity, https://react.dev/learn/adding-interactivity

Originally published at https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/react-router-pages-that-change-without.html
