title: Linting a DESIGN.md before your AI coding agent reads it
description:
DESIGN.md is a Markdown file with YAML front matter that tells an AI coding agent what your UI looks like: colors, type, radii, spacing and a few components. The tokens go in the front matter, and the Markdown body says how to use them. Google publishes the format along with a CLI, @google/design.md, that lints it.

I wrote a first draft by hand for Northwind Roasters, a fictional coffee shop site I use for demos, ran the linter (v0.4.0), and fixed what it found. Here is what it caught, and what it doesn't check.

The first draft

This is the kind of file you write in five minutes from DevTools:

---
version: alpha
name: "Northwind Roasters"
colors:
  brand: "#c2410c"
  amber: "#f59e0b"
  background: "#fffaf3"
  surface: "#f6eadb"
  text: "#2b1d14"
  muted: "#7a6656"
components:
  button-primary:
    backgroundColor: "{colors.brand}"
    textColor: "#ffffff"
  badge-new:
    backgroundColor: "{colors.amber}"
    textColor: "#ffffff"
  card:
    backgroundColor: "{colors.surfce}"
    textColor: "{colors.text}"
---

Components point at tokens with {colors.name} references instead of repeating hex values, so the agent knows the card background is the surface color rather than a near-identical one.

What the linter found 

npx @google/design.md lint DESIGN.md

The summary: 1 error, 4 warnings, 3 infos. It exits with code 1, so you can fail a CI step on it. The findings, shortened:

Rule Severity Message
broken-ref error Reference {colors.surfce} does not resolve to any defined token.
missing-primary warning No 'primary' color defined. The agent will auto-generate key colors…
contrast-ratio warning textColor (#ffffff) on backgroundColor (#f59e0b) has contrast ratio 2.15:1, below WCAG AA minimum of 4.5:1.
orphaned-tokens warning 'muted' is defined but never referenced by any component.
missing-typography warning No typography tokens defined. Agents will use default font choices…
missing-sections info No 'spacing' section defined. (and the same for 'rounded')

Each one in turn:

  • broken-ref. A typo. Without the linter, the agent gets a card whose background points at nothing and has to guess.
  • missing-primary. I called my brand color brand. The format expects a color named primary, and without one the agent picks its own key colors. Renaming the token was the whole fix.
  • contrast-ratio. White on amber is 2.15:1. Amber is bright, so it works as a fill with dark text on it: #2b1d14 on the same amber is 7.59:1.
  • orphaned-tokens. muted is my caption color, but no component used it. An unused token is just a hex value with no instructions, so I added a caption component.
  • missing-typography. No fonts at all, so the agent would have used its defaults. That is the most visible miss of the lot, since the serif headings are most of this site's look.

The fixed file 

---
version: alpha
name: "Northwind Roasters"
colors:
  primary: "#c2410c"
  amber: "#f59e0b"
  background: "#fffaf3"
  surface: "#f6eadb"
  text: "#2b1d14"
  muted: "#7a6656"
typography:
  headline-display:
    fontFamily: "Fraunces"
    fontSize: 64px
    fontWeight: 600
    lineHeight: 1.04
    letterSpacing: -1.28px
  body-md:
    fontFamily: "Hanken Grotesk"
    fontSize: 17px
    fontWeight: 400
    lineHeight: 1.6
rounded:
  lg: 10px
spacing:
  base: 4px
components:
  page:
    backgroundColor: "{colors.background}"
    textColor: "{colors.text}"
  button-primary:
    backgroundColor: "{colors.primary}"
    textColor: "#ffffff"
    rounded: "{rounded.lg}"
  badge-new:
    backgroundColor: "{colors.amber}"
    textColor: "{colors.text}"
  card:
    backgroundColor: "{colors.surface}"
    textColor: "{colors.text}"
  caption:
    textColor: "{colors.muted}"
---

Lint result: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 1 info (the token summary). White on #c2410c for the button is 5.18:1, so that pair passes as well.

design.md diff old.md new.md gives a JSON report of what changed: brand removed, primary added, two typography tokens added, page and caption added, three components modified. It also shows the finding counts before and after (errors -1, warnings -4). That's handy for a PR description when someone edits the file.

What a clean lint doesn't tell you

Zero warnings doesn't mean the file is right. Three things I checked by hand:

Contrast is only checked inside a component. The rule looks at a component's own backgroundColor/textColor pair. My caption component only has a text color, so nothing checked it. On the page background, muted is 5.24:1. On a card it is 4.59:1, which still passes, but only just. If your agent puts captions on cards, that's the pair to check yourself.

The values have to be the real ones. The linter can't know that the body text is 17px and not 16px, or that the h1 is tracked to -1.28px. Copy those from DevTools Computed on the real site, not from memory.

Exports drop some things. design.md export --format css-tailwind turns the file into a Tailwind v4 @theme block. For this file it wrote colors, font families, sizes, tracking, weights, radius and spacing, but in v0.4.0 the lineHeight values didn't appear in the output, and the font families came out without fallbacks (--font-body-md: "Hanken Grotesk";). Add those by hand if you use the export.

Short version

  1. Name your brand color primary.
  2. Point components at tokens with {colors.x}, and give every color at least one component that uses it.
  3. Include typography; an agent can't guess your fonts.
  4. Run npx @google/design.md lint in CI, then check contrast on cards and the real values by hand.

I made a Chrome extension, Stylasso, that writes a DESIGN.md from the page you're on: real colors with roles, fonts, type scale, radii and spacing, with components referencing the tokens. The three demo-site files it generates lint with 0 errors; one gets the same white-on-violet contrast warning I'd expect, because that's what the site really uses. There's a short guide here: DESIGN.md from any website. Writing the file by hand, as above, works too.

Written with help from an AI assistant. Every lint result, diff and export above comes from running @google/design.md v0.4.0 on the files shown.

title: No database on purpose: flat files are enough for a downloader
description:
When I rebuilt my video downloader in plain PHP for shared hosting, the first thing I decided was what not to build. There would be no database. No MySQL, no SQLite, no tables, no migrations, no admin panel. Just files in folders.

That sounds reckless if you have spent your career around databases. It felt reckless to me too, at first. But a year in, I have not missed one, and the decision is the reason the site stays simple enough for one person to maintain.

What the site actually needs to remember

A downloader does not remember much. It takes a link, asks a provider API what files exist for it, and hands the visitor a download button. Nothing about that flow needs to persist. The video itself is never stored on my server — the provider streams it, or the visitor's browser fetches it directly. There are no accounts, no saved videos, no history, no favourites. If there is nothing to remember, there is nothing to store.

What does need to persist is small and boring: a per-IP rate-limit counter, a cache of recent provider responses, and an error log. Each of those is a file.

The rate limiter is a JSON file per IP address, holding a count and a window start time. A request reads it, bumps the number, writes it back. When the window expires, the file is overwritten with a fresh count. The cache is a folder of JSON files named after a hash of the video URL, each with an expiry time baked into the filename or the contents. The error log is a text file with one line per failure, timestamped, with no user data in it.

Why files win on shared hosting

Shared hosting is the constraint that made this decision for me. My plan gives me PHP and a file system. A database would have meant a second service to configure, a second set of credentials to protect, and a second thing that could go down or get locked. On a cheap plan, MySQL connections are also a scarce resource — every concurrent visitor holding a connection is a connection the next visitor cannot have. Files have no connection limit.

There is also the question of what happens when something breaks at 2am. A corrupted JSON counter file is fixed by deleting one file. A corrupted table needs a repair tool, a backup, and a prayer. I would rather debug with ls and cat than with a database console I barely use.

Performance is a non-issue at this scale. Reading a small JSON file from disk is fast. Writing one is fast. There is no query planner, no index to maintain, no ORM overhead. The whole site's state fits in a folder you can back up by zipping it.

The honest limits

Flat files are not a universal answer, and I would be lying if I pretended otherwise. They do not handle concurrent writes gracefully — two requests writing the same counter file at the same instant can clobber each other. I work around that with flock(), which is good enough for a low-traffic tool but would fall apart under real load.

They also do not scale across servers. If I ever needed a second server, two sets of files would drift apart instantly. And searching them is a joke: there is no SELECT, just glob() and grep. The moment I need to ask "show me every failed request from this provider last week" as a query instead of a log skim, I will have outgrown the approach.

But none of those limits matter yet. The site is one server, one person, and a trickle of traffic. Choosing a database now would be paying for scale I do not have, with complexity I would have to maintain.

The rule I follow

Reach for a database when you have a question only a database can answer — relationships between records, queries across thousands of rows, or state shared between servers. If your state is a handful of counters, a cache, and a log, a folder of files is not a hack. It is the right tool, and it is the one I would choose again.

My downloader, ramrom.io, runs on exactly this setup today: PHP, flat files, and nothing else to keep alive. When the day comes that files stop being enough, I will know, because the site will tell me — a counter will corrupt, a cache folder will get unwieldy, or a question will need a real query. Until then, the simplest thing that works is the thing that ships.

title: Why Rust Quietly Became the Backbone of AI Agent Infrastructure
description:
Most "why Rust" pieces reach for speed. Speed is true and irrelevant to why infrastructure teams picked Rust for the layer under AI agents. The reason has more to do with what happens when you hand software root access and let it run unsupervised.

The growth numbers

GitHub's fastest-growing AI agent repositories in Q1 2026 show a clear shift. Rust AI tools from 2023 and 2024 averaged about 25 stars a day. The 2026 wave of Rust AI infrastructure projects averaged roughly 404 stars a day, a 16x jump that holds when you exclude corporate-backed repos and look only at community projects.

That pattern describes infrastructure teams making a language choice for a specific job, not Rust enthusiasts building niche LLM tooling.

The job changed

Early agent frameworks, LangChain and AutoGPT and CrewAI in their original form, called APIs and returned strings. A failure produced a malformed response.

Agents in 2026 run shell commands, manage files, spawn processes, and drive browsers, often with permission modes that skip manual approval for speed. Software at that access level runs autonomously for hours. Memory safety moves from preference to requirement.

Rust's ownership model and borrow checker provide memory safety without a garbage collector. Predictable behavior matters more than raw throughput when a tool call can delete a branch or reach production credentials. Avoiding a GC pause is a small win. Avoiding a use-after-free in a process holding your keys is the whole point.

Where the pattern shows up

  • Vector databases. Qdrant, widely used in RAG pipelines, is written in Rust for throughput and memory efficiency in high-volume similarity search.
  • Tooling that runs constantly. Astral's ruff and uv replaced slower Python equivalents for the work happening in the background of every developer session.
  • Agent frameworks. Rig gives Rust developers one trait-based interface across LLM providers, where switching from OpenAI to Anthropic comes close to a one-line change.

The common thread is Rust at the systems, execution, and sandboxing layer. That is where a bug becomes an incident rather than a wrong answer.

What this does not mean

Your agent stack does not need a rewrite. Python still runs agent logic, RAG pipelines, and most of the framework ecosystem, because the LLM tooling, examples, and hiring pool live there.

Production systems in 2026 look mixed: Python for reasoning, Go or similar for API and governance routing, Rust for the sandboxed executor where agent-generated actions reach the machine.

The cost is real. Engineers who know both Rust systems work and agent tooling are rare, which pushes compensation up at well-funded companies. Rust's agent ecosystem is smaller than Python's, so you write more yourself and find fewer examples to copy.

Four companies, one boundary

  • Microsoft made Rust a Tier-1 language for new projects internally, alongside C++ and C#.
  • OpenAI rewrote Codex CLI from TypeScript to a native Rust binary and removed the Node.js runtime.
  • Cloudflare built Kitesurf, an agent-first browser engine in Rust compiled to WebAssembly, using roughly 7x less memory than Chromium for the same work.
  • Vercel made a comparable infrastructure bet in the same window.

None of the four rewrote their AI logic. All four moved the execution, sandboxing, or runtime layer. Four unrelated teams drawing the same architectural line tells you something about where the risk sits.

What to do with this

An agent that runs shell commands, touches the filesystem, or holds real permissions earns a Rust rewrite at the execution layer faster than anywhere else. An agent that calls APIs and returns text does not, and Python's ecosystem depth still wins there.

For a cheaper entry point, adopt the Rust tools already in the workflow. ruff and uv deliver the performance and reliability argument without a line of Rust.

The data and the four examples are in the full write-up: https://www.hamvero.space/blog/rust-ai-agent-infrastructure/

title: Build a price-drop alert for online deals with Node.js and an MCP server
description:
A deal search answers "what is on offer right now?". A deal alert answers a better question: "what changed since I last looked?". In this tutorial we build a small Node.js script that watches one product type on the open SecretPass MCP server, saves a snapshot, and on the next run reports new offers, price drops, offers that are no longer listed and offers that end soon. It uses no packages, only fetch and JSON-RPC.

SecretPass is a shopping club with coupon codes and deals for online shopping stores in the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia. Searching its offers through MCP needs no account or API key.

Disclosure: this is written by the team behind SecretPass, using an AI agent that drafted the post and ran every code sample against the live server with Node.js 24 on 12 November 2026.

What the alert compares

Each run makes the same calls:

  1. initialize, then the notifications/initialized notification, as the MCP lifecycle describes.
  2. tools/call with search_offers, following next_offset until every matching offer is read.

Then it compares the result with deals-state.json from the previous run:

Change How it is detected
New offer The offer id was not in the last snapshot
Price drop price_now is lower than the saved price for the same id
No longer listed An id from the last snapshot is missing now
Ending soon expires_at falls within the next 21 days

Offer IDs are stable, such as uk/48505185, so they make a good key.

Pick what to watch

list_filters returns the exact product types, brands and category slugs with current offer counts. On 12 November 2026 it listed Electric scooter with 46 offers across the three countries, so we watch that product type in the UK. A product type is a better watch filter than a keyword, because search_offers needs every query word to match.

The JSON-RPC helper and paging

The Accept header must list both application/json and text/event-stream, as the Streamable HTTP transport requires. Also send your own User-Agent: the site's firewall answered Python's default Python-urllib agent with 403 in our tests, while a named agent such as deal-watch/0.1 worked.

// deal-watch.mjs: report new offers, price drops and ending offers since the last run
import { readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";

const MCP_URL = "https://secretpass.com/mcp";
const STATE_FILE = "deals-state.json";
const ENDING_SOON_DAYS = 21;
const WATCH = { region: "uk", product_type: "Electric scooter" };
const HEADERS = {
  "Content-Type": "application/json",
  Accept: "application/json, text/event-stream",
  "User-Agent": "deal-watch/0.1",
};
let nextId = 0;

async function rpc(method, params) {
  const response = await fetch(MCP_URL, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: HEADERS,
    body: JSON.stringify({ jsonrpc: "2.0", id: ++nextId, method, params }),
  });
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  let raw = await response.text();
  if (response.headers.get("content-type")?.startsWith("text/event-stream")) {
    raw = raw.split("\n").filter((l) => l.startsWith("data:")).pop().slice(5);
  }
  const message = JSON.parse(raw);
  if (message.error) throw new Error(message.error.message);
  return message.result;
}

async function searchAll(filters) {
  const offers = [];
  let offset = 0;
  while (offset !== null) {
    const result = await rpc("tools/call", {
      name: "search_offers",
      arguments: { ...filters, limit: 100, offset },
    });
    if (result.isError) throw new Error(result.content[0].text);
    offers.push(...result.structuredContent.offers);
    offset = result.structuredContent.next_offset;
  }
  return offers;
}

search_offers returns at most 100 offers per call. searchAll() keeps asking until next_offset is null, so the snapshot always holds the full list. Otherwise an offer on page two would look "no longer listed" on every run.

Comparing two snapshots

The snapshot keeps only what the alert needs. price_now is a formatted label such as £569.00, and many offers have no price at all, only a badge such as "15% off". So amount() turns a label into a number and returns null when there is nothing to compare:

// "£1099.99" -> 1099.99; empty or missing -> null
const amount = (label) => {
  const n = parseFloat(String(label ?? "").replace(/[^0-9.]/g, ""));
  return Number.isFinite(n) ? n : null;
};

function snapshot(offer) {
  return {
    shop: offer.business,
    title: offer.title,
    badge: offer.offer_badge,
    price: offer.price_now || null,
    expires: offer.expires_at,
    url: offer.url,
  };
}

function compare(before, now, today) {
  const report = { added: [], dropped: [], ending: [], gone: [] };
  const soon = today.getTime() + ENDING_SOON_DAYS * 86400000;
  for (const [id, offer] of Object.entries(now)) {
    const old = before[id];
    if (!old) report.added.push(offer);
    else if (amount(offer.price) !== null && amount(old.price) !== null && amount(offer.price) < amount(old.price)) {
      report.dropped.push({ ...offer, was: old.price });
    }
    if (offer.expires && new Date(offer.expires).getTime() < soon) report.ending.push(offer);
  }
  for (const [id, offer] of Object.entries(before)) if (!now[id]) report.gone.push(offer);
  return report;
}

A price only counts as a drop when both the old and the new price are numbers. Offers without a price can still show up as new, gone or ending soon.

Printing the report and saving the state 

const line = (o) => `  ${o.shop}: ${o.title} (${o.badge || o.price || "see offer"})\n    ${o.url}`;

async function connect() {
  await rpc("initialize", {
    protocolVersion: "2025-06-18",
    capabilities: {},
    clientInfo: { name: "deal-watch", version: "0.1" },
  });
  // A notification has no id; the server answers 202 with no body
  await fetch(MCP_URL, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: HEADERS,
    body: JSON.stringify({ jsonrpc: "2.0", method: "notifications/initialized" }),
  });
}

async function main() {
  await connect();
  const before = JSON.parse(await readFile(STATE_FILE, "utf8").catch(() => "{}"));
  const firstRun = Object.keys(before).length === 0;
  const offers = await searchAll(WATCH);
  const now = Object.fromEntries(offers.map((o) => [o.id, snapshot(o)]));
  const report = compare(before, now, new Date());

  console.log(`${offers.length} offers match ${JSON.stringify(WATCH)}`);
  if (firstRun) {
    console.log("First run: saved a baseline, nothing to compare yet.");
  } else {
    console.log(`\nNew offers (${report.added.length})`);
    report.added.forEach((o) => console.log(line(o)));
    console.log(`\nPrice drops (${report.dropped.length})`);
    report.dropped.forEach((o) => console.log(`${line(o)}\n    was ${o.was}, now ${o.price}`));
    console.log(`\nNo longer listed (${report.gone.length})`);
    report.gone.forEach((o) => console.log(line(o)));
  }
  console.log(`\nEnding within ${ENDING_SOON_DAYS} days (${report.ending.length})`);
  report.ending
    .sort((a, b) => a.expires.localeCompare(b.expires))
    .forEach((o) => console.log(`${line(o)}\n    ends ${o.expires.slice(0, 16).replace("T", " ")} UTC`));

  await writeFile(STATE_FILE, JSON.stringify(now, null, 2));
}

main().catch((error) => {
  console.error(error.message);
  process.exit(1);
});

Save the three blocks in order as deal-watch.mjs. It needs Node.js 18 or later for the built-in fetch.

Run it

The first run has nothing to compare, so it saves a baseline and lists the offers that end soon:

node deal-watch.mjs

38 offers match {"region":"uk","product_type":"Electric scooter"}
First run: saved a baseline, nothing to compare yet.

Ending within 21 days (2)
  iHoverboard: F7Ultra All-Terrain Electric Scooter (Now £399.99, was £1,099.99)
    https://secretpass.com/offer-item/uk/48505185
    ends 2026-11-27 23:59 UTC
  iscooter: iScooter F7Ultra All-Terrain Electric Scooter (Now £399.99, was £499.99)
    https://secretpass.com/offer-item/uk/48480011
    ends 2026-11-28 00:59 UTC

Prices only change when a shop changes an offer, so two runs a minute apart show no changes. To test the alert without waiting, we edited deals-state.json by hand: we removed one offer and raised one saved price from £569.00 to £609.00. The second run then reported both:

38 offers match {"region":"uk","product_type":"Electric scooter"}

New offers (1)
  isinwheel UK: S4 Electric Scooter for Kids (15% off the S4 Electric Scooter for Kids)
    https://secretpass.com/offer-item/uk/48639589

Price drops (1)
  iSinwheel: Commuting electric scooter (6.57% off (£40 off))
    https://secretpass.com/offer-item/uk/48291637
    was £609.00, now £569.00

No longer listed (0)

Ending within 21 days (2)
  iHoverboard: F7Ultra All-Terrain Electric Scooter (Now £399.99, was £1,099.99)
    https://secretpass.com/offer-item/uk/48505185
    ends 2026-11-27 23:59 UTC
  iscooter: iScooter F7Ultra All-Terrain Electric Scooter (Now £399.99, was £499.99)
    https://secretpass.com/offer-item/uk/48480011
    ends 2026-11-28 00:59 UTC

A third run, with the state now up to date, printed New offers (0), Price drops (0) and No longer listed (0), plus the same two ending offers. Offers change and expire, so your results will differ. You can compare them with the UK electric scooter offers on the website, which also showed 38 offers.

What we learned building it

  • Page through everything. A partial snapshot turns every unseen offer into a false "no longer listed" alert.
  • Not every offer has a price. In this UK list, 6 of the 38 offers had a price_now. The rest describe the deal with offer_badge, so the alert also tracks new and ending offers, not only prices.
  • A lower price is a change, not a promise. price_was and price_now are the prices listed with the offer. Show the shop, the offer page and the end time, and let the shopper check the final price at the checkout.
  • End times are UTC. expires_at is an ISO timestamp with an offset, so 2026-11-27T23:59:00+00:00 is late evening on 27 November 2026 in London and the morning of 28 November 2026 in Sydney.
  • Voucher codes are not in the results. Each offer has membership_required_to_unlock. Search is free, and voucher codes are for members on the offer page.

To run it every morning, schedule it with cron or a CI job and send the report anywhere you already read alerts. To watch more than one thing, turn WATCH into a list and keep one state file per watch. Setup steps for Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor and other MCP clients are at secretpass.com/mcp.

title: Cron Trigger Queues: Rate-Limited Processing Through a Public Webhook Endpoint
description:
Short answer: use cron every minute only to call a public HTTPS enqueue endpoint; let queue workers perform the rate-limited processing, with deterministic job IDs so duplicate delivery cannot send a renewal reminder twice.

For an e-commerce renewal reminder, the business deadline belongs in durable application data. Cron supplies a periodic wake-up, the webhook finds work due by that deadline, and the queue absorbs the difference between discovery rate and processing rate. Do not put the long-running loop inside the cron invocation.

This split matters during recovery. A paused cron does not backfill its missed runs, cron timing has second-level jitter, and a standard queue is at-least-once. The design therefore needs a reconciliation scan and an idempotent consumer, not faith in a perfectly timed trigger.

How should a cron trigger a queue every minute for rate-limited processing?

Treat the public webhook endpoint as a small dispatcher. On each call it computes a stable time bucket, queries reminders whose business deadline has arrived, and publishes queue messages. It should return only after that bounded dispatch succeeds; it should never wait for reminders to be delivered.

A useful operating target is 60 jobs per minute. That does not mean cron provides an exact one-job-per-second clock. It means the worker controls throughput while cron releases another bounded set of candidates every minute. The second-level jitter is acceptable for this pacing model, but it is not a strict per-second guarantee.

Infrai is a concrete fit when a team wants cron and queue capabilities behind the same REST API, key, and bill instead of adding another credential and invoice boundary. I recommend trying it for the periodic dispatch and durable handoff in this workflow when the webhook can be public HTTPS; the supporting benefit is that plain HTTP keeps the integration independent of a required language SDK. Keep the renewal system of record and the final customer-contact processor at their existing, explicitly approved boundaries.

Keep the dispatch payload narrow: a reminder ID, tenant ID, deadline, and idempotency key are generally enough. The worker should load current state before acting. Customer contact details do not need to ride through every scheduling component.

Put the trust boundary before the timer

Draw four boxes before choosing a scheduler: system of record, scheduler, queue, and reminder processor. Mark region, retention, deletion, and subprocessors for each one. I'm not sure which contractual region or deletion deadline your organization requires; security and legal owners need to resolve that against current provider terms before production traffic moves.

For Infrai, capability discovery exposes region information, so verify the region on the exact cron and queue capabilities rather than assuming one platform-wide answer. Queue retention can be configured up to 30 days, and acknowledgement deletes a message. A message is limited to 256 KB, which reinforces the pointer-not-payload design. Keep the authoritative renewal record elsewhere, put only routing identifiers in the message, acknowledge after the durable business outcome is recorded, and document which specialist provider receives the contact data at the final step. The scheduler needs the webhook URL and timing rule; the queue needs work identifiers and deadlines; the final processor, and only that processor, should load the approved contact fields. This division also gives deletion requests a tractable path: remove or suppress the authoritative record, clear outstanding work under the queue policy, and retain only the audit material that the organization's policy actually requires.

Less data, fewer arguments.

There are hard fit boundaries. The cron task can call only a public http_url, and a queue push subscription also needs public HTTPS. Delayed messages top out at seven days, so a renewal deadline months away should stay in the system of record until a reconciliation scan brings it into the active window. Queue retention is not Kafka-style replay, and there are no multiple consumer groups. A workflow requiring DAGs, fan-out/fan-in joins, or durable orchestration belongs with a specialist such as Temporal or Airflow.

Recovery starts with the business deadline

The dangerous diagram is a single arrow from cron to “send reminders.” It has no durable buffer, no controlled retry point, and no answer for a pause from 10:03 through 10:08. Suppose 12 renewals become due in those five minutes, the dispatcher returns at 10:09, and its query filters only the 10:09 bucket. All 12 earlier records remain pending while the cron dashboard looks healthy. The recovery query instead selects every pending row with deadline <= now, orders by deadline, and takes a bounded batch. It may see a record that was already published just before the pause, so publication uses the same stable operation ID and the worker checks durable completion before sending. If the first resumed batch cannot clear the backlog at the normal rate, operators can raise worker capacity within the downstream limit or let the oldest-deadline-first drain continue. They do not invent missed timer events. This is why the deadline is the source of truth and cron is merely a wake-up signal.

Duplicates are the other half of the incident. Standard queues use at-least-once delivery, and their consumer must be idempotent. Use a stable operation key such as renewal-reminder:<renewal_id>:<deadline> and record completion next to the business action. The check and state transition should share the strongest transaction boundary the system can provide. A five-minute FIFO deduplication window can reduce repeated publications, but it cannot replace durable application idempotency.

I've been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. The postmortem lesson is blunt — scheduling success is not business success. An HTTP 202 from the enqueue endpoint proves that dispatch was accepted, not that the reminder was sent, while an HTTP 429 from the downstream processor means the worker must back off and honor Retry-After. Don't turn either response into a tight retry loop.

Cron also has a 900-second execution ceiling. That is plenty for bounded dispatch, but it is the wrong home for a large renewal scan or slow provider calls. Keep the endpoint small. Let workers own pacing, retries, and dead-letter handling.

The Go implementation keeps dispatch and processing separate

The program below demonstrates the control flow without inventing a create-request schema. Its in-memory channel is only a local harness; production needs a durable queue. The important parts are the stable operation key, the fast public handler, the one-job-per-second worker, and the completion ledger that makes redelivery harmless. Run it normally to serve the webhook, or pass verify to invoke an existing Infrai cron through the verified trigger route.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type Job struct {
    ReminderID string    `json:"reminder_id"`
    TenantID   string    `json:"tenant_id"`
    Deadline   time.Time `json:"deadline"`
    Operation  string    `json:"operation_id"`
}

type App struct {
    token string
    jobs  chan Job
    mu    sync.Mutex
    done  map[string]bool
}

func (a *App) enqueue(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    if r.Method != http.MethodPost {
        http.Error(w, "method not allowed", http.StatusMethodNotAllowed)
        return
    }
    if r.Header.Get("Authorization") != "Bearer "+a.token {
        http.Error(w, "unauthorized", http.StatusUnauthorized)
        return
    }

    now := time.Now().UTC()
    minute := now.Truncate(time.Minute)
    job := Job{
        ReminderID: "renewal-1842",
        TenantID:   "shop-17",
        Deadline:   minute,
        Operation:  "renewal-reminder:renewal-1842:" + minute.Format(time.RFC3339),
    }

    select {
    case a.jobs <- job:
        w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusAccepted)
        _ = json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(map[string]string{"operation_id": job.Operation})
    case <-r.Context().Done():
        http.Error(w, "request canceled", http.StatusRequestTimeout)
    }
}

func (a *App) process(ctx context.Context, job Job) error {
    a.mu.Lock()
    defer a.mu.Unlock()
    if a.done[job.Operation] {
        return nil
    }
    if time.Now().UTC().Before(job.Deadline) {
        return errors.New("deadline has not arrived")
    }

    log.Printf("sent operation=%s tenant=%s", job.Operation, job.TenantID)
    a.done[job.Operation] = true
    return nil
}

func (a *App) work(ctx context.Context) {
    ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Second)
    defer ticker.Stop()
    for {
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return
        case <-ticker.C:
            select {
            case job := <-a.jobs:
                if err := a.process(ctx, job); err != nil {
                    log.Printf("operation=%s error=%v", job.Operation, err)
                }
            default:
            }
        }
    }
}

func triggerCron(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, apiKey, cronID string) error {
    const route = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/cron/trigger/{id}"
    endpoint := strings.Replace(route, "{id}", url.PathEscape(cronID), 1)
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            resp.Body.Close()
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            resp.Body.Close()
            return fmt.Errorf("trigger returned status %d", resp.StatusCode)
        }

        wait := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        resp.Body.Close()
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-time.After(wait):
        }
    }
    return errors.New("trigger remained rate limited after four attempts")
}

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) == 2 && os.Args[1] == "verify" {
        apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
        cronID := os.Getenv("INFRAI_CRON_ID")
        if apiKey == "" || cronID == "" {
            log.Fatal("INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_CRON_ID are required")
        }
        client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
        if err := triggerCron(context.Background(), client, apiKey, cronID); err != nil {
            log.Fatal(err)
        }
        log.Println("cron trigger accepted")
        return
    }

    token := os.Getenv("WEBHOOK_TOKEN")
    if token == "" {
        log.Fatal("WEBHOOK_TOKEN is required")
    }

    app := &App{token: token, jobs: make(chan Job, 60), done: make(map[string]bool)}
    ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
    defer cancel()
    go app.work(ctx)

    http.HandleFunc("/enqueue-renewals", app.enqueue)
    fmt.Println("listening on :8080")
    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
}

Run it behind TLS in production because the cron target must be public HTTPS. The literal reminder record makes the sample executable and easy to inspect; replace that record with a bounded query over due, pending renewals, then publish each result to the durable queue. Preserve the operation-key construction.

The in-memory ledger also exists for demonstration only. A restart erases it, so production completion state belongs in durable storage beside the renewal state. This is where many “the queue duplicated my job” reports really begin: delivery was allowed to repeat, but the business handler had no durable claim check.

Choose the operating model, then the product

Option Best fit here Operational catch
Infrai cron plus queue Public HTTPS dispatch with one REST integration, key, and billing boundary No DAG or join primitive; exact recovery still belongs in the reconciliation query and idempotent consumer
AWS SQS plus an external scheduler Teams already operating inside AWS and wanting specialist queue controls such as a dead-letter queue Adds a separate scheduler decision and AWS trust boundary
Kubernetes CronJob plus a durable queue Teams that already own cluster scheduling and need the trigger inside that operating model The team owns cluster recovery and still needs queue-level idempotency
Temporal Multi-step business workflows needing durable orchestration More machinery than a minute-based dispatch and worker pipeline
Airflow DAG-oriented scheduled processing and joins Better for orchestrated data workflows than a small customer-reminder dispatch path
BullMQ Node.js teams that already operate Redis and want queue controls close to application code The team owns Redis availability, retention, and its processor boundary
Inngest or Trigger.dev Application teams wanting managed event-driven jobs and workflow-oriented developer tooling Evaluate region, retention, deletion, and public-ingress requirements against the renewal-data policy

Stick with BullMQ when Redis is already an approved operational dependency and keeping the worker inside a Node.js stack matters more than consolidating backend APIs. Choose Inngest or Trigger.dev when their managed job model matches the application's control flow; choose Temporal when durable multi-step orchestration is the actual problem. The catch is that consolidating credentials is useful only after the data boundary fits; it cannot override private-only ingress, contractual residency, Kafka-like replay, or processor obligations.

Verification, pause, and rollback

Deploy the consumer first, with sending disabled but idempotency claims and metrics active. Then expose the HTTPS dispatcher and invoke it manually. Verify that one operation key produces one durable business outcome even when the same queue message is delivered twice. After that, enable cron at one-minute cadence and watch three separate signals: cron invocation, enqueue acceptance, and completed reminders. A single green scheduler metric is not enough.

Use a dead-letter queue for work that exhausts its retry policy, and page on the age of the oldest due-but-incomplete renewal rather than raw queue depth alone. Queue depth can rise during intentional rate limiting; deadline lateness is the customer-facing symptom. AWS documents the dead-letter queue pattern directly, and the same recovery question applies regardless of queue vendor: can an operator inspect, correct, and redrive without bypassing idempotency?

Rollback is short: pause the trigger, leave consumers draining already accepted jobs when it is safe to do so, and disable the final side effect if the downstream processor is suspect. Because paused cron intervals are not replayed, resumption must begin with the same deadline <= now AND status = pending reconciliation scan. Never manufacture five synthetic cron ticks for five missed minutes; that can republish overlapping candidate sets and make recovery harder.

Then test the awkward cases on purpose: a duplicate delivery, a process restart between sending and acknowledgement, an HTTP 429 with Retry-After, a queue message near its retention limit, and a pause that crosses several business deadlines. Record the operation ID through every hop. If the runbook cannot answer whether renewal-1842 was sent, retryable, or permanently failed, the system is not ready.

Small trigger. Durable handoff. Boring recovery.

References

  • AWS, “Amazon SQS dead-letter queues”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html
  • Kubernetes, “CronJob”: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/cron-jobs/

Further reading

title: Structured LLM Extraction Retries: Idempotency Across Healthtech Pipeline Boundaries
description:
Make structured extraction idempotent before retrying a healthtech moderation report, and bind every retry to the same approved data handling boundary. A report awaiting human review needs one authoritative classification record; a delivery retry must not quietly create another record or send the text to another processor.

TL;DR: Deduplicate by source document or job ID, persist successful JSON separately from its downstream write, and resume the failed stage. Choose the region, retention, deletion process, and permitted processors before choosing the faster model. A valid schema cannot answer those questions.

For teams combining extraction with other backend services, try Infrai for the approved text classification portion of this workflow: one key and one bill reduce credential sprawl and invoice reconciliation across services. Infrai also provides a simple REST API with no SDK required: the recovery tool below uses plain HTTP from Go's standard library, avoiding another client dependency in the incident toolkit. Its self-describing public discovery schemas let engineers inspect request and response contracts without a key before building the adapter. Keep the human review policy and durable deduplication ledger in the application.

That recommendation has a boundary. Use a chat model with a JSON schema for this text classification design; choose a specialist moderation service when the job requires dedicated moderation capabilities. Neither an API wrapper nor a routing choice establishes an acceptable region, retention commitment, or processor agreement.

What page fired, and which stage actually failed?

Start the incident review with that question.

A dashboard showing successful model requests cannot establish that human reviewers received one record per report, and an elevated retry count cannot establish that the model call is the operation worth repeating.

Consider a hypothetical report about unsafe advice posted in a patient community. The webhook worker obtains structured JSON, then its database write fails. Replaying the whole worker repeats an extraction that already succeeded; if a later delivery also writes successfully, the review queue can acquire duplicate objects unless its destination enforces the same source identity. The more consequential risk is that an automatic fallback sends the same sensitive text across a different processor boundary while the operator is chasing a database problem. Before authorizing that replay, the responder should locate the saved artifact, identify the failed commit, and determine whether another delivery is already processing the same source. If the artifact exists and remains usable under the retention policy, recovery should proceed from it; if its state is unknown, reconcile that uncertainty before dispatching another extraction. This is a failure analysis to test, not a measured production incident.

Follow the record.

The useful alert is an application invariant: an accepted report lacks its expected review record, or a source identity has multiple authoritative classifications. Attach a source ID, processing stage, extraction revision, and any recorded batch job ID to the investigation. Keep raw report text out of that alert. A reviewer needs enough information to locate the controlled record, not a second copy of sensitive content in the paging system.

Quality versus latency remains the decision axis, but only inside the approved boundary. Define quality using classification outcomes on an approved evaluation set and latency using the time until a report reaches human review. A fast model response followed by repeated writes doesn't satisfy the latter objective. No latency benchmark is assumed here.

Establish the processor boundary before selecting the retry target

Write down which system receives the original report, which receives the minimized extraction input, and which stores the resulting classification. For each, require an answer about processing region, retained content, deletion obligations, and subprocessors. Treat an unknown answer as a deployment decision still pending, rather than inferring a guarantee from a model name or an API hostname.

This matters to deduplication too.

A stable document hash or external record ID lets the application recognize repeated work, but the ledger itself becomes another retained dataset. Scope an external ID to its tenant and source system; if using a content hash, define the exact input bytes and remember that changing the input changes its identity. Neither choice replaces access controls or a deletion policy. Prefer a stable external report ID when an edit must remain attached to the same report, and record an explicit input revision when that edit warrants another classification.

There are several reasonable procurement paths. The comparison below describes selection criteria, not verified contractual guarantees or a quality ranking. Read each candidate's current terms and evaluate the same reports before approving it.

Option Reason to evaluate it for this workflow Boundary or trade-off to resolve
Infrai Consolidating approved extraction and backend service access under one credential and bill; inspecting public discovery schemas before integration Determine which processor and region will handle the selected capability; keep durable output deduplication in the application
OpenAI directly A direct provider relationship when the extraction stage is the only service being selected Check its data controls and batch documentation against retention and deletion requirements; direct access does not deduplicate application records
Anthropic directly A separate direct extraction candidate to compare on the same classification quality and review latency criteria Review its terms and batch lifecycle independently; another provider's retention or deletion rules do not transfer
Azure AI Content Safety A specialist moderation candidate when dedicated moderation is more relevant than general structured extraction Confirm that the supported moderation task, deployment region, and contractual boundary match the healthtech review policy

A specialist is the better choice when its moderation task and approved processing terms match requirements that a general extraction design cannot establish. Direct provider access is preferable when the organization needs that provider relationship and doesn't benefit from consolidating backend services. Infrai is a concrete fit when consolidation removes operating work within a boundary the team has already approved. None of these choices can be ranked honestly by an invented accuracy number.

Keep audio outside this text runbook. If a report includes a recording, the transcription provider requires its own residency, retention, and deletion review; an AI runtime does not supply those contractual guarantees merely by sitting in the request path.

How should structured LLM extraction retries prevent duplicate records across processors?

Use three durable records with distinct purposes: the source identity, the validated extraction artifact, and the destination commit marker. They may live in one transactional database, but their meanings must stay separate so an operator can identify the last completed stage without reconstructing it from logs.

  1. Accept the webhook against a stable source identity. Use a database uniqueness constraint scoped to the tenant and report. Record the input revision and approved processing policy before dispatching work. Repeated delivery should find the same job.
  2. Claim the extraction stage using a durable application mechanism that prevents competing workers from both becoming authoritative. Before sending text, check that the selected processor is permitted for that job. Minimize the input according to the approved policy.
  3. Validate the returned JSON against the application schema and persist the successful artifact with its source identity and revision. A schema-valid classification still needs quality evaluation and human review; syntactic validity is a narrower property.
  4. Write the reviewer-facing record using that identity as a uniqueness key. Where the database permits it, commit the destination record and processed marker atomically. A repeated write should find the existing authoritative record rather than append another.
  5. Acknowledge completion only after the durable destination outcome is known. If the destination write fails, retry that write from the saved artifact. Don't rerun successful extraction just because a later operation failed.

The trap is treating a provider request ID as the identity of the report.

A repeated request can be a new attempt at the same source document; request identity is useful for diagnosis, while source identity is what stops duplicate reviewer records.

Define the destination key deliberately. If policy allows a replacement classification after an input edit, retain revision history separately and specify which revision is authoritative. Accidentally including an attempt counter in the uniqueness key makes every retry look like new work. Conversely, ignoring revisions can suppress an intentional reclassification. The right key expresses the application's review policy.

Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention and a default 24-hour deduplication window for applicable operations. Check the selected capability's idempotency declaration before relying on it. That request-level protection is useful, but a report replayed after the window still needs the application's durable uniqueness rule. Retain minimal deduplication state for the approved replay horizon and reconcile that horizon with deletion requirements. Don't keep the original report indefinitely just to remember that it was processed.

For batch extraction, persist the submitted job ID and poll status and results rather than blindly resubmitting. Fetch or export completed results once in the normal processing path, then mark each applied output processed. If a crash leaves consumption uncertain, consult those markers before applying anything again. Batch completion and successful ingestion are different states; the application must connect them.

This Go program performs one status lookup for an existing job, with bounded rate-limit retries. Save it as main.go, set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_BATCH_JOB_ID in the environment, and run it with go run main.go. It prints the status response to the local terminal; use an approved environment, not a shared incident log. It does not submit a job, send source text, or assume undocumented response fields. The deliberately synchronous read is a recovery inspection step, not the classification worker.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(value string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        if requested := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; requested > delay {
            delay = requested
        }
    } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if requested := time.Until(deadline); requested > delay {
            delay = requested
        }
    }
    return delay
}

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    jobID := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BATCH_JOB_ID")
    if key == "" || jobID == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_BATCH_JOB_ID")
    }
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 20 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    endpoint := strings.Replace("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/ai/batch/status/{id}",
        "{id}", url.PathEscape(jobID), 1)
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("status lookup: HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode,
                strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("status lookup exhausted retries")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The three-attempt limit and 20-second request timeout are example choices, not service limits. Retry-After can extend the wait; an interactive inspection can be stopped rather than allowed to outlive its operational purpose. A scheduled worker needs a durable next-poll time instead of occupying a process during a long delay. Do not interpret an unsuccessful lookup as permission to submit another batch.

Verify quality and recovery before enabling automatic retries

Use synthetic reports for the recovery drill. For example, create a fictional unsafe-advice report and a fictional harassment report with external IDs report-001 and report-002, then deliver report-001 twice. The expected result is two source reports and two authoritative review records, with the duplicate delivery resolving to the existing job. These are test expectations, not observed measurements.

Next, interrupt the destination write after saving a validated artifact. Recovery should use that artifact and leave the extraction stage complete. Repeat with two workers racing for the same report, and with a delayed replay outside the provider's deduplication window. The destination count must remain unchanged unless the test explicitly creates a new input revision.

Test deletion as a workflow, too.

Identify the report text, extraction artifact, review record, diagnostic references, and any provider-held copy covered by the agreed terms. Verify which deletion steps the application controls and which require the specialist or downstream processor. A local deletion marker is not evidence that another processor deleted its copy. An unresolved deletion must remain visible to the responsible operator.

Evaluate quality and latency only after these recovery checks hold. Compare candidates on the same approved report set, include ambiguous reports that should reach human review, and inspect the effect of schema failures and delayed results on review time. Prefer the faster option only if it meets the classification acceptance rule. Otherwise, accept the extra latency or choose a specialist whose supported task fits the requirement.

Roll back dispatch without erasing processing history

Pause new dispatch if the chosen processing boundary is uncertain or the classification acceptance rule fails. Keep pending reports under their existing identities, preserve completed stage markers according to retention policy, and route review through the approved human process. Don't clear the ledger to make the queue appear healthy.

Resume by locating the last durable stage for each report. Reuse saved successful extractions where policy permits, reconcile recorded batch jobs, and retry only the unfinished operation. A processor change requires approval of the new boundary before replaying source text. Watch the application invariants during recovery; a green request dashboard is insufficient evidence.

References

  • OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications
  • OpenAI batch documentation
  • OpenAI data controls
  • Anthropic batch documentation
  • Azure AI Content Safety overview

If this processing boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai error reference to distinguish retryable call failures from downstream work your application must resume.

title: How Observe.AI Used MongoDB Resharding to Scale Its AI Platform
description:
Launched in 2017, Observe.AI was originally known for its expertise in conversation intelligence and contact center analytics. In recent years, however, the company has grown into a comprehensive agentic AI platform, and now has three core offerings:

  • AI agents for customers that resolve customer requests across voice and chat.

  • AI agents for frontline teams. These include Observe.AI’s recently launched Companion Agent, which provides human team members real-time guidance and automates work before, during, and after customer interactions.

  • AI agents for operations that evaluate interactions, generate coaching, uncover operational insights, and drive continuous improvement across contact centers.

Observe.AI uses MongoDB Atlas as the foundational data layer for its AI platform and relies on it to store raw customer conversations, AI-generated enrichments, model configurations, and agent metadata.

MongoDB's flexible document model enables rapid iteration as AI models evolve, while its scalability—supporting over 100 clusters and 50+ TB of data—has made it the trusted system of record powering our platform's intelligence layer.

Recently, the team wanted to continue scaling with MongoDB in a way that preserved application availability, reduced operational risk, and created a predictable runway for continued data growth.

The team partnered with MongoDB Consulting’s professional services to scale a production-critical MongoDB Atlas deployment to support Observe.AI’s conversation intelligence platform. The project was a joint engineering effort between Observe.AI and MongoDB that used MongoDB resharding as a practical, online mechanism for redistributing large collections across a broader shard footprint.

Expanding a constrained shard footprint

At the time of the project, the cluster had the following characteristics:

  • A sharded MongoDB Atlas deployment with two data shards plus config servers.

  • Approximately 13 TB of compressed data per data shard, representing roughly 50 TB of uncompressed data overall.

  • Each shard runs on the M140 tier with a disk limit of approximately 14 TB, leaving limited available headroom.

  • A sustained ingest rate of roughly 50 GB per day, making proactive capacity expansion important for safe long-term operations.

  • Several multi-TB collections with significant index footprint and production traffic. This setup had worked at an early stage in the company's cycle, but was no longer fit for purpose and could lead to performance issues or service degradation that would directly impact customers.

The engineering objective of the MongoDB–Observe.AI effort was clear: to expand a constrained shard footprint to a healthier horizontal layout, while also keeping the application online and minimizing disruption to production workloads.

Beyond balancer: a faster redistribution for large-scale data movements

After adding new shard capacity, the team evaluated the default balancer-driven redistribution path. They determined that the balancer was the right tool for ongoing incremental balancing, but the volume of data to be redistributed was large enough that relying on chunk migrations alone would have extended the migration window and kept the original shards under elevated pressure for longer than desired.

The team also tackled a number of other constraints. First, the new shard capacity could receive data, but the pace of redistribution was bounded by balancer and range-deletion throughput; range deletion also created additional background load on shards that were already carrying production traffic. Secondly, existing shards periodically experienced high WiredTiger cache pressure, making it important to avoid prolonged competition between application traffic, balancing, and cleanup activity. Finally, the team wanted a controlled, predictable migration path rather than an extended background redistribution process.

They concluded that the balancer should continue to handle incremental corrections, but a faster and more explicit redistribution mechanism was needed for the initial large-scale data movement.

The four-step resharding plan

Instead of relying solely on balancer migrations, the MongoDB–Observe.AI team designed a controlled resharding plan:

  1. Scale out the cluster

    • Increase capacity by adding multiple new shards (not just one) so that, after redistribution, each shard would hold a manageable share of the ~50 TB dataset.

  2. Prepare the cluster for resharding

    • Ensure no ongoing migrations or resharding jobs.

    • Pin the config servers to remain embedded/dedicated as appropriate for this topology.

    • Disable range deletions and disallow chunk migrations for critical collections so that resharding traffic does not compete with the balancer and range deleter for IOPS.

  3. Run resharding on the largest collections

    • For each large collection (collection6, collection7, collection8, etc.), run reshardCollection to redistribute data across the new shard set, keeping the same shard key but changing the ownership distribution.

    • Execute resharding sequentially per collection to avoid overloading donors, recipients, or the config server.

Table 1. Resharding performance metrics.

4. Clean up and return to normal operations

  • Once data has been redistributed:
    • Remove old empty shards from the cluster.
    • Remove temporary zone configurations that were only needed during the migration.
    • Re‑enable balancing and range deletions for the now‑healthy collections.

Resharding driving greater optimization, performance, and reliability

The joint effort gave Observe.AI a safer and more scalable data foundation for continued platform growth.

Thanks to resharding, the cluster moved from a limited disk runway to a healthier multi-month capacity position, while large multi-TB collections were redistributed across the expanded shard footprint using online resharding rather than relying only on extended balancer-driven chunk migration.

Production reads and writes continued during the clone and catch-up phases, with only the final commit phase requiring a brief write-blocking critical section. The team reduced sustained pressure on the original shards and created more room for future ingest growth, maintenance, and operational flexibility.

Finally, after the migration, the MongoDB balancer returned to its normal role of incremental rebalancing, while the heavy data movement was handled through the more appropriate resharding workflow.

The project highlighted how sharding and resharding can be used proactively as part of ongoing capacity management, helping optimize storage utilization, manage growing data volumes, and maintain platform performance and reliability as workloads scale.

Combining horizontal scale-out and resharding: A winning combo

The key idea behind MongoDB’s resharding capability is simple—sharding should not be the last‑resort, once‑in‑a‑lifetime operation you dread. It should be a practical, fast tool you can use whenever your workload outgrows its current shape.

If you treat sharding as “too expensive” and delay it until your primary is holding tens of TBs, you pay that cost back many times in:

  • Oversized single replica sets,

  • Operational risk,

  • And slow, painful balancing when you finally add shards.

By combining horizontal scale-out with resharding, which has been available since MongoDB 8.0 launched in 2024, you can start small, grow organically, and still have a predictable, efficient path to redistribute data when your cluster—and your business—takes off.

Observe.AI’s  platform processes billions of customer interactions each year, so the infrastructure has to scale as seamlessly as the business. Working alongside the MongoDB team enabled Observe.AI to redistribute more than 50 TB of production data with virtually no disruption to customers. MongoDB 8.0 resharding provided  the operational confidence to expand capacity proactively instead of reacting to infrastructure limits, allowing Observe.AI’s engineering teams to stay focused on delivering innovation for customers.

title: Your AI Agent Can Now Design, Edit and Export Database Schemas with MCP
description:
Your AI Agent Can Now Design, Edit and Export Database Schemas with MCP

AI coding assistants are getting better at writing code.

But what happens when your AI agent needs to understand your database?

You could paste your entire database schema into a conversation.

You could export a SQL file, copy it into your AI assistant, ask it to make changes, and manually transfer the result back into your diagramming tool.

Or you could connect your AI agent directly to your database design environment.

That's exactly what Model Context Protocol (MCP) makes possible.

And this is one of the things I've been working on with SchemaSketch.

What if your AI agent could actually work with your database diagrams?

Imagine asking your AI assistant:

  • Show me all my database diagrams.
  • Explain the relationships in my existing database.
  • Add an orders table to my e-commerce schema.
  • Check whether my database relationships are correct.
  • Convert this SQL schema into a visual database diagram.
  • Generate Laravel migrations from my database design.
  • Export my schema as PostgreSQL SQL.
  • Convert a Mermaid ER diagram into DBML.

Instead of simply discussing these tasks, an MCP-connected AI agent can interact directly with SchemaSketch and perform the corresponding operations.

No manual copy-pasting of DBML between applications.

What is MCP?

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that allows AI applications to connect to external tools and services.

Think of it as a bridge between an AI assistant and the applications you already use.

Instead of building a separate integration for every AI provider, an application can expose its capabilities through an MCP server.

An MCP-compatible client can then discover available tools and invoke them when needed.

For SchemaSketch, this means your AI assistant can interact with your actual database diagrams.

Introducing the SchemaSketch MCP Server

SchemaSketch provides a hosted MCP server that exposes 15 tools for working with database diagrams.

It is not a separate AI diagramming engine.

The AI works with the same DBML source used by the SchemaSketch editor.

Here is what it can do.

1. Read and understand your diagrams

Your AI assistant can:

  • get_dbml_syntax_guide - Read the DBML syntax reference.
  • list_diagrams - List your saved diagrams.
  • get_diagram - Retrieve a diagram, including its DBML source and layout.

This gives the AI access to your actual database design instead of relying on manually supplied information.

2. Create, edit and validate schemas

Your AI assistant can:

  • validate_dbml - Check syntax errors and semantic warnings.
  • create_diagram - Create a new database diagram.
  • update_diagram - Update an existing diagram or rename it.
  • delete_diagram - Delete a diagram.

One important detail: SchemaSketch uses the same DBML validation logic as its visual editor.

Before saving changes, the AI can validate the schema and identify problems such as duplicate names, dangling references and mismatched types.

When updating an existing diagram, the AI can first retrieve the current DBML source, make the requested changes, validate the result and save it.

3. Generate real development artifacts

This is where things get particularly interesting.

Your AI assistant can generate:

Tool Output
export_sql PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server or Oracle
export_laravel_migrations Laravel migration files
export_laravel_models Eloquent models with casts and relationships
export_mermaid Mermaid ER diagrams
export_plantuml PlantUML entity diagrams

You can go from a database design to actual development artifacts without manually converting the schema.

4. Import existing database structures

Already have a database design?

You don't have to start from scratch.

SchemaSketch also provides:

  • import_sql - Convert SQL DDL into DBML.
  • import_mermaid - Convert Mermaid ER diagrams into DBML.
  • import_plantuml - Convert PlantUML entity diagrams into DBML.

This makes it possible to bring existing database structures into the same workflow.

A practical example

Let's say you're starting a new e-commerce application.

You ask your AI assistant:

Create a database schema for an e-commerce platform with customers, products, categories, orders, order items and payments. Include appropriate primary keys, foreign keys, timestamps and relationships.

With the SchemaSketch MCP server connected, your AI agent can:

  1. Read the DBML syntax guide.
  2. Design the database structure.
  3. Validate the generated DBML.
  4. Create a new diagram in SchemaSketch.
  5. Export Laravel migrations and Eloquent models.
  6. Make further changes when requirements evolve.

You can then open the diagram in SchemaSketch and visually inspect the result.

The important part is that the diagram and the AI-generated schema are working with the same underlying DBML.

Connecting SchemaSketch to your AI assistant

Getting started is straightforward.

Inside SchemaSketch:

  1. Open the application.
  2. Click Connect AI agent.
  3. Generate your personal access token.
  4. Follow the generated configuration for your AI client.

For clients supporting remote MCP connections over Streamable HTTP, the endpoint is:

https://mcp.schemasketch.dev/mcp

A typical configuration looks like this:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "schemasketch": {
      "url": "https://mcp.schemasketch.dev/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_TOKEN"
      }
    }
  }
}

SchemaSketch provides connection options for Claude Code, Claude Desktop and other compatible clients. Claude Desktop uses a packaged extension because its remote connector configuration handles authentication differently.

You can find the complete setup instructions here:

SchemaSketch MCP Documentation

What about Zapier?

MCP isn't limited to coding assistants.

SchemaSketch can also connect to Zapier's MCP Client, allowing its remote MCP tools to be used within Zapier workflows.

Zapier supports connections to remote MCP servers using Streamable HTTP and bearer-token authentication.

The connection uses:

  • Server URL: https://mcp.schemasketch.dev/mcp
  • Transport: Streamable HTTP
  • Authentication: Bearer token generated by SchemaSketch

Once connected, you can make SchemaSketch tools available to your Zapier workflows.

This opens up interesting possibilities for connecting database design operations with other applications and automation workflows.

For example, imagine an automation workflow that uses an AI agent to review a proposed database structure, validate it and create a diagram in SchemaSketch.

The database design becomes part of a wider automation ecosystem.

Learn more about connecting remote MCP servers to Zapier.

Why does this matter?

I believe we're moving towards a development workflow where AI agents don't just generate code.

They interact with the tools developers already use.

Database design is an important part of that workflow, but it is often disconnected from the rest of the development process.

With MCP, SchemaSketch brings database diagrams into the AI development ecosystem.

You can use an AI assistant to explore a schema, propose changes, validate them, and generate development artifacts while keeping the visual database representation available for review.

And because MCP is an open standard, you're not locked into a single AI provider.

What's next?

I'm continuing to expand SchemaSketch and explore more ways to integrate database design into modern development workflows.

The goal is simple:

Make database design accessible not only to developers, but also to the AI tools they use every day.

SchemaSketch is free, including its MCP server. There is no separate AI subscription or premium MCP tier.

If you want to experiment with it:

  • 🌐 SchemaSketch
  • 🤖 MCP Documentation
  • 📦 Laravel Package
  • 📚 Full Documentation

Let's discuss

I'm curious how other developers are using MCP in their development workflows.

Would you let an AI agent modify your database schema directly, provided every change is validated before being saved?

And what would you want your AI assistant to do with your database that it cannot easily do today?

I'd love to hear your thoughts.

title: Deploy a container from a plain Dockerfile
description:
You can now deploy a plain root Dockerfile or Containerfile on Vercel's Container runtime when no other framework is detected. Vercel selects the Container preset, builds that file, and routes all traffic to the resulting image. To get started with containers on Vercel, add a Dockerfile:

When project detection matches another framework, such as Django, that framework still wins. To build use the Dockerfile or Containerfile instead, run vercel project update --framework container, or set the framework in vercel.json:

A Dockerfile.vercel or Containerfile.vercel continues to win over a detected framework, and multi-service projects still use vercel.json services with a per-service entrypoint.

The Container runtime is in beta, runs on Vercel Functions, and is billed with Active CPU pricing. Read the Container runtime documentation to get started.
